title: Affairs? Drugs? You could ask Dolly Parton about anything and get a laugh. Just stay away from politics … | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: One autumn day in 2023 I bathed in the luminous glow of this utterly authentic star – and while she did have one weak spot, her life and music will speak for themselves
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: One autumn day in 2023 I bathed in the luminous glow of this utterly authentic star – and while she did have one weak spot, her life and music will speak for themselves
Content: Beatific … Dolly Parton in 1987.Photograph: Craig Sjodin/Disney General Entertainment Content/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBeatific … Dolly Parton in 1987.Photograph: Craig Sjodin/Disney General Entertainment Content/Getty ImagesDolly PartonAffairs? Drugs? You could ask Dolly Parton about anything and get a laugh. Just stay away from politics …One autumn day in 2023 I bathed in the luminous glow of this utterly authentic star – and while she did have one weak spot, her life and music will speak for themselvesCelebrity tributes pour in for Dolly PartonDolly Parton’s 10 best deep cutsAlexis Petridis on Dolly Parton’s peerless careerEmine SanerWed 26 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 17.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe great privilege of my kind of journalism is to get the chance to meet extraordinary people – some famous, many not – and very occasionally that person is beyond extraordinary.Dolly Parton, you may not be surprised to learn, was one of them. I’ve only come across it a handful of times. It has nothing to do with extreme fame – I’ve met plenty of A-listers who are dead behind the eyes. It’s not charm or extroversion either, nor beauty, and it’s not what we’d call “star quality” because it’s less showy than that. It’s almost indescribable, but “luminous” probably comes closest. I think it’s partly innate – God-given, Parton might have said – but it also comes from living with humility, gratitude and humour. Parton was luminous, and it wasn’t just the rhinestones.The cliche that you should never meet your heroes because you’ll only be disappointed only stands if you think famous people have somehow transcended the deep character flaws that make the rest of us human. Everyone has off days, or off years. Still, I’d been slightly dreading interviewing Parton. The machinery that surrounds a superstar interview – the holding rooms, the allotted time slots, the officious publicists – is designed to be intimidating, and it was all present on that autumn day in 2023. And then it was just Parton and me in a London hotel room, borderline uncomfortably close on a sofa, but unusually, no publicist sitting in, taking notes.Dolly Parton on style, stardom and sexists: ‘I know how to push men off and get the hell away’Read more13:53Dolly Parton: why the world loved the queen of country - The LatestShe was funnier than I expected, and warmer. Parton’s artifice – the look, the folksiness, the ready quips – was clearly part of her armour. You can deflect any tricky question, or criticism, with a well timed boob joke. But somehow it didn’t feel fake. It was her creation, but it was stillher. I had no illusions I’d get to the real Parton, whatever that was, in our hour together – she even went to bed with her makeup on, she said, because she didn’t want to go to bed “looking tacky” for her husband.Certain things don’t make it into interviews because written down they look trite, or lose power, but re-reading my transcript, I think I underestimated how spiritual Parton was. “You need to believe in something bigger than yourself,” she said. “You need to believe in at least a higher power, the higher wisdom, whether you call it nature or whatever, to get you out of yourself.” She would often break into reciting her lyrics (“Whatever you are, be that / Whatever you do, do that / Everything else is just an act”) which, in person, felt like being preached to by a beatific being.She could deal, with humour and grace, with the sort of questions other celebrities – or at least their PRs – would throw you out for. Had she or her husband had affairs? “If there [were], we don’t know about it.” Had she ever been tempted? “I didn’t say I’d never been tempted,” she said with a laugh. “I said I’m married, not dead. Nor blind.” We were meeting partly to discuss her book about fashion, and she’d written about partying at Studio 54: how many drugs had she taken? Nothing hard, she said. “I don’t really want anything to change me. I don’t want to mess with my brains.” It didn’t makemy piece– even with follow-up questions, her deflection was too practised, her answers too opaque. It’s more an illustration that she was game.4:00How Dolly Parton’s glamorous career transcended stereotypes – video obituaryThe only thing that was off-limits was her politics. Much as I admired her, I thought this was Parton’s weak spot. Her apolitical stance seemed, to me, about protecting her career, her money. If you’re political, she said, “you’re gonna lose half your audience. I’ve got as many Democrats, as I do Republicans as fans, and I’m not going to insult any of them because I care about all of them.” It was the same reason she didn’t describe herself as a feminist, she said – she didn’t want to alienate men.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI needled her (she remained good-humoured) because it seemed a cop-out – this was 2023, and life had become frightening and intolerable for many people. Tennessee, her home state, had not long banned abortion in almost all cases. At what point does silence, given her platform, start looking like complicity? “I have my own opinion about everything,” she said, “but I don’t have to march in the streets for it, I don’t have to insult other people for it. I don’t think that makes me a hypocrite. I think it makes me a loving, caring human being.”Three years on I’ve softened towards Parton’s refusal to add to the noise, to label herself, to take sides, to inevitably alienate and polarise and condemn. Deeds not words. Parton’s deeds – living as a feminist, if not calling herself one, and her philanthropy, and of course her music – speak for themselves. I had it for an hour in that hotel room, just the hack who happened to be chosen for that assignment, but we were all lucky to be touched by Parton’s light.Explore more on these topicsDolly PartonCountryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My mum has died – and there is one kind of response I can’t stand | Polly Hudson | The Guardian
description: The platitudes, euphemisms and cliches are excruciating. But the people who say nothing at all are the worst, writes Polly Hudson
Author: Polly Hudson
Headline: The platitudes, euphemisms and cliches are excruciating. But the people who say nothing at all are the worst, writes Polly Hudson
Content: Say anything …Photograph: Posed by models; Juanmonino/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenSay anything …Photograph: Posed by models; Juanmonino/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionDeath and dyingMy mum has died – and there is one kind of response I can’t standPolly HudsonThe platitudes, euphemisms and cliches are excruciating. But the people who say nothing at all are the worstWed 26 Aug 2026 11.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareLuckily, I already knew having a comic thought at a tragic moment is anatural stress response, or I might have worried. My mum has died, making me an orphan – and what first popped into my head was how annoyed Larry David would be.InCurb Your Enthusiasm, when Marty Funkhouser’s mother’s wheelchair was run over by a car, he proclaimed himself an orphan. David informed him he was too old to be an orphan. Funkhouser insisted that if your parents are dead,you’re an orphan.“You could be 70 and be an orphan?” David challenged.“You could be 100 and be an orphan!’ Funkhouser maintained.“You can’t be 100 and be an orphan.”“Yeah, you can.”“OK, Little Orphan Funkhouser,” concluded David.Images of Annie-like red curls aside, the people who brought you into the world both having left it is pretty profound. I’m lucky to have a lot of support, but it’s a hard knock in life. A singularly specific brand of aloneness; the natural order that feels anything but. It’s so weird. There’s no one to tell me off any more, either. I wonder what I may get up to. What if I fall in with a bad crowd?My mum “had a good innings though”, as I have been reminded roughly thrice daily. It’s been 14 years since my dad died, and there’s so much I’d forgotten about the grief game – namely the platitudes, the strange language, and how terrible so many of us are at dealing with it. The best reaction so far was a bloke who replied to my breaking of the news for sadmin purposes with: “OK, that’s fine.” At least he gave me a good story.The main disclaimer here is that I do believe everyone is trying their best. It’s a serious minority who are deliberately attempting to offend or upset you “at this difficult time”. Most human beings are just hopeless at talking about death.I also know that a lot of this is subjective. For example, it’s safer to err on the side of caution and use fluffy euphemisms such as “passed away” and “resting”. However, as a dyed-in-the-wool fan of simply saying “died”, that fluff grates. “Please accept my condolences” is ridiculous, because it sounds as if there’s a chance you might reply in the negative, outraged at the very idea. My least favourite is “I don’t know what to say” – and then a blank, expectant look, as though they are genuinely hoping you’ll provide a shortlist of suggestions. I’m also not that into “you have to be strong”. Because, why do I have to? The best way out is always through, surely.But the absolute worst thing to say to the bereaved is nothing at all. Richard E Grant has spoken before about some longstanding friends who crossed the road to avoid him after his wife’s death. This week,he said that he’d never forgive them.“I’m very unequivocal, black and white, all or nothing,” he said. “I’ve tried to go for the grey areas but it’s not succeeded for very long. There are people that have been edited out of my life and I will never see them again. If I had done that to them, I wouldn’t be able to look them in the face ... No, portcullis down, goodbye.”What Grant endured was extreme, but most people who have “lost” (which sounds like absent-mindedly mislaying something) somebody have experienced the deafening sound of silence. You’re conversing with someone who doesn’t acknowledge the enormous way your universe has shifted, and it’s as if you’ve grown a second head that they pretend not to notice. Again, they’re almost definitely not doing it intentionally – they aren’t mentioning it because you seem OK right at this second (AKA you aren’t crying), and they don’t want that to change, or to remind you what’s happened, just in case you have completely forgotten. They mean well, and focusing on that fact is how you manage not to snap at them. (Grief can make you really tetchy, another aspect of it that had slipped my mind.)So now I’m back in the sad saddle, a PSA that platitudes, euphemisms and cliches are excruciating. However, nothing is as awful as having to interact with somebody for whom all words on the subject have dearly departed. Even arguing about the age limit for claiming orphan status is better than that.Polly Hudson is a freelance writerDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The great Snowdon queue-skipping row – is it really OK to jump the line if you’re not taking a selfie? | Walking | The Guardian
description: The crowds at the top of Yr Wyddfa, the highest mountain in Wales, are now so huge that seasoned hikers and climbers are simply walking past them. Is everyone just making a mountain out of a molehill?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The crowds at the top of Yr Wyddfa, the highest mountain in Wales, are now so huge that seasoned hikers and climbers are simply walking past them. Is everyone just making a mountain out of a molehill?
Content: Get in line! … walkers queue to reach the summit of Yr Wyddfa.Photograph: Dylan Garcia/AlamyView image in fullscreenGet in line! … walkers queue to reach the summit of Yr Wyddfa.Photograph: Dylan Garcia/AlamyPass notesWalkingThe great Snowdon queue-skipping row – is it really OK to jump the line if you’re not taking a selfie?The crowds at the top of Yr Wyddfa, the highest mountain in Wales, are now so huge that seasoned hikers and climbers are simply walking past them. Is everyone just making a mountain out of a molehill?Wed 26 Aug 2026 07.20 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:The Snowdon queue.Age:A decade and a half, give or take.Appearance:Frustratingly long.This isn’t new.You’re right. The presshas been reportingon the queueto reach the summit of Yr Wyddfa in north Wales (known in English as Snowdon) since 2013.I have never understood that.Really? Yr Wyddfa is an important national landmark, in one of the most beautiful parts of the UK. It’s bound to attract crowds – so people should expect to queue!British people aresoweird …It isn’t just British people. In 2019, peoplequeued for so long to reach the summitof Mount Everest that some of them actually died. If you want to climb a mountain in 2026, expect to join a line.You still haven’t explained why this is suddenly newsworthy.No, I haven’t, and for good reason. What I’m about to tell you will shake you to your very core. You might want to brace yourself.This sounds awful.It’s worse than awful. Get this: people have started skipping the queue.View image in fullscreenA moment of calm? Walkers on the Llanberis path at Yr Wyddfa.Photograph: Dylan Garcia/AlamyWHAAAT?!I know, and I’m sorry. People just aren’t having it any more. Social media has been flooded with Yr Wyddfa queue jumpers. “Imagine queueing on a mountain. No chance,” a climber huffs in one video, as he’s heckled by his more patient compatriots.And it’s not a terrible one-off?If only. Another queue jumper posted a video, captioned: “Won’t catch me hiking for two hours to spend 30 minutes queueing at the top.”This is the least British thing I have ever heard.Put yourself in their position, though. You’ve spent hours literally climbing a mountain, but then you have to stop near the top so a long line of bozos can take selfies at the peak to prove they made it. What would you do in that situation?I would queue up, because I understand that some things are sacred.Yes, actually, I would, too. Skipping a queue is the least British thing of all time. It’s like insulting Paddington Bear.Someone needs to be blamed for this.I mean, we could blame the rampant culture of overtourism that sent all these people there in the first place. About600,000 people reach Yr Wyddfa’s summit every year, each bringing litter, traffic and vegetation erosion with them. Maybe some of them could go elsewhere?No, that’s not it.Maybe, then, we could blame social media for increasing the time spent at the peak? If everyone was banned from taking a selfie at the top, the lines would almost certainly speed up a bit.Can’t we just blame the queue jumpers?Oh God, yes, let’s just do that. Who do they think they are, disrespecting national etiquette like this?Do say:“Queue jumpers are the scourge of Yr Wyddfa.”Don’t say:“But maybe the problem has … peaked?”Explore more on these topicsWalkingPass notesMountaineeringWalesSnowdonia holidaysWales holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ayyoub Bouaddi: maths student, chess fan and Manchester City’s new Rodri | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: The £85m midfielder passed his exams a year early, is studying for a degree and is ready to tackle Premier League learning curve
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: The £85m midfielder passed his exams a year early, is studying for a degree and is ready to tackle Premier League learning curve
Content: Ayoub Bouaddi is described by a former coach as a ‘very intelligent boy who adapts quickly, capable of playing in every position in the middle’.Photograph: Manchester City FCView image in fullscreenAyoub Bouaddi is described by a former coach as a ‘very intelligent boy who adapts quickly, capable of playing in every position in the middle’.Photograph: Manchester City FCManchester CityAyyoub Bouaddi: maths student, chess fan and Manchester City’s new RodriThe £85m midfielder passed his exams a year early, is studying for a degree and is ready to tackle Premier League learning curveWill UnwinWed 26 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“He’s like a computer,” the former Lille head of academy recruitment, Mathieu Frison, says of the €100m (£85.7m)Manchester City recruit Ayyoub Bouaddi. “You teach him something, he learns it and can do it immediately.” Bouaddi has the mountainous challenge at his new club of replacing the world’s best central midfielder. It would be difficult for anyone but at 18 it feels monumental, although those who know the Morocco international best would not bet against him.Bouaddi has known onlyLilleand Ligue 1 but is entering one of the biggest clubs in the world where a season without a trophy is deemed a failure. For someone so young, however, he has plenty of experience. He made his European debut three days after his 16th birthday and has played three full seasons in the first team, culminating in a place at the World Cup this summer.Manchester City confirm Bouaddi signing as Marmoush and González head outRead moreAt 13, Lille beat off competition from France’s elite to sign Bouaddi, after showing his parents the pathway he could follow to the first team. There was never lengthy discussion over money, just what would be best for a boy who wanted to reach the highest level. Lille’s track record is impressive, the club bringing through Bouaddi’s soon-to-be Premier League rivals Carlos Baleba and Leny Yoro, among others, in recent times.Frison visited the Bouaddi family in Creil, an hour north of Paris, to explain why a move to Lille would be beneficial after scouts spotted Bouaddi playing for his home town team in a tournament. “He was not here at the beginning of the meeting with his parents, and he came in the house with the ball on a string,” Frison recalls. “He did a very good trick; he always had this ball in his hand and he always played in his house, so he was already very talented technically.”City have faith in him, although plenty of the expenditure is based on promise rather than a finished article. He is not someone who creates highlight reels, but does the dirty work and plays for the team. Others may have sought someone with more miles in their legs, but Enzo Maresca is rebuilding a midfield for the long term after Rodri’s departure for Barcelona and with a £52m deal agreed for Nico González to join Newcastle. The 23-year-old Elliot Anderson arrived from Nottingham Forest as the first cog in the machine, and Enzo Fernández is also wanted by his former manager at Chelsea.Bouaddi, the only boy of four siblings, passed all his exams a year early, is studying for a mathematics degree remotely and speaks English. He is a deep thinker, someone able to cut out the distractions at home and on the pitch. “On the bus, while everyone is watching YouTube videos or listening to music, he will play chess for one or two hours,” Frison says. “In the evening when all the players played Fifa or were on their phones, he studied mathematics, physics, science. His parents didn’t need to push him to do this – he wanted to learn.”View image in fullscreenAyyoub Bouaddi plays for Morocco after representing France, the country of his birth, up to under-21 level.Photograph: Mauro Pimentel/AFP/Getty ImagesBouaddi represented the country of his birth, France, from under-16 to under-21 and is regarded as a huge loss forLes Bleus. “Bouaddi, for me, is one of the smartest players I’ve known in my coaching career,” says the former France under-18 coach Landry Chauvin, who had Bouaddi in his squad for the Lafarge tournament in Limoges in 2024. “He reminds me a lot of Yoann Gourcuff, who I saw in Rennes a few years ago. As soon as the tournament was over, I toldLes Espoirs[France’s Under-21s] that he should have nothing more to do with me, that he had to continue to progress and go above and beyond.”Rodri has won everything worth winning over the past decade while Bouaddi was growing up. Emulating the Spaniard will not be straightforward for a player who is a long way from being fully developed. “When Maresca asks him to do something tactically, he knows that 100% Ayyoub will take the best position for the team,” Frison says.View image in fullscreenAyyoub Bouaddi celebrates Lille’s Champions League victory over Real Madrid on his 17th birthday.Photograph: Benoît Tessier/Reuters“He will respect the game model with intensity, even when he is tired; he will respect the process. Everyone wants a player who can make the difference individually because they can help you to win the game but you need reliable players who you can trust 100% during 60 games of the season. And Ayyoub, he’s this kind of player.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenAyyoub Bouaddi and his family chose Lille because of the pathway to the first team.Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty ImagesBouaddi has consistently mixed with – and surpassed – older players, quickly improving as he rapidly went through each step to the top. He was 16 when he featured for Chauvin’s France Under-18s and on his 17th birthday he faced Real Madrid in the Champions League, playing 90 minutes in a 1-0 win against Jude Bellingham et al.“A very intelligent boy who adapts quickly, capable of playing in every position in the middle, capable of evolving in a changing environment, permanently working hard, but also always with his head held high,” Chauvin says. “He has the ability to scan the actions very quickly, to take the information before the others. Very comfortable technically, he always has the right position on the field. And on top of that, he’s a boy who’s charming in everyday life; very respectful, very well educated, who knows all the rules.“The man who hides behind the footballer is simply a very beautiful person. Every time I went to Lille, I would send him a little text, and immediately he came to greet me, even though he was already a pro. Many in his place would have snubbed the under-18 coach, but not Ayyoub.”Explore more on these topicsManchester CityLillefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: With Nige still sulking, it was left to Honest Bob to unveil Reform UK’s latest ‘policies’ | John Crace | The Guardian
description: The sense of futility hanging over the room was almost overwhelming as Robert Jenrick took the stage
Author: John Crace
Headline: The sense of futility hanging over the room was almost overwhelming as Robert Jenrick took the stage
Content: Even with Nige there, the event would have been an uphill struggle. With Honest Bob it was dead in the water before he had said a word.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenEven with Nige there, the event would have been an uphill struggle. With Honest Bob it was dead in the water before he had said a word.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAThe politics sketchReform UKWith Nige still sulking, it was left to Honest Bob to unveil Reform UK’s latest ‘policies’John CraceThe sense of futility hanging over the room was almost overwhelming as Robert Jenrick took the stageWed 26 Aug 2026 11.26 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 16.02 EDTShareIt’s turning out to be one of the longer sulks in Nigel Farage’s already sulk-filled career. Few politicians are better at having a strop and holding a grudge than Nige. At least on this side of the Atlantic. Donald Trump could give Farage a run for his money, but skin doesn’t come much thinner than Nige’s. He’s the soul of the Reform party as long as he’s the centre of attention and the yes-men and women – that’s everyone – around him are saying yes. But the moment reality challenges his narcissism, the mirror cracks.There was a time when you couldn’t keep Nige away from a TV camera or a gathering of reporters. It’s what he lived for. But ever since the Guardian revealed his £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, Farage has gone all shy. Unable to bear the humiliation of being seen for the man he really is. The posh. The entitled. The venal. The grifter. Everything he has spent the last 25 years trying to persuade people he isn’t.Even with the Reform party conference just over a week away and the pressure on him to be at his sparkling best, Nige is still playing hard to get. His one concession has been to give the softest of soft interviews to Jeremy Kyle, Reform’s pet stooge from TalkTV. When GB News is too challenging for Nige, then you know he is in a very delicate state. Nor is there any sign of his self-imposed exile having improved his frame of mind. His latest fantasy is that immigrants are on the verge of forming their own standing army and going to war with the UK. Not even Kyle could quite keep a straight face. Fever dreams all round.So for the latest instalment of the Reform summer press conference-athon, we were back toRobert Jenrick. Back, because the front-of-house formalities have been almost exclusively left to him and Dicky Tice, and it was Honest Bob’s misfortune to have drawn the short straw on Wednesday morning. The sense of futility hanging over the room was almost overwhelming. Even had it been Nige on stage, the event would have been an uphill struggle. With Honest Bob at the helm it was dead in the water before he had said a word. Reform are tanking in the polls and, in any case, to see Honest Bob is to dislike him. A little goes way too far. The stench of opportunism is overpowering.The purpose of the presser was supposedly to highlight Reform’s latest – unfunded, natch – promises to small business. Though as no one was really listening and were instead wondering what sins they had committed in a previous life to have to endure 45 minutes of a burbling, fantasy-driven Honest Bob, this was really a public demonstration of the sort of waste of time Reform was trying to save businesses from. Though its possible that someone in Reform HQ has recently developed a meta-brand of existential humour and is now actively toying with the media to see how long it is before anyone realises the party has nothing to say and no longer bothers to show up.Honest Bob raced through the sell. A relaxation of the rules on data protection. Who cares if Big Tech get their mitts on your personal information? They will mine your data one way or the other, so we might as well make it as easy as possible for them. The VAT level for business would be raised to £150K and anyone kept on hold by HMRC for 30 minutes would be entitled to a £30 tax credit. Cue the whole country ringing HMRC at the same time just to save a bit of money. You don’t even have to listen to the music when you’re put on hold because no one is ever going to answer. Do this several times a day and you might never have to pay tax again.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReform UK hates ‘Mickey Mouse’ degrees – apprenticeships in dodgy crypto, anyone?Read moreThis is personal for me, said Honest Bob. Look into my eyes. Trying to sound sincere. Though it’s hard to trust a man with a track record of betrayal and dishonesty. Nige, Dicky, Zia and Bob. All working-class boys from the wrong side of the tracks. It’s as if he had never read this speech before, passing it off as his own. The whole point of Reform is that everyone at the top of the party is posh and has absolutely no idea of what it’s like to have no money. Nor are they even on each other’s side, let alone that of small business. Zia can’t stand Honest Bob and Nige seems to hate everyone at the moment.Then the final giveaway. Grandparents and parents would be able to invest £250k in a child’s business tax free. Because everyone has a quarter or a mill to spare. It was just delusional. Honest Bob doesn’t understand himself, let alone the average Brit. And don’t worry about where all the money to pay for all these giveaways would come from. Just offset them from the imaginary savings they had made from last week’s nonsensical pressers. Dicky Tice extolling the virtues of marital fidelity was quite the moment.There was just time for a few questions. More out of habit than genuine inquiry. All of which merely exposed Honest Bob’s limitations. Like trying to pretend that the energy price increase had nothing to do with the war with Iran that Nige had insisted the UK would be better off joining. Then there were the polls which really, really didn’t show that the Reform surge had long since peaked. But there were moments of light relief, such asJenrick going for Kemi Badenochover her invented conversations with Giorgia Meloni. It takes one delusionist to spot another.It took the reporter from the Press Association to mention the elephant in the room. The crushing sense of ennui. Please could Reform get around to talking about defence, foreign affairs and health, because they had long since exhausted all the topics for which they had spokespeople. Honest Bob hesitated. Reform not having any MPs it could trust on defence, foreign affairs and health should be taken as a sign of strength not weakness. No way was the party a reclusive one-man band. There was Dicky and Honest Bob after all. Not forgetting Honest Bob and Dicky.Explore more on these topicsReform UKThe politics sketchRobert JenrickNigel FaragenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It destroyed me’ – your top true-crime TV shows of all time  | Television | The Guardian
description: From influencers gone (really, really) bad and the outrageous Joe Exotic to the greatest reveal in television history – here are Guardian readers’ favourite real-life documentaries and whodunnits
Author: Alfie Packham
Headline: From influencers gone (really, really) bad and the outrageous Joe Exotic to the greatest reveal in television history – here are Guardian readers’ favourite real-life documentaries and whodunnits
Content: Timid as a pussycat? Joe Exotic in Tiger King.Photograph: Netflix US/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTimid as a pussycat? Joe Exotic in Tiger King.Photograph: Netflix US/AFP/Getty ImagesTelevision‘It destroyed me’ – your top true-crime TV shows of all timeFrom influencers gone (really, really) bad and the outrageous Joe Exotic to the greatest reveal in television history – here are Guardian readers’ favourite real-life documentaries and whodunnitsAlfie Packhamand Guardian readersWed 26 Aug 2026 02.57 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 09.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnsolved: The Boy Who Disappeared (2016)I watched the BBC’s Unsolved: The Boy Who Disappeared when it came out andDamien Nettles, its subject, still pops up in my mind sometimes. It’s a comprehensive, empathetic and gripping investigation into a case I had never heard of. TheSerial/Making a Murderer-style approach of showing the investigation, rather than just presenting information, gives the series a much more human angle. I thought it might turn up new evidence; that level of faith in the work being shown is a testament to how thorough it was.AJ, Devon, UKMurder on a Sunday Morning (2001)View image in fullscreenCould have been my brother … Murder on a Sunday Morning.Photograph: YoutubeI remember watching this with my dad. It came on TV late, as part of the Storyville strand, when I was about 20 and working in a pub, living at home. We were captivated by this story about a wrongly accused Black teenager and his trial for allegedly shooting an older white woman. It opened my eyes to police corruption, mistaken identity in lineups and the deep-rooted racism that underlies them. The accused boy is so incredibly normal, like friends of mine at the time, or my younger brother – and the impossibility that he decided to rob and shoot someone on a Sunday morning seems obvious. It is a beautiful piece of sensitive, non-sensationalist film-making with humanity at its heart.Rose, Wakefield, UKTiger King (2020)I’m not a fan of true crime TV, but I did seethe outrageous Tiger Kingand found it immensely watchable. Big-cat enthusiast Joe Exotic – who was jailed for animal abuse and two counts of attempted murder for hire, for plotting to kill a rival feline conservationist, Carole Baskin – is the kind of over-the-top character who seems as if he had sprung from a work of fiction.Bruce, Florida,USDevil in the Family: the Fall of Ruby Franke (2025)View image in fullscreenMaintaining the facade … Ruby Franke.Photograph: BBC/Disney/Passion PicturesTo call this a favourite is maybe not the right word; it’s thestory of the family vlogger Ruby Franke and the the severe child abuse she committed. The camera footage – the story unfolding before us – made the documentary about this unforgivable crime difficult, albeit engaging, to watch. It’s horrific seeing educated people punishing children in a very cruel way. It helped to know before watching that the two perpetrators were jailed.Judith, Tyne and Wear, UKHometown: A Killing (2019)This series, which focused on a murder in journalist Mobeen Azhar’s hometown of Huddersfield, was fantastic. Starting with the investigation of a single crime, the story evolves unexpectedly into a really interesting dive into societal and cultural issues, and Azhar’s personal connection to the place means he is clearly invested. It’s one of the best explorations of crime in modern Britain that I’ve seen and it’s available on BBC iPlayer.NeilMarshall, 43, Glasgow, UKConfessions With a Killer: The Ted Bundy Tapes (2019)I watchedConfessions With a Killer: The Ted Bundy Tapesfor the first time with a friend during my first year of uni – and then maybe 100 times since. It’s the high-water mark of an anthology series that also featured Charles Manson and John Wayne Gacy, balancing the sensational and truthful admirably, and giving due respect to the victims. It also allows Bundy to continually dob himself in, emphasising his monstrous ego and lack of empathy. Psychologically and in highlighting the police successes and failures, I still find it fascinating. It’s led to a lifelong fascination with true crime.Issy, 27, London, UKDear Zachary: A Letter to a Son About His Father (2008)View image in fullscreenPrepare to cry … Kurt Kuenne and Zachary.Photograph: David BagbyI saw this about 15 years ago on a Thursday afternoon when I was off sick from work. It destroyed me. My girlfriend (now wife) came home to find me in floods of tears over the amazing David and Kathleen Bagby and how they dealt with the murder of their son, Andrew, and then the murder-suicide of his former partner, Shirley Turner (the main suspect in Andrew’s death), and one-year-old baby son, Zachary. I made everyone watch it, with the caveat that it will make you cry uncontrollably. Even typing this now, it’s making me teary, not least as it was made by Kurt Kuenne – a close friend of Andrew’s.John Fitzgerald, 58, Manchester, UKThe Staircase (2022)The Staircase first appealed to me for its intimate view into a family in crisis. It’s a dramatisation, starring Colin Firth and Toni Collette, of a French documentary that first aired in 2004, about the case of an American novelist accused of murdering his wife (but who he claims fell down the stairs). From there, the rollercoaster progresses – slowly but no less exhilaratingly. The sentiments go from “there are just too many coincidences, he must be guilty”, to “he may be guilty, but the evidence is shoddy at best”, to “even if he is guilty, the American justice system is the real bad guy here and he should never have been convicted”, to ultimately believing that he probably is innocent. As a brother to a criminal defence lawyer, I always prefer true crime that helps unjustly convicted people. The Staircase is a great example of that.Michiel Pauw, 38, Amsterdam, the NetherlandsOJ: Made in America (2016)View image in fullscreenOJ Simpson, before the infamy.Photograph: ESPN filmsOJ: Made in America is such a great journey, using the story of OJ Simpson’s life, career and crimes to explain the history of modern civil rights in America. At the end of the series, you feel so captivated by the intertwining themes that you need time to synthesise it all. It’s a well put together series that shows the antecedents to broader societal trends.Anonymous, AustraliaThis is a Robbery: The World’s Biggest Art Heist (2021)View image in fullscreenThe aftermath of the Isabella Stewart Gardner museum robbery.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixThis is a Robbery is an in-depth look at theIsabella Stewart Gardner museum heist in Boston in 1990. It remains unsolved and the artwork has never been found. It’s really well done and digs into all the weirdness and oddities that were part of the crime. What makes it especially wild is that Isabella Gardner’s will meant that the paintings couldn’t be replaced – so to this day, the spaces on the wall remain empty.JoseRamirez, 55, Tewksbury, Massachusetts,USThe Jinx: The Life and Deaths of Robert Durst (2015)View image in fullscreenShould have turned the mic off … Robert Durst in The Jinx.Photograph: HBOThe Jinx is probablythe greatest true crime TV show of the modern era, certainly since Errol Morris’s The Thin Blue Line. Durst – who was suspected of killing his first wife, and was convicted for the murder of a friend and then a neighbour in 2000-01 – is a remarkable subject: a manipulative Jekyll and Hyde-type figure clearly with a great capacity for violence, but charismatic and vulnerable with it, and who is finally undone by his own entitlement and hubris. Watching him ignore the advice of his lawyers and wander inexorably into self-incrimination is highly entertaining. Andrew Jarecki is a fantastic storyteller, and the story itself unfolds with all the twists and turns to keep you completely engrossed. What it demonstrates about what wealth does to people, and how it leverages the legal system, is instructive. Combine all this with the jaw-dropping final reveal and it is about as good as true crime gets!Yvette, Bristol, UKUnsolved Mysteries (1987–2010)View image in fullscreenUnsolved Mysteries presenter Robert Stack, in 1989.Photograph: THA/ShutterstockUnsolved Mysteries is the granddaddy of the true crime TV genre. Robert Stack was the perfect host (when he died in 2003, Dennis Farina took take over hosting duties until the end of its first run), spinning intriguing and sometimes wild and weird mysteries that you wished you could help solve. I’m sure that series helped inspire many of the armchair internet sleuths that popped up in the decades that followed.Robert Graves, 58, Los Angeles,USWho murdered Sister Cathy? Netflix takes true crime to the next levelRead moreThe Keepers (2017)The Keepers explores the unsolved murder of Sister Catherine Cesnik in 1969, after she grew to suspect that a priest at the Catholic high school she taught at in Baltimore had sexually abused students. This was the first true crime documentary that caught my attention. I watched and rewatched it several times, perhaps because I lived in the area in Maryland where the case happened.Susan Wilt, New York,USAmerican Murder: The Family Next Door (2020)View image in fullscreenChilling … the Watts family.Photograph: NetflixMy favourite crime series has to be American Murder: The Family Next Door on Netflix. The way it’s filmed is equally enthralling and infuriating. The effect of Chris Watts’s attempts to cover up the murder of his pregnant wife and children in the town of Frederick, Colorado, in 2018 is chilling. You feel so much for his late wife, as one horrible man goes on a tear to change his life.Dane Klingaman, 40, Phoenixville, Pennsylvania, USLast Stop Larrimah (2023)View image in fullscreenOne for the road … Paddy Moriarty.Photograph: MAXTrue crime dramas have become a guilty pleasure in retirement. Like many viewers, I justify the prurient aspect by thinking they might teach us how to avoid similar events and that they honour the victims. Last Stop Larrimah tells the story of the disappearance of an elderly, eccentric Irish immigrant from the tiny Australian outback “town” of Larrimah – population 11, falling to 10. Despite the underlying human tragedy of Paddy Moriarty’s disappearance, I found myself laughing out loud as we meet the inhabitants of Larrimah and hear their stories. As the series progresses and we begin to learn of the tensions between the residents, the tone becomes darker. In the end, this series shines a light on the human condition and Larrimah becomes a microcosm of the wider world.Tim Powell, 67,Worcestershire, UKExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTiger KingOJ SimpsonRobert DurstTV crime dramafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Burnham drops support for political funding cap aimed at curbing mega-donors | Party funding | The Guardian
description: PM said he would set bar at £500k, but trade unions say funding reforms could undermine their ability to donate to Labour
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: PM said he would set bar at £500k, but trade unions say funding reforms could undermine their ability to donate to Labour
Content: Labour MPs have urged Andy Burnham to strengthen ‘timid’ elections  bill with amendments.Photograph: Richard Pohle/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenLabour MPs have urged Andy Burnham to strengthen ‘timid’ elections  bill with amendments.Photograph: Richard Pohle/AFP/GettyParty fundingBurnham drops support for political funding cap aimed at curbing mega-donorsPM said he would set bar at £500k, but trade unions say funding reforms could undermine their ability to donate to LabourKiran StaceyPolicy editorWed 26 Aug 2026 15.08 EDTFirst published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 15.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has dropped his support for capping political donations, causing anger among activists and Labour MPs who have long campaigned for change to the way parties are funded.The prime minister has decided not to back amendments to the elections bill, which would cap the amount a person or an organisation can give in a single donation, according to government sources.The decision comes after alobbying campaignfrom Labour’s trade union backers, who said amendments to the bill, which returns to parliament for its remaining stages next week, could undermine their ability to donate to the party. It is also a retreat from the support Burnham gave to the idea just a few weeks ago, whenhe emailed a campaignerfor electoral reform to say he would support a donations cap of £500,000.Stella Creasy, one of the Labour backbenchers who has tabled an amendment calling for a donations cap, said: “Millionaires are increasingly treating British politics as their plaything – splashing the cash to get the outcome they want and the next election as their cup final.“The public won’t forgive us if we miss this chance to clean up Westminster because we are squabbling with each other.”Shaun Bowler, the campaigner to whom Burnham promised his support in May, said: “Andy Burnham promised me a proper cap on political donations and a ‘wholesale culture change’ in Westminster. If his government now refuses to back a donations cap, then he has broken the promise he made to me – and to voters.“I wanted to believe the positive message he gave me. I wanted to believe that someone was finally going to take on the culture that has left so many people feeling that their voices don’t matter and that wealthy people can buy influence over our government.“But words mean nothing if they disappear the moment power is won. Large political donations are not democratic. They create influence, whether politicians want to admit it or not. The prime minister has one chance to start rebuilding trust: therepresentation of the people act.“He told me he wanted change. Now he needs to keep his promise and act.”Darren Hughes, the chief executive of the Electoral Reform Society, said: “Huge donations have a corrosive effect on trust in politics as they leave the public wondering what donors expect in return for their money.“A donations cap is a crucial step to ending the impression that our politics is for sale to the highest bidder and rebuilding that trust, which is currently at record lows.”However, aLaboursource said: “The representation of the people [elections] bill has been designed to deliver our manifesto commitments on votes at 16 and strengthen political donation rules to guard against foreign interference and that’s what the government is prioritising.”The elections bill, which returns to the Commons next week, is one of the most hotly contested of Burnham’s first few months in office. The bill was intended to lower the voting age to 16 and limit donations by foreign donors, but many in the Labour party believe it should go further in a number of areas.Rushanara Ali, the Labour MP who helped write the bill when she was a minister in the communities department, recentlytold the Guardianthat she felt it was too “timid” and “incremental”, and urged Burnham to strengthen it with amendments.Some Labour MPs intend to use the next stage of the bill to try to introduce clauses banning cryptocurrency donations and cracking down on social media misinformation at election times.Others want Burnhamto back their ideaof a national commission on changing the voting system – something the former Greater Manchester mayor has repeatedly backed in the past.The government has already saidit intends to capdonations by British people living abroad at £100,000, but a big fight is now brewing over whether to apply a similar cap to domestic donations.In May, Burnham signalled he would back a £500,000 cap, telling Bowler over email that he thought a donations cap “would guard against the perception of any one party being unduly influenced or swayed by one person or organisation”.He added: “As to the level, I think that would have to be subject to wider review of political funding but my gut feeling would suggest somewhere in the region of £500k.”Once Burnham got into office however, some of Britain’s biggest trade unions mounted a campaign against the idea, urging MPs not to back an amendment by Creasy to cap donations at £100,000 or another by her backbench colleague Alex Sobel to set the bar at £1m.Last month,GMBwrote to 80 MPs who are members of the union warning: “We believe this amendment risks having significant unintended consequences. Trade unions are already subject to a level of statutory regulation over political expenditure that no other membership organisations face.”Creasy is now changing her amendment in a move to placate union worries, proposing a £500,000 cap that would be gradually reduced until ministers intervene to set it at a level with which they feel comfortable.She said: “Our new amendment would give British democracy the breathing space to get a donations cap right.”However, even this compromise does not appear to have done enough to win ministerial support, which is likely to be crucial for securing enough votes to pass.Those close to the process say capping donations is not a priority for Burnham and not a subject over which it would be worth triggering a fight with Labour’s biggest backers.Explore more on these topicsParty fundingAndy BurnhamLabourTrade unionsGMB unionElectoral reformStella CreasynewsShareReuse this content

title: London neurosurgeons perform first successful AI-assisted operation to remove brain tumour | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Surgeons aided by real-time analysis of camera footage that identified critical anatomy in brain to be avoided
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Surgeons aided by real-time analysis of camera footage that identified critical anatomy in brain to be avoided
Content: Rhys Hibbert, right (with neurosurgeon Hani Marcus, left) was the first patient to have a brain tumour successfully removed in an AI-assisted operation. He was operated on at the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery in London.Photograph: UCLH/PAView image in fullscreenRhys Hibbert, right (with neurosurgeon Hani Marcus, left) was the first patient to have a brain tumour successfully removed in an AI-assisted operation. He was operated on at the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery in London.Photograph: UCLH/PAAI (artificial intelligence)London neurosurgeons perform first successful AI-assisted operation to remove brain tumourSurgeons aided by real-time analysis of camera footage that identified critical anatomy in brain to be avoidedAndrew GregoryHealth editorWed 26 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNeurosurgeons inLondonhave performed the world’s first successful AI-assisted operation to remove a brain tumour, saving the sight of a 48-year-old man, health officials have said.The surgery was performed in May at the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery (NHNN), part of University College London hospitals NHS foundation trust, but details were kept secret until Thursday while the patient, Rhys Hibbert, recovered.While the surgical team remained in full control, the AI system analysed live camera footage during the operation, helping identify key structures such as nerves and blood vessels that should be avoided near the 11mm (0.4in) tumour on Hibbert’s pituitary gland.“When I came round … I could see everything in the room clearly,” said Hibbert, who was able to walk independently without glasses or sticks within a week of the surgery.He has since returned to work as a customer service manager. “It feels like I’ve got a 360‑degree panoramic view of everything around me,” he said.The surgeons operated on Hibbert using new AI technology which helps to identify tiny anatomy in the brain by colour-coding important structures to help surgeons recognise them safely.The hospital had previously used the technology as a research tool but the operation was the first time it had been used on a patient.The pituitary gland, blood vessels and nerves controlling vision are tightly packed together, and “going a millimetre wrong can make a critical difference”, health officials said, potentially leading to blindness, stroke or death.Dr Sophia Bano, an associate professor in robotics and AI at UCL and the technical lead for the AI system, said: “By learning from hundreds of surgical videos, [the system] has been exposed to a breadth of surgical examples that would take a surgeon many years to encounter.“It is designed to help recognise critical anatomy, surgical instruments and tissue interactions in real time, supporting the surgeon during highly delicate procedures.”Initially managed without surgery, Hibbert’s symptoms had worsened since his diagnosis in 2024, and included severe hormone imbalance and vision problems. Without the operation, he faced going blind, health officials said.Hibbert, from Bedfordshire, said: “The NHNN was founded in 1859 … and was the world’s first dedicated neurosurgical hospital. So to me, it seems very fitting that the same hospital should also be the world’s first to carry out an AI-assisted neurosurgery.”Prof Mike Lewis, the scientific director for innovation at the National Institute forHealthand Care Research (NIHR), which funded the operation as part of a clinical trial, said the “pioneering surgery” highlighted the potential of advanced AI to support surgeons and improve patient care.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)HospitalsLondonUCL (University College London)NeuroscienceEnglandHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Plug-in balcony solar panels to go on sale in UK for first time | Solar power | The Guardian
description: DIY system will be stocked by big retailers, starting with Argos, enabling more homes to lower bills by generating own electricity
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: DIY system will be stocked by big retailers, starting with Argos, enabling more homes to lower bills by generating own electricity
Content: The systems can be plugged into a standard wall socket to generate solar power from a balcony, terrace, shed roof or any other outdoor space.Photograph: Ronald Rampsch/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe systems can be plugged into a standard wall socket to generate solar power from a balcony, terrace, shed roof or any other outdoor space.Photograph: Ronald Rampsch/AlamySolar powerPlug-in balcony solar panels to go on sale in UK for first timeDIY system will be stocked by big retailers, starting with Argos, enabling more homes to lower bills by generating own electricityJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentWed 26 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlug-in solar panels will go on sale in the UK for the first time from Thursday, allowing households unable to use rooftop panels to also generate their own cheap electricity.Households across the country will be able to join the millions across mainland Europe who generate their own renewable electricity using “balcony solar panels”, which will be stocked by some of the UK’s biggest retailers.Argos will be the first to offer the DIY solar systems this week, helping people living in flats or rented homes without roof access to lower their billsby generating their own electricity.The rival retailers Amazon, Currys, B&Q and Screwfix are also expected to stock their shelves with plug-in panels within the coming weeks at prices starting from about £400 to £500 depending on the capacity of the system.The devices are already popular in Spain and Germany, wherethey are known asBalkonkraftwerk(balcony power plant) because they can be plugged into a standard wall socket to generate solar power from a balcony, terrace, shed roof or any other outdoor space.The solar power flows directly into the property’s electrical circuit to power appliances without needing to buy as much from the grid. Each solar system must be registered so Great Britain’s NationalEnergySystem Operator can gauge how the cumulative impact of these panels could cut the need for gas-fired power or imports.View image in fullscreenThe solar power flows directly into the property’s electrical circuit to power appliances without needing to buy as much from the grid.Photograph: Climate CentralIn the UK the 800-watt solar systems due to go on sale will be about a fifth of the size of a typical residential rooftop solar set-up, meaning they are unable to provide enough energy to power a home but they could save the average household up to £110 a year on their annual electricity bill.Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said: “Plug-in solar is a simple, affordable way for households to take control of their energy bills and start saving straight away.”Graham Biggart, the managing director for Argos, said: “By making this technology more accessible, we’re putting more power in the hands of our customers and helping them explore practical ways to manage energy use at home.”The savings possible from each solar system will depend on how much solar power is generated, which could be affected by the orientation of each solar panel and the weather on any given day.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSavings will also depend on whether the household is able to use the electricity while it is being generated – perhaps by running washing machines or dishwashers during sunny spells – because plug-in batteries were not included in thenew legislation allowing plug-in solar salesto begin.Emily Seymour, the energy editor at the Which? consumer group, said: “These smaller systems will generate less electricity than conventional rooftop solar and won’t be suitable for every home. People may need planning permission or the consent of the building owner before going ahead, so it will be important to check your own circumstances before making a purchase.“There are also important safety considerations, particularly around the suitability of older electrical systems, the safe mounting of panels and the potential for people to use products or equipment incorrectly.”Joanna O’Loan, a manager at Energy Saving Trust, said: “While the savings will vary from home to home, plug-in solar panels will give more people greater control over their energy use and costs. As these products become more widely available, access to clear and reliable information is essential to help people make informed choices that are right for their home and budget.”Explore more on these topicsSolar powerEnergy industryRenewable energyEnergy billsRetail industryEnergyConsumer affairsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Amol Rajan warns BBC destined to shrink at ‘accelerating rate’ | BBC | The Guardian
description: Presenter says he is moving to YouTube to avoid being left ‘behind the curve’ as media landscape changes
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Presenter says he is moving to YouTube to avoid being left ‘behind the curve’ as media landscape changes
Content: Amol Rajan announced earlier this year that he was leaving BBC News to ‘unleash my inner entrepreneur’ in the creator economy.Photograph: Aled Llywelyn/AlamyView image in fullscreenAmol Rajan announced earlier this year that he was leaving BBC News to ‘unleash my inner entrepreneur’ in the creator economy.Photograph: Aled Llywelyn/AlamyBBCAmol Rajan warns BBC destined to shrink at ‘accelerating rate’Presenter says he is moving to YouTube to avoid being left ‘behind the curve’ as media landscape changesMichael SavageMedia editorWed 26 Aug 2026 14.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 14.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe outgoing Today programme presenterAmol Rajanhas warned that the BBC is destined to “get smaller at an accelerating rate”, as he prepares to depart for a new project on YouTube.Rajan, who announced earlier this year that hewas leaving BBC Newsto “unleash my inner entrepreneur” in the creator economy, said he was making the shift to ensure he was not “behind the curve”.It comes with the BBC making savings of£500m over the next two yearsas it contends with the falling value of its licence fee funding and an increase in the number of people opting not to pay it.The corporation, along with other traditional broadcasters, isdemanding to be given prominence in the algorithmsof platforms such as YouTube and TikTok as it faces mounting pressures from an increasing shift away from linear television viewing.Speaking to the Political Currency podcast, Rajan said Radio 4’s Today programme was “the last big mass-market news programme” – an exception in a world where consumers are increasingly turning to digital platforms.Auntie v influencers: why YouTubers are ready for battle with the BBCRead more“I’ve worked for 20 years in the media,” he said. “I had a wonderful 10 years in newspapers, a wonderful 10 years in TV and radio and I’ve always been a bit behind the curve, basically. And I feel that I’ve always been basically in areas of rapid and accelerating decline.“The Today programme … does not fit with this argument, so I’m arguing against myself, but the BBC and BBC News is in the years to come going to get smaller at an accelerating rate, and I want to go to where the action is, and that’sYouTube.”Rajan’s comments come with the TV world fretting over the rise of digital platforms. The BBC has already responded by announcing anew partnershipto produce content dedicated to YouTube. Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, has set reaching younger audiences as one of his top priorities.Pedro Pina, YouTube’s head for Europe, Middle East and Africa, has insisted that the platform is “not the villain” set to destroy the TV industry.“That is how the story usually goes, like a well-scripted tragedy,” Pina said on Wednesday in the keynote MacTaggart lecture at the Edinburgh TV festival. “We have our once great hero, we have their terrible downfall, and – in platforms like YouTube – we have an obvious villain. It’s a powerful story. An emotive story. The trouble is that it is not true.”He said broadcasters could flourish alongside new digital platforms, just as painters continued to flourish after the invention of the photograph. However, he said TV companies no longer had the monopoly they enjoyed in the heyday of linear television.BBC hires 26-year-old entrepreneur to help reach younger audiencesRead morePina warned against the idea of the government forcing YouTube to give greater prominence to content from traditional broadcasters – an idea that hascaused fury among content creatorswho believe it will mean their videos will be relegated. The idea has been pushed as a solution to online misinformation.Pina said: “Forced prominence would impair the public interest by unfairly shifting focus from independent creators and production companies, and by recommending that all our viewers watch the same things, disregarding personal taste.“If this becomes law, many UK-based creators and production companies will see their livelihoods threatened. UK viewers will have to wade through content they may not want, which in itself could undermine the trust that UK public service broadcasters have built up. Forced prominence won’t help anyone succeed – not new independent talent, not viewers and definitely not public service media.”Elsewhere at the festival, Kevin Lygo, ITV’s managing director of media and entertainment, suggested YouTube’s investment in the UK was tiny compared with that of Britain’s public service broadcasters.Observing YouTube’s recent £3m commitment to investing in the UK’s creator economy and TV industries, Lygo said the figure “made him chortle” when he compared it with ITV’s estimated £1.2bn spend on content this year.Explore more on these topicsBBCAmol RajanRadio 4BBC licence feeEdinburgh International Television FestivalTelevision industryRadio industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Tim Curry, star of The Rocky Horror Picture Show and Stephen King’s It, dies aged 80 | Movies | The Guardian
description: A prolific performer across stage, screen and TV, the actor starred in Legend, Clue and It, but will always be associated with the flamboyantly camp rock’n’roll musical in which he made his breakthrough
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: A prolific performer across stage, screen and TV, the actor starred in Legend, Clue and It, but will always be associated with the flamboyantly camp rock’n’roll musical in which he made his breakthrough
Content: Mr versatility ... Tim Curry in 2008Photograph: Michael Tran/FilmMagicView image in fullscreenMr versatility ... Tim Curry in 2008Photograph: Michael Tran/FilmMagicMoviesTim Curry, star of The Rocky Horror Picture Show and Stephen King’s It, dies aged 80A prolific performer across stage, screen and TV, the actor starred in Legend, Clue and It, but will always be associated with the flamboyantly camp rock’n’roll musical in which he made his breakthroughTim Curry on sexuality, surviving a stroke – and 50 years of stardomFarewell, Dr Frank N Furter: why Tim Curry’s Rocky Horror Show will go onClowns, corsets and kings: Tim Curry – a life in picturesAndrew PulverWed 26 Aug 2026 11.47 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 17.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTim Curry, the versatile performer of screen and stage, who made his name as the flamboyant Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Show, has died aged 80.Reports sayCurry died at his home in Los Angeles.Farewell, Dr Frank N Furter: why Tim Curry’s Rocky Horror Show will go onRead moreThe actor’s manager confirmed to Variety that he died peacefully. No cause of death is known as yet.Ironically, Curry’s best-known roles all required a considerable physical transformation, to the extent that he was unrecognisable in all of them. Frank-N-Furter, Rocky Horror’s deranged scientist, saw him daubed in garish makeup and wearing stockings and suspenders, for the stage show (which debuted in 1973) and the film adaptation (released in 1975). In the Ridley Scott-directed fantasy Legend (1985), he was equipped with giant horns and scarlet skin as the Lord of Darkness. And in 1990, Curry was transformed with full-face clown pancake to play Pennywise in the TV miniseries It, based on theStephen Kingnovel.View image in fullscreen… Tim Curry in The Rocky Horror Picture Show.Photograph: PRAlongside these show-stopping incarnations, Curry enjoyed a successful parallel career in film, TV and theatre. Born in 1946, he earned a degree in drama and English from the University of Birmingham in 1968 and embarked on a stage career. His first significant role was in the original cast for the first West End production of the controversial musical Hair, in 1968 – where he met Richard O’Brien, who would go on to cast him in his own musical, TheRocky Horror Show. Curry went on to play Tristan Tzara in Tom Stoppard’s Travesties (taking over the role from John Hurt and Robert Powell), and Mozart in the Broadway transfer of Amadeus in 1980. Later highlights included King Arthur in the Broadway run of the Monty Python musical Spamalot.‘Risky is the best way to be’: Tim Curry on sexuality, surviving a stroke – and 50 years of stardomRead moreCurry worked regularly in film, in roles including that of Robert Graves in Jerzy Skolimowski’s sinister The Shout, and later as Jeremy in the Ian McEwan-scripted political drama The Ploughman’s Lunch. Later, Curry found himself working largely in comedies – including Home Alone 2: Lost in New York, Muppet Treasure Island, Scary Movie 2, and McHale’s Navy – before providing voiceovers for numerous animated films, such as Garfield: A Tail of Two Kitties, A Turtle’s Tale: Sammy’s Adventures and Ribbit.View image in fullscreenPennywise for them … Tim Curry as the killer clown in It.Photograph: Allstar/Cinetext/Lorimar TelevisionCurry was also a regular presence on TV for more than four decades, playingWilliam Shakespearein John Mortimer’s six-part biography of the playwright in 1978, Bill Sikes in the 1982 US TV adaptation of Oliver Twist, and the wizard Trymon in the adaptation of Terry Pratchett’s The Colour of Magic in 2008. He voiced a stream of animated series (Duckman, Sonic the Hedgehog, The Mask and Star Wars: The Clone Wars) and was cast in many guest roles in established series, including Psych, Poirot and Criminal Minds.“I’ve had the opportunities,” he said to theGuardian in 2025, “and I’m still showing up. You know? I think that’s what you have to do. You have to keep showing up.”Clowns, corsets and kings: Tim Curry – a life in picturesRead moreIn 2012, Curry had a stroke while receiving a massage and received brain surgery. He was left with mobility issues and his short-term memory was also affected. “It was an odd thing, because my father had a stroke and died very soon afterwards,” he said. “I knew I had to force myself to relax and just take the opportunity to float a little.”In 2025, he released his memoir Vagabond.“I’m very aware that I’m lucky,” Curry said last year. “I’m astonished actually at how ambitious I’ve been. I didn’t think of myself as ambitious at all.”Luke Evans, who played the role of Dr Frank-N-Furter in the recent Broadway production of The Rocky Horror Show, paid tribute onInstagram. The actor called him “a force, a bright fierce flame” and “an inspiration”. He added: “There will only be one Tim Curry.”Rocky Horror Picture Show co-star Susan Sarandoncalledhim a “funny sexy original” in an online post. “Even wheelchair bound he continued to be so sweet and generous with his fans,” she wrote. “Thank you Tim for meaning so much to so many people.”Carol Burnett, who starred with Curry in Annie, also paid tributeonline. “Nobody could play lovable villains better than he could,” she wrote. “He was a dear friend. I was blessed to know him.”Curry’s Clue co-star Michael McKeansharedon X: “My last conversation with Tim Curry was about life and love and laughter. The grim physical state he found himself in has now ended, a blessing. Our blessing was that we had Tim Curry in our lives. RIP, my friend.”Explore more on these topicsFilmTim CurryRocky Horror ShowLegendStephen KingFilm adaptationsTelevisionShareReuse this content

title: ‘Work is good for you’: how UK scheme could help tackle youth mental health crisis | Youth unemployment | The Guardian
description: Paid employment can boost confidence and wellbeing, says Pat McFadden as jobs guarantee scheme gets under way
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Paid employment can boost confidence and wellbeing, says Pat McFadden as jobs guarantee scheme gets under way
Content: Pat McFadden and Juliet Campbell, MP for Broxtowe, with Saqib (right), a Boots warehouse employee in Nottingham.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAView image in fullscreenPat McFadden and Juliet Campbell, MP for Broxtowe, with Saqib (right), a Boots warehouse employee in Nottingham.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAYouth unemployment‘Work is good for you’: how UK scheme could help tackle youth mental health crisisPaid employment can boost confidence and wellbeing, says Pat McFadden as jobs guarantee scheme gets under wayHeather StewartWed 26 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWork must be “part of the answer” to the mental health crisis among young people, the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, has said as he met some of the first beneficiaries of Labour’syouth jobs guarantee scheme.He was speaking on a visit to Boots’s headquarters in Nottingham on Wednesday, where several 18- to 21-year-olds were taken on under the job guarantee – with their wages paid by the taxpayer for six months.Some of the recruits were packing and labelling boxes of products to be posted out to households, and others are in administrative roles. They told McFadden about long periods of fruitless jobhunting.“It was just amazing for me to hear their stories,” McFadden said of the recruits. “These are young people who have been out of work for one, two, up to four years. Most of them have been working here for a few weeks. And you can already see how it’s changed their confidence in themselves – their sense of belief in themselves.”A rise in cases of mental illness is widely cited as one cause for the increase in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) in recent years.But McFadden said the reasons could run the other way, too. “Work is part of the answer. Work is good for you. It’s bad for your mental health to be sitting at home, isolated.View image in fullscreenYoung people told Pat McFadden that their social lives had improved and they had clearer daily routines as a result of being in paid work.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA“I see this not only as an economic thing, but as a response to greater instances of mental health problems for young people. The last thing we want to see is a diagnosis of problems leading to a life on benefits.”At a roundtable discussion, McFadden asked each of the young people how they felt as a result of their move into paid work. They cited better social lives and clearer daily routines.“I’m so conscious, having done this job for almost exactly a year now, that belief and confidence is a big part of the picture,” McFadden told journalists afterwards. “We mustn’t blame young people for the challenges they are facing in the labour market.”The number of Neets in the UK recently topped 1 million – with the latest data due out on Thursday.Alan Milburn, the Blair-era cabinet minister reviewing youth inactivity for the government, has warned that the numbercould hit 1.25m by 2030, without intervention. His final report is due in the autumn.McFadden made clear that welfare reform would probably be part of the government’s response, criticising the “black and white” distinction in the current universal credit system.“There’s a design flaw in the universal credit system, which too readily separates people into ‘fit for work’ and ‘unfit for work’, and when they are unfit for work, leaves them without any support or any conditions,” he said. “That’s what I call the culture of ‘signed off and written off’. I think we need to change that.”He highlighted a recent initiative under which claimants with no obligation to look for work have been asked to attend voluntary interviews with work coaches at their local Jobcentre.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMcFadden had started the day at a branch of Sainsbury’s in London, stacking shelves in the bread aisle, alongside the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the London mayor, Sadiq Khan.View image in fullscreenPat McFadden, Sadiq Khan and Andy Burnham help to stack shelves at Sainsbury’s in Nine Elms, London.Photograph: Richard Pohle/ReutersThe trio were highlighting the fact that Sainsbury’s is offering 10,000 internships for young people.McFadden praised Boots and Sainsbury’s, and encouraged other big employers to play their part in what he called the “national cause” of tackling youth unemployment.Asked whether it was a good use of public money to be subsidising corporations to take on young people, he said: “I’m enthused when businesses like Boots or Sainsbury’s – or any business in the country – steps up and says: ‘I want to play my part here.’ And if there’s a bit of a financial incentive in it, that’s fine.”The jobs guarantee scheme will eventually be available to 18- to 24-year-olds in Great Britain who have been claiming universal credit and seeking work for at least 18 months, with the aim of creating 90,000 subsidised placements over the next three years.It is initially being piloted in six areas with high unemployment, including central and east Scotland, Birmingham and Solihull, and south-east and south-west Wales. The government intends it to be nationwide by November.Explore more on these topicsYouth unemploymentUnemploymentYoung peopleMental healthWork & careersBootsWelfarenewsShareReuse this content

title: How to lose Trump’s trade war: test Canada’s resolve with threats to hockey sticks | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: The US president expected Ottawa to bow to tariff demands, but Canada is striking back – and it could cost Americans
Author: Adam Gabbatt
Headline: The US president expected Ottawa to bow to tariff demands, but Canada is striking back – and it could cost Americans
Content: Donald Trump in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, on 21 August and Mark Carney in Quebec, Canada, on 24 August.Photograph: Saul Loeb,andrej Ivanov/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, on 21 August and Mark Carney in Quebec, Canada, on 24 August.Photograph: Saul Loeb,andrej Ivanov/AFP/Getty ImagesThis Week in TrumplandTrump tariffsAnalysisHow to lose Trump’s trade war: test Canada’s resolve with threats to hockey sticksAdam GabbattThe US president expected Ottawa to bow to tariff demands, but Canada is striking back – and it could cost AmericansThis was originally published in This Week in Trumpland.Sign up to receive it in your inbox every WednesdayWed 26 Aug 2026 14.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 14.49 EDTShareEarlier this year, a survey found thatCanada, along withSwitzerland, wasthe best-liked countryin the world. We all know this kind of polling is about as scientific as a high school popularity contest, but at least anecdotally, Canadians have a reputation for being friendly and welcoming, respectful and polite. Many people would find it difficult to dislike Canadians.But not Donald Trump, who in a “hold my beer” moment this week demonstrated that he, at least, finds it easy to resent Canadians. The US president called the country “difficult and unreasonable”, and in a particularly hysterical moment,threatened to rename a lake, after trade talks collapsed.Days earlier, Trump had claimed a deal withCanadawas imminent, which would avoid the new taxes.Wiped out: US faces surging toilet paper prices amid trade war with CanadaRead moreBut, in a development that surely galled the Art of the Deal author, there was no agreement.Instead, Trump and his team demonstrated the art of collapsing the deal, as trade talks fell apart due to what Canada said wereunreasonable, last-minute demandsfrom the US side.It meant that the US tariffs duly came in on Saturday, applied to various Canadian exports including hockey sticks and tongue depressors, but if Trump expected Canada to bow to his demands – the president was seeking more favorable terms on things like steel and aluminum – he was disappointed.Instead,Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister who has emerged as a rare world leader willing to stand up to Trump, said Canada had been “attacked”, and announced retaliatory tariffs on about $20bn worth of US goods, including steel, dairy products, appliances and farm equipment.All this means US consumers are seeing surging prices on all kinds of products – including toilet paper. My colleague Lauren Aratanireports that“the US accounts for more than 20% of global tissue consumption despite having only 4% of the world’s population”. And this outsize usage has grown more expensive. “Though American toilet paper and tissues are often made domestically, they heavily rely on lumber-rich Canada for raw materials,” she writes.It’s fair to say that Canada’s retaliation upset Trump, who famously loves to win. On Tuesday, he claimed the US “is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer” – we’ll see how that goes – and has dubbed Canadian negotiators“clowns”.Earlier this week, TrumpcomparedDoug Ford, the premier of Ontario, unfavorably to his deceased brother Rob, the scandal-plagued former mayor of Toronto, whose time in office saw himadmit to smoking crack cocaineand being “hammered” in public.And while Trump was flailing about, JD Vance was doing his best Scrappy Do, “lemme at ’em” impression, lobbing insults at Canadafrom the safety of a Republican rallyin Maine. Vance claimed that Canada and China are “the two worst countries when it comes to trade policy anywhere in the world”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis Week in TrumplandA deep dive into the policies, controversies and oddities surrounding the Trump administrationEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe added: “We have to remember, Canada is a state. Sorry. Freudian slip. That was actually an accident.” The satisfied look on his face didn’t make it seem like one.Vance went on to add that Canada “quite literally would get invaded by a foreign country were it not for the umbrella of protection provided by the United States of America”.
