It was an interesting take, given the only country that has mused about invading Canada is the US – as recently as last year Trump wasthreatening to annex the nation.So in a nutshell:Donald Trumphas led the US into an unsavory spat against the world’s most popular country, a scrap that could result in Americans – less than three months out from crucial midterm elections in which Republicans face an uphill battle – struggle to pay for a roll of toilet paper.Win!Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsThis Week in TrumplandDonald TrumpMark CarneyTariffsCanadaAmericasanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘9 to 5? She was full-on round the clock!’ Dolly Parton celebrated by kd lang, Peggy Seeger, Annie Lennox and more | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: Musicians and performers pay tribute to the country legend who managed to be a generational talent, a formidable entrepreneur, a dedicated philanthropist and a truly kind person
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: Musicians and performers pay tribute to the country legend who managed to be a generational talent, a formidable entrepreneur, a dedicated philanthropist and a truly kind person
Content: ‘She was in a class of her own’ … Dolly Parton in 1978.Photograph: Richard E Aaron/RedfernsView image in fullscreen‘She was in a class of her own’ … Dolly Parton in 1978.Photograph: Richard E Aaron/RedfernsDolly Parton‘9 to 5? She was full-on round the clock!’ Dolly Parton celebrated by kd lang, Peggy Seeger, Annie Lennox and moreMusicians and performers pay tribute to the country legend who managed to be a generational talent, a formidable entrepreneur, a dedicated philanthropist and a truly kind personAs told toDave SimpsonandOwen MyersWed 26 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 22.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Not just a big-bosomed singer of great songs’Shirley Collins, singer-songwriterI don’t really follow pop music or country and western very much, butDolly Partonwas always something special – separate from it all, in a way. She seemed absolutely indomitable. Coming from a large family in a mountain home and being brought up in poverty, she broke through to have this incredible career and you couldn’t help feeling fond of her. How she did it I don’t know, but nothing seemed to faze her.I was always impressed by her perception of things. Like in Jolene, the carelessness of someone taking someone’s husband “just because [she] can” is really clever. Dolly could see stuff and then write about it in ways that nobody else could.A few years ago, someone sent me a book called The Pack Horse Library, about women in the Appalachians in the 1930s who rode pack horses or mules in this wilderness country and took library books to all the isolated cabins with huge families, who wouldn’t normally get near a library. In modern times, Dolly has done exactly the same thing, but on such a massive scale,posting books to children around the world. She wasn’t just a big-bosomed singer of great songs – and she wrote so, so many great songs – but a fabulous human being. I think we’re all really rather privileged to have been able to see her.I wouldn’t talk like this about any other pop singer, but as a singer and a person she was in a class of her own. It’s a sad, sad day, but people will always think of her and smile.‘She embodied the ideal of live and let live’kd lang, singer-songwriterView image in fullscreenkd lang.Photograph: Carolyn Contino/BEI/ShutterstockShe was a plain-clothed prophet. She transcended all misconceptions of what a Christian is, what an American is, what an artist is or what an ally is. She came from a southern, Christian, country and western place and she never wavered inher support of the LGBTQ+ communityor the Black community – all those that have suffered at the hands of those with a far-right mentality.I believe in the divine timing of things and I think that, in her departure, there’s a gift, too, because I can’t think of anyone who had a more cohesive effect on people than Dolly Parton. Her exaggerated physical presence – her hair and her boobs and her hips and her clothes – was a caricature, one we sometimes laughed at. But the joke was on us, because she embraced who she was and never judged anyone else. She truly embodied that way of being – just live and let live.Of all her songs, I really likeCoat of Many Colors. I’m not a Christian, but there’s something so down-home about that. I truly believe that it is a story from Dolly’s life. She used the tools she was given and one of them was being from a large country family that was raised Christian. She took the very essence of the teachings and illuminated them to the highest degree. May she have a swift rebirth.‘She sent me a big, home-cooked meal’Joan Osborne, singer-songwriterView image in fullscreenJoan Osborne in London, 2024.Photograph: Robin Little/RedfernsI had the honour of singing her songDo I Ever Cross Your Mind?for a Dolly compilation called Just Because I’m a Woman in the early 00s. During the recording session, she sent over a big, home-cooked meal, that she had made herself, to give to the musicians and me so we wouldn’t get hungry while we worked. When the album was done, she sent me a very gracious handwritten letter, saying that my version of her song had made her cry. I wish I could lay my hands on that letter right now. It’s buried somewhere in my archives. But I do remember it very well and someday I’ll unearth it and frame it for my studio.I always admired the way that Dolly hid in plain sight. She was an immensely talented songwriter and beautiful singer, a serious artist and a brilliant businesswoman, but she wrapped herself in the disguise of a comic blond bombshell. Her presentation was probably a result, at least in part, of her desire to fulfil the fantasies of a little girl who grew up in poverty, but it was also a very smart career strategy.‘She was honest, brash, daring and way ahead of her time’Peggy Seeger, singer-songwriterDolly was a one-off – and I mean off the wall. Honest, brash, daring and way ahead of her time, yet very present in her own time. She wasn’t a 9 to 5 woman; she was full-on round the clock. I followed her career throughout and adored everything she did. She’s left us way too soon, yet left us so much.‘Her presence could fill 10 football stadiums’Annie Lennox, singer-songwriterView image in fullscreenAnnie Lennox(far right)at the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony with Dolly Parton(centre).Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for The Rock and Roll Hall of FameOn 5 November 2022, Eurythmics had the unforgettable experience of performing Jolene with the legendary Dolly Parton, joining alongside an exceptional mix of musical acolytes, representing a cross-section of musicians who were all being inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. When we arrived for the dress rehearsal, there she was, standing centre stage, a surprisingly tiny figure in vertiginous high-heeled boots and full rocker regalia, dressed head to toe in a figure-hugging outfit of black skintight PVC, adorned with suspended pendants of silver chains. As tiny as she was, her presence was big enough to fill 10 football stadiums.She was warm and personable, with a tremendously dry sense of humour. We all felt extremely favoured to be part of that song performance. It was a special moment with no pedestals in sight … except for the one we placed her upon that night.Rest in power, Dolly Parton … the REAL deal.‘She came along like Attack of the 50 Foot Woman’Billy Bragg, singer-songwriterView image in fullscreenBilly Bragg.Photograph: Guitarist Magazine/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesWe’ve lost someone who was an embodiment of a type of American exceptionalism that has been eclipsed by the Trump carnival of people who say: “Empathy is toxic.” She was the opposite of that. Her faith was based on the idea that, as she once said: “I just want everybody to be treated good.” That quote came from someoneasking her about anti-trans legislationin her home state of Tennessee. She didn’t hedge it. She went on to say: “We are all God’s children and how we are is who we are.” She didn’t stop at trans people, or American people, or white people. She extended that to everybody.When people are saying empathy is toxic, you need someone like Dolly Parton to come along like the Attack of the 50 Foot Woman and put them back in their box. Everyone talks about a divided America, but her superpower was to bring people together. She completely transcended her role and became a universal figure, a bit like the queen, and similarly the reaction to her passing has been exceptional.Obviously, as a songwriter, she was incredible. Everyone knows about the great songs that have been all over the radio in the last 24 hours, but for me her artistry also lies in the more obscure songs such as Do I Ever Cross Your Mind? – the chord changes are to die for – orDown from Dover, a heartbreaking song where a young woman is pregnant and waiting for her boyfriend to come back. He doesn’t come and the baby dies. It’s a heart-rending song that doesn’t just put the position of unwed young women at the centre; it also plumbs into that great Appalachian tradition of tragedy songs, which she heard when she was growing up and will have seen first-hand.She was tougher than any man. Her second album was called Just Because I’m a Woman. She was saying: don’t be messing with me, because I see through your pernicious attitudes towards me as a woman and I’m gonna turn that back on you. And she was incredibly powerful at doing that. She had kindness and empathy, but she wasn’t like a little flower. She had the strength to broadcast her empathy to the world. She was the epitome of that rhinestone, vaudeville, bouffant, over-the-top America that I’ve always been attracted to, but also the best of humanity. She really was the best of us.‘She silenced the crowd at Glastonbury’Jonny Woo, drag performerView image in fullscreenJonny Woo’s troupe at Glastonbury in 2014.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverEveryone loved Dolly. How could you not? She was the archetype of joy and beauty and generosity – and the music was amazing. The first time she came into my psyche was watching her in9 to 5and she’s the best person I’ve seen at Glastonbury in 20 years of going. When she was talking, just in her normal voice, the crowd were absolutely silent. Her voice was immaculate. Her storytelling was just joyous. I think there were more people watching her than the Rolling Stones.So, of course, my drag troupe and I all dressed up as her. That image is so joyous. It’s not derogatory to call her a camp icon. Like Céline Dion or Cher, she was very aware of the pleasure of her visual appeal. They’re celebratory and stylish, using their femininity and sexuality to lift your mood.9 to 5 review – Dolly Parton’s quietly radical office revenge satireRead moreShe said: “It costs a lot of money to look this cheap.” But on stage she was like a diamond: her music shone, her voice shone and her image shone. It’s just hard not to smile when you think of her.Because she came from such an extraordinarily poor background, she could connect with the working-class experience around the world. She was interested in people: “Tell me where you come from. What’s your life about?” I don’t know how much country music embraces queer culture – possibly not much – but she was hugely supportive of us.She was the kind of person who got on with it: did the job, got her money and helped people out, rather than making a big song and dance about it. She was strong without being aggressive and would rebut people without being unkind, which is a great skill. You just knew she had the back, not just of queer people, but of all people who face shit in their lives. She was looking out for you and singing for you. She’ll be hugely missed, but thinking of her immediately fills us with joy, rather than sadness.‘She could wrap anyone in warmth and love’KT Tunstall, singer-songwriterDolly was beyond the greatest. She was a world-leveller, in her immeasurable talent and in her ability to wrap anyone and everyone together in warmth and love. She’ll for ever be one of the best examples of how to spend a life on Earth.‘She represented anyone down on their luck’Kelly O’Brien, ‘the world’s No 1Dolly Parton tribute’View image in fullscreenKelly O’Brien with Dolly Parton.Photograph: Courtesy of Kelly O’BrienI don’t think I’ve had time to properly process Dolly’s passing. Every time I hear a bit of a song, it gets me started. I grew up in Australia. My parents would play her records and I’d go to sleep listening toLove Is Like a Butterflyand Jolene. As you get older, you think: “Wow, this woman’s clever. She’s no dumb blonde. She knows exactly what she’s doing.” Talking to interviewers, she would make fun of herself before anybody else could. From her entrepreneurism and humanitarianism to her philanthropy, she was a very clued-up woman.I started mucking around being Dolly 30 years ago. Being Dolly takes a lot of practice. I really studied her voice a lot, because I wanted to represent her in the best way possible. That meant going on a very strict diet, learning the accent, learning all the songs, her mannerisms. The costumes had to be right and the wigs had to be perfect. I based my work on her perfection.She means a lot to so many people in a world that’s gone a little bit mad. She’s this constant, kind, big-hearted, wholesome girl. She represented not only women, but anybody down on their luck, singing about unwedded women back in the early 70s and aworld on fire. She reached a whole new younger generation of admirerswhen she performed at Glastonbury in 2014, because she was Miley Cyrus’s godmother and so glamorous.She didn’t really approach politics, but then I think with her Rockstar album in 2023 she probably got a bit fed up and so became even more outspoken about LGBTQ+ rights and things like that. She used to have gay days at Dollywood and I think she used to get death threats, but she stood her ground. She’d go: “No, this is who these people are. They’re born this way. God accepts them and you have to do the same.” She brought some badass ideas to the deep south.I met her in 2011, backstage at the O2. I was dressed as her – unexpectedly, we had matching gold outfits! – and we were the same height. It was terrifying, because I was going to meet my idol, but she said she loved what I did and loved all the drag queens and Dolly impersonators everywhere. It was just magical, which she was.‘She wrote what she knew with great eloquence and skill’Paul Jepson, director of themusical 9 to 5View image in fullscreenPaul Jepson.Photograph: Andy Casey Upright MediaShe was an extraordinary person and very talented. We wanted to honour her extraordinary spirit. Our show’s music supervisor, Mark Crossland, and choreographer got to know Dolly. She had a lot of involvement in the development of the musical. Obviously, it’s her songs [and was originally a Broadway production, based on the 1980 movie], but everyone commented on how incredibly generous she was. She recorded herself singing, and bits of speaking, and sent them down the line from the US. Afterwards, she would ask if we needed to make any changes or needed anything else. She was the consummate pro. People often make this stuff up, but she was genuinely lovely and everybody loved her.One of the numbers in the show is Backwoods Barbie, which Karla Tracey – as Doralee – does exceptionally well. It’s actually a confession: she’s talking about where she comes from and she’s upset, because everyone has been horrible to her. Dolly got that: she was writing about something she knew very well with great eloquence and skill. A lot of people don’t know that the 9 to 5 song and movie was based on a real organisation, 9to5,that still existsand is still fighting discrimination and pushing for workers’ rights.I’m very glad the show has been touring in places such as Worthing, Bridlington and Darlington, which aren’t known as primary dates for this level of attention. They’re places that haven’t always been shown a lot of love – a bit downtrodden, if you will – and we wanted to stand up for them. I’d like to think that Dolly would have approved. It seemed a very Dolly thing to do.‘She dedicated much of her life to helping children’The Wiggles, children’s music groupWe are heartbroken to hear of the passing of Dolly Parton. Dolly brought so much joy, kindness and music into this world and we feel incredibly lucky to have spent time with her and to have called her our friend.Her extraordinary legacy goes far beyond the songs we all know and love. Dolly dedicated so much of her life to helping children dream big, including through herImagination Library,which has put millions of books into the hands of children around the world.Getting to make music with Dolly was something we will treasure for ever. But even more special was experiencing the warmth, generosity and joy that made her so deeply loved by generations of families. Thank you for the music, the laughter, the stories and everything you did for children everywhere. We will always be friends. We love you, Dolly. Rest peacefully.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick hereExplore more on these topicsDolly PartonCountryCelebrityAmericanafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Farewell, Dr Frank-N-Furter: why Tim Curry’s Rocky Horror Show will go on | Movies | The Guardian
description: The versatile stage performer will always be remembered for his defining film role in The Rocky Horror Picture Show, which turned him into an icon of 70s underground cinema and proto-punk
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: The versatile stage performer will always be remembered for his defining film role in The Rocky Horror Picture Show, which turned him into an icon of 70s underground cinema and proto-punk
Content: Tim Curry in The Rocky Horror Picture Show.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenTim Curry in The Rocky Horror Picture Show.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/ShutterstockMoviesFarewell, Dr Frank-N-Furter: why Tim Curry’s Rocky Horror Show will go onPeter BradshawThe versatile stage performer will always be remembered for his defining film role in The Rocky Horror Picture Show, which turned him into an icon of 70s underground cinema and proto-punkTim Curry, star of The Rocky Horror Picture Show and Stephen King’s It, dies aged 80Tim Curry on sexuality, surviving a stroke and 50 years of stardomClowns, corsets and kings – a life in picturesWed 26 Aug 2026 12.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 22.45 EDTShareOver the past decade, the issues of trans identity and gender fluidity couldn’t have been more contemporary, andTim Currywas an integral part of what might be called their pre-history in pop culture. He was an icon – though maybe now a dimly remembered icon – of the 70s underground cinema and proto-punk.How we made: The Rocky Horror Picture ShowRead moreCurry was a good-looking actor with a tremendous speaking and singing voice, and a versatile performer – he got Tony nominations for his varied stage work on Broadway as Mozart in Amadeus, Alan Swann in My Favorite Year (the part Peter O’Toole played on screen) and as King Arthur in Monty Python’sSpamalot. But it was his strange destiny to be remembered for one role: at once indelibly prominent and weirdly peripheral. He was the sensational Dr Frank-N-Furter in the thoroughly outrageous Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975), the screen version of the 1973 stage show.This was the drop-dead gorgeous “sweet transvestite from Transsexual, Transylvania” in mascara and fish-nets, a vampiric sex outlaw who challenges the dull complacency of the timid American teen couple, Janet and Brad, played by Susan Sarandon and Barry Bostwick. These hapless straights had got lost and found themselves in his exotic domain. Curry himself said that the movie stymied his film career for many years, because of typecasting in a role that could not really ever be repeated, and in fact a great deal of his income from screen work from then on derived from voiceovers. But he also hinted that it was a kind of pension, perhaps because of royalties from the million-selling soundtrack LP.View image in fullscreenStage star … David Hyde Pierce and Tim Curry (right) in Monty Python’s Spamalot at the Shubert theatre, New York, in 2005.Photograph: Evan Agostini/Getty ImagesCurry defined the role, defined the movie, and helped define other things besides. Without Curry and Rocky Horror, there might be no Vivienne Westwood Sex boutique and no punk. He was a part of the sexual peacock movement that was upending the dullness and drear of the 70s. Curry swam briefly alongside Bolan and Bowie on a tide of glam.There was something else. Curry described the awfulness of sitting with 20th Century Fox executives at early private showings of Rocky Horror and hearing the deathly silence that reigned in the screening room afterwards. But it was a smart young Fox publicity director, Tim Deegan, who realised what a draw Tim Curry and Rocky Horror could be in the burgeoning “midnight” circuit in New York. He booked the movie in, and its growing word-of-mouth success and audience participation rituals virtually created the underground cult film scene. The stylishly sexual Tim Curry drew in the crowds and created a market for movies such as Alejandro Jodorowsky’s El Topo, George Romero’s Night of the Living Dead, John Waters’s Pink Flamingos, Perry Henzell’s The Harder They Come, and David Lynch’s Eraserhead.Tim Curry and Rocky Horror were wacky and campy: they grew out of the hokey B-movie tradition of sci-fi and horror. (One of Dr Furter’s lines is “We could take in an old Steve Reeves movie” – a tongue-in-cheek reference to the beefcake bodybuilder who starred in many daft sword-and-sandal movies after the war; he was the Schwarzenegger of his day, with a lively gay following.)Furter was wildly popular, but it always threatened to box Curry into a niche image. Many actors find themselves through sheer random fate chained to some lucrative TV or soap opera role. But there is usually some chance of developing in other directions. Tim Curry’s screen career certainly stayed healthy enough, and he even enjoyed a kind of miniature version of his earlier cult celebrity in the wacky novelty murder-mystery flick Clue in 1985, based on the board game Cluedo, released with three alternative endings. Curry played the fruity butler Wadsworth, manically rushing about explaining everything.But of course there could be no way of topping the extraordinary, brief impact of Dr Frank-N-Furter and Rocky Horror – not on screen anyway, although his stage musical work was admired for its variety. Curry’s Furter gave the world a blast of subversive fun.This article was amended on 27 August 2026. The original version of this article stated that Curry played Salieri in the Broadway production of Amadeus; he actually played Mozart.Explore more on these topicsFilmTim CurryRocky Horror ShowcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Never Ending Murder review – behind the lurid title, there is a family’s heartbreaking story  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: In 1991, 18-year-old Nicola Payne went missing and has never been found. It’s easy to assume this documentary is a sensationalist dig into her case – but there is much more depth to such a haunting real-life nightmare
Author: Rachel Aroesti
Headline: In 1991, 18-year-old Nicola Payne went missing and has never been found. It’s easy to assume this documentary is a sensationalist dig into her case – but there is much more depth to such a haunting real-life nightmare
Content: Nicola Payne, who disappeared in 1991.Photograph: PAView image in fullscreenNicola Payne, who disappeared in 1991.Photograph: PATV reviewTelevision & radioReviewThe Never Ending Murder review – behind the lurid title, there is a family’s heartbreaking storyIn 1991, 18-year-old Nicola Payne went missing and has never been found. It’s easy to assume this documentary is a sensationalist dig into her case – but there is much more depth to such a haunting real-life nightmareRachel AroestiWed 26 Aug 2026 18.05 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 18.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWell done, I suppose, to whoever came up with the title of this documentary about the 1991 disappearance of 18-year-old Nicola Payne. It’s a concept so exceptionally horrifying – a brutal killing that continues on indefinitely – that it stands out even in the oversaturated and grimly sensationalist true-crime landscape. At least it bears no connection to the facts: there isn’t any suggestion that Nicola was subject to an unusually protracted death. Instead, The Never Ending Murder is about one family’s infinite struggle to endure such a loss.It’s also a nightmarishly surreal title for what turns out to be not only a sensitive true-crime series, but a very conventional one. The story, narrated primarily by Nicola’s relatives, unfolds strictly chronologically. From her father, brothers and friends we learn that she was the longed-for daughter after four boys, a “tomboyish” girl who could often be found in the pub with her mates in the friendly working class area of Coventry she grew up in. At the time of her disappearance, she and her boyfriend Jason had recently had a baby boy called Owen, to whom she was utterly devoted.View image in fullscreenNicola with her mother, Marilyn.Photograph: Channel4It was a misty December day when she left Jason’s house alone and set off for her family home. It should have been a six-minute journey across a piece of land nicknamed the Black Pad, so-called because it was once a railway line used for coal, which would stain the surrounding ground. Her father was quick to notice that Nicola hadn’t arrived and went out looking for her. Soon, the police joined him. As days turned into weeks and months, they investigated a vast number of leads and identified two suspects via a distinctive car. The men’s statements were “full of holes,” says Malcolm Ross, who led the initial investigation, but the evidence was ultimately insufficient. The pair fled to France, witnesses changed their stories and DNA testing was not yet widespread. The police couldn’t build a case against them.Months turned into years and decades. Another detective took on the case. Martin Slevin was obsessive in his commitment to finding out what had happened to Nicola, and used modern technology to gather enough proof to charge the same two men in 2015. Yet, flaws in the original handling of some material evidence proved ruinous in court.Knowing in advance that Nicola’s body has never been found and nobody has ever been convicted of her murder doesn’t prevent this programme from being a stomach-churningly stressful watch. In fact, it makes it worse: a strong sense of doom prevails as rewards are offered, new leads uncovered and hopes raised, before all potential breakthroughs dissolve into nothing.There is a point when you wonder whether The Never Ending Murder Investigation might have been a better title. But that isn’t completely true either. When this series was originally released on Prime Video in 2023 (it has now been acquired by Channel 4), the case was still open but not particularly active. Yet, at that point the Payne family were making a considerable effort to keep the crime in the public consciousness in the hope that more witnesses would come forward. An aunt interviewed here says the next generation seemed keen to take on the mantle of publicising the case. Last year, however, Nicola’s brother, Nigel, announced they were closing the social media pages they had been using as a way to seek information related to her disappearance, telling the BBC that “for our own sanity, we’ve got to move on and live our own lives”. It’s a development that also calls into question the ethical justifications for re-broadcasting this programme.View image in fullscreenMartin Slevin, the detective who gathered enough evidence to charge two men for Nicola’s murder.Photograph: Channel4Still, conveying the emotional toll on those left behind is something this series does respectfully and effectively. Nicola’s mother Marilyn died in 2023, but we hear her discuss her feelings with heartrending frankness in footage broadcast on TV over the years. In 2001, she told a reporter that time had been no healer: “I feel worse now than I did the first Christmas that she went.” Later, she admitted that as more time passed, the more she felt she was “letting Nicola down”.It can be interesting to hear how investigations get revived after long periods – numerous cold-case detective dramas are testament to that – but a reluctance to twist the case into salacious shapes means The Never Ending Murder is less a gripping true-crime thriller than a haunting portrait of ordinary people dealing with a heinous event. It’s about the long tail of grief for a missing person, the disappointments of a lengthy investigation, and the constant threat of violence against women. It will leave you with a sinking feeling and a profound sense of sorrow.The Never Ending Murder is on Channel 4 nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionDocumentaryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Whimsical shortlist announced for Edinburgh comedy award 2026 | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: A shortlist rich in kookiness sees Lara Ricote tipped for the main prize, alongside returning nominees and a new generation of eccentric fringe acts
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: A shortlist rich in kookiness sees Lara Ricote tipped for the main prize, alongside returning nominees and a new generation of eccentric fringe acts
Content: Woozy … UK-based Li Jin Hao from Singapore is nominated for Falling from a Moon.Photograph: Rebecca Need MenearView image in fullscreenWoozy … UK-based Li Jin Hao from Singapore is nominated for Falling from a Moon.Photograph: Rebecca Need MenearEdinburgh festival 2026Whimsical shortlist announced for Edinburgh comedy award 2026A shortlist rich in kookiness sees Lara Ricote tipped for the main prize, alongside returning nominees and a new generation of eccentric fringe actsBrian LoganWed 26 Aug 2026 13.23 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 13.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe shortlist has been announced for the annual Edinburgh comedy award, and it’s a list that majors in whimsy. With an act hymning his belief in healing crystals, another dreamily counting sheep and a third whose show is about “mystery and messages” – and that’s before we even get to the loopy DIY comedy of TV veteran Spencer Jones – this year’s “Oscars of comedy” nominees (for both the best show and best newcomer prize) suggest an art form exploding with creativity but also increasingly oriented towards woo-woo: in full flight, perhaps, from our troubled times.The award favourite is Mexican-American comic Lara Ricote, co-star of Sam Campbell’s Channel 4 mockumentaryMake That Movieand former fringe best newcomer. Ricote’sInklingis a remarkable hour about picking up on the messages that come one’s way, and how that’s complicated by, in the 29-year-old’s case, being hard of hearing.View image in fullscreenAward favourite … Lara Ricote.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanReturning to the annual shortlist, for an award once known as the Perrier, are Chris Cantrill (a three-time nominee whose double act sidekickAmy Gledhillwon in 2024), shouty MancunianDan Tiernan(nominated twice before) with Quartz and All and goofball prop comic Jones (also nominated twice before). Jones is the veteran of this year’s list with his own BBC show, The Mind of Herbert Clunkerdunk, already under his belt.On a shorter list than we’ve seen in recent years, they are joined by Cornwall’sHarriet Dyer, recently announced as a participant in the Halloween edition of Amazon Prime’s smash hit Last One Laughing UK, and whose show Easily Distra … celebrates her inability to stay on topic; andLi Jin Hao, the UK-based Singaporean whose show Falling from a Moon develops the brand of woozy philosophical comedy pioneered in his2024 show Swimming in a Submarine.The most egregious omissions from the lineup, which is selected by industry and public panellists, are Elf Lyons with The Woman on the Edge,an extraordinary breakup showthat’s got everyone talking; Aussie stunt-comedy offeringMan Sings the Same Song Over and Over Again for an Hour; and the Radio 4 sketch trioCrybabieswith their brilliantly executed horror pastiche The Scaring.View image in fullscreenInventive … Limerick comic Marty Gleeson.Photograph: Rachel SherlockOn the best newcomer shortlist – for an award previously won by Sarah Millican, Tim Minchin and Harry Hill – there’s more whimsy still. Too many kooks, you might say, at a festival where socially engaged or political comedy is vanishingly thin on the ground. Or you could celebrate the surfeit of invention among acts that include Limerick’s Marty Gleeson, a quartet of US clowns performing theirUnderground Monk Show, and Birmingham teacher turned oddball Tom Towelling, with a show that binds its audience together in wool.Completing the newcomer nominees, at a time when the proficiency of first-time Edinburgh acts seems to be rocketing, there are Dom McGovern with Prize Hog, TV regular but fringe rookie Fatiha El-Ghorri withCockney Stacking Doll, Freddie Meredith with the terrific Need a Light? and Omar Badawy with Guided Detour.Chair of the judging panel Liz Lewin, director of comedy series at Netflix UK, said of the lists: “These are the people shaping the comedy landscape and we can’t wait for audiences beyond Edinburgh to enjoy them as much as we did”. The awards will be handed out at a ceremony this Saturday by2016 winner Richard Gaddand last year’s best newcomer and now SNL:UK starAyoade Bamgboye. The winners will receive £10,000 for best show (sponsored by Audible), and £5,000 for best newcomer. Recent winners of the main award include Rose Matafeo, Hannah Gadsby and last year’s champ Sam Nicoresti.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalAwards and prizesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Stephen Libby on fashion: I’m on a mission to revive the jumpsuit – they’re practical and stylish | Fashion | The Guardian
description: The 70s was a golden era for the jumpsuit, but I’m happy they’re back, thanks to Harry Styles, Benson Boone and – of course – me
Author: Stephen Libby
Headline: The 70s was a golden era for the jumpsuit, but I’m happy they’re back, thanks to Harry Styles, Benson Boone and – of course – me
Content: Photograph: David Newby/The Guardian. Styling: Sam DeamanView image in fullscreenPhotograph: David Newby/The Guardian. Styling: Sam DeamanGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Stephen Libby on men's fashionFashionStephen Libby on fashion: I’m on a mission to revive the jumpsuit – they’re practical and stylishThe 70s was a golden era for the jumpsuit, but I’m happy they’re back, thanks to Harry Styles, Benson Boone and – of course – meStephen LibbyWed 26 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince appearing on The Traitors, I’ve become synonymous with jumpsuits. In fact, I’ve been required to wear one at every public appearance I have made since it aired, despite only wearing two on the show. That’s the power of the jumpsuit, I guess.When I was packing for the show, I wasn’t even sure I would bring them – and not everyone watching liked them. Lots of people did, but I got messages saying: “What the hell is he wearing?”. The memes were also phenomenal. My favourite was my head on John Travolta’s body in a still fromSaturday Night Fever.I now own five jumpsuits – which is probably five more than almost any other man – and they all tend to be quite 70s in style. This was a golden period for the men’s jumpsuit, when David Bowie and Elton John wore them, and they really became a part of popular culture. They’ve since faded into obscurity and now the only men we see wearing them are those who are very comfortable with their sexuality, such asBenson Booneand Harry Styles.You can see echoes of the 70s in some modern men’s clothes, whether it’s a geometric pattern or a wide lapel, but jumpsuits seem to be a bridge too far for most people. I love them because they’re so practical. I take quite a while to get ready at the best of times, and they are a whole outfit in one. As for going to the loo, it’s easier than with trousers because there’s no button, just a zip.I bought my first jumpsuit six years ago. It was from a brand called Palomo Spain, cost about £300 and I saved up for 18 months to buy it. It’s orange and blue with short sleeves, and one of the ones I wore on TV. The moment I wore it out of the house, that was it: it became the gateway drug to my jumpsuit era. People have referred to it as a boilersuit, but I would never get under the bonnet of a car wearing that beautiful garment.double quotation markSome call them boilersuits, but I’d never get under a car bonnet in such a beautiful garmentThe next one I bought was also Palomo Spain. It was black and white and very chic. You might recognise it from the finale of Traitors – though I very nearly didn’t wear that either. I bought it a while before filming started, and then discoveredHarry Styles had worn the same one on tour. Nothing against Harry, but I pride myself on trying to be as unique as possible, so I’d already earmarked a beautiful micro-checked 70s suit for the finale. The problem was, when I put it on, we discovered the print was causing the camera to strobe. The only thing I hadn’t worn was the jumpsuit, so I ended up wearing that. And of course, I became “Stephen from Traitors in the jumpsuits”.A good jumpsuit can really elongate your body. The trick is making sure the waist sits where the waist of your trousers would sit. For me, that’s quite high up, but you can get things altered to what works for you. Unlike a lot of menswear, the jumpsuit is the main event, so you don’t need to accessorise much. I’d probably wear a loafer, or a Cuban heel – just not trainers. Jumpsuits aren’t really casual items of clothing so trainers would just look a bit off.Stephen Libby on fashion: so many men have asked me for clothes advice since The TraitorsRead moreI’ve not seen many affordable jumpsuit options for men, who tend to favour overalls orboilersuits(as far as I’m concerned, these are different garments with a slouchy fit or a drop crotch). My tip is to buy a women’s one and just get it altered. Reiss do some fantastic denim jumpsuits which you can get in a longer leg, as do Me+Em. Other than that, it’s vintage all the way.I’m always on the hunt for the perfect jumpsuit. I remember seeing a photo ofDavid Bowie leaving Studio 54wearing one by Willie Brown. It’s not a classic 70s style, and is in fact quite loose, but I said to myself: “ I need to own something like this in my lifetime.” I still haven’t found the exact one, but I’m about to bid on a purple disco number from the 1970s. Wish me luck!Styling: Sam Deaman. Stylist’s assistant: Charlotte Gornall. Grooming: Alice Theobald at Arlington Artists using Benefitand Dr Hauschka.Jumpsuit, £240, Reiss.Belt, £195, Elliot Rhodes.Bracelet, £295, Dower & Hall.Prada loafers, £75,DepopExplore more on these topicsFashionStephen Libby on men's fashionMen's fashionThe TraitorsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rainbow Warrior review – spies bomb activists in truly gasp-inducing TV | Television | The Guardian
description: The bizarre story of French secret agents blowing up a Greenpeace ship in New Zealand is rivetingly retold by the eco-veterans – revealing an increasingly unhinged litany of lies, denials and James Bond-style antics
Author: Sarah Dempster
Headline: The bizarre story of French secret agents blowing up a Greenpeace ship in New Zealand is rivetingly retold by the eco-veterans – revealing an increasingly unhinged litany of lies, denials and James Bond-style antics
Content: Two divers plant a bomb on the Rainbow Warrior ship.Photograph: SkyView image in fullscreenTwo divers plant a bomb on the Rainbow Warrior ship.Photograph: SkyTV reviewTelevisionReviewRainbow Warrior review – spies bomb activists in truly gasp-inducing TVThe bizarre story of French secret agents blowing up a Greenpeace ship in New Zealand is rivetingly retold by the eco-veterans – revealing an increasingly unhinged litany of lies, denials and James Bond-style anticsSarah DempsterWed 26 Aug 2026 19.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen DS Terry Batchelor received the call informing him of the whereabouts of the French couple suspected of bombing the Rainbow Warrior, he was eating a pie. The suspects were in Auckland, he learned, preparing to return their hired Toyota HiAce campervan to the rental depot. A scoop! Batchelor, who was based nearby, gathered his team and set off in hot – and ultimately successful – pursuit. And the pie? “Actually,” reflects the retiree, peering at us over his moustache, “I hadn’t started the pie yet.” A pause, heavy with the threat of italics. “ButI was about to.”There is a lot of this sort of thing in Sky Documentaries’ Rainbow Warrior, a feature-length retelling of the events surrounding the July 1985 sinking of the titularGreenpeaceflagship. That is to say; granular recollections, delivered by elderly men with combative facial hair, seemingly irrelevant in isolation but riveting and oddly comforting when viewed as part of a startling and frequently unhinged whole.View image in fullscreenThe sinking of the Rainbow Warrior.Photograph: SkyBy the time the documentary docks in New Zealand, we have already been on quite the journey. Greenpeace was, by 1985, an international endeavour, an extraordinarily effective campaigning network that had ballooned from a Vancouver-based collection of be-denimed eco-activists and anti-war protesters into a million-member network featuring – as one astonished archive report splutters – “paid researchers and computers!” Its successes were, by that point, quite something. Here, a pressure-led ban on large-scale whaling; there, the evacuation and relocation of the residents of the Rongelap Atoll in the Marshall Islands, after US nuclear tests in the 1950s had led to decades of illness and birth defects.View image in fullscreen‘The rest is the violent history’ … Greenpeace veteran Rex Weylor.Photograph: SkyLittle wonder, then, that when the rusting former fishing trawler known as the Rainbow Warrior chugged into Auckland’s Marsden Wharf, it was met with whoops and banners of the “WE LOVE THE FUTURE OF OUR KIDS” variety. Its mission? To head to the South Pacific and monitor France’s imminent neutron warhead tests.Oh no vous don’t, replied the French government, busily preparing to put paid to the activists’ aims with a plan of its own. “And the rest is history,” says Greenpeace veteran Rex Weyler. “The rest is the violent history.”Enter, stagegauche,Opération Satanique, a top-secret mission involving “the crème de la crème” of France’s foreign intelligence agency, the DGSE. Chief among said operatives were Dominique Prieur (dark glasses, collar turned up, “an expert in hand-to-hand combat”) and her colleague Maj Alain Mafart (weak chin, air of near-parodic Gallic indifference, “an accomplished marksman, parachutist and wildlife photographer in his free time”). Together they would pose as Swiss newlyweds honeymooning around New Zealand in their rented campervan. Among their fellow operatives were two expert frogmen (assigned cover story: “gym instructors at a girls’ college in Tahiti”)and one Dr Xavier Maniguet, who wore a Milk Tray polo neck and would later die while attempting to land his plane on a glacier.It’s all very mid-period Bond, with much archive footage of yachts and speeding police cars, and snippets from a 2005 interview with Maniguet in which he claims his team would’ve gotten away with it if it hadn’t been for those pesky New Zealanders and their hopelessly démodé penchant for justice and not blowing people up. “If we’d known about the culture in New Zealand,” he honks, “perhaps we would have been more discreet.”View image in fullscreenThe photographer Fernando Pereira, who drowned when the Rainbow Warrior sank.Photograph: SkySignificantly less fun times is the bombing itself, which resulted not just in the destruction of the Rainbow Warrior, but the death of the freelance photographer Fernando Pereira. Similarly shameful is the litany of lies and denials that followed, with the French government attempting to reduce murder and international terrorism to the level of scuttlebutt and paranoia. It’s gasp-inducing stuff,even if the documentary is at pains to keep the mood fizzy via skittish editing and a soundtrack consisting of wine-bar jazz and, inexplicably, Wang Chung.The last word goes to Terry Batchelor, who eventually tired of a life of half-eaten pies and is now an actor. “The biggest surprise was the arrogance of the French,” he chuckles.“Thinking that they could come to New Zealand, plant a bomb on a ship and somehow get away with it.”Quelle idée!Rainbow Warrior aired on Sky Documentaries and is on NowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewGreenpeacereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Deirdre McSharry obituary | Magazines | The Guardian
description: Editor of Cosmopolitan in its 1970s heyday when it was famous for addressing women’s careers, health and their sex lives
Author: Hettie Judah
Headline: Editor of Cosmopolitan in its 1970s heyday when it was famous for addressing women’s careers, health and their sex lives
Content: Deirdre McSharry was a powerful inspiration when she was at the helm of Cosmo and a formidable boss, not shy of criticism, but always interested in the lives and opinions of her staffView image in fullscreenDeirdre McSharry was a powerful inspiration when she was at the helm of Cosmo and a formidable boss, not shy of criticism, but always interested in the lives and opinions of her staffMagazinesObituaryDeirdre McSharry obituaryEditor of Cosmopolitan in its 1970s heyday when it was famous for addressing women’s careers, health and their sex livesHettie JudahWed 26 Aug 2026 12.10 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 12.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDeirdre McSharry, who has died aged 94, edited Cosmopolitan in the magazine’s golden era. As fashion editor when the UK magazine launched in 1972, within a year she was elevated to the top spot. Under McSharry, “Cosmo” was witty and forthright, addressing women’s careers, style, health and, notoriously, their sex lives. Like its editor, it was guided by joie de vivre.A 1973 documentary captured a conversation between McSharry and one of Cosmo’s occasional nude centrefolds. The model was irked – the centrefold showed him laughing. He preferred to smoulder.As he explained to McSharry that women found a sultry look sexier, her smile broadened and her eyebrows rose. She knew better. The jollity of the centrefold was part of the point, she told the documentary crew: “For years, men have been picking up magazines with pictures of busty ladies, and we thought it was a good joke to simply reverse the role and make the man the sex object.”For her team, she was a powerful inspiration and a formidable boss, not shy of criticism, but always interested in their lives and opinions. All were “Cosmo girls”, representing the magazine’s readership. They gathered weekly for editorial meetings and exercise classes. “What she couldn’t tolerate was lack of ambition,” recalls Pattie Barron, Cosmopolitan’s then health and beauty editor.McSharry was ambitious for her staff in return: “It was typical Deirdre to push everyone to the max and then push them out of the Cosmo nest, never holding them back to keep working for her. She wanted to see us fly.”Caroline Coon, a regular contributor in the 1970s, recalls the cultural impact of the magazine and its feminist editor: McSharry “promoted actual change that could be achieved, with a dollop of glamour and fun”.She was born in West Ham, eastLondon, to Mary (nee O’Brien) and Jack McSharry, an Irish doctor who worked with tuberculosis patients before succumbing to the disease himself. In 1939, newly widowed, Mary moved with her two children to Dublin. Deidre was sent to a convent school and her mother went to work, becoming editor of Woman’s Life magazine.View image in fullscreenDeirdre McSharry modelling an Aran jumper in the 1950sIt came as a shock to realise that her schoolfellows pitied her for having a mother with a career. She “always made work seem very special and glamorous,” Deirdre recalled.In the holidays, she and her brother Sean were taken to the theatre, to lunches at the Stephen’s Green Club, and to the magazine office, where Deirdre learned to type and to paste articles into the “dummy”. Her mother encouraged her to paint and steered her towards biographies of clever women. All this proved formative.At Trinity College Dublin studying English, McSharry started to write and act. Her mother died just before she reached 21. She did not graduate but turned to the theatre, performing with the Dublin Players and in late-night revues at the Pike theatre. Throughout her life she retained the crisp diction and elegant poise of an actor.Joining the Gate theatre under the founding directors Hilton Edwards and Micheál Mac Liammóir, she was part of the ensemble during a two-month tour in Egypt in 1956. The trip was a revelation, introducing McSharry to exquisite textiles and richly patterned designs that became an enduring obsession.Following a brief marriage to Linton Stone in 1955, McSharry moved toNew York. There she made a definitive shift from theatre into journalism, with a role on Women’s Wear Daily.Later in the 1950s she moved to London as a fashion writer. A photograph shows her modelling an Aran jumper for a magazine shoot – the reverse carries a wry note that she was “saving the price of a model for George Newnes, publisher of Woman’s Own (circulation 4m)”. That figure was no exaggeration. In 1958, Time magazine cited “Britain’s proliferating women’s weeklies” as having a collective circulation of 10.4m. The newspapers paid attention: McSharry was lured on to theDaily Expressas fashion editor.She was a natural tastemaker, curious and enquiring, confident in her judgment. In 1966, she so liked the look of a model used for a daringly short haircut by Leonard’s of Mayfair that she called her in to the Express and commissioned a shoot. McSharry’s headline proclaimed the teenager, dubbed Twiggy, “the face of 1966”.She married her second husband, Peter King, in 1967. The end of that marriage, in 1984, caused a period of ill health that precipitated her departure from Cosmo. After recuperating, in 1985 she became founding editor of Country Living, a magazine that reflected an era of growing affluence and social mobility in the UK.McSharry identified a middle-class readership for whom renovating rural property was aspirational. She promoted eclectic, inventive interior schemes that were understood as expressions of their owners’ personalities. Designers, makers and artists she admired were promoted both on the page and off. After encountering Candace Bahouth at the Crafts Centre in Covent Garden, the artist made frequent appearances in Country Living and became a close friend. Kevin McCloud, then a lighting designer, recalls her as “a sparkling and tireless champion of other people”, and admits that his “career in no small part started thanks to her”.McSharry was twice awarded editor of the year by the Professional Publishers Association – in 1981 for Cosmopolitan, and in 1987 for Country Living. In the mid 80s she met Ian Smyth, with whom she lived in a sequence of beautiful homes in the UK and US, before settling in Bath, where she became a cornerstone of the city’s cultural scene. The couple married in 1999 and remained devoted until Smyth’s death in 2022.McSharry is survived by her sister Mary and her brothers Sean, Harry, Frank and James, and by her stepchildren Matthew, Lucy, Malachi and Patrick.Deirdre Mary McSharry, magazine editor, born 4 April 1932; died 14 August 2026Explore more on these topicsMagazinesLondonIrelandTheatreNew YorkDaily ExpressobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham should rip up our undemocratic first past the post system – even if some in Labour disagree | Neal Lawson | The Guardian
description: Rearguard reactionaries may try to block the idea of a national commission into proportional representation, but we should want more not less democracy, says Neal Lawson, director of Compass
Author: Neal Lawson
Headline: Rearguard reactionaries may try to block the idea of a national commission into proportional representation, but we should want more not less democracy, says Neal Lawson, director of Compass
Content: Burnham speaking after his victory in the Makerfield byelection in June. The prime minister is a longstanding supporter of electoral reform.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBurnham speaking after his victory in the Makerfield byelection in June. The prime minister is a longstanding supporter of electoral reform.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesOpinionElectoral reformAndy Burnham should rip up our undemocratic first past the post system – even if some in Labour disagreeNeal LawsonRearguard reactionaries may try to block the idea of a national commission into proportional representation, but we should want more not less democracyWed 26 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 13.36 EDTShareApoll in the Mail on Sunday at the end of June was remarkable. It had not just Reform as low as 21%, but alsoLabourand the Tories. It was remarkable because it starkly demonstrated the fragmented landscape of the UK’s electoral terrain, as well as the electoral weakness of its main players.Polls since have varied, not least with the Burnham bounce, butthis week’s YouGov voting intention figuresput Reform, Labour and the Tories on 23%, 22% and 20% respectively (although it almost no longer matters which exact figure applies to which party). Add in the Greens and the Liberal Democrats on 13% apiece, the SNP dominating Scotland and Plaid Cymru Wales, then Restore UK and independent candidates and you have an unprecedented variety of options laid out before the British electorate.And all this despite the first past the post (FPTP) electoral system, which has for so long upheld two-party politics. It does so by punishing any party outside the duopoly by refusing to match votes to seats. If this unprecedented level of fragmentation exists in the face of a voting system that coerces people to back only their least bad option, then how diverse would this landscape be if people could vote with their heart and know that their vote really counted?This now complete mismatch between what voters want and what they get is the root cause of the governing crisis destabilising British politics. Labour won two-thirds of the seats in the Commons in 2024 on just a third of the vote, and its leadership assumed that this result conferred it legitimacy in the eyes of the public. But governments increasingly find that a Commons majority upheld by an unrepresentative voting system is more vulnerable to voter backlash. In this context, support quickly melts away, as Keir Starmer and Morgan McSweeney found out.If Britain continues under FPTP, then this governing chaos will deepen, and the only beneficiaries will be anti-democratic extremists.But now there is a golden chance to change all this. Next Wednesday, the representation of the people bill will come before parliament for its final stages. An amendment has been tabled to set up a national commission to look at which system of proportional representation (PR), which does match votes to seats, would best suit our country. It has huge backing in the Commons,in the Labour partyand among the public. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, is also alongstanding supporterof electoral reform. The political conditions have never been more favourable to begin making changes to the voting system. What could possibly go wrong?This: a minority but powerful view within the upper reaches of the Labour party, the cabinet and the party bureaucracy is vehemently opposed to PR and the plural politics of cooperation it demands. According to this tribal view, only Labour, governing alone, can represent the interests of “their voters”. And so it is preferable to lose all power than to share it. Labour winning – however tiny its share of the vote – is more important than democracy working. At best, those with this view may calculate whether PR or FPTP delivers the most Labour MPs, equating self-interest with the national interest.But all their paternalistic calculations miss the very big point: democracy should not be designed around what is best for Labour – or any party – but around what works best for the country.Labour’s rearguard reactionaries will try to block the idea of a national commission, water it down or kick it bureaucratically into touch. They will say only the cost of living matters, and that no one brings up PR on the doorstep. But it is precisely our rotten voting system that denies the changes people want, because it prioritises the cautious views of a few swing voters in a few swing seats and impels Labour to pander to them.The game is over for this old top-down, command-and-control politics. The myth of strong government from FPTP is dead. It is time for change, to do what Willy Brandt, the fabled leader of the German Social Democrats, implored the left to do in 1969, and “dare more democracy”. That means finally embracing multiparty government, and ensuring everyone’s vote is counted equally: it is the only way to end the cycle of chaos.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRadical Manchesterism beats in our prime minister’s heart. There, he made big changes happen by listening to voices beyond Labour and working cross-party to build a long-term consensus to transform a region. Next week, by backing himself and his best instincts on PR, he can transform the country.Neal Lawson is director of the cross-party campaign organisation CompassExplore more on these topicsElectoral reformOpinionLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: The London stock market dodged a bullet with Shein | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: China’s fashion giant will list in Hong Kong with a shrunken price tag – and big questions over its business model
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: China’s fashion giant will list in Hong Kong with a shrunken price tag – and big questions over its business model
Content: Mannequins at a factory in Panyu District, Guangdong province, China.Photograph: Go Nakamura/ReutersView image in fullscreenMannequins at a factory in Panyu District, Guangdong province, China.Photograph: Go Nakamura/ReutersNils Pratley on financeSheinThe London stock market dodged a bullet with SheinNils PratleyChina’s fashion giant will list in Hong Kong with a shrunken price tag – and  big questions over its business modelWed 26 Aug 2026 12.21 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 14.19 EDTShareIn a parallel world, we might now be preparing for the arrival on the London stock market ofShein, the giant Chinese-founded fast-fashion retailer. Or it could have happened already.The possibility of a London flotation was a running storyduring 2024and into last year as politicians from both main parties engaged in behind-the-scenes wooing. Shein was seen as a shot of tech adrenalin for a listless local listings scene, and an opportunity to advertise the UK’s openness to international capital.Instead, Sheinwill float next week in Hong Kong. To which one can only say: thank goodness for that.In a listings context, Shein was a cast-off. The company had rejected New York amid tensions between Washington and Beijing and hostile questions from US lawmakers over labour practices in its supply chains in China. London was merely the next-best option for a company whose owners seemed suspiciously anxious to find a stock market home in the west.London did its reputation no favours with its willingness to jump. The Financial Conduct Authority, in charge of listings, took the view that it was“not unusual”for UK-listed companies to carry legal risks around the world and that what mattered was disclosure to allow investors to form their own view. The Labour government sounded keen. Donald Tang, the banker hired as Shein’s chair, did a round offeelgood meetings.This positivity was punctured, however, in January last year when Shein’s general counsel in Europeappeared at the Commons business select committeeand stone-walled.Did Shein source cotton from China, asked the committee chair, Liam Byrne. The company representative was not qualified to reveal such “detailed operational information”. Byrne had not even been asking at that point about allegations of use of cotton produced in the Xinjiang region, which has been linked to Uyghur forced labour.The company, it should be added, had already said it had signed statements of compliance to modern slavery acts in the US, UK and elsewhere. But Byrne’s view was entirely fair: “The reluctance to answer basic questions has frankly bordered on contempt of the committee.”The idea of listing in London soon went away – encouraged, it seemed, by pressure from Beijing. And so,Hong Kongit is.Note, though, how the company’s price tag has shrunk from the £50bn that was talked about during the London leg of the global tour. The valuation will be $27bn (£20bn).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat figure also reflects the other issue that has dogged Shein: political and societal resistance to the practice of shipping goods in small packages out of China to take advantage of tax breaks on low-value imported goods. The US has alreadyclosed such “de minimis” exceptionsas part of President Trump’s tariffs wars; the EU says it will phase them out;the UK intends to get there by 2029. Shein used to argue that its business model did not depend on tax breaks, but the reduced valuation suggests that investors do not regard the issue as irrelevant.In a world in which Shein had somehow managed to list in London last year, the valuation drop would have been felt here. The supposedly hot prize would look substantially less so. London dodged a bullet on this one. Those politicians who encouraged the flirtation might reflect that, while the stock market is obviously desperate for exciting newcomers, you’ve got to choose your targets carefully. Nobody is talking about a missed opportunity.Explore more on these topicsSheinNils Pratley on financeIPOsStock marketsFinancial sectorHong KongInternational tradecommentShareReuse this content

title: Around the world, people are rejecting divisive and dangerous politics. We can – and must – build on that | Gordon Brown | The Guardian
description: The vast majority of the global public supports international cooperation on human rights, climate and AI. Like-minded countries must stand together to deliver, says former UK prime minister Gordon Brown
Author: Gordon Brown
Headline: The vast majority of the global public supports international cooperation on human rights, climate and AI. Like-minded countries must stand together to deliver, says former UK prime minister Gordon Brown
Content: Composite: Alex Mellon for the Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Alex Mellon for the Guardian/Getty ImagesOpinionUS foreign policyAround the world, people are rejecting divisive and dangerous politics. We can – and must – build on thatGordon BrownThe vast majority of the global public wants international cooperation on human rights, climate and AI. Like-minded countries must stand together to deliverWed 26 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 08.47 EDTShareBritain’s new prime minister,Andy Burnham, is already having to make one of his gravest decisions. He has to issue the instructions that he alone gives to the military, setting out the UK response in a doomsday scenario of a nuclear weapons attack on us. He will, as I did two decades ago, sign a piece of paper telling commanders whether or not to retaliate and, if so, whether through targeting civilian conurbations or military sites. These instructions are written down in the aptly named“letter of last resort”.Now, more than at any time since the 1960s Cuban missile crisis, theEuropean public fears a third world war. With the nuclearDoomsday Clockdeveloped by atomic scientists moving ever closer to midnight, and Japan, South Korea, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Egypt, Poland and Germany contemplating either acquiringnuclear weapons or siting them on their soil, our world is descending from a rules-based order to a power-based one, where might is deemed right and brute force dominates.Russianpresident Vladimir Putinhas abandoned any pretence of supporting international law – “no one is ready to play by rules set by one person somewhere far away,” he has said – while China’spresident Xi Jinpinghas warned that reunification with Taiwan “cannot be stopped by any force or anyone”. And with Donald Trump’srecent threatof genocide against the Iranian people – “a whole civilisation will die tonight, never to be brought back again” – and his further threat to evenbomb an ally, Oman, the American president has demonstrated yet again his contempt for every single pillar of the previous US-led order: human rights, multilateral cooperation, humanitarian aid and the rule of law itself.But what should give us a measure of hope, is that people’s rising fears of conflict are now matched by a clear demand that the world come together to counter this collapse into chaos. This has been revealed in a survey covering more than36,000 people in 34 countries, conducted formy new bookby Focaldata, on behalf of the Rockefeller Foundation (for whom I am a trustee).Donald Trump can’t beat Iran and Nigel Farage can only beat a bin. When it counts, these populists are just losers | Jonathan FreedlandRead moreWe asked a most demanding question: whether people would support “international cooperation”, even if it meant some compromise of their “country’s national interest”. The55%who said yes, with only 20% saying no, were clearly signalling their rejection of the “America first”, “Russia first”, “China first”, “my country first” dogmas that view life as no more than an endless struggle between an “us” and a “them”. Clearmajoritiesin every continent oppose those populist nationalist leaders, who would pull up the drawbridge and see geopolitics as a zero-sum game in which their country can only do well if other countries do badly.Indeed, more than70%of the global public want their governments to uphold human rights and the rule of law, take action on the climate crisis,AI and cyber securityand fund humanitarian aid. Follow-up research shows that an even larger group –80%worldwide – now believe there should be a global system to ensure the existence of policies that not only engender peace and stability but also promote the dignity of all, requiring action against poverty, disease, hunger and illiteracy.Most important of all, we now know how support for cooperation can be increased. In every country, it is the very people who are active in their own communities, and who have connections that cross ethnic and religious divides, who are50%more likely to support international cooperation, even when it involves some sacrifice of national interest. The message is clear: to rebuild support for cooperation across borders, we should start by rebuilding communities at home.But even if there is an emerging consensus on what to do, the question is: who can bring people together, now that we are moving from a unipolar world, where the US sets the agenda and could enforce its will, to a more multipolar world, with many competing centres of decision-making power, not least a risingChina?We find that the big three nuclear-weapon powers – the US, China and Russia – are more unloved than ever. Instead, the global public looks to other countries – principally Canada, Australia, Italy, Japan, the UK, France, Brazil and South Korea, and in that order – as potential unifying forces. These also turn out to be the countries whose own peopleare the most eager to cooperate and take on a leadership role, advocated byCanadian prime minister Mark CarneyandFinnish president Alexander Stubb.But can a new concert of countries ever overrule the US and China on the big issues such as nuclear disarmament or AI and cyber regulation? Unlikely, given those two countries’ coercive power through military threats, tariffs, trade bans and sanctions, and the US’s singular power toweaponise the dollar. Still, now is the time to discuss how we move from a world where technology dominates the state, as in the US, or the state dominates technology, as in China.Already, the rest of us are creating a new system forarbitrating trade disputesand foroutlawing crimes against humanity. TheEU and Asian-led CPTPPmay yet form the biggest trade alliance the world has ever seen. How many battalions do the lesser powers have, one might ask, adapting the questionStalin is said to have asked of a previous pope? But, up against the power to compel, we can counterpose the legitimacy accorded by most fair-minded people to international human rights and humanitarian law.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCountries other than Russia, China and the US and their satellites control 75% of the votes at theInternational Monetary Fundand theWorld Bank, and have huge majorities at the World Trade Organization and the World Health Organization, as well as 12 of the 15 votes – and two of the five vetoes – on the UN security council. So there is no reason why we cannot make progress on agreeing principles of cooperation, and reforming these institutions, to deliver on the climate crisis, humanitarian aid, peacemaking and the global war against poverty. When a new UN secretary-general is appointed,to begin work in the new year, I would urge like-minded countries to agree with her or him a programme of action for 2027.The US public also prefers cross-border cooperation to going it alone. They want the US to lead by persuasion, not by coercion. And they can be convinced that the US that used to act multilaterally in a unipolar world should stop acting unilaterally in what is becoming a multipolar world.But, for the time being, progress will depend upon a coordinated push by the UK and cooperation-minded powers. The message from our survey of global opinion is that our citizens do look out in hope of a better world – and a troubled world looks to us. That’s an issue for Britain’s new PM – and for everyone.Gordon Brown is the UN’s special envoy for global education and was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010The future starts with us:Gordon Brown in conversationOn Thursday 10 September, join Hugh Muir and Gordon Brown to discuss the intricate connections between global instability and civic decline, as explored in Brown’s new book,The Future Starts With Us.
