title: Goodbye, Dolly Parton: a gay icon whose appeal reached across age, class and politics, and into the Maga heartlands | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: Straight women loved her, so did Eminem. Even Donald Trump found something nice to say. Her allure had no boundaries and was truly unique, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: Straight women loved her, so did Eminem. Even Donald Trump found something nice to say. Her allure had no boundaries and was truly unique, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Content: Parton performing in 1978. ‘The queen of country and crossover pop was beloved by so many communities – many antagonistic to each other.’Photograph: Ira Berger/AlamyView image in fullscreenParton performing in 1978. ‘The queen of country and crossover pop was beloved by so many communities – many antagonistic to each other.’Photograph: Ira Berger/AlamyOpinionDolly PartonGoodbye, Dolly Parton: a gay icon whose appeal reached across age, class and politics, and into the Maga heartlandsEmma BrockesStraight women loved her, so did Eminem. Even Donald Trump found something nice to say. Her allure had no boundaries and was truly uniqueWed 26 Aug 2026 08.33 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 22.37 EDTShareIwas at the National Theatre in London on Tuesday night, at a production ofPride, which tells the story of the unlikely alliance between gay activists and Welsh miners during the 1984 miners’ strike, when news broke of Dolly Parton’s death. Well. Against the sadness, one couldn’t help smiling. At a very gay production, attended by a majority gay audience, I half expected them to stop the show or call out a team from St John Ambulance bearing stretchers. In the script for Pride, references to Judy Garland and Ethel Merman serve as shorthand for gay sensibilities, but it could just as easily have been Dolly Parton. The queen of country and crossover pop was beloved by so many communities – many antagonistic to each other – but it was perhaps her gay fans who claimed her most vociferously and publicly.When we got home my friends and I danced around to9 to 5, and on Wednesday morning it was Here You Come, Again (“looking better than a body has a right to” – oh, Dolly) on a loop, along with her 1971 hit Coat of Many Colors.Parton was, in some ways, an unlikely gay icon. She was studiously neutral on a great many subjects, including politics, and while she could be funny and waspish, the person she most often poked fun at was herself. In my colleague Alexis Petridis’slovely tribute, he mentions Parton’s 1977 encounter with Barbara Walters – a woman so rich in spite and Chanel suits as to win her her own following in corners of the gay community. She asked Dolly: “Do you ever feel that you’re a joke?” One was struck by Parton’s smiling response – “I’m sure of myself as a person. I’m sure of my talent” – relative to how Katharine Hepburn, a gay icon with a more traditional way of handling things, responded to similar nastiness from Walters. When the journalist asked her, “Do you ever wear a skirt?”, Hepburn clapped back: “I have one. I’ll wear it to your funeral.” In a million years, Parton wouldn’t have been rude like that.View image in fullscreenFans outside the Castro Theater in San Francisco 25 August 2026.Photograph: Dan Hernandez/San Francisco Chronicle/APAll of which, you might think – and despite the bouffant hair and rhinestone wardrobe – might have lessened her appeal to gay audiences. But Parton had something else. The voice, of course, but to me it was also a question of sincerity. She meant it: every rhinestone, every teased, backcombed strand of hair in the blowout. She could joke about her image with the best of them, but we all knew that when it came down to it, Parton was deadly serious about the way she looked. There is a hard, gleaming gemstone at the core of camp culture that isn’t funny at all. It exists in absolute earnest, a private space of joy and pain and beauty undiluted by judgment. It’s hard to say precisely how one knows the difference between the endless fake, gay-baiting uses to which this tone is put and the real thing, but one does. Gay rights was one of the few issues on which Parton didn’t stay neutral – she threw the Bible at homophobes, asking them who they thought they were to pass judgment – but it wasn’t that. You just knew.And yet if there’s another thing we knew about Dolly Parton, it was her genius to cross every barrier of age, sexuality, race and politics. In arecent pollconducted by the University of Massachusetts Lowell, Parton was the only person in the survey to win higher than a 50% approval rating from Democrats, Republicans and independents. She crossed class barriers, too. While the Democratic Socialists of America praised Parton for being “a hero of the working class”, the now-billionaire president, Donald Trump, issued possibly the most positive statement he has ever made about another human being, saying of Parton: “There has never been anyone like her, and never will.”Eminem posted a tribute. Straight women loved her, including one of my aunts, who when she went platinum blond in her 60s was fond of quotingParton’s famous line– “It costs a lot of money to look this cheap” – by way of justification. Parton owned it all, and was god-level smart and as kind as they come, which may have been at the root of how she pulled off the seemingly impossible feat of being genuinely adored by all. When Trump ordered the nation’s flags to be lowered, one marvelled again at her unique status as someone as beloved in rural Kentucky as she was in Hell’s Kitchen.View image in fullscreenJane Fonda, Lily Tomlin and Dolly Parton in 9 to 5.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/Kobal/ShutterstockOn Wednesday morning, my friends and I only had eyes for the gay stuff, including astatement released by Jane Fonda, with whom she starred, alongside Lily Tomlin – what a triumvirate – in the 1980 film 9 to 5. Fonda said: “To her gay and trans fans, I want you to know that she loved you.” Meanwhile Parton’s nephew, Bryan Seaver, who was her head of security, as was his father, Larry, before him, issued avideo statementon behalf of the family. “Dolly has lived in the light,” he said, movingly. When Bryan said: “May god bless you all, she will always love you,” I had my biggest wobble.To quote another gay icon, Barbra Streisand: it’s the laughter we’ll remember. At the production of Pride on Tuesday night, my friend told me his Dolly story. I hope it’s alright to mention this; I can’t help but think Dolly would’ve enjoyed it. He was at a (gay) wedding deep in rural Tennessee a few years ago and thought he’d take a quick look at Grindr, the gay hook-up app. As expected, in that grimly traditional part of the US, it was an absolute gay desert, except for a bizarre cluster in a single spot about 40 miles down the road. Surprised, my friend glanced at the map and burst out laughing. Of course:Dollywood. What a gift she was to all of us – but to some of us, perhaps, more than others. Thank you, Dolly, for everything. God, we’ll miss you.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEmma Brockes is a Guardian columnist13:53Dolly Parton: why the world loved the queen of country - The LatestExplore more on these topicsDolly PartonOpinionLGBTQ+ rightscommentShareReuse this content

title: This is the question Democrats should ask voters in order to win this November | Robert Reich | The Guardian
description: They should ask the question Reagan asked at the end of his debate against Jimmy Carter: ‘Are you better off now than you were before this presidency?’
Author: Robert Reich
Headline: They should ask the question Reagan asked at the end of his debate against Jimmy Carter: ‘Are you better off now than you were before this presidency?’
Content: ‘Unless you’re very, very rich, the answer is obviously: “No, I’m worse off.”’Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Unless you’re very, very rich, the answer is obviously: “No, I’m worse off.”’Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionDemocratsThis is the question Democrats should ask voters in order to win this NovemberRobert ReichThey should ask the question Reagan asked at the end of his debate against Jimmy Carter: ‘Are you better off now than you were before this presidency?’Wed 26 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 18.17 EDTShareThe midterm elections are already upon us, and every Democrat and independent running against a Republican should ask voters the question Ronald Reagan asked on 28 October 1980, at the end of his televised debate against Jimmy Carter: “Are you better off now than you were before this presidency?”Unless you’re very, very rich, the answer is obviously: “No, I’m worse off.”Start with his tariffs, which are costing every American household an average of $1,100 annually, according to theYale Budget Lab. (If you don’t trust Yale, the conservative Tax Foundation estimated last year’s tab to be $1,000 a household.)Even cleaning supplies and toilet paper areup at least 5%. Household furnishings,up at least 8%. Clothing,up at least 14%. Trump’s tariffs have also increased the costs of big-ticket items such ascarsand made it more expensive to buildnew homes.Other studies find that the tariffs have added as much as0.7and0.5percentage points to the consumer price index and the personal consumption expenditures price index, respectively.The Guardian view on Trump’s economic threats: bullies can overplay their hand | EditorialRead moreThen there’s Trump’s war in Iran, which is driving up energy and food prices, as oil tankers remain stranded in the strait of Hormuz.The war is costing more at the gas pump – about $670 more a household since the war began. Americans face what the Century Foundation and Protect Borrowersdescribeas “a worsening utility debt crisis”. The groups wrote in an analysis published last month:Energy bills have increased three times faster than the rate ofinflationwhile Trump has been president. The national average monthly utility bill reached $280 in early 2026, a 12% increase since the end of 2024, just before the secondTrump administrationtook office.What’s the Republican response to soaring energy utility prices? Eliminate billions in clean energy subsidies and tilt the scales toward costlier, dirtier fossil fuels.Also driving up the cost of electricity are AI datacenters. They’re also using up huge amounts of water and creating noise pollution. And who’s been pushing these datacenters?Trumpand, beforerecent backlash, many Republicans.Trump’s war and the blockage of the strait are also causing fertilizer shortages, which are sending food prices upward. Millions of Americans are nowstruggling to afford groceries.Meanwhile, Trump’s huge tax cuts – which mostly benefited big corporations and the super-wealthy – are being paid for, in part, by Republican cuts to Medicaid and Medicare.Trump announced last month that he is ending Medicare subsidies that have kept drug prices low for seniors; Republican cuts to the Affordable Care Act have deprived millions of Americans of health insurance.Hell, even Trump’s executive order to divide the measles, mumps, rubella vaccine into three shots instead of one is adding burdens to the typical American family.As the Republican senator Bill Cassidysaidon ABC’s This Week: “This is why the president’s poll numbers are down, because you’ve lost sight of affordability for the parent. You’ve lost sight of the convenience for the American family. You’ve lost sight of that which is driving higher costs in healthcare – for example, more doctor’s visits … for something which has no rationale in science.”Trump’s obsession with gutting the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has denied Americans billions in foregone rebates and settlements.The regime spent $464m of taxpayer dollars in a no-bid contract for a special fleet of jets intended to deport immigrants. The planes have almost never been used.On and on it goes.Trump says theUS economyis “doing unbelievably from the standpoint of Wall Street”.Maybe, but most Americans live on Main Street and own few if any shares of stock. The richest 1% holds more than half of the value of stocks listed on US stock exchanges; the richest 10%, 92%. Even including retirement accounts, only 16% of adult Americans have assets exceeding $100,000.The stock market boom reflects a boom in corporate profits. Thepharmaceutical industry,big oil, and other sectors are posting banner earnings. Second quarter earnings for S&P 500 companies are on pace to rise a remarkable50% year over year, the highest growth rate since the second quarter of 2021.Why are progressives winning across the United States? It’s not complicated | Bernie SandersRead moreBut average working Americans are struggling to keep their heads above water.Trump’s comments about the roaring stock market came the same day thatnew datashowed US consumer sentiment dropped in August. Americans’ outlook on the country’s economic conditions have worsened among Republicans as well as among Democrats.TheJuly jobs reportshowed the US economy shedding 23,000 jobs, wage growth slowing, and theunemploymentrate falling because more people left the workforce.My humble advice to Democratic candidates in the midterms: don’t be distracted. Don’t take the bait and discuss socialism, “wokeism”, or anything else.Just ask this simple question: are you better off now than you were before this presidency? And explain how badly Trump and congressionalRepublicanshave shafted average working people.You’re better off than you were before the start of this presidency only if you’re a major investor in the stock market, a top corporate executive or a beneficiary of Trump’s largesse to his billionaire backers.But if you’re an average working American, you’re indubitably worse off. Hopefully, you’ll vote your economic interests on 3 November and deposit Trump’s congressional lapdogs into the dustbin of history.Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is atrobertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, isout now in the USandin the UKExplore more on these topicsDemocratsOpinionUS politicsUS-Israel war on IranUS economyUS healthcareRepublicansTrump administrationcommentShareReuse this content

title: Americans say they lose weight in Europe – and I think I know why | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Is it because of differences in the flour that’s being consumed? Or something to do with the European approach to getting around, asks Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Is it because of differences in the flour that’s being consumed? Or something to do with the European approach to getting around, asks Arwa Mahdawi
Content: The Italian job – but is it quality pasta or just more legwork that’s aiding American weight loss abroad?Photograph: RossHelen/Getty Images (Posed by a model)View image in fullscreenThe Italian job – but is it quality pasta or just more legwork that’s aiding American weight loss abroad?Photograph: RossHelen/Getty Images (Posed by a model)OpinionEuropean Union holidaysAmericans say they lose weight in Europe – and I think I know whyArwa MahdawiIs it because of differences in the flour that’s being consumed? Or something to do with the European approach to getting around?Wed 26 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTShareIt’s not just the mass shootings you have to watch out for in the US, it’s also thelettuce– a dodgy bit of iceberg could leave you sick with cyclosporiasis. And then there are the frozenblueberries, recently recalled because of a “reasonable probability” they could “cause serious adverse health consequences or evendeath”. And the alfalfasproutsthat may harbour salmonella. And the fruit bars that may becontaminatedwith glass. I could go on: there’s been asurgein foodborne illnesses in the US this year and food recalls have been getting a lot of attention.Europe obviously isn’t immune to foodborne illnesses either. More than 200 people have become sick in the UK this summer and one person has died because of asalmonella outbreaktied to imported eggs. Still, Europe iswidely seenas having far more robust regulations and food policies than the US. There’s endless anecdata online from Americans who claim that American bread and pasta makes them feel bloated and sick, but they can eat whatever they want in Europe and feel great.Podcaster Joe Rogan, for example,has saidpasta and bread “wreck” him in the US, but not in Italy. He cited US health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr’s theory that heavily processed (“enriched flour”) in the US could be to blame. Social media is full of people with similar claims. Earlier this month, the Wall Street Journalpublisheda piece called My Secret Diet is a Trip to Europe, showcasing Americans who dropped weight while eating their way across the continent.I’m about as qualified to weigh in on this matter as RFK Jr, so here’s my personal hypothesis: for most of these Americans, I think it’s less about the food, and more about the fact that they are walking a lot more on their holidays than they do at home. People in the US look at me like I must be either indigent ordeeply eccentricwhen I tell them I don’t have a car. Beyond a few cities, you can’t actually walk anywhere in the US because there are no pavements and the infrastructure is hostile to pedestrians. In the 1920s, the auto industry even lobbied for “jaywalking” laws tocriminalisecrossing the road and cast pedestrians as ridiculous simpletons. I’m no scientist, but I reckon my theory has legs.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsEuropean Union holidaysOpinionEuropeFoodcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on electoral reform: don’t wait for a crisis to fix a broken system  | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: In an era of multiparty politics, first past the post risks generating perverse outcomes that delegitimise the democratic process
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: In an era of multiparty politics, first past the post risks generating perverse outcomes that delegitimise the democratic process
Content: Andy Burnham and Bev Craig celebrate her victory in the Manchester mayoral election on 1 August, which used the supplementary vote system.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and Bev Craig celebrate her victory in the Manchester mayoral election on 1 August, which used the supplementary vote system.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAOpinionElectoral reformThe Guardian view on electoral reform: don’t wait for a crisis to fix a broken systemEditorialIn an era of multiparty politics, first past the post risks generating perverse outcomes that delegitimise the democratic processWed 26 Aug 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareIf the system that elects MPs to Westminster was obviously the most democratic one available, there would be no need to use alternative modes when electing the UK’s devolved assemblies or England’s regional mayors. The fact that first past the post (FPTP) was not preferred when establishing those institutions reflects an acceptance that there are better ways to turn popular opinion into fair political representation. So why should the Commons stick with an inferior system?This question is raised by anamendmenttabled to the representation of the people bill, which returns to parliament next week. The call to establish an independent national commission on electoral reform has beenendorsedby 185 MPs.Andy Burnham has backed electoral reform in the past and, as the Guardian reported this week,pressure is growingon the prime minister to translate that view into action: 98 Labour MPs have signed the amendment. For technical reasons related to the scope of the bill, the electoral reform question is unlikely to be put to a vote, but the scale of backbench support compels the prime minister to reaffirm his commitment to change.Downing Street has made it clear that Mr Burnham does indeed back reform but, in deference to the manifesto he inherited from Sir Keir Starmer, accepts that there is no mandate to legislate this side of a general election. That is the constitutionally proper position, but it doesn’t preclude steps that will help win the argument when the time comes. Electoral reformers arehaunted by defeatin the 2011 referendum on switching to the alternative vote model – a flawed rival to FPTP that was opposed by the Tories, then the senior party in coalition with the Liberal Democrats. The Labour party in opposition was divided.Back then, the two largest English parties expected their duopolistic hold on Westminster to continue indefinitely. They had few incentives to change a system that suppresses small-party representation. What suited Labour and theConservativesdid not tally with voter preferences, as demonstrated by a steady trend of fragmenting allegiances.Opinion polls show Labour, the Conservatives and Reform UKjostling for supportat levels between one-fifth and one-third of national vote share. In devolved and local elections, the Greens, Liberal Democrats and Scottish and Welsh nationalists complicate the picture still further.With multiple parties polling within a few points of each other, FPTP can propel a candidate to victory on a tiny margin and against the wishes of a clear majority of voters. This is a recipe for chaos and disenchantment – conditions that British politics has endured too much in recent years.Delivering stable government is supposed to be a virtue of FPTP. Another is the link between MPs and their constituents, although elements of this can be retained with hybrid systems that also have a proportional element, such as multimember constituencies or combined list and constituency ballots.There is no perfect voting system, but the potential pitfalls of alternatives are not a good enough reason to stick with a status quo that threatens such a perverse outcome as to delegitimise the democratic process. The clamour for reform would then be irresistible. Preparations to modernise the way parliament is elected, and win public support for change, should begin well before that crisis point is reached.Explore more on these topicsElectoral reformOpinionFirst past the postMayoral electionsDevolutionAndy BurnhamGeneral electionsLocal politicseditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on child marriage: girls should not be wives | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: There’s growing agreement that under-18s need to be protected – but international turmoil is pushing many towards wedlock
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: There’s growing agreement that under-18s need to be protected – but international turmoil is pushing many towards wedlock
Content: A billboard features the president and first lady in Sierra Leone, which raised the minimum marriage age to 18 in 2024.Photograph: Saidu Bah/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA billboard features the president and first lady in Sierra Leone, which raised the minimum marriage age to 18 in 2024.Photograph: Saidu Bah/The GuardianOpinionChild marriageThe Guardian view on child marriage: girls should not be wivesEditorialThere’s growing agreement that under-18s need to be protected – but international turmoil is pushing many towards wedlockWed 26 Aug 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareEvery minute, 23 girls around the world wed, according to theGirls Not Bridescampaign, a coalition of more than 1,000 organisations across 100 countries. No child should be married. But girls are far more likely to be affected than boys, accounting for nine in 10 of those wed before 18, and their spouses are often much older men. The consequences, beyond the immediate threat of sexual violence, include the shortening of their education, increased risks of poverty and domestic abuse, and poor health, including high rates of maternal mortality. In spring, the Center for Global Development thinktankestimatedthat child marriage costs $175bn annually in lost productivity and increased health risks.The good news is that the last decade has seen a drop in rates; last year alone, Grenada, Bolivia, Burkina Faso, Kuwait and Portugal introduced bans. But there are disturbing signs of regression elsewhere. In May, the Talibanissued a new judicial codeenabling child marriage below the previous minimum age of 16, and preventing wives from ending marriages they entered as children if their husbands object. Previous protections were inadequate and often poorly enforced; now even those have been swept away. Activists say forced and early marriages have soared since the Taliban returned to power in 2021, thanks to the ban on secondary education and the state of the economy.Child marriage is almost double the global average in countries experiencing conflict or other crises, with more than one in three girls marrying before they turn 18, Girls Not Bridesreports. The breakdown of economic and support systems, and the exacerbation of factors driving child marriage, such as patriarchal values, can leave families seeing marriage as the only way to protect their daughters – even though they frequently face violence from their husbands. In Gaza, the rate of child marriages dropped from more than 28% in 2009 to just under 18% in 2022. The war has reversed that progress, says the UN Population Fund, with case workers reporting steeply rising rates.Yet child marriage happens in the developing world too. Under-18s could marry in all 50 states of the US until 2018; 17 states have now passed bans, but three – New Mexico, California and Mississippi –still have no age floor. England and Wales raised the minimum age to 18 in 2023; in Northern Ireland, those aged 16 and older can marry with parental consent, and in Scotland they can marry without it. In Australia, 16- and 17-year-oldsmay marry“in exceptional circumstances”.There is still cause for optimism. Although laws are often evaded – sometimes through corruption, more frequently because marriages are not officially registered – they still send an important message. In Sierra Leone, which raised the minimum marriage age to 18 in 2024,the first trial has begunover the forcible marriage of a 17-year-old. Four men, including the girl’s father and alleged groom, face jail sentences of at least 15 years or fines. The new law allows even guests at the wedding of a child to be imprisoned.Advocacy targeting girls as well as their communities is essential, helping some to resist marriage. Cuts to overseas aid now threaten such work.Child marriagewill not end until girls also have educational and economic opportunities, reproductive healthcare and some measure of security. This must be a priority.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ADHD is no myth – but we should interrogate it all the same | Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Gina Rippon’s criticism of a controversial TV documentary about attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Gina Rippon’s criticism of a controversial TV documentary about attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
Content: Dr Max Pemberton, an NHS psychiatrist and the presenter of the Channel 4 documentary The Great ADHD Myth?Photograph: Minnow ProductionsView image in fullscreenDr Max Pemberton, an NHS psychiatrist and the presenter of the Channel 4 documentary The Great ADHD Myth?Photograph: Minnow ProductionsAttention deficit hyperactivity disorderLettersADHD is no myth – but we should interrogate it all the sameReaders respond to Gina Rippon’s criticism of a controversial TV documentary about attention deficit hyperactivity disorderWed 26 Aug 2026 12.06 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareThree months ago, at 42, I was diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Unlike many adults prior to receiving a diagnosis, I had not spent years wondering whether I had ADHD. In fact, I was oblivious until quite recently, when I strongly identified with several things a colleague said about their own experience of ADHD. The more I learned, the more I found myself thinking: “Wow, that’s me.”My forgetfulness, distractibility, messiness, chronic need for organisation and memory strategies, constant lateness, tendency to lose things daily, persistent perfectionism and habit of going, tyres screeching, right up to the last minute of every deadline suddenly made sense. Things I had spent my life viewing as daily frustrations or personal failings had an explanation. I had ADHD, and had always had it. There was a reason for the constant chatter and noise in my brain, with any gaps filled with, or interrupted by, a song. Honestly, literally anything can trigger a song.The diagnosis brought an unexpected, enormous sense of relief. I could finally look at aspects of myself that I had previously been frustrated by and understand them differently – with a new kindness toward myself. And then I heard about a documentary claiming that ADHD isn’t even real, as discussed in Gina Rippon’s article (There is nothing scientific about The Great ADHD Myth? ‘documentary’, 20 August). My first reaction was confusion. Then embarrassment. Then actual shame. Had I just been a fool? Was the explanation that had brought me so much relief actually all just fiction?Of course, it is healthy and worthwhile to question shaky science where the evidence is lacking. But to question the existence of a condition supported by decades of clinical research and scientific evidence is astonishing – and potentially so damaging to so many lives. For people like me, this isn’t an abstract argument about a trend or fashion. An ADHD diagnosis can fundamentally change how you understand your entire life.I hope the documentary will continue to be thoroughly challenged. People who have found a framework for understanding and accepting themselves deserve better than to have that understanding so casually and thoughtlessly undermined by a documentary lacking even basic scientific rigour.Daisy JonesBristolIn her critique of the recentChannel 4documentary on ADHD, Prof Gina Rippon apparently thinks that, when addressing the issue of how much validity the diagnosis has, all we need do is gather more scientific evidence about it. But huge amounts of evidence have already been accumulated. What she fails to consider is the question of how existing evidence should be interpreted, because she seems to assume that the status of ADHD as a genuine neurological disorder is indubitable. However, any body of data can be open to different interpretations. Moreover, she does not consider the fact that much research on ADHD has been conducted with the assumption that it is a distinct disorder and, unsurprisingly, has achieved results that support this. This assumption needs to be questioned, and there is nothing unscientific about doing so.Prof Rippon also criticises the case study of Mason, used in the documentary, for not being a scientific experiment. But this implies a very narrow positivist view of what scientific inquiry involves. Single-case methodology, such as was used here,isscientific and has a long history of use in psychology, including neuropsychology. The salient question is the extent to which the results may be generalisable to a larger population. If sufficient such case studies are conducted with consistent results, stronger conclusions can be drawn.Dr Richard HassallHonorary research fellow, department of philosophy, University of NottinghamAn independent prevalence review which has taken into accountall the research on childhood and adult ADHDwill shortly be published, answering many of the issues brought up in this extremely biased programme. I would now urge Channel 4 to commission a much more accurate programme based on this review. It could be called ADHD: The Truth.Dr Val HarpinConsultant neurodevelopmental paediatricianI was diagnosed with severe ADHD long before the current rise in adult diagnoses. I struggled profoundly to process and retain information at school and was moved back a year. At nine, I had to leave my prep school because of my learning difficulties. I was eventually accepted by Millfield school, where I was taught in very small classes.My parents did not choose medication lightly. I was monitored by paediatricians for years and was also part of Prof Sir Michael Rutter’s English and Romanian Adoptees study following my adoption from Romania.I am now 37 and run a successful dog-grooming business. In many ways, I found a life that suits the way my brain works: practical, creative, fast-moving and hands-on. But ADHD has not disappeared. Without medication, paperwork piles up, conversations become harder to follow and my organisation noticeably deteriorates.I completely support careful diagnosis and sensible prescribing, and I understand concerns about overdiagnosis. But there is a difference between occasionally feeling distracted and having difficulties severe enough to shape your entire childhood.Medication did not suddenly make education easy. Even with it, following tasks, instructions and courses could still be difficult. I wanted to learn, but processing and retaining information remained a struggle and sometimes stopped me taking on new courses because I knew how overwhelming they could become.But medication gave me the chance to find myself, discover what I was good at and build confidence.It did not make me someone else. It gave me a better chance to become myself.Rosieanna EdelmanBathAs a 45-year-old recently diagnosed with ADHD, I find the central question of Max Pemberton’s Channel 4 documentary The Great ADHD Myth? – namely, whether ADHD is a genuine neurodevelopmental disorder, or simply a set of tendencies – somewhat extraneous.It is not only schools that fail to accommodate brains or behaviours that are deemed untypical. Our entire economy is predicated upon the idea that competition rewards hard work – and while that is fine for adults who are able to focus consistently on the demands of work and life, it is ill-suited to those who are not. Thus, adults with an ADHD diagnosis are often forced to choose between protecting our creative, sometimes chaotic true selves – our “fun-ness”, as Mason, the boy in the programme, put it – and medication that can make us feel more stable and productive, but also flat and uninspired.Yes, it feels dystopian to potentially overdiagnose and overmedicate kids. But it is a different type of cruelty to throw those same kids out into a world that is not designed for them, without the language to understand why they struggle or how best to cope.Simon LeeTunbridge Wells, KentHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Only sanctions imposed on Israel will work | Israel | The Guardian
description: Letter: The UK’s response to flagrant breaches of international law is pathetic, writes Bernie Evans, and sanctions against a few individuals have no effect
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: The UK’s response to flagrant breaches of international law is pathetic, writes Bernie Evans, and sanctions against a few individuals have no effect
Content: ‘It is likely that people such as Israeli minister of national security Itamar Ben-Gvir see sanctions as some sort of badge of honour.’Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘It is likely that people such as Israeli minister of national security Itamar Ben-Gvir see sanctions as some sort of badge of honour.’Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty ImagesIsraelLettersOnly sanctions imposed on Israel will workThe UK’s response to flagrant breaches of international law is pathetic, writesBernie Evans, and sanctions against a few individuals have no effectWed 26 Aug 2026 12.06 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareHow long does it take for the penny to drop in Downing Street and the Foreign Office (Israel’s Ben-Gvir posts video of gallows site for hanging Palestinians, 20 August)? Israeli individuals have hadsanctions imposed on them for over a yearwith absolutely no effect, and it is likely that people such as Itamar Ben-Gvir, the minister of national security, see them as some sort of badge of honour.Andy Burnham andEd Milibandmust realise by now that the only sanctions likely to have any effect are those imposed against the state of Israel, so denouncing the issue of tenders for the E1 settlement near Jerusalem as an “unacceptable and destructive act ” is just box-ticking.It’s all very well for Miliband to say that all Israeli settlements in theWest Bankare a “flagrant breach of international law”, but their construction has been going on for years; had the UK and others had the courage to take action when the first ones were built, who knows how many lives could have been saved?Now, with the UN international commission of inquiryreporting that there is ongoing genocide in Gaza, war crimes andethnic cleansing being carried out in the West Bank, and thecallous murder of journalistsand“ecocide” in southern Lebanon, criticising recent events as illegal and inhumane, while taking no effective action, is frankly pathetic.Bernie EvansLiverpoolHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Birds have an eerie association with death | Death and dying | The Guardian
description: Letter: Responding to an article in which birds comforted Helen Harris during bereavement, Angela Smith describes her own experience
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Responding to an article in which birds comforted Helen Harris during bereavement, Angela Smith describes her own experience
Content: ‘Some years later, at school, a blackbird flew into a glass door and died. … That evening, I discovered that a good friend had died at about the same time.’Photograph: Nature Photographers Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Some years later, at school, a blackbird flew into a glass door and died. … That evening, I discovered that a good friend had died at about the same time.’Photograph: Nature Photographers Ltd/AlamyDeath and dyingLettersBirds have an eerie association with deathResponding to an article in which birds comforted Helen Harris during bereavement,Angela Smithdescribes her own experienceWed 26 Aug 2026 12.06 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareHelen Harris’s experience (A moment that changed me: my husband died – and birds began behaving strangely towards me, 19 August) chimes with that of a friend of mine who had many close encounters with robins after the death of her father. She too had birds flying into her house as never before but, unlike Helen, she believed that this was the person’s spirit making contact.My own association between birds and death is rather different. The day my mother-in-law died, a wren had flown into the window of the classroom where I taught, and I found it dead on the ground outside. When we took her ashes to be scattered in the sea, a pheasant hit the car windscreen and died.Some years later, at school, a blackbird flew into a glass door and died. “I hope this doesn’t mean someone is about to die,” I said to another teacher, explaining why I thought it might. That evening, I discovered that a good friend had died at about the same time.I can offer no explanation, but for me there does seem to be an association between birds and death. Visiting robins are more uplifting than birds sacrificing their own lives, though.Angela SmithNorwichHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Trump’s deep-sea mining plan flouts international law | Deep-sea mining | The Guardian
description: Letters: Britain and other signatories to the UN convention on the law of the sea should protest against US proposal to lease seabed for mining, says Guy Standing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Britain and other signatories to the UN convention on the law of the sea should protest against US proposal to lease seabed for mining, says Guy Standing
Content: US territories in the Pacific, including Guam (pictured), oppose the plan to lease out millions of hectares of seabed near the Mariana Trench for deep sea exploration.Photograph: Artimente/AlamyView image in fullscreenUS territories in the Pacific, including Guam (pictured), oppose the plan to lease out millions of hectares of seabed near the Mariana Trench for deep sea exploration.Photograph: Artimente/AlamyDeep-sea miningLettersTrump’s deep-sea mining plan flouts international lawBritain and other signatories to the UN convention on the law of the sea should protest against US proposal to lease seabed for mining, saysGuy StandingWed 26 Aug 2026 12.06 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 12.08 EDTShareYour article on Donald Trump’s plan to lease millions of hectares of seabed in the Pacific for deep-sea mining correctly points to the ecological disaster that this could unleash (US territories hit out at Trump plan to explore deep sea mining in the Pacific, 24 August).However, it does not mention that this plan contravenes international law in the form of Unclos, the UN convention on the law of the sea, which has been ratified by 171 countries and the European Union. The US has not ratified it, but since 1982 has agreed to abide by its rules and procedures.Under Unclos, no deep-sea mining may be undertaken until an international code on environmental assessments has been agreed and, crucially, an international agreement has been reached on sharing the economic benefits among all countries. These have not been agreed by the International Seabed Authority, the body responsible for drawing them up.The UK government, among 171 others, should protest vehemently at this reckless and lawless plan.Guy StandingAuthor, The Blue Commons: Rescuing the Economy of the SeaHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Sávio savours debut goal as Spurs coast to emphatic Carabao Cup win over Charlton | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: Sávio came off the bench to score Tottenham’s fourth goal in a 5-1 Carabao Cup win against Charlton, with Mikey Moore and Dominic Solanke also on target
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Sávio came off the bench to score Tottenham’s fourth goal in a 5-1 Carabao Cup win against Charlton, with Mikey Moore and Dominic Solanke also on target
Content: Sávio of Tottenham Hotspur celebrates after scoring his team’s fourth goal after coming off the bench.Photograph: Ashley Western/Colorsport/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSávio of Tottenham Hotspur celebrates after scoring his team’s fourth goal after coming off the bench.Photograph: Ashley Western/Colorsport/ShutterstockCarabao CupSávio savours debut goal as Spurs coast to emphatic Carabao Cup win over CharltonDavid Hytnerat the Tottenham Hotspur StadiumWed 26 Aug 2026 16.58 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 19.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA new season at the snazziest modern stadium in England and something extremely welcome for Tottenham. A home win over domestic opposition. There were only four of them last time out; three in the Premier League with the final one – over Everton on the last day – helping them to avoid relegation. Had they lost that, thisCarabao Cupfixture against Charlton would also have been played in the Championship.Spurs needed this tonic for another reason – to begin the clean-up operation after Saturday’sawful 3-0 defeat at Brentford.The season could not have started any worse. With no European football, a decent cup run or runs are imperative and Spurs got themselves up and running in this competition on a night when everything came together perfectly.Thierno Barry fires hat-trick as ruthless Everton sweep Preston asideRead moreFor a good while, it looked as though Mikey Moore was going to be the story.The homegrown 19-year-old broke the deadlock with a vicious drive from the edge of the area; it was the purity of the strike that made it. But then came Sávio.Spurs were 3-0 up with further goals from Dominic Solanke and the substitute, Kevin Danso, when Roberto De Zerbisent on his £75m signingfrom Manchester City for his debut. It was a devastating cameo from Sávio, something to wet the whistle for the bigger challenges ahead. “A perfect day for him,” De Zerbi said.It took Sávio just 11 minutes to score and it was a lovely goal – a glide inside from the right, his markers close and yet nowhere near, his control of the situation total before the fizzing low finish into the near corner. De Zerbi has said he wants end product from Sávio, especially goals and he challenged him afterwards to score 10-12 before the end of the season. This was a good start. There was more.Once again, it was Sávio on the right, cutting back, closer to goal this time. He put one would-be challenger down and skated around another. It was all about the composure. The shot hit his teammate, Ben Davies, and went in. The goal was credited to Davies, who was pretty unapologetic about it.The Charlton manager, Nathan Jones, made wholesale changes to his preferred lineup – 10 in total from Saturday’s win at West Ham – and it was a difficult evening for his team. “Absolutely disastrous,” as he put it. “This was a game we didn’t need.” Charlton did enjoy the last word when another substitute, Lloyd Jones, headed home from a corner.View image in fullscreenMikey Moore of Tottenham Hotspur scored their first goal.Photograph: Elli Birch/IPS/ShutterstockThe major take-away was the sense of possibility brought by Sávio, with De Zerbi insisting he was not daunted by being drawn to face Liverpool at Anfield in the next round. “It’s a great game,” he said. “If we want to win the competition, we have to win these games.”It was a night when there was a focus on De Zerbi’s selection. There was a sense of the calvary returning. The manager started Destiny Udogie, Rodrigo Bentancur, Mateus Fernandes and Solanke, players that were fit enough only for the bench at Brentford. Pedro Porro and Micky van de Ven, who did not kick a ball in pre-season and were not available for Brentford, were among the substitutes. They got on. There was no Marcos Senesi or Sandro Tonali in the squad. They will be ready for Newcastle here on Saturday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQuick GuideCarabao Cup: Bradford stun Burnley, plus third-round drawShowBradford City extended Burnley’s uncomfortable start to the season with a 4-2 penalty shootout victory in their second-round Carabao Cup tie. Bantams keeper Jon McCracken [pictured] saved from Jacob Bruun Larsen after Zeki Amdouni had hit the post with Burnley's first spot-kick.Both teams missed chances to win the game inside 90 minutes as it ended goalless. The Burnley head coach, Nicky Hayen, made nine changes from Sunday's defeat to West Brom, but the visitors could not break down the Bradford defence, which has now kept four clean sheets in a row.The 2013 League Cup finalists and current League One leaders will face another third-tier side, Leyton Orient, away from home in the last 32. Standout third-round ties include Liverpool v Tottenham, Ipswich v Arsenal, Manchester United v Brighton, Coventry v Aston Villa and holders Manchester City v Norwich.Third-round drawCrystal Palace v MiddlesbroughManchester United v BrightonManchester City v NorwichSunderland v HullIpswich v ArsenalCoventry v Aston VillaBournemouth v LincolnLiverpool v TottenhamChelsea or Luton v LeedsMillwall v NewcastleFleetwood v Sheffield UnitedEverton v WolvesLeyton Orient v BradfordReading v BrentfordPeterborough v BarnsleyWest Ham v Fulham or AFC WimbledonTies to be played in weeks commencing 7 and 14 SeptPhotograph: Sean Chandler/Shutterstock EditorialWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Spurs were always going to dominate the ball. The question concerned what they could create with it. The answer at the outset was very little. Spurs did not threaten until the 30th minute when Solanke had a shot blocked and Archie Gray extended the goalkeeper, Tiernan Brooks, with a low prod on the rebound. Charlton might have been in front by then. Greg Docherty exploded a drive through a crowd that Antonin Kinsky did well to save while Nathan Asiimwe headed narrowly off target.Spurs upped the tempo after the Brooks save from Gray. Fernandes impressed. There was a flicker from Moore, even if the end product was not there. Then it was. Gloriously. When Moore moved inside from the right, the Charlton player close to him – Millenic Alli – slipped. Moore knew what he had to do and the sweetness of the left-footed connection took the breath. The shot ripped through the hands of Brooks.View image in fullscreenDominic Solanke displays textbook technique to double Tottenham’s advantage.Photograph: Jacques Feeney/Offside/Getty ImagesWhat Charlton did not need shortly afterwards was hesitant defending inside their box on a bouncing ball. Lucas Bergvall saw a shot blocked and Timothy Ouma seemed to freeze. When it broke for Solanke, he swept a clinical finish into the bottom corner.Moore’s only other goal for Spurs was against Elfsborg in the Europa League in January 2025. After that game, his teammate, James Maddison, compared him to Neymar. Moore’s career trajectory has not been as steep as once envisaged but he remains young. He wanted to do more in the second half and there was a swagger about him on the ball; some lovely skills and darting runs. The home crowd saluted him. He remains a loan target for FC Köln before the transfer window shuts. As De Zerbi acknowledged, he needs regular football.De Zerbi introduced Porro, van de Ven and Danso after Gray had once again worked Brooks. It was some entrance from Danso, his first touch a header past Brooks from Fernandes’ free-kick. He was bloodied into the bargain, caught in the aerial challenge by the Charlton substitute, Danny McNamara. Sávio stood and watched. He was stripped and ready while Danso had treatment. He had to wait. When he got on, he more than made his mark.Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupTottenham HotspurCharlton Athleticmatch reportsShareReuse this content

confirmed on Monday that Carse had briefly been detained on suspicion of “being drunk and disorderly” before being “de-arrested”, but the Guardian has been told that their investigation remains live.In a subsequent statement released on Wednesday, first reported by the Telegraph, Derbyshire police confirmed they are investigating allegations of assault. “We are investigating allegations of assault in Derby city centre,” the statement read. “No arrests have yet been made and the investigation is ongoing.”It is unclear at this stage whether Carse had any involvement in the alleged assault, but the revelation that the arrest may have involved more than a row over a spilled drink will intensify the spotlight further on England’s cricketers following a torrid few months dominated by headlines involving late-night misbehaviour.Eight England players including Stokes and the white-ball captain Harry Brook have been involved in alcohol-related incidents since last November, with the returning Test captain, Joe Root, admitting on Tuesday that hewas “hacked off”by Carse’s arrest just days after he announced he was lifting a midnight curfew that had been imposed by management on England’s players because he believes they should be treated as adults.As previously reported by the Guardian, the phone footage of Carse was filmed after he was denied re‑entry to the bar shortly before closing time at around 4am on Sunday morning.The 31-year-old had left the building following “an exchange of words” with a member of the public who spilled a drink on him.The England and WalesCricketBoard announced on Monday that Carse would not be available to face Pakistan this week, after he was released from the squad from last week’s first Test victory at Headingley, which led to him playing for Durham against Derbyshire.Carse will remain unavailable for England pending the outcome of an inquiry by the Cricket Regulator, but with the police still investigating that process has yet to begin so he could face a lengthy exile. He has been selected byDurhamfor Thursday’s home County Championship match with Gloucestershire.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRoot expressed concern for Carse’s wellbeing at Lord’s on Tuesday, but made no attempt to hide his displeasure at the incident. “If I’m being brutally honest, I’m really hacked off, I’m really disappointed,” he said. “I’ve spoken to Brydon, and when I first found out my main concern was him as a person.“I don’t think I’m speaking out of turn by saying he’s very upset, very apologetic and understands his actions. I’m sure that when he gets his chance he will say that himself.“But I don’t think it’s the isolated incident itself, it’s the fact we keep making stupid mistakes away from the game and it’s detracting from what we’re doing on the field.”Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamEngland v Pakistan 2026CricketDurhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Debutant Malard breaks Chelsea duck after Real Sociedad threaten WCL shock | Women's Champions League | The Guardian
description: Melvine Malard scored twice on her Chelsea debut to set up a 5-2 win against Real Sociedad in the first leg of their Women’s Champions League qualifier
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Melvine Malard scored twice on her Chelsea debut to set up a 5-2 win against Real Sociedad in the first leg of their Women’s Champions League qualifier
Content: Melvine Malard rounds  Real Sociedad’s goalkeeper to put Chelsea 3-2 up.Photograph: Patrick Khachfe/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMelvine Malard rounds  Real Sociedad’s goalkeeper to put Chelsea 3-2 up.Photograph: Patrick Khachfe/Getty ImagesWomen's Champions LeagueDebutant Malard breaks Chelsea duck after Real Sociedad threaten WCL shockThird qualifying round, first leg: Chelsea 5-2 Real SociedadGirma 29, Buurman 54, Malard 67 88, James 74; Marín 7, Marcos 59Suzanne Wrackat Cherry Red Records StadiumWed 26 Aug 2026 15.50 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 19.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChelsea’s sluggish start in the first leg of their Champions League qualifier against Real Sociedad will have made far from satisfying viewing for their suspended head coach, Sonia Bompastor, but two goals from the new signing Melvine Malard contributed to a five-goal haul as the Blues came from behind to give themselves a three-goal cushion going into next week’s return fixture.“It was a tough game, a tough first half because Real Sociedad is a really great team but I think we had a good reaction,” said Camille Abily, the assistant coach to Bompastor, who was serving a one match ban followingher red cardin Chelsea’s quarter-final second leg against Arsenal last season. “We were so much better in the second half, there was more space also. It’s a good win – a tough win but a good win.”Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 6: ChelseaRead moreChelsea looked rusty at the Cherry Red Records Stadium, their new home for domestic cup competitions, with WSL fixtures being played at Stamford Bridge. A commercially focused pre-season jaunt to New Zealand and Australia perhaps did not provide the best of preparatory tests prior to this fixture.Their sluggishness was contrasted by Real Sociedad’s sharpness and a confidence that was perhaps delivered by a strong end to their pre-season which included a 1-1 draw with the eight-time European champions OL Lyonnes.View image in fullscreenMelvine Malard (right) is Chelsea’s impact sub off the bench, scoring twice in the second half.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAThe visiting team were tenacious and well organised and opened the scoring in style when a corner was cleared to the edge of the box and the forward Ainhoa Marín, who joined from Deportivo this summer, met it unmarked, sending a looping shot in at the far post.Despite looking far from their best, the home team drew level in the 30th minute, when Katie McCabe’s corner looked to take the smallest of touches off the captain, Naomi Girma, as it was swept in.After the break it was a different story. Chelsea played with an energy that implied they had had the riot act read to them, or read it to themselves. They maintained their momentum despite the visiting team cancelling out Veerle Buurman’s goal from a Lauren James corner that had given them the lead for a brief four minutes.Chelsea were a tad unlucky that Buurman’s precise sliding tackle delivered the ball to the feet of an arriving Cecilia Marcos who fired past Hannah Hampton to pull them back level. The Real Sociedad bench erupted and the goalscorer, who suffered back-to-back anterior cruciate ligament injuries in 2021 and 2023 and only fully rediscovered her form last season, was engulfed by her teammates.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenVeerle Buurman rises highest to put Chelsea 2-1 up in new surroundings at AFC Wimbledon.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/ReutersExcept Chelsea had a stronger bench, greater experience and exploited the high line of the visitors to far greater effect as legs tired. It took the substitute Malard 12 minutes to make her mark on her Chelsea debut as they kept their momentum despite conceding. The France striker collected Sjoeke Nüsken’s poked through-ball, sat down a defender and waited coolly for the goalkeeper to commit before rolling the ball into the empty net.Bristol City ready to ‘supercharge growth’ and prove women’s clubs can fly soloRead moreJames delivered Chelsea’s fourth and gave them a more comfortable lead when she turned in Ellie Carpenter’s ball from close range. Carpenter delivered similarly for her former Lyonnes teammate Malard to get her second as the clock ticked down to put the hosts a step closer to the league phase.On whether it is an advantage to have these tough competitive games ahead of the start of the new domestic season next week, Abily said: “For sure. We saw we started slow. We started slow, even though we’ve played some friendly games. We also played against the boys last week. It’s not the same though, it’s not competition. It’s important to have this kind of game.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's Champions LeagueWomen's footballChelsea WomenShareReuse this content

Content: Serena and Venus Williams reunited to play doubles at the Cincinnati Open earlier this month.Photograph: Robert Prange/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSerena and Venus Williams reunited to play doubles at the Cincinnati Open earlier this month.Photograph: Robert Prange/Getty ImagesUS Open Tennis 2026Serena and Venus Williams will play doubles together at the US OpenSisters to appear in New York for first time since 2022Serena played mixed doubles with Alcaraz on TuesdayAssociated PressWed 26 Aug 2026 10.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 10.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSerena andVenus Williamsare teaming up again at the US Open.The sisters will play doubles at the tournament after receiving a wild card on Wednesday into the event they have won twice.Serena Williams thrills New York crowd on US Open return with Carlos AlcarazRead moreSerena Williams returned to tennis this summer after a four-year absence, and the sisters were set to play at Wimbledon before Serena had to withdraw after injuring her knee in her singles loss. title: Ten-man Hearts stun Rapid Vienna in shootout to reach Conference League | Conference League | The Guardian
description: Beau Reus saved two spot-kicks as Hearts advanced to the Conference League’s main phase despite Tomas Magnusson’s red card
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Beau Reus saved two spot-kicks as Hearts advanced to the Conference League’s main phase despite Tomas Magnusson’s red card
Content: Hearts players celebrate with goalkeeper Beau Reus after his saves helped them defeat Rapid Vienna on penalties.Photograph: Christian Hofer/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenHearts players celebrate with goalkeeper Beau Reus after his saves helped them defeat Rapid Vienna on penalties.Photograph: Christian Hofer/ShutterstockConference LeagueTen-man Hearts stun Rapid Vienna in shootout to reach Conference LeaguePlayoff second leg: Rapid 2-2 Hearts (aet, 3-4 on pens)Kara 34, Cvetkovic 119; Kabore 79, Miller 100PA MediaWed 26 Aug 2026 16.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 22.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBeau Reus made two penalty saves as heroic Hearts overcame Tomas Magnusson’s red card to pull off a stunning shootout victory away to Rapid Vienna, and book themselves a return to the Conference League’s main phase.Following a 2-2 draw in the first leg at Tynecastle, the Jambos’ European journey looked to be fizzling out when they were reduced to 10 men in the 75th minute of the playoff round second leg, while already trailing to Ercan Kara’s first-half goal.Football Daily | Celtic raise the bar for calamitous capitulations in EuropeRead moreSubstitute Landry Kaboré equalised a few minutes later before Calvin Miller volleyed 10-manHeartsahead in the 10th minute of extra-time. Rapid hit back in the 119th minute, Nenad Cvetkovic’s goal making it 4-4 on aggregate.But Hearts rediscovered their poise to edge the shootout 4-3 and secure what may be their most significant result in Europe for more than two decades. It means they will compete in the Conference League proper for the third time in five seasons.The visitors suffered a blow in the 15th minute when Tom Renaud was carried off after Rapid attacker Petter Dahl fell awkwardly on his leg while being fouled by Jordi Altena. ­Magnusson replaced the Frenchman but Hearts were struggling to get a foothold early on, and the breakthrough came for Rapid in the 34th minute.View image in fullscreenCalvin Miller finishes acrobatically to put Hearts ahead in extra timePhotograph: Lukas Grinaj/SNS GroupDemir’s low shot from the right took a nick off Oisin McEntee and broke kindly to the unmarked Kara, who slotted into the empty net from six yards out. Hearts were almost handed a way back into it when Cláudio Braga seized on a loose pass but his angled shot from inside the box was beaten away by Niklas Hedl.Hearts enjoyed a spell of pressure towards the end of the half, with Josh McPake and McEntee threatening with shots from outside the box. After the break, the Jambos captain, Blair Spittal, volleyed just wide from 20 yards out, before James Wilson and Braga both spurned opportunities.Quick GuideChampions League: Fenerbahce stun Lyon, Viking march onShowFenerbahceupset Lyon in the Champions League playoffs on Wednesday to advance, whileViking Stavangerjoined fellow Norwegians Bodø/Glimt in the league phase with victory over Dinamo Zagreb.With the teams locked at 1-1 from the first leg in Istanbul a week ago, the Turkish giants opened up a 2-0 lead in the first half of the return fixture in France. Vedat Muriqi and English defender Archie Brown [pictured] were on target for the visitors, with winger Malick Fofana giving Lyon faint hope in the second half.Viking hit back from a goal down on the night against Dinamo Zagreb, winning 3-1 in Norway and 5-3 on aggregate. Albania's Arber Hoxha gave Dinamo an early lead but Zlatko Tripic equalised from the penalty spot just eight minutes later. Two early goals in the second half from Edvin Austbø and Tobias Moi sealed Viking’s progress to their first Champions League group phase.Barnabas Varga scored a double and former Real Madrid forward Luka Jovic added another asAEK Athenscruised into the league phase with a 4-0 thrashing of Levski Sofia. Romania's Razvan Marin added a penalty as the Greeks booked their progress following a 0-0 draw in the first leg in Bulgaria.Panama’s Cristian Martínez scored the extra-time winner forSlovan Bratislavaas they overcame Slovenian champions Celje. After a 1-1 draw in the first leg, Andraz Sporar gave the Slovakians an early lead at Celje but Svit Seslar equalised fom the penalty spot, before Martínez secured a 3-2 aggregate success.AFPChampions League: qualified teams and predicted potsPot 1:Paris Saint-Germain, Bayern Munich, Real Madrid, Liverpool, Internazionale, Manchester City, Arsenal, Barcelona, Atlético Madrid.Pot 2:Dortmund, Roma, Sporting CP, Aston Villa, Porto, Manchester United, Club Brugge, Real Betis, PSV Eindhoven.Pot 3:Feyenoord, Lille, Bodø/Glimt, Napoli, RB Leipzig, Villarreal, Fenerbahce, Shakhtar Donetsk, Galatasaray.Pot 4:Slavia Prague, Slovan Bratislava, Stuttgart, AEK Athens, Lask, Como, Lens, Viking, Sabah.Photograph: AnadoluWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Magnusson then sent a close-range header wide from a Spittal free-kick, but the Icelandic midfielder’s night was cut short when he was shown a second yellow card for a trip on Jannes Horn in the 76th minute.Despite the setback, Wouter Vrancken’s side drew level within three minutes, as Kaboré adjusted his body and chested Spittal’s corner into the net at the near post, sending the game to extra time.Remarkably, Hearts went ahead in the 100th minute when Miller acrobatically volleyed in a cross from substitute Rogers Mato. But just as the depleted Jambos looked like hanging on, Cvetkovic knocked in Moulaye Haidara’s cross in the 119th minute to force penalties.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenHearts keeper Beau Reus saves a penalty from Marco Tilio and send his side into the Conference League.Photograph: Christian Hofer/ShutterstockMiller, Altena, Mato and Sabah Kerjota all scored from the spot for Hearts, with McEntee the only Hearts player to miss. Reus saved two kicks, denying Haidara and Marco Tilio to emerge as the hero in Vienna.Victory brought welcome relief for Vrancken after a punishing run of European results, with his side losing 6-0 on aggregate to Sturm Graz in the Champions League qualifiers. Hearts then lost 6-1 in Lisbon and 7-2 on aggregate to Benfica in the Europa League, dropping into the Conference League playoffs as a result.“We played a really bad first half, a little bit similar [to] Benfica. We had a game plan and we didn’t show the guts to follow up,” Vrancken told BBC Scotland. “We were already pretty angry at half-time, and we came out, we did much better. We took the game in our hands, we were dominant.”“They have to learn that they’re a good team, that they’re good players, that they can show it and show the guts every time, every week, every game,” the Belgian added. “Because in the last away games in Europe, you see that they’re a little bit scared to do things, to take risks or to give spaces away.“But the progress of the team is amazing. The team spirit, I saw it from the first session. They want to learn. They wanted to have feedback, they want to go into it and the kind of football we played. This is the result, they get rewarded, and I’m so happy for them.”Explore more on these topicsConference LeagueHeartsRapid ViennanewsShareReuse this content

title: Mbappé hat-trick sinks Real Sociedad after Real Madrid jeered by home fans | La Liga | The Guardian
description: Kylian Mbappé’s hat-trick earned Real Madrid a 4-1 win against Real Sociedad but José Mourinho’s side were jeered on his return to Bernabéu as head coach
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Kylian Mbappé’s hat-trick earned Real Madrid a 4-1 win against Real Sociedad but José Mourinho’s side were jeered on his return to Bernabéu as head coach
Content: One, two, three for Kylian Mbappé against Real Sociedad.Photograph: Cesar Cebolla/PRESSINPHOTO/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenOne, two, three for Kylian Mbappé against Real Sociedad.Photograph: Cesar Cebolla/PRESSINPHOTO/ShutterstockLa LigaMbappé hat-trick sinks Real Sociedad after Real Madrid jeered by home fansReutersWed 26 Aug 2026 17.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 19.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKylian Mbappé scored a hat-trick as Real Madrid beat Real Sociedad 4-1 at the Bernabéu on Wednesday ⁠in their first home match since the return of José Mourinho as head coach.Mbappé put Madrid ahead in the 40th minute before Luka Sucic levelled four minutes later, but the ⁠France forward restored the ⁠hosts’ lead on ​the hour. Vinícius Júnior added a third in the 68th minute before Mbappé completed his treble 10 minutes from time.Julián Álvarez walks alone at Atlético in transfer saga with no end – and no winners | Sid LoweRead moreIt was a winning return ⁠to the Bernabéu for Mourinho, more than 13 years after his previous home match in charge of the club, as Madrid recovered from a disjointed first half ⁠with a ruthless display after the break.Madrid were jeered before half-time after a sluggish opening in which they ​looked short of rhythm, careless in possession and ‌vulnerable on the counterattack.“There’s always a sense of justice in the ​boos and the applause, and the odd boo now ‌and then doesn’t do anyone any ‌harm – it helps you grow,” Mourinho said at full time. “We all know the Santiago Bernabéu and just how demanding the fans ‌are here, and I’m very pleased with how my players responded under pressure and put in a great second half, in which we could even have scored more goals.”Real Sociedad carried ‌the sharper threat early on and almost went ahead in the 10th minute when Takefusa Kubo intercepted ‌a loose pass near the edge of the box and slipped in Mikel Oyarzabal, whose close-range effort was kept out by Thibaut Courtois.Quick GuideChampions League: Fenerbahce stun Lyon, Viking march onShowFenerbahceupset Lyon in the Champions League playoffs on Wednesday to advance, whileViking Stavangerjoined fellow Norwegians Bodø/Glimt in the league phase with victory over Dinamo Zagreb.With the teams locked at 1-1 from the first leg in Istanbul a week ago, the Turkish giants opened up a 2-0 lead in the first half of the return fixture in France. Vedat Muriqi and English defender Archie Brown [pictured] were on target for the visitors, with winger Malick Fofana giving Lyon faint hope in the second half.Viking hit back from a goal down on the night against Dinamo Zagreb, winning 3-1 in Norway and 5-3 on aggregate. Albania's Arber Hoxha gave Dinamo an early lead but Zlatko Tripic equalised from the penalty spot just eight minutes later. Two early goals in the second half from Edvin Austbø and Tobias Moi sealed Viking’s progress to their first Champions League group phase.Barnabas Varga scored a double and former Real Madrid forward Luka Jovic added another asAEK Athenscruised into the league phase with a 4-0 thrashing of Levski Sofia. Romania's Razvan Marin added a penalty as the Greeks booked their progress following a 0-0 draw in the first leg in Bulgaria.Panama’s Cristian Martínez scored the extra-time winner forSlovan Bratislavaas they overcame Slovenian champions Celje. After a 1-1 draw in the first leg, Andraz Sporar gave the Slovakians an early lead at Celje but Svit Seslar equalised fom the penalty spot, before Martínez secured a 3-2 aggregate success.AFPChampions League: qualified teams and predicted potsPot 1:Paris Saint-Germain, Bayern Munich, Real Madrid, Liverpool, Internazionale, Manchester City, Arsenal, Barcelona, Atlético Madrid.Pot 2:Dortmund, Roma, Sporting CP, Aston Villa, Porto, Manchester United, Club Brugge, Real Betis, PSV Eindhoven.Pot 3:Feyenoord, Lille, Bodø/Glimt, Napoli, RB Leipzig, Villarreal, Fenerbahce, Shakhtar Donetsk, Galatasaray.Pot 4:Slavia Prague, Slovan Bratislava, Stuttgart, AEK Athens, Lask, Como, Lens, Viking, Sabah.Photograph: AnadoluWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The visitors went close again in the 34th minute, Sergio Gómez flashing a fine volley just wide of the far post, as the Bernabéu crowd began to voice its frustration.Mbappé briefly changed the mood five minutes before half-time with a flash of class. Fede Valverde collected ‌the ball just beyond midfield and split the defence with a superb pass, allowing Mbappé to surge into the box, cut left and lash a shot into the top ​corner.View image in fullscreenJosé Mourinho was in the home dugout at the Bernabéu for the first time in 13 years.Photograph: Diego Souto/Getty ImagesBut Madrid’s defensive uncertainty returned four minutes later. Ibrahima Konaté, Dean Huijsen and Álvaro Carreras were all caught out after Job Ochieng latched on to a long ball, his deflected effort falling to Sucic on the right, who had time to steady himself and drill a low shot past Courtois.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMourinho sent on Marc Cucurella at ⁠half-time and Madrid emerged transformed, with Vinícius and Mbappé stretching the visitors ​with direct running and greater intensity.The ​hosts regained the lead on the ​hour when Mbappé and Jude Bellingham exchanged a sharp one-two, leaving the France captain ​free inside the box to ‌beat Álex Remiro ​with a low finish. Eight ​minutes later, Bellingham’s pressing won the ball back near the byline and his low cross gave Vinícius the simplest of tap-ins from close range.Mbappé completed the win in the 80th minute after Vinícius slipped a clever pass behind the defence, the forward lifting a composed chip over Remiro to seal his hat-trick.“This guy is incredible,” Mourinho said of Mbappé. “I see him really hungry to make history withReal Madrid, and I see a team where, despite Kylian being Kylian, it’s hard for me not to talk about the team.”Explore more on these topicsLa LigaReal MadridReal SociedadKylian MbappéEuropean club footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Uefa to lift boycott threat after Fifa promises no World Cup sale repeat | Uefa | The Guardian
description: Uefa is to drop its threatened boycott of Fifa competitions after receiving concrete guarantees that the global governing body will never attempt a repeat of Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell stakes in the World Cup
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: Uefa is to drop its threatened boycott of Fifa competitions after receiving concrete guarantees that the global governing body will never attempt a repeat of Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell stakes in the World Cup
Content: Gianni Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal sparked a backlash, including from Uefa.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal sparked a backlash, including from Uefa.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAUefaUefa to lift boycott threat after Fifa promises no World Cup sale repeatUefa has received guarantees after ill-fated Infantino planEuropean sides will go to under-20 Women’s World CupExclusive byNick AmesandMatt HughesWed 26 Aug 2026 07.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUefa is to drop itsthreatened boycottof Fifa competitions after receiving concrete guarantees that the global governing body will never attempt a repeat ofGianni Infantino’s plan to sell stakesin the World Cup.European teams have been cleared for participation in the upcoming Under-20 Women’s World Cup, along with subsequent tournaments, afterFifaprovided the binding assurances that no equivalent of its president’s ill-fated scheme will be put on the table.Uefa had threatened the ­boycott after Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal was revealed and ­doubled down after it was ­withdrawn, saying the condition that “such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again” had not been met.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Despite exchanging barbs in ­public, Uefa and Fifa are understood to have been having private ­discussions over the terms of ­removing the ­boycott threat for several weeks, with the European governing body finally ­getting the reassurances it required.When Fifa confirmed its decision to abandon FFE four days after it became public it neglected to pledge that a similar privatisation plan would not be repeated, but it has now done so in private correspondence.The decision to drop the boycott allows England, who named their squad for the under-20 tournament last week, to travel to Poland in time for the opening game against Canada on 5 September. France and Spain had also listed their travelling party in anticipation that the boycott threat would be lifted. Portugal, Italy and the host nation are the other European countries due to compete.View image in fullscreenEngland’s under-20s will travel to the World Cup in Poland.Photograph: Carlos Rodrigues/The FA/Getty ImagesFifa welcomed the end of the boycott , saying: “Fifa is pleased that all qualified teams ‌will be participating in the upcoming Fifa Under-20 Women’s World Cup. Fifa strongly believes that football has the power to unite, even in challenging circumstances, and looks forward to welcoming all teams and players to Poland.”The boycott is yet to be publicly dropped by Uefa, whose executive committee and federation chiefs meet in Monte Carlo on Thursday. The 55 heads of Uefa’s member associations will convene before the Champions League draw during what is traditionally a significant few days in the European football calendar.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUefa’s position that Infantino must be replaced has not changed and further steps regarding its stance towards the Fifa leadership will also be discussed at the meeting.Italy’s football federation (FIGC) on Wednesday became the latest to publicly withdraw support for Infantino. “This decision is intended to clearly and transparently express the FIGC’s position … regarding the recent initiatives promoted by the Fifa president concerning the governance and development of international competitions,” it said.There will be relief in some quarters that younger players, in particular, will not become embroiled in the volatile battle for football’s future.
