But the fact that Fifa has been forced to mitigate for its president’s actions is another humiliation for a persistently scandal-hit organisation.Explore more on these topicsUefaFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Nothing ever seemed to faze him’: Ken Oliver, former racing editor of the Guardian, dies aged 86 | Horse racing | The Guardian
description: Tributes are paid to the much-loved former racing editor of the Guardian who also tipped as Larry Lynx
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: Tributes are paid to the much-loved former racing editor of the Guardian who also tipped as Larry Lynx
Content: The legendary Guardian racing editor, Ken Oliver.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe legendary Guardian racing editor, Ken Oliver.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianHorse racing‘Nothing ever seemed to faze him’: Ken Oliver, former racing editor of the Guardian, dies aged 86Tributes are paid to the much-loved and respected Fleet Street veteran who also tipped as ‘Larry Lynx’Greg WoodWed 26 Aug 2026 12.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 15.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKen Oliver, who has died at the age of 86, was the Guardian’s racing editor for many years until his retirement in 2004, at the end of a lifetime in racing journalism at publications including the London Evening News, the Sporting Life, the Sun, the London Daily News, the Sunday People – where he tipped as Larry Lynx – and as the editor of Ruff’s Guide to the Turf, the racing equivalent of Wisden.Ken was the racing editor when I joined the Guardian in 2001 and he was a joy to work with: an old-school veteran of the glory days of Fleet Street, blessed with an encyclopaedic knowledge of the sport and steeped in all the rhythms and traditions of daily papers that would soon be ushered into history by the internet. He was also unflappable, understanding when a story or plan went awry, and the best possible company for a pint or two in a local watering hole once the first edition had been put to bed.The long lunch was another Fleet Street tradition that Ken maintained diligently. “What a great operator he was,” Chris Hawkins, a racing writer with the Guardian for nearly 30 years, says. “Nothing ever seemed to faze him. He also loved a pint, a game of snooker and was a great trencherman. I remember one Sunday, we were having the full works for lunch in the Albion. Ken was getting stuck into the roast beef when the landlady shouted out: “Ken, the Dovers are in.” He said: “Right, when I finish this, I’ll have one. And he did.”Like many Fleet Street journalists in the post-war era, Ken Oliver started out as a teaboy in his teens – in his case, on the London Evening News in an era when it was the biggest-selling evening paper in the world – and then worked his way through the ranks.“He was the most affable, easy-going person you could ever, ever come across,” Dennis Sherriffs, a former Guardian colleague, says. “Ken would never get up or down, it was always smooth as smooth, and then it was: ‘Come on Den, let’s go for a pint.’ As a person, you would not have got a nicer guy. That’s how he was with everybody, he was just a nice guy that everybody liked.”In retirement, Oliver remained a regular racegoer at West Country tracks – Wincanton was his particular favourite – for many years, and he died a few months after celebrating the 60th anniversary of his wedding to Sylvia.Tony Paley, Oliver’s successor as the Guardian’s racing editor, said: “I owe a lot to Ken and will always be eternally grateful for his faith in me when recommending my application to the sports editor for a place on the racing desk at the Guardian.“What a pleasure it was to be there in the final pre-internet-dominated days when he would always insist on having lunch out when he was on duty.“Totally unflappable, Ken had the most amazing eye for a print edition and could redesign pages in the light of breaking stories faster than anyone I have ever seen. He was kind, had an engaging sense of humour and was always ‘the life and soul’. I know he will be very sorely missed by his family, friends and all his ex-colleagues.”Explore more on these topicsHorse racingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: US issues sanctions against UK-based direct action group Palestine Action | Palestine Action | The Guardian
description: US labels group ‘global terrorist’ as Palestine Action challenge against proscription in UK nears supreme court hearing
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: US labels group ‘global terrorist’ as Palestine Action challenge against proscription in UK nears supreme court hearing
Content: A Palestinian flag flown by a protester outside the group’s high court hearing in London in February.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenA Palestinian flag flown by a protester outside the group’s high court hearing in London in February.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/GettyPalestine ActionUS issues sanctions against UK-based direct action group Palestine ActionUS labels group ‘global terrorist’ as Palestine Action challenge against proscription in UK nears supreme court hearingHaroon SiddiqueLegal affairs correspondentWed 26 Aug 2026 13.45 EDTFirst published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 13.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US ⁠has ​issued sanctions against ⁠the UK-based direct action organisationPalestine⁠Action, describing it as a “transnational terror group”.The US Department of the Treasury labelledPalestine Actiona specially designated global terrorist on Wednesday, which allows the US to freeze the assets of foreign individuals and entities.Palestine Action becamethe first direct action group to be proscribedunder the UK’s Terrorism Act in July last year, placing it alongside the likes of Islamic State and Boko Haram. The UK ban is the subject of a legal challenge thatwill be heard by the UK supreme courtin November.The powers used to sanction the organisation in the US were introduced by President George W Bush shortly after the 9/11 attacks by al-Qaida on the twin towers in New York.Announcing the sanctions on Palestine Action and two other organisations, the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said: “Far-left extremists, their fronts, and their enablers should be on notice: we will bring the full weight of our economic tools to bear. Political terrorism has no place in our society and we will continue to cut the financial lifelines of these groups until they are eliminated.”The co-founder of Palestine Action, Huda Ammori, who is behind the legal challenge to the UK ban, said in response: “Palestine Action’s activities in the US and elsewhere have always been about saving lives by disrupting the Israeli war machine, which is committing a genocide in Gaza with the support of the US government. Trump has been at the centre of the mass murder of Palestinians, enabling the Zionist regime at every turn.View image in fullscreenHuda Ammori, the co-founder of Palestine Action, said the fact that Trump was taking inspiration from Britain’s repression of the movement should be a wake-up call to anyone who cared about civil liberties.Photograph: Abdullah Bailey/Alamy“The fact that Trump is now taking inspiration from Britain’s repression of the movement for Palestinian freedom exposes just how dangerous this ban is and should be a wake-up call to anyone who cares about free speech and civil liberties. By banning a direct action protest group under terrorism legislation for the first time in British history, Keir Starmer’s government has created a blueprint for authoritarian governments around the world to suppress political dissent, and to criminalise British citizens who travel or live abroad.“Trump’s decision to adopt Keir Starmer’s designation of Palestine Action as a ‘terrorist’ group should be the final nail in the coffin of this dangerous, draconian and disproportionate ban.”Palestine Action ban will be overturned, group’s co-founder vowsRead moreAs well as freezing the assets of those sanctioned, the listing forbids US citizens and entities from doing business with them.The US Treasury website said the group had “supported numerous acts of terrorism since July 2020, including acts that have physically injured UK law enforcement personnel, as well as acts intended to intimidate lawful commercial enterprises and coerce the UK government. The group’s actions include multiple high-profile instances of breaking into defense infrastructure and British military installations, and causing millions of dollars’ worth of damage to military equipment.”It said the group had promoted its activities on social media, “encouraging the use of similar tactics internationally, including within the United States and along the US-Mexican border”.In the UK, Palestine Action has focused largely on factories run by the Israeli weapons firm Elbit Systems, as well as other companies that do business with it.In March last year, Donald Trump’s Turnberry golf course on the west coast of Scotlandwas targeted by protesters. The clubhouse at the five-star resort in Ayrshire was graffitied and the course dug up and painted with the words “Gaza is not 4 sale”.The then UK foreign secretary, Yvette Cooper, moved to ban the group last year after recommendations from officials, who nevertheless conceded that proscribing Palestine Action would be “relatively novel” as “there was no known precedent of an organisation being proscribed on the basis that it was concerned in terrorism mainly due to its use or threat of action involving serious damage to property”.Explore more on these topicsPalestine ActionTrump administrationPalestineUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nvidia’s quarterly revenue doubles to nearly $100bn as CEO declares ‘golden age’ | Technology | The Guardian
description: The $5tn firm beat Wall Street expectations for yet another blockbuster quarter, though the stock made only modest gains
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: The $5tn firm beat Wall Street expectations for yet another blockbuster quarter, though the stock made only modest gains
Content: Nvidia’s logo displayed at their headquarters in Santa Clara, California.Photograph: Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNvidia’s logo displayed at their headquarters in Santa Clara, California.Photograph: Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty ImagesTechnologyNvidia’s quarterly revenue doubles to nearly $100bn as CEO declares ‘golden age’The $5tn firm beat Wall Street expectations for yet another blockbuster quarter, though the stock made only modest gainsJohana BhuiyanWed 26 Aug 2026 18.57 EDTFirst published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 18.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNvidia announced on Wednesday that its quarterly revenue had doubled in a year to nearly $100bn. Jensen Huang, the founder and CEO, jubilantly declared that demand is accelerating as the AI industry had reached a “golden age”.The chipmaker, the most valuable company in the world with a $5tn market cap, brought in $96.2bn in revenue, beating Wall Street expectations of $92bn in the second quarter. That’s 106% more than the company saw in revenue this time last year. The company expects its revenue to continue to grow to $108bn by the end of the third quarter, higher than analysts predicted.The company saw $89bn in datacenter revenue in the second quarter, a closely watched metric that likewise rose 117% year over year. The chipmaker also posted in $2.22 in earnings per share, surpassing Wall Street expectations of adjusted earnings of $2.09.“AI has reached its inflection point. It’s doing useful work. Its tokens are productive and profitable. Now, compute is revenue,” said Huang.The stock rose nearly 4% after the earnings call after initially slipping, as investors look to Nvidia to set the bar for the rest of the AI industry.As the manufacturer of the best-regarded chips of the AI boom, Nvidia’s earnings reports serve as a proxy for the entire industry. While many of the companies Nvidia supplies are working to decrease their reliance on it and build their own chips, Huang said that he remained confident that these companies will be buying from Nvidia for a long time.“I have 100% confidence that our technology will continue to be extraordinary for them,” Huang said on the company earnings call.“Nvidia is a platform – an entire AI factory platform that spans the entire AI lifecycle, which you can use in any cloud,” he continued. “It’s in every cloud. So we built something very different.”Emarketer analyst Jacob Bourne said the company “provides a strong argument for the durability of its position”.“Even extraordinary growth can fail to satisfy investors as scrutiny of AI spending and its financing intensifies,” said Bourne. “Yet Nvidia continues to deepen its relevance across the AI stack, expanding beyond training into inference, models, networking, and broader AI infrastructure.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChip stocks have generally seen a downturn over the last few months with renewed questions about whether the billions of dollars AI companies are investing into building out AI will be worth it bubbling to the surface. Critics have also questioned the circular nature of Nvidia’s financing deal with its major clients.Nvidia has attempted to ease those concerns by working with BlackRock, Blackstone, KKR, Apollo, Brookfield and Goldman Sachs to put together a$500bn pool of capital. The company also inked a deal to build out an 8GW datacenter in Ohio.Explore more on these topicsTechnologyNvidianewsShareReuse this content

title: Judge awards Blake Lively $400,000 in legal fees in Justin Baldoni case | Blake Lively | The Guardian
description: The actor had sought $8m in attorney costs resulting from her protracted legal battle with Baldoni
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: The actor had sought $8m in attorney costs resulting from her protracted legal battle with Baldoni
Content: Blake Lively leaves the US district court in New York, on 11 February 2026.Photograph: Eduardo Muñoz/ReutersView image in fullscreenBlake Lively leaves the US district court in New York, on 11 February 2026.Photograph: Eduardo Muñoz/ReutersBlake LivelyJudge awards Blake Lively $400,000 in legal fees in Justin Baldoni caseThe actor had sought $8m in attorney costs resulting from her protracted legal battle with BaldoniOwen MyersWed 26 Aug 2026 13.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 13.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBlake Livelyhas been awarded more than $400,000 in attorneys’ fees after her 18-month legal battle with Justin Baldoni.On Wednesday, judge Lewis Liman awarded the actor $363,245.40 in attorneys’ fees and $44,206.35 in costs, figures far lower than the $8m Lively hadsought.In aruling, the judge found that Lively was entitled to only “reasonable” fees. He found that her lawyers’ billing rates were “not unreasonable” in a case of this complexity, but “the number of hours for which Lively seeks reimbursement is unreasonable.”Liman added that her documentation was incomplete: “Lively has submitted the declaration of a purported attorney fee expert who has reviewed the billing records […] Lively has not submitted the invoices themselves.”In December 2024, Lively accused Baldoni of sexual harassment and fostering a hostile work environment on the set of domestic abuse drama It Ends With Us; the directorfileda counter-defamation lawsuit against Lively the following month.In May, theysettledtheir dispute just weeks before it went to trial, with only the issue of attorneys’ fees and costs remaining. Today’s ruling draws a line under their long legal battle.In July, Baldoni and his wife, Emily,spoke outabout the “injustice and pain” they said they had endured as part of the legal battle.“We’ve had to wrestle with so many things and try to understand so many things,” said Emily in a video posted to Instagram. “Like, how could something like this even happen? Let alone disguised as a fight for women.”Lively has made high-profile appearances at the Met Gala and at the World Cup final after the settlement but has yet to speak publicly about the legal battle. Last month, she was absent at Taylor Swift’s wedding amid reports that the pair’s friendship had fractured after the singer was subpoenaed by Baldoni’s legal team.Explore more on these topicsBlake LivelyDrama filmsLaw (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: Two women accuse former Fat White Family member Saul Adamczewski of physical and emotional abuse | Music | The Guardian
description: Insecure Men singer has now been dropped by his record label and had tour dates cancelled after two women shared allegations about his behaviour
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: Insecure Men singer has now been dropped by his record label and had tour dates cancelled after two women shared allegations about his behaviour
Content: Saul Adamczewski performing with the Fat White Family in 2014.Photograph: Hugo Marie/EPA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSaul Adamczewski performing with the Fat White Family in 2014.Photograph: Hugo Marie/EPA/ShutterstockMusicTwo women accuse former Fat White Family member Saul Adamczewski of physical and emotional abuseInsecure Men singer has now been dropped by his record label and had tour dates cancelled after two women shared allegations about his behaviourLaura SnapesWed 26 Aug 2026 11.42 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 15.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSaul Adamczewski of Insecure Men and formerly ofFat White Familyhas been dropped by his record label and had tour dates cancelled after two women shared allegations of physical and emotional abuse against the musician.One woman said that the pair had a short relationship that resulted in a pregnancy, after which, she alleged, Adamczewski “made it his duty to make me suffer. He has been violent, pushed me, thrown glass bottles at me, showered me with beer […] insulted me, taken my passport from me, stolen my money and more, all while I had our baby.”She claimed that Adamczewski – who has been candid about his use of crack cocaine and heroin, and was kicked out of Fat White Family and sent to rehab – used her “as an excuse to get more money for doing smack, while I would have no money to feed myself and had to steal after he promised he would take care of me.”She said that in her third month of pregnancy, she moved to “be with my family and away from him” and shared screenshots appearing to show abusive messages from Adamczewski.The musician Jessica Winter commented on the post saying she had “witnessed this man’s physical and emotional abuse on two women and other men”, and claimed that Adamczewski had “threatened and abused me to try and silence me”.Another alleged victim described multiple incidences of physical violence. She also alleged that he folded her inside a sofa bed and “held me inside”.The Guardian has contacted representatives for Adamczewski for comment. The band’s management and UK publicist have severed ties and the Instagram profile for Insecure Men has been removed.Insecure Men were signed to the US indie label Fat Possum and have now been dropped. In a statement, the label said: “We take the accusations against Saul Adamczewski very seriously. Fat Possum will no longer be working with Insecure Men.” The band have been removed from the label’s online roster.The band’s set at the Green Man festival did not go ahead this weekend, nor a planned date in Manchester. A subsequent date at Rough Trade Liverpool has also been cancelled, a staff member confirmed to the Guardian, along with the band’s November tour of the UK. No official reason for the cancellation has been shared.Adamczewski co-founded the Metros in 2006 and found minor indie sleaze-era success including having a song on the soundtrack to US teen TV series Gossip Girl.In 2011, he co-founded Fat White Family, a band that gained notoriety and acclaim for their debauched behaviour. He left the band before the completion of their 2024 album Forgiveness Is Yours. He was also a member of Warmduscher from 2014 to around 2018.Explore more on these topicsMusicFat White FamilynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘National scandal’: extreme heat linked to 40,000 deaths in England between 1988 and 2025 | Extreme heat | The Guardian
description: ONS data shows rising toll of climate crisis, with officials warning this summer on track to set further records
Author: Damian Carrington
Headline: ONS data shows rising toll of climate crisis, with officials warning this summer on track to set further records
Content: The figures do not include this summer, when England is on track to record its highest ever number of heat-related deaths.Photograph: SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe figures do not include this summer, when England is on track to record its highest ever number of heat-related deaths.Photograph: SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesExtreme heat‘National scandal’: extreme heat linked to 40,000 deaths in England between 1988 and 2025ONS data shows rising toll of climate crisis, with officials warning this summer on track to set further recordsDamian CarringtonEnvironment editorWed 26 Aug 2026 07.45 EDTFirst published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 05.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 40,000 extra people died on the hottest days in England between 1988 and 2025 than would be expected in normal temperatures, according todatapublished by the Office for National Statistics on Wednesday.The figures do not include this summer, when England has sweltered under a succession of heatwaves and is on track to record itshighest ever number of heat-related deaths. The UK Health Security Agency announced on 30 July that an estimated 2,877 people had died in the May and June heatwaves alone. The total is almost double the figure for the whole summer in 2025.The number of people dying prematurely due to high temperatures is expected to rise further as the climate crisis caused by the burning of fossil fuels continues to push up temperatures and the population ages. Elderly people, as well as children and the unwell, are particularly vulnerable to heat.Emergency departments in England’s hospitals have experienced theirbusiest period everthis summer, with almost 2.5 million patients attending A&E each month in May, June and July and the heat cited as a main reason. Nurses were collapsing during shifts amid “inhumane and impossible” conditions caused by extreme heat, theirunion warnedearlier in August.View image in fullscreenEmergency departments in England’s hospitals have experienced their busiest period ever this summer.Photograph: sturti/Getty ImagesLondon had the highest number of deaths attributable to the hottest temperatures, the ONS said. The London ambulance service has dealt with25,000 more callsthis summer than last, surpassing the record number seen during the peak of the Covid-19 pandemic.Nearly all English regions, andWales, experienced a 50% increase in the risk of a person dying when temperatures passed 24C. More than 2,000 deaths in Wales were associated with the hottest days from 1988 to 2025 and 10,000 deaths with the coldest.Historically, more excess deaths happened on the coldest days than the hottest. There were 139,000 deaths associated with the coldest days in England between 1988 and 2025, according tothe ONS data. However, James Tucker at the ONS said: “Our results show that the gap between heat- and cold-related deaths has narrowed in recent years as the proportion of heat-related deaths has increased.”ChartDr Clair Barnes, a statistician at Imperial College London investigating the impacts of climate change on extreme weather, said: “We now face the very real prospect of heat deaths overtaking those that occur on the coldest days. As this summer has made abundantly clear, the risk from extreme heat is a fast growing problem that will only worsen without further action to reduce emissions and provide cooling.”“Many climate change deniers and net zero opponents callously claim that heat-related deaths do not matter because of higher winter deaths, but all these lives matter,” said Bob Ward, of the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change at the London School of Economics.“Most of these cold- and heat-related deaths are preventable,” Ward said. “This is a shocking national scandal.”In the most recent year in the ONS data, the 2,805 heat-related deaths inEnglandand Wales were more than the 2,244 cold-related deaths.ChartEmma Howard Boyd, the chair of theNational Heat Risk Commission, said: “Behind these numbers are people, families and communities. The challenge now is to ensure that our homes, neighbourhoods, infrastructure and public services are better prepared to protect those most vulnerable.”The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, has beencriticised for a low-key responseto the summer heatwaves and the climate crisis, and formoving to cut electric vehicle salestargets and accept new North Sea oil and gas drilling.Government advisers at the Committee on Climate Change have long warned thecountry is not preparedfor the impact of the climate crisis. TheCCC saidin May that air conditioning should be installed in all hospitals and care homes within the next 10 years and in all schools within 25 years, and that the government should set a maximum temperature for indoor and outdoor working.In continental Europe, at least35,000 more people diedduring the baking hot summer than would normally be expected, according to figures available so far from barely half the continent.The heatwave that scorched western Europe in late June was themost severe and widespread ever recordedand was only possible due to the climate crisis driven by fossil fuel burning, scientists found. The World Health Organization said in May that heat-related mortality in its European region had increased by more than 30% over the past 20 years.Gareth Redmond-King, of the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, said: “If we don’t speed our way to net zero emissions – the only solution to bringing our climate back into balance – then this hot and dangerous summer will be one of the coolest of the rest of our lives.”The heat in 2027 will be further exacerbated by thesuper El Niñoweather system now building in the Pacific Ocean.Extreme heat more dangerous for people 60 and over than previously thoughtRead moreMillie Brown, of the Centre for Ageing Better, said the ONS statistics were “extremely worrying”. She said: “The threat of heatwaves is exacerbated by our ageing and poor-quality housing stock that heat up quicker and more intensely than homes in Europe. Often these homes are designed for a temperate climate that no longer exists.”The ONS data focused on the hottest 2.5% of hottest and coldest days, representing a range of about 0C to 20C. The researchers used a statistical model to estimate the relationship between temperature and mortality. This accounted for some factors that influence the risk of dying, such as air pollution, but not other including deprivation and household overcrowding.The minister for climate transition, Katie White, said:“These shocking figures represent thousands of families who have lost someone they love. We’re not waiting for climate change to arrive, we’re living in the middle of it, and this summer’s record-breaking heat has brought that home.“That’s why we’re taking some of the biggest action in a generation, preparing hospitals for extreme heat, rolling out air-to-air heat pumps to cool as well as heat homes, and accelerating clean homegrown power to tackle the root causes of climate change.”The Guardian’s climate forum 2026On Tuesday 20 October, join Damian Carrington and our panel of experts, including ProfAndy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman, for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening. Book ticketshereor atguardian.liveExplore more on these topicsExtreme heatExtreme weatherClimate crisisEnglandNHSOffice for National StatisticsGreenhouse gas emissionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘You can taste the ash’: surviving in America’s wildfire smoke capital | US news | The Guardian
description: A magical corner of Oregon has the highest US rate of wildfire smoke deaths. How do residents live with the haze – and grief?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A magical corner of Oregon has the highest US rate of wildfire smoke deaths. How do residents live with the haze – and grief?
Content: Sara on the property of her mother Joy’s art gallery, which is called It’s a Burl, in Kerby, Oregon.Photograph: Ricardo Nagaoka/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSara on the property of her mother Joy’s art gallery, which is called It’s a Burl, in Kerby, Oregon.Photograph: Ricardo Nagaoka/The GuardianUS news‘You can taste the ash’: surviving in America’s wildfire smoke capitalA magical corner of Oregon has the highest US rate of wildfire smoke deaths. How do residents live with the haze – and grief?John D Sutter with photographs by Ricardo NagaokaWed 26 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTShareDriving into the county, you can’t miss the sign.“IT’S THE CLIMATE”.The letters are so big they form an arch over 6th Street in Grants Pass.Locals tell me it’s a flex – or was before the irony set in. This evergreen corner ofOregon, near the California border, is a beautiful tangle of mountains and forest carved out by the Rogue and Illinois rivers. Once upon a time, the climatewasthe draw. Cool and wet in the winters, sunny but not too hot in the summers. The forests protected you from unbearable heat beyond the ridge.Now, you don’t hear the term summer much.Just “smoke season”.May-ish to October-ish.Across the US and Europe this summer, people have choked beneath red skies and endured extraordinarily unhealthy air – scenes that would be grimly familiar to anyone in the American west.Josephine county is the deadliest place for wildfire smoke in the US, according to a2025 studypublished in Nature magazine. It ties with Trinity county, California, as having the highest rate of wildfire smoke deaths linked to climate breakdown between 2006 and 2020, the years the researchers analyzed, with an estimated 17 premature deaths per 100,000 people.View image in fullscreenA neighborhood in Grants Pass, Oregon.Photograph: Ricardo Nagaoka/The GuardianEveryone here has a story about how bad it can get.They describe ash falling from the sky and coating their cars like snow. “You can taste it!” says Cynthia Hewitt, a retiree andrestaurant owner. When the smoke is particularly thick, she wets towels and wedges them around her doorframes to try to prevent the haze from coming into her living room. “It gets on the furniture and everything,” she says.Everything includes wine. If you taste certain bottles from bad smoke years, I’m told, that campfire tang clings to the grapes.Randi Maldonado, a beautician I met in a hair salon with two workers and three air purifiers, tries to calm her toddler’s lungs by sitting in the bathroom with the door closed and hot water roaring from the bathtub faucet. “Like a humidifier,” she says. It helps her child breathe.Her mother, Kim Williams, the other salon worker, tells me that her client’s husband died not long after leaving the windows open overnight during a wildfire smoke inundation.View image in fullscreenA sign downtown Grants Pass.A local nurse, Joann Reed, says the smoke has gotten so bad in recent years that even hospitals can’t keep it out. She recalls a summer, a few years ago now, when a hospital where she was working tasked employees with standing near exits, in part to shut doors as fast as possible. “You could see a smoke cloud, just a haze, as you walked up and down the hallways,” she tells me. “There’s no filtration system strong enough to get rid of that much constant smoke.”Some wear masks. Others wish they were brave enough to wear masks but they get tired of the stares from people who still see masks as code for “woke America”. (Josephine county is far more conservative than Oregon’s familiar “Portlandia” tropes. More than one person suggests to me that the way to solve the wildfire problem is to log or even clearcut the forest so there’s less of it to burn.)It is true that the area’s forests are thick, and its valleys are deep, trapping smoke in place for weeks or sometimes months at a time. “Socked in” is a phrase you hear a lot – as in, we’re just socked in with smoke.“We stay kind of like a convection oven,” says SusanAlbright, a family nurse practitioner who works at an urgent care in Grants Pass. “Everything just kind of stews.”View image in fullscreenSusan Albright, a family nurse practitioner at the urgent care clinic she works at.Throw in an aging population and high rates of poverty and you have a county that’s being ravaged not by one particularly bad fire but by years of insidious haze.I tell Joy Shinerock, who owns a woodworking art gallery along Redwood Highway, about the statistics – the high death rate, the worst in the nation.“Jeez,” she says.She pauses, and I imagine she’s thinking about her late husband, Harvey.“I can see why.”Here’s the thing: Despite the hazy red skies and smoky, 1970s-casino tinge of the air, Josephine county is an extremely lovable place – and it is loved fiercely by people like Joy.It’s kind of like the wood in Joy’s art gallery, which is calledIt’s a Burl.A burl – and I didn’t know this – is the knotty growth on the trunk or branch of a tree, sometimes caused by stress or disease. It’s a tumorous blob that can grow to the size of a car. Joy had just given birth to their youngest child, Sara (“It’s a girl!”), when her late husband named the place. Sara is a mother to two now, and the gallery’s manager.View image in fullscreenHolton Creek, next to the It’s A Burl gallery.I find Joy this afternoon in the back corner of her art gallery, an air purifier buzzes at her feet. She is wearing purple headphones and watching Korean soap operas while doing Sudoku and talking to me. She’s more gen Z-coded than most 78-year-olds.Behind her is a watercolor portrait of Harvey, her late husband. In it, he’s wearing overalls, his signature look, and peering over glasses. Harvey was a woodworker and started the gallery with Joy. He died during the summer of 2013 after the smoke rolled into the valley and his illness worsened.Their love is still palpable.“I couldn’t believe him. I just couldn’tbelievehim,” Joy says, still awestruck. “He was so easy. It seemed like I’d always sort of just struggled in relationships with people who were not really there.“He was just so grounded.”View image in fullscreenJoy in the backroom of her art gallery.They fell in love over art and moved to Oregon from California in 1987.Wildfireshad been flaring up more often in California, she says, and she wanted to get away from those. Oregon felt cooler and wetter – and therefore safer.There were cruel twists of fate on the way, though. In 1995, the gallery burned down in a chimney fire. The family was safe, but nearly all of their art was lost. With the help of neighbors, they rebuilt another gallery, home and woodshop. But the shop burned down a decade later – another accident – and then, while the family was trying to clean up brush to prevent another fire, the replacement shop didn’t burn down so much as melted in a third fire, Joy says.The experience had a way of bringing them closer to the community. The rebuilt gallery has stood for decades now, with countless burls carved into wizard faces watching visitors from the walls.When she’s at the gallery, Joy feels like Harvey is still here with her, too. “It’s his soul,” she says. His soul lives here among all this knotted wood.“People always tell me it’s magical,” she says.View image in fullscreenJoy holds a photograph of Joy and Harvey, her late husband.It’s not the flames that kill. It’s the smoke.The Camp Fire in Paradise, California, killed85 people. TheMaui fire killed 102.With far less attention, wildfire smokecontributed to an estimated 164,000 premature deathsin the US between 2006 and 2020, according to the same 2025 study in Nature.That’s an average of nearly 11,000 deaths per year.By 2050, if industry keeps warming the planet with such reckless abandon, that number is estimated to jump to70,000 Americanskilled by wildfire smoke per year.Lately, more attention is being paid to the ways smoke sickens wildland firefighters. The Trump administration last yearreverseda longstanding ban on members of the US Forest Service wearing masks on wildfire assignments. Masks are now being passed out to firefighters.In Josephine county, fires are coming straight to the people. They live inside plumes of smoke much of the time. And it’s getting worse as the climate crisis worsens.Between 2016 and 2025,Grants Pass saw 94 dayswith air that was unhealthy for sensitive groups or worse because of wildfire, according to data from the Oregon department of environmental quality. Compare that with only 16 days in the decade before, the data shows.View image in fullscreenLeft to right: a sign in-between Kerby and Grants Pass; one of the many fiberglass bears at the Grants Pass post office; ‘no burn’ signs on a tree in Grants Pass.Wildfire smoke burrows deep into the lungs, causing inflammation and in some cases choking off the ability to breathe. That makes people with COPD, asthma, allergies and congestive heart failure especially vulnerable. Local people say it can feel like someone is standing on your chest.Josephine county’s residents are doing their best. Officials drive through the more remote parts of the area – near Cave Junction, out by Joy – making megaphone announcements about evacuations, says Laura Mancuso, who started a local non-profit, Illinois Valley Wellness Resources, that distributes home air purifiers. Neighbors who don’t have solid mobile phone coverage, she says, have even banded together on a Citizens Band radio network to alert each other to fire danger.Chris Granville, 73, carries a handwritten note in her purse during wildfire season, warning people about her severe asthma and allergies that can cause her to temporarily stop breathing. “Allergy reaction,” the note says in purple ink. “Lose ability to talk. Have my own meds. Don’t call EMS. Allergic to their med. 20 minutes after I take meds, [I should] get voice back.”She tells me the note is important because she doesn’t want anyone to worry about her, and she trusts that she can revive herself with medicine without the hassle of an ambulance. The worst part about having to stay inside during smoke season? Chris is unable to volunteer, she says. She drivesotherseniors to appointments and to get groceries – and she worries about them needing her.View image in fullscreenSara, Joy’s daughter, weighing out a burl that a customer is purchasing.“I just want to show kindness,” she says. “I wish [the smoke] would go over the ocean where nobody is.”The smoke snuck up on them that summer.It was 2013, and Joy would look out the odd-shaped windows in their home and see Harvey asleep outside in a hammock while soup-thick smoke clung to the sides of the valley.Then there was the night-time cough. The cough – and an intense fatigue – had started in the late spring, before the summer fires, she says, but it deepened and started to rattle.Harvey went in and out of the hospital for tests, frustrated and sometimes leaving before he could get answers. By late summer, he entered the hospital for the final time.Diagnosis: pneumonia, according to Joy and their daughter, Sara. Both believe the wildfire smoke contributed to and accelerated the illness. They could hear his breathing deteriorate.View image in fullscreenAn air purifier inside Sara and Joy’s home, which is in the back of the gallery.“That fire seemed to go on forever,” Joy says.“It was apocalyptic,” says Sara.He died on 7 August.Doctors listed Harvey’s cause of death as sepsis, according to Sara. That may seem unrelated butwildfire smoke has been shownto weaken the immune system and increase risk of sepsis.It’s difficult to link any individual death to wildfire smoke exposure. Studies show that long-term exposure to wildfire smoke is unhealthy, and deadly, and is analogous to smoking cigarettes. To die from wildfire smoke, quite often, is to be pushed there by illness combined with smoke.Sara and Joy both believe Harvey died too soon because of the wildfires.How do we still love our home when it’s dangerous? When there are cancerous knots in the wood?Joy doesn’t talk about it much, but she has congenital heart failure and a heart arrhythmia. She knows the smoke is extra-risky for her, just as it was for Harvey.View image in fullscreenJoy watching soap operas at her desk.She checks the weather. There’s still that wildfire one county over – called the East Evans Creek Fire. Her fire-watch app shows a patchwork of red and orange evacuation zones. It’s not visible from the gallery, but a cauliflower cloud of smoke has been blooming on the horizon.The next afternoon, that smoke is still rising unseen in the distance. The evacuation zone grows. The sky remains blue above the gallery, though, and classic rock is on the radio.A woman in high-waisted shorts and a crop top walks into the back. She’s on vacation for a friend’s 50th birthday and snuck away for the afternoon to make a trip to the Oregon coast.“I just stumbled across this, and – I mean – every single inch of this entire space is just filled with creativity and magic and love,” the visitor tells Joy. “I’m just like, ‘Wow, this kind of place exists.’“It’s a reminder that there is real magic still in the world.”Joy smiles.She agrees.John D Sutter is an assistant professor of environmental media at the University of Oregon, as well as an independent climate journalist and film-maker. He lives in Eugene, Oregon

title: Mood-boosting benefits of birdsong drowned out by traffic noise, study finds | Birds | The Guardian
description: Even low levels of traffic noise can negate the benefits of listening to natural sounds, researchers say
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Even low levels of traffic noise can negate the benefits of listening to natural sounds, researchers say
Content: Bird song has previously been associated with lowering stress and positive mood changes.Photograph: Toby Houlton/AlamyView image in fullscreenBird song has previously been associated with lowering stress and positive mood changes.Photograph: Toby Houlton/AlamyBirdsMood-boosting benefits of birdsong drowned out by traffic noise, study findsEven low levels of traffic noise can negate the benefits of listening to natural sounds, researchers sayNatalie WintWed 26 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHearing the trill or whistle of a bird while going about daily life is well known to boost people’s mood. But a new study suggests thepsychological benefits of hearing birdsongare being threatened by traffic noise.Researchers found that even low levels of traffic noise negatively affected the benefits to wellbeing that could otherwise be derived from listening to natural sounds.Bird song haspreviouslybeen associated with psychological benefits, including stress reduction and positive mood changes, while noise from traffic has been linked to both stress and annoyance.“Bird sounds tend to be one of the elements of nature soundscapes that people perceive as being most relaxing, most pleasant, beneficial for them psychologically,” said Dr Eleanor Ratcliffe, associate professor in environmental psychology at the University of Surrey, and co-author of the studypublishedin People and Nature.View image in fullscreenListening to birdsong was found to have a psychological benefit.Photograph: Denis Thorpe/The GuardianThe study involved more than 1,500 participants who listened to nine simulated soundscapes consisting of both birdsong and traffic noise and were asked questions about how they made them feel.“We set up the study with the interest of looking at these differences in the objective properties of the soundscape, these levels of acoustic complexity that relate to different levels of biodiversity,” Ratcliffe said. “And our hypothesis was that these would lead to different effects on wellbeing and restoration and stress recovery.”Gen Z flocks to BirdTok as birding takes flight: ‘It’s a craving for something real’Read moreHowever, listening to birdsong was found to have a psychological benefit, irrespective of its acoustic characteristics. “It shows us that we should support and protect nature for the sake of nature, regardless of whether or not humans have some increased utility benefit from it,” said Ratcliffe.In comparison, the presence of traffic noise negatively affected the psychological benefits of nature’s sounds. Analysis of complementary heart rate measurements on a group of participants showed significantly lower variability for those listening to soundscapes including traffic noise, indicating a greater physiological stress response.View image in fullscreenNoise from traffic has been linked to stress and annoyance.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAThe negative effect was found to be more evident when the acoustic characteristics of soundscapes were at high levels, something which may be attributed to overstimulation.Researchers also analysed how differently aged participants responded. Younger participants reported higher feelings of wellbeing than their older peers, something suggested to result from their better hearing and enhanced acoustic experience.Interestingly, the researchers found that greater feelings of wellbeing were recorded when participants perceived greater diversity in the types of birds they were listening to. This increased for participants who claimed greater knowledge of birds, suggesting perceptions of bird species richness may boost the benefits.The work has design implications, the researchers said. “With urban planning now including more green spaces it is important that steps are taken so that people enjoy such areas to their fullest,” said Ratcliffe.Suggested measures to minimise traffic noise include reducing speed limits and increasing the density of ground-level vegetation around parks. The study also has implications at an individual level. “Listening to birds is quite an accessible way to engage with nature. So, I think it’s something that people can do without a lot of effort,” she added.Explore more on these topicsBirdsMental healthAnimalsHealthWildlifeRoad transportAccess to green spacenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Pack of lies’: Robert Jenrick launches personal attack on Kemi Badenoch | Robert Jenrick | The Guardian
description: Reform MP seeks to heap pressure on Tory leader amid confusion around details of meeting with Giorgia Meloni
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Reform MP seeks to heap pressure on Tory leader amid confusion around details of meeting with Giorgia Meloni
Content: Robert Jenrick has described his former boss as a fantasist.Photograph: Victoria Jones/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRobert Jenrick has described his former boss as a fantasist.Photograph: Victoria Jones/ShutterstockRobert Jenrick‘Pack of lies’: Robert Jenrick launches personal attack on Kemi BadenochReform MP seeks to heap pressure on Tory leader amid confusion around details of meeting with Giorgia MeloniBen Quinnand Amelia Casey-RerhayeWed 26 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 16.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRobert Jenrick has accused Kemi Badenoch of telling “a pack of lies” about her meeting with the Italian prime minister,Giorgia Meloni, as he launched a deeply personal attack on his former boss.TheReform UKMP sought to heap pressure on the Conservative leader amid confusion about whether Meloni urged Badenoch at a meeting in Rome to “be her own woman” and resist doing a deal with his party.A Conservative spokesperson denied the party had suggested the Italian leader made such comments, after the Times initially reported she had. This was later removed from the newspaper’s report.Jenrick described the leader of his former party as a fantasist. “It was obviously very, very embarrassing forKemi Badenoch. My advice, if you go and visit a foreign leader, is don’t make up a pack of lies about what they say,” said Jenrick, who defected to Reform this year after losing out to Badenoch in a leadership contest.View image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch met Giorgia Meloni for an hour in Rome on Monday.Photograph: @KemiBadenoch/Twitter/XThe Tory leader met the Italian prime minister for an hour in a cafe in Rome on Monday morning and in a post on X afterwards she praised the handling of the Italian economy by Meloni, whose own Brothers of Italy party is underpressure from a new rival.A spokesperson for Badenoch denied theConservativeshad made any false claims about the Meloni meeting, saying Reform was “just making things up” and “peddling conspiracy theories to distract [people]”. They went on to refer to the £5m gift the Reform leader, Nigel Farage, received from the Thailand-based businessman Christopher Harborne.Jenrick said: “As regards Kemi, look, we could tell she was making it up. She lives in a fantasy of her own making. She made up that she got a degree offer from an American university for her CV, she claims she is going to be the next prime minister. There is a lot of fantasies going on at the moment in Kemi’s life.”The university comment was a reference toa previous claimthat Badenoch received an offer from Stanford University at the age of 16, which became the subject of controversy after former admissions staff said she had described an impossible scenario.Jenrick and Badenoch featured in fresh claims this week that she had plotted with fellow Conservative cabinet ministers toremove Rishi Sunakas prime minister months before the general election.A new book by Anthony Seldon alleges that after Jenrickresigned as immigration ministerin 2023 over the details of Sunak’s plan to deport asylum seekers to Rwanda, Badenoch discussed telling Sunak she would resign from the cabinet if he did not amend the policy, with some people recounting she “had promised she would ‘take him out’”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJenrick was speaking at an event in London where he announced a raft of polices including plans to scrap Britain’s data protection laws and widen a tax-relief scheme for investors in small businesses in the UK in an attempt to allow relatives to claim advantages more easily.People on calls to HMRC who are left on hold for more than half an hour would get a £30 credit off their tax bill under Reform, Jenrick pledged, and he also announced plans to scrap the mandate for all new car and van sales to be zero-emission by 2035. “Let white van men choose the vehicle that they want to drive for their businesses,” he said.Labour criticised Reform’s plans to replace GDPR with a “light-touch” privacy law modelled on New Zealand’s. “Robert Jenrick can’t say which important data safeguards he would scrap and whether it would put people’s personal details at risk. He’s making it up as he goes along,” a Labour spokesperson said.Explore more on these topicsRobert JenrickKemi BadenochConservativesReform UKGiorgia MeloninewsShareReuse this content

title: Inquest opens into death of former Cambridge professor Jason Arday | Jason Arday | The Guardian
description: Academic was found unresponsive by family members, inquest told, as coroner adjourns proceedings to later date
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: Academic was found unresponsive by family members, inquest told, as coroner adjourns proceedings to later date
Content: Floral tributes left at the University of Cambridge for Jason Arday.Photograph: Chris Radburn/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFloral tributes left at the University of Cambridge for Jason Arday.Photograph: Chris Radburn/AFP/Getty ImagesJason ArdayInquest opens into death of former Cambridge professor Jason ArdayAcademic was found unresponsive by family members, inquest told, as coroner adjourns proceedings to later dateHaroon SiddiqueLegal affairs correspondentWed 26 Aug 2026 09.44 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 15.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA coroner has formally opened an inquest into the death of Jason Arday, whoresigned as a professor at the University of Cambridgeamid allegations of plagiarism.Arday, 41, died at his home in Battersea, south London on 14 August, nine days after his resignation. Family members watched the 10-minute hearing at London inner south coroner’s court via a video link.The senior coroner, Dr Julian Morris, said: “London ambulance service and the Met police attended the home address after he’d been found unresponsive by returning family members. Sadly, despite resuscitative efforts, he was pronounced dead at the scene. The Met police confirmed that the scene was not suspicious.”He said that given the circumstances, he would launch an investigation into Arday’s death, adjourning the inquest until an unspecified later date.Morris also implored the media to be “mindful of your reporting” and to have regard for Arday’s family and the public.There has been an intense debate over media handling of the allegations against Arday, with his family and supporters highly critical of the coverage and others defending it. In a statement announcing his resignation, Arday said he was driven to resign because the “relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love”.Arday was appointed professor of sociology of education at Cambridge in 2023, when he became the university’s youngest-ever black professor. He said he had been nonverbal until the age of 11, requiring extensive speech and language therapy, as well as being illiterate until 18.Arday resigned after accusations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career and achievements.He was initially accused of plagiarising another academic’s work for his PhD thesis. But he denied the accusations, and an investigation by Liverpool John Moores University earlier this year upheld its decision to award him a PhD.In a statement, Arday’s family condemned what they said was a “campaign of misinformation” against him and described him as an “amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son”.They added: “We won’t comment further at this point beyond asking the press to leave us alone now, and to stop the campaign of harassment which has been waged against Jason and his family for too long.”Explore more on these topicsJason ArdayRace in educationUniversitiesRaceHigher educationUniversity of CambridgenewsShareReuse this content

title: Devon man becomes first person to swim Switzerland’s 10 largest lakes | Swimming | The Guardian
description: Neil Gilson completes 230-mile challenge after a ‘tough’ 22-hour crossing of Lac Léman
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Neil Gilson completes 230-mile challenge after a ‘tough’ 22-hour crossing of Lac Léman
Content: Neil Gilson has become the first person to swim the 10 largest lakes in Switzerland, a total of about 230 miles.Photograph: Jamie HancockView image in fullscreenNeil Gilson has become the first person to swim the 10 largest lakes in Switzerland, a total of about 230 miles.Photograph: Jamie HancockSwimmingDevon man becomes first person to swim Switzerland’s 10 largest lakesNeil Gilson completes 230-mile challenge after a ‘tough’ 22-hour crossing of Lac LémanSteven MorrisWed 26 Aug 2026 09.58 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe staggered rather than sprang out of the lake but it wasn’t surprising.Neil Gilson, a former international athlete, could be forgiven for feeling a little wobbly, having become the first person to swim the 10 largest lakes in Switzerland, a total of about 230 miles (370km).Over the last two summers, Gilson, a father of three from Devon in the English West Country, has ticked the lakes off and on Wednesdayhe finished swimming the 45-mile lengthof Lac Léman (Lake Geneva), taking just over 22 hours.His 12-year-old daughter, Lily, and 10-year-old son, Jack, were in the water waiting as he neared the end to accompany him across the finishing line.“They swam the last 200m with me,” Gilson said. “There were tears in my goggles. For the whole challenge, I was envisioning that moment. It kept me going through some difficult times – lovely.”Gilson, 40, was once ranked second in Britain for the 1500-metre freestyle and after finishing race swimming,turned to endurance challenges.In 2024, he swam across Lac Léman in 22 hours and nine minutes, a world record. But it wasn’t enough. He decided to tackle 10 Swiss lakes.View image in fullscreenNeil Gilson, seen here on Sandy Cove beach, trained for his Swiss lakes challenge in the sea off North Devon.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianGilson put in countless hours in the pool at a leisure centre, the sea off the northDevoncoast and the gym to prepare.There have been blips. Gilson admits that a swim of about 40 miles in Lake Maggiore this summer almost broke him. It was colder than he anticipated and he had to swim more quickly to get his core temperature up, which meant he used more energy than planned. He had “nothing left” for the last few miles.Lake Thun proved surprisingly difficult as the pressure to complete the challenge – and the physical effort – caught up with him. After clambering out of the lake, he said: “My arms don’t like me and I feel shattered.”Gilson said he found swimming in lakes more demanding than the sea. “They’re more unpredictable. You can get some really choppy conditions because of the wind and you can hit walls of cold water.”He began Léman on Tuesday morning and finished on Wednesday lunchtime. He admitted that 18 hours into the swim, he thought of giving up. “It was so tough in the night – the current was strong. I felt really close to stopping but what kept me going was my family waiting there.”View image in fullscreenNeil Gilson’s support team said ‘the right things’ to keep him going, he said.Photograph: Jamie HancockGilson said his support team, which accompanied him in a boat, helped by giving him coffee – and saying “the right things”.He just missed out on beating his own world record for Léman, but is confidentGuinness World Recordswill recognise him as the first to complete what has been billed the Legend of the Lakes challenge – and in subsequent years, that other ultra-swimmers may try to do it more quickly.As well as doing the swim as an extraordinary challenge, Gilson is seeking to draw attention to a neuropsychiatric condition, Pandas, that affected his son at 18 months old. People withPans or Pandasexperience a variety of symptoms ranging from mental health symptoms to changes in behaviour and difficulties with movement.Jack was diagnosed with Pandas after catching tonsillitis. “He went to bed a happy, healthy little boy, and woke up as someone we didn’t recognise, gripped by aggression, OCD [obsessive-compulsive disorder], tics and intense fear; he refused to eat, wouldn’t leave the house or even speak. It was terrifying,” Gilson said.Jack is doing well – as shown by his joining his dad for the last leg of his swim – but Gilson said: “The challenge has always been about more than swimming. Every lake, every kilometre and every difficult moment has been about raising awareness of Pans and Pandas.“It’s a condition that isn’t rare but is rarely diagnosed. Raising awareness of it means more than anything.”Explore more on these topicsSwimmingSwitzerlandDevonEnglandEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Flight attendant’s breast cancer was occupational disease, court rules | Breast cancer | The Guardian
description: Sophie Lainault, who worked for Air France, wins legal case linking illness to more than 12,600 hours on flights
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Sophie Lainault, who worked for Air France, wins legal case linking illness to more than 12,600 hours on flights
Content: Sophie Lainault began working as a flight attendant for Air France in 1989.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSophie Lainault began working as a flight attendant for Air France in 1989.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto/ShutterstockBreast cancerFlight attendant’s breast cancer was occupational disease, court rulesSophie Lainault, who worked for Air France, wins legal case linking illness to more than 12,600 hours on flightsAgence France-Presse in ParisWed 26 Aug 2026 10.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 18.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA flight attendant inFrancehas succeeded in having her breast cancer recognised as an occupational disease, a first for the country’s aviation industry, her lawyer and a trade union said.The ruling, which recognised that Sophie Lainault, a former flight attendant forAir France, had frequently worked at night and been exposed to passive smoking, could pave the way for similar claims, the lawyer and the CFDT union said.Lainault, from Anglet in south-west France, told the news agency AFP that she hoped her legal victory could help other women.“It is truly my dearest wish that this opens the way for other women who might not have dared until now,” the 59-year-old said.Now in remission, Lainault said she worked for Air France, the country’s flagship carrier, between 1989 and 2019 as a flight attendant and later as a purser on long-haul flights, accumulating more than 12,600 flight hours, including more than 6,500 at night.PBS should fund drug to treat breast cancer, endometriosis and gender dysphoria, experts recommendRead moreThe ruling, seen by AFP, came from a court in the city of Bayonne in early July and recognised the occupational origin of Lainault’s cancer.The court highlighted the role of night work, exposure to ionising radiation and passive smoking. Smoking was permitted on Air France flights until 2000.Two regional committees responsible for recognising occupational diseases had previously concluded that no link had been established.Breast canceris not included in France’s official list of occupational diseases, meaning that obtaining recognition can be a lengthy and difficult ordeal for patients.Lainault said that she had fought for two-and-a-half years for the recognition, supported by CFDT activists. She said the ruling would allow her to take early retirement.Lainault’s lawyer, Elisabeth Leroux, said the court decision set a legal precedent. The ruling was final and no appeal had been lodged, she added.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSome studies have suggested that women who regularly work night shifts may face a higher risk of developing cancer.Air France said it “was not a party to the proceedings and has not been informed of the court’s reasoning”.The airline said: “The health and safety of employees at work is an absolute priority.”In 2023, a French nurse who had worked night shifts for 28 years and been exposed to radiation succeeded in havingher breast cancer recognisedas an occupational disease.With nearly 13,000 deaths each year, breast cancer is the deadliest cancer among women in France.Explore more on these topicsBreast cancerAir transportFranceWorkers' rightsWork & careersEuropeAir France/KLMnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mpox is back – and in new countries. How can this outbreak be contained? | Global health | The Guardian
description: The public health emergencies in 2022 and 2024 saw the virus reported in 145 countries, but in the new cases children appear particularly affected
Author: Kat Lay
Headline: The public health emergencies in 2022 and 2024 saw the virus reported in 145 countries, but in the new cases children appear particularly affected
Content: A man infected with mpox at a hospital in Burundi.Photograph: Tchandrou Nitanga/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA man infected with mpox at a hospital in Burundi.Photograph: Tchandrou Nitanga/AFP/Getty ImagesGlobal healthMpox is back – and in new countries. How can this outbreak be contained?The public health emergencies in 2022 and 2024 saw the virus reported in 145 countries, but in the new cases children appear particularly affectedSupported byAbout this contentKat LayGlobal health correspondentWed 26 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 11.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA fresh outbreak of mpoxin Guinea Bissau– the country’s first – means the virus formerly known as monkey pox is back in the headlines. So what has changed?Since 2022, there have beenalmost 190,000 lab-confirmed casesof mpox reported worldwide in 145 countries. Before then, outbreaks of mpox tended to be relatively small and in a handful of African countries, where the viral infection was known to be endemic.What is mpox?Mpox is an infectious disease that typically starts with flu-like symptoms, including fever, chills and aching muscles. These are followed by a distinctive rash, beginning as raised spots that turn into blisters filled with fluid before forming scabs.View image in fullscreenA colourised electron microscope image shows Mpox virus particles, represented in green, found within infected cultured cells, represented in blue. The virus particles are in various stages of maturity, which accounts for their differences in shape.Photograph: APIt used to be called monkeypox, because the virus was first discovered in captive monkeys in 1958. But during an international outbreak in 2022, there were concerns that the name was fuelling racist and stigmatising language on and offline, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to recommendchanging it to mpox.It is endemic to many parts of Africa, with outbreaks historically starting when people ate meat from infected wild animals. But in recent years it has spread beyond the usual areas, with sustained chains of human-to-human transmission. The Atlanta-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said this month that mpox wason course to become endemic in the US.Why is it spreading to new countries?There are, broadly, two types of mpox, known as “clades”. Clade I was once called the “Congo Basin clade” and clade II the “West African clade”.The latter sparked a major global outbreak in 2022 when it appeared to undergo some changes that allowed it to spread more efficiently from person to person. It is passed on via close contact – in that outbreak, mostly by sexual contact, with men who have sex with menat the highest risk.View image in fullscreenA Red Cross worker disinfects a tent in the Don Bosco camps for internally displaced people in Goma, in the Democratic Republic of Congo.Photograph: Moise Kasereka/EPAIn June 2024, researchersraised the alarmabout a new variant of clade I in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), which also appeared to be spreading more easily between people. That grew into another major international outbreak, which was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the WHO on 14 August 2024.“Emergence of mpox in more countries in west Africa is to be expected,” said Prof Michael Marks, of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine and University College London hospital. “Mpox outbreaks have now been declared in a number of countries in the region, including Guinea and Sierra Leone within the last 12 months.“Mpox spreads by close physical contact. This makes it suitable to spread in a variety of different contexts, such as in close sexual networks, as was seen during the 2022 global pandemic, or areas where many people are living closely together such as settings with refugees and internally displaced people, as was seen in the DRC outbreak over the last few years,” Marks said.What happened to those two big outbreaks?The 2022 outbreak was declared a public health emergency in July that year. After contact-tracing and mass vaccination programmes, the status was lifted in May 2023. There had been about 90,000 infections.View image in fullscreenA passenger passes mpox alerts at Chennai airport in India.Photograph: R Satish Babu/AFPThe 2024 outbreak had its international public health emergency statuslifted in September 2025, not because the disease had disappeared but because numbers of cases and deaths were declining and officials felt the situation had become better controlled.If genetic testing reveales a new variant, or surveillance suggested an outbreak was spreading particularly fast, making people particularly sick or proving more deadly, global health authorities would be likely to step in again.How worrying is the new outbreak?Cases had not been reported in Guinea Bissau before this outbreak. Unicef said it was concerned that of 46 suspected cases, 23 were children aged under 15 and most of those were aged under four.“The concern about children is that they are at the highest risk of severe disease and death from mpox,” said Dr Aula Abbara, a senior lecturer at Imperial College London and adviser to Médecins Sans Frontières UK. “Young children can become much sicker than healthy adults.”View image in fullscreenFuraha Elisabeth applies medication to the skin of her child, Sagesse Hakizimana, at a health centre near Goma, in the DRC.Photograph: Arlette Bashizi/ReutersHowever, she cautioned that the apparent over-representation of children in the outbreak data should be interpreted carefully. She said: “There may also be some bias in the data. Families are often more likely to seek healthcare for a sick child than for an adult, particularly in a resource-constrained setting with a fragile health system, such as Guinea-Bissau.”Marks added: “Children have close physical contact with their parents and with each other, and in settings such as Guinea-Bissau are often living in cramped conditions, which make close physical contact and transmission more likely.”Confirmed cases do not appear linked to each other, which suggests the virus is circulating more widely in the community and there are unidentified cases.Are there vaccines and treatments?The WHOrecommends two vaccines, which can be given to people at high risk or offered to people who have been in contact with a known case to prevent further spread. The question is where they are available.Marks said: “The major challenge remains that supplies of vaccines are best in high-income countries but worst in low-income settings, where the need and conditions for mpox transmission are highest.”A new global stockpile isdue to be launchedwithin weeks, which should mean vaccines can be deployed more rapidly to quell outbreaks. Officials also hope it will allow manufacturers to plan ahead and produce more of the jabs by providing a clear, concrete demand.View image in fullscreenA young mpox patient receives treatment at the Kavumu hospital in Karanrhada, in the Democratic Republic of Congo.Photograph: Michael Lunanga/EPAAn antiviral called tecovirimatdid not appear any better than a placebowhen tested on patients with mpox clade I in the DRC, although the question of whether it might help some immunocompromised patients – such as those living with HIV – remains open. That trial did show, however, that giving patients good, supportive care dramatically improved their chances of survival.While vaccines remained an important tool for outbreak control, basic supportive care could be lifesaving, Abbara said. She added that strengthening surveillance, testing, contact tracing and broader public health measures would be critical to understanding and containing the outbreak.“Vaccines are important, but outbreaks are not controlled by vaccines alone,” she said. “Early detection, contact tracing, supportive care and strong public health surveillance remain absolutely essential.”Explore more on these topicsGlobal healthMpoxGuinea-BissauInfectious diseasesWorld Health OrganizationHealthMicrobiologynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Escape wizard’ who has broken out of four prisons is arrested in Spain | Spain | The Guardian
description: Albanian criminal has cut bars, descended sheets and even used human pyramid in escapes in Italy and Belgium
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Albanian criminal has cut bars, descended sheets and even used human pyramid in escapes in Italy and Belgium
Content: Toma Taulant, who was serving a prison sentence due to end in 2048, escaped from a maximum-security prison in Milan eight months ago.Photograph: SFM Press Reporter/AlamyView image in fullscreenToma Taulant, who was serving a prison sentence due to end in 2048, escaped from a maximum-security prison in Milan eight months ago.Photograph: SFM Press Reporter/AlamySpain‘Escape wizard’ who has broken out of four prisons is arrested in SpainAlbanian criminal has cut bars, descended sheets and even used human pyramid in escapes in Italy and BelgiumSam Jonesin MadridWed 26 Aug 2026 12.22 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 18.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice in Spain have arrested a dangerous Albanian criminal nicknamed the “escape wizard” who has managed to break out of four jails inItalyand Belgium by sawing through bars, clambering down knotted sheets and even using a human pyramid to breach prison walls.The fugitive, who has not been officially named, was arrested after officers from the Policía Nacional force discovered he was living in the north-eastern Spanish city of Tarragona. He was the subject of a European arrest warrant issued by the Italian authorities.Spanish police identified the man by the initials TT, which correspond to those of Toma Taulant, an Albanian national known in Italian media as the“mago della fuga”, or “escape wizard”.Before escaping from a maximum-security prison in Milan eight months ago, he was serving a prison sentence due to end in 2048 for a series of offences including violent robbery, theft and drug dealing, according to Italian media reports cited by Agence France-Presse.“It sounds like something out of a film, but sometimes reality is stranger than fiction,” the Policía Nacional said in a statement that described him as “the master of escapes”.“He escaped from a jail in [the Umbrian city of] Terni in 2009, from a jail in Parma in 2013 and from a Belgian prison that same year after using a human pyramid to climb over the wall,” the police said. “His latest escape, in December 2025, came after he managed to break out of a maximum-security prison in Italy after sawing through the bars and climbing out of the window down knotted sheets.”According to the statement, the “very dangerous” fugitive was arrested in Tarragona last Friday, putting up “strong and active resistance” as officers swooped.“The man was accompanied by a number of his compatriots who tried to stop him being arrested, including one man who struck and injured two officers,” the force said. Police are still looking for the assailant but have recovered a Sig Sauer pistol that was discarded by one of the suspect’s associates.Once in custody, the man was found to be in possession of fake identity documents, which revealed that he had a criminal record in the Catalan city of Girona for possession of weapons and explosives. He was also found to be carrying two €500 banknotes that are thought to have been counterfeited, which have been sent to the Bank ofSpainfor investigation.The suspect was denied bail and has been remanded in custody at a jail in Tarragona while he awaits extradition to Italy.Explore more on these topicsSpainItalyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Wiped out: US faces surging toilet paper prices amid trade war with Canada | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: Paper products among hardest-hit sectors after trade negotiations broke down, with 25-50% tariffs estimated
Author: Lauren Aratani
Headline: Paper products among hardest-hit sectors after trade negotiations broke down, with 25-50% tariffs estimated
Content: A customer picks up a pack of toilet paper from a store shelf in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, on 2 March 2025.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA customer picks up a pack of toilet paper from a store shelf in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, on 2 March 2025.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesTrump tariffsWiped out: US faces surging toilet paper prices amid trade war with CanadaPaper products among hardest-hit sectors after trade negotiations broke down, with 25-50% tariffs estimatedAre you a Canadian boycotting US products? We’d like to hear from youLauren Arataniin New YorkWed 26 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUsing the bathroom or having a cry is about to become more expensive for North Americans as theUSandCanadaenter a full-fledged trade war that threatens to flush away decades of peaceful trading between the two nations.After trade negotiationsbroke downbetween the two countrieslast weekend, Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister,vowedto match US tariffs “dollar for dollar” andunveiledalistof nearly 900 American goods that will face 25% to 50% tariffs starting on 8 September.Paper products are among the hardest-hit sectors, withCanadathreatening to put tariffs of between 25% and 50% on “toilet paper or face tissue stock” from 8 September in retaliation for a 50% hike from Washington DC.Though American toilet paper and tissues are often made domestically, theyheavily relyon lumber-rich Canada for raw materials. Procter & Gamble, the owner of Charmin toilet paper,saidlast year that it would have to increase prices amid tariffs that were in place at the time.Canada announces retaliatory tariffs on wide range of US goodsRead moreThe US imported $328m worth of toilet paper from Canada in 2024, according to theWorld Bank, making it by far the largest exporter of the product to the US. Retailersincluding Costcosource much of their paper products from the country.The US accounts for more than 20% of global tissue consumption despite having only 4% of the world’s population. The average Americanuses 141 rollsof toilet paper per year, making them No 1 for No 2s globally, just ahead of Germans, each using an average of 134 rolls annually.It’s not just paper products that could rise in price.
