Thetrade warhighlights the deep economic ties shared between the two countries as consumers continue to worry about inflation on both sides of the border.US tariffsare specifically affecting Canadian liquor, including popular whiskey brands Crown Royal and Canadian Club, which are currently under a 50% tariff.While Canada has not introduced a tariff on American liquor, most Canadian provinces have introduced their own bans on American alcohol, in retaliation for earlier tariffs on Canadian products.Donald Trumpused these province-wide bans on American alcohol as part of hislegal justificationfor his new tariffs against Canada.Carney has asked province leaders to consider putting American liquor back on the shelves, though as the Nova Scotia premier Tim HoustontoldCBC News: “Whether Nova Scotians or Canadians will actually buy it when it’s back on the shelves, that’s a whole other discussion.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrump announces new 50% tariff on Canadian cars, trucks and steelRead moreTrump also said that his new tariffs are in retaliation for Canadian levies against theAmerican dairy industry. Heintroduceda 50% tariff on nearly all Canadian dairy products, with the exception of Canadian cheese.In response, Canada has a 50% tariff on American dairy products, along with a 25% tariff on American cheese.Canada also took a swing at the US fishing industry, with a 25% tariff on American fish and seafood, including frozen lobster. The move prompted Republican senator Susan Collins, facing a tough re-election battle in lobster-capital Maine, to call Trump’s latest move“a mistake”.A 25%tariff on Canadian cars and auto partsis set to affect the American auto industry, which relies heavily on Canadian parts for manufacturing. Trump has threatened todouble the tariffto 50% if a deal isn’t made by 1 January 2027.With negotiations down the drain, it’s unclear if or when the tariffs will be lifted. But the Trump administration is adamant that“there’s no possible way”the trade dispute with Canada will affect US consumers, according to Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative.“The fundamentals are good,” he said. “I don’t think this is going to affect anything.”Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsCanadaMark CarneyDonald TrumpAmericasTariffsTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Women using HRT at lower risk of dementia, study suggests | Dementia | The Guardian
description: Scientists found those who had used hormone replacement therapy were 10% less likely to be diagnosed with dementia
Author: Hannah Devlin
Headline: Scientists found those who had used hormone replacement therapy were 10% less likely to be diagnosed with dementia
Content: The study tracked more than 180,000 postmenopausal women over an average of 13 years.Photograph: Anchiy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe study tracked more than 180,000 postmenopausal women over an average of 13 years.Photograph: Anchiy/Getty ImagesDementiaWomen using HRT at lower risk of dementia, study suggestsScientists found those who had used hormone replacement therapy were 10% less likely to be diagnosed with dementiaHannah DevlinScience correspondentWed 26 Aug 2026 09.16 EDTFirst published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 08.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHormone replacement therapy may reduce the risk of dementia, a study has found.Scientists tracked more than 180,000 postmenopausal women in the UK in the largest study of its kind. They found that those who had used HRT were 10% less likely to develop any type of dementia and 16% less likely to be diagnosed with Alzheimer’s, the most common form, compared with those who had never used it.The greatest reduction was seen in women using HRT who had undergone surgical menopause, with a 26% lower risk of developing any type of dementia compared with non‑users.Prof Anne-Marie Minihane, the director of the Norwich Institute for Healthy Ageing at the University of East Anglia, who led the study, said: “While HRT has long been prescribed primarily to relieve menopausal symptoms such as hot flushes and night sweats, this work suggests it may also play a role in long‑term cognitive health for some women.”Women are more likely to develop dementia than men because they live longer. It may also be related to the effects of menopause on brain metabolism and the impact of the main risk gene for Alzheimer’s,Apoe4, being greater on women.Minihane said: “We wanted to better understand how HRT could prevent dementia and to assess if particular groups of women may respond differently.”Can antihistamines really help with PMDD and menopausal symptoms?Read moreUsing data from the UK Biobank, 183,450 postmenopausal women were tracked over an average of 13 years, during which time almost 4,000 cases of dementia were identified. The scientists looked at whether using HRT of any kind for at least one year changed women’s risk of developing dementia.Women who naturally had lower oestrogen exposure during their lifetime, owing to starting their periods late or early menopause, seemed to benefit more from HRT, with a 16% lower risk of any type of dementia.Genetics also played a role. The associations between HRT use and dementia were stronger in women who carried the Apoe4 gene variant. “This is really important because Apoe4 carriers are typically considered at higher risk and have fewer established prevention options,” said Minihane.The findings, published in the journal Alzheimer’s &Dementia, come with the caveat that they are based on observational data rather than being the gold standard randomised-controlled trial, so it is not possible to prove a causal link.Those using HRT had a higher average level of education than non-users, for instance. Although socioeconomic factors were taken into account in the analysis, it is still possible that differences between the two groups aside from HRT influenced dementia risk.Dr Susan Kohlhaas, the executive director of research and partnerships at Alzheimer’s Research UK, said: “This study alone isn’t enough to tell us whether HRT should be used to reduce dementia risk, but it provides further evidence that the timing of HRT and a woman’s hormonal history may matter.“We now need research that can establish whether HRT itself is responsible for these differences in dementia risk and understand which forms of HRT may have an effect.“Anyone considering starting or stopping HRT should speak to their GP about the potential benefits and risks for them.”Explore more on these topicsDementiaAlzheimer'sWomenHealthMenopauseWomen's healthMedical researchnewsShareReuse this content

title: London rollout of robotaxis delayed amid lack of guidance for firms to follow | Self-driving cars | The Guardian
description: Uber and Wayve had said they would start trips ‘later this summer’ but launch now looks unlikely this year
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Uber and Wayve had said they would start trips ‘later this summer’ but launch now looks unlikely this year
Content: A Wayve autonomous car. Wayve and Uber have said more than 100,000 Londoners are on their waiting list for self-driving taxis.Photograph: tim@timandrew.co.uk/WayveView image in fullscreenA Wayve autonomous car. Wayve and Uber have said more than 100,000 Londoners are on their waiting list for self-driving taxis.Photograph: tim@timandrew.co.uk/WayveSelf-driving carsLondon rollout of robotaxis delayed amid lack of guidance for firms to followUber and Wayve had said they would start trips ‘later this summer’ but launch now looks unlikely this yearBusiness live – latest updatesMark SweneyWed 26 Aug 2026 04.48 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe rollout of robotaxis on the streets ofLondonis unlikely to happen this year, as regulatory and technical hurdles push back the ambitious schedule set out by the UK government.Only weeks ago Uber and London-based Wayve were granted the first minicab licences in the capital to allow them to offer self-driving taxi rides to paying customers – but with a human safety driver in place, for now – and said they would start trips“later this summer” before a full public launch.In 2025, Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, accelerated the proposed timeline for commercial trials of fully driverless taxi services by a year, announcing that they would start in the spring of this year.However, progress has slowed in recent months and Transport for London (TfL) has still not published the guidance that companies wanting to offer services must follow to win its approval.Last month, Christina Calderato, TfL’s director of strategy, told the London assembly’s transport committee that the transit authority would not be in a position to start accepting applications “for some time”.She said: “I do not think we are in a rush to get [the guidelines] out. There is a huge amount of work going on behind the scenes.”Uber and Wayve have said that more than 100,000 Londoners were on their waiting list for self-driving taxis.They are racing against Google-owned Waymo and its Chinese equivalent, Baidu’s Apollo Go, to launch self-driving taxi services in London. Robotaxis are now available to hire in more than 20 cities across the US, China and the Middle East.Earlier this month Zagreb became the first European city to offer autonomous rides to the general public, through Uber, but the service still has a human driver for “onboard monitoring”.On Tuesday, Waymo announced that it plans to launch commercial operations in Munich, Germany, late next year.Ben Loewenstein, Waymo’s head of policy and government affairs for the UK and Europe, told the Financial Times that the company was currently “working through the safety approval process” with the transport department and was waiting on TfL’s guidance to gain consent.He added that Waymo was working towards launching a fully autonomous service “by the end of this year” but would not say whether the company would be able to offer paid rides to the general public in that timeframe.TfL has granted 15 private hire vehicle licences to Ford Mustang Mach-E vehicles equipped with Wayve’s artificial intelligence driving software, as well as surround cameras and radar.A TfL-licensed private hire driver will sit in the driver’s seat during trips to intervene if necessary, although the software is expected to control the car.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUber and Wayve plan to launch small-scale commercial pilots with a driver behind the wheel soon.For its fully driverless launch Wayve plans to switch to a new Nissan Leaf vehicle that is still in production and is due to launch later this year.Alex Kendall, Wayve’s chief executive, said the company never claimed it would have a fully driverless operation this year.“I don’t want to put a timeline on it because we want to make sure we pass through [the regulatory process],” he told the FT. “This work is continuing at pace. London is a significant step up in complexity compared to Phoenix or San Francisco.”Baidu only began testing vehicles in London at the end of last month and has said it plans to launch public rides next year.Operating taxis without a driver requires approval via a new process, known as an automated passenger services permit, with the government’s Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency. So far, no vehicles have been approved by the DVSA.TfL was contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsSelf-driving carsAutomotive industryLondonTfLUberTechnology sectorAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A mockery’: how offshore tax havens are thwarting the UK’s transparency push  | Tax havens | The Guardian
description: Critics say ownership registers are too costly and too complicated, scuppering attempts to expose alleged money laundering
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: Critics say ownership registers are too costly and too complicated, scuppering attempts to expose alleged money laundering
Content: The Cayman Islands has quite a long, drawn-out process for requesting company records in its jurisdiction. Transparency campaigners say aspects of the system in the British Virgin Islands are even worse.Photograph: LOOK Die Bildagentur der Fotografen GmbH/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Cayman Islands has quite a long, drawn-out process for requesting company records in its jurisdiction. Transparency campaigners say aspects of the system in the British Virgin Islands are even worse.Photograph: LOOK Die Bildagentur der Fotografen GmbH/AlamyTax havens‘A mockery’: how offshore tax havens are thwarting the UK’s transparency pushCritics say ownership registers are too costly and too complicated, scuppering attempts to expose alleged money launderingRob DaviesWed 26 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 12.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince Britain’s offshore secrecy jurisdictions caved in topressure from Westminsterto embrace corporate transparency, finding out who owns a company in one of these island havens is, in theory at least, a piece of cake.Take theCayman Islands.All you have to do is show that you have a “legitimate interest” in the data by proving that you are a researcher, journalist, member of a civil society group or a business person considering a transaction with the subject of your inquiry.Next, you must explain how the information will be used for “preventing, detecting, investigating, combating or prosecution money laundering or its predicate offences or terrorist financing”.There is a fee of at least $75 (£55) for each application. Until recently, this could only be done via the tricky method of an international wire transfer, although card payments are now available.Now, fill out a lengthy form outlining exactly what information you’re after, cross your fingers and wait.It isn’t exactly Companies House (for all itsfaults).Even when the form has been submitted, the subject of the inquiry can apply for a three-year “protection from disclosure” (at a cost of $1,000) to stop the information being sent on, on the basis that corporate transparency could expose them to harm.These applications are refused more often than not, a Cayman Islands spokesperson said, but justifications for exemption appear to be drawn quite widely.Reasons could include revealing any connections to “activity such as testing products on animals, which might lead to them being targeted by activists”, according to guidelines written by the Cayman Islands government. This is not an uncommon precaution. It is also available in the UK for a fee of £100.Transparency campaigners believe aspects of the system in theBritish Virgin Islands(BVI) are even worse.There, officials will inform the subject of any inquiry – perhaps a powerful oligarchor a narco-trafficker– of the name of any organisation asking the inconvenient questions, though not the names of individuals.Don’t expect a quick outcome either.“Three months ago we asked whether a sanctioned Russian oligarch still owns a company holding millions worth of UK property,” said Steve Goodrich, the head of research and investigations at the anti-corruption campaign group Transparency International. “We still haven’t had a reply.”Margaret Hodge, the veteran anti-corruption campaigner, said that the sclerotic and unpredictable nature of these corporate registries “makes a mockery of their purpose”.Legitimate interest access registers of beneficial ownership (or Liarbos for fans of ironic acronyms) have come about after a seven-year campaign by the UK government to bring overseas territories – and crown dependencies such as Jersey and Guernsey – to heel.The campaign has gathered steam amid mounting real-world examples of how Britain’s offshore havens had been used to launder money, avoid taxes or otherwise flout laws or other norms, such as the financial rules governing football.Cayman Islands entities played a central role inthe 1MDB scandal, one of the largest corruption cases in history.The Russian oligarch Roman Abramovichsecretly funded Chelsea FC with cash funnelled through companies in the BVI, a Guardian investigation revealed last year.The BVI was the single most-used jurisdiction in the now infamousPandora papersleak.By earlier this year, afterseveral missed deadlines, all of the overseas territories had responded to the drive to introduce Liarbos.But, according to Stephen Abbott Pugh, of the transparency group Open Ownership, the registers are “too costly, too complicated and [it] takes too long to access this crucial information.“So it remains locked away in most cases out of the reach of users with a legitimate interest in accessing it.”A spokesperson for the Caymans said only 25 applications for information had been received in 19 months, citing this as evidence of lack of demand, rather than difficulty in accessing the system.The spokesperson rejected criticism that the register was hard to use or costly and defended the islands’ reputation.“In spite of the public perception created by Hollywood fiction, misguided NGOs, and the politicians whom they have influence over, no credible evidence has ever been presented that Cayman has a problem with illicit finance,” they said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe new registers, according to the UK government’s own rhetoric, are only supposed to be an “interim step” towards fully public corporate registers accessible to all.Dispute over the pace of progress towards greater transparency has fuelled simmering tension between London and offshore outposts.Last year, Hodge – the government’s “anti-corruption champion” – was dispatched to the BVI on what was officially called a fact-finding mission but looked more like a shot across the bows.View image in fullscreenThe British Virgin Islands were criticised by British MPs campaigning against corruption.Photograph: Hemis/AlamyCriticism of the BVI by two other leading anti-corruption voices in Westminster – Phil Brickell MP and Joe Powell MP – led to one BVI media outlet printing a cartoon of the duo.Wearing thick boots, they were depicted kicking lumps out of Riley Right – a cartoon parakeet in a suit who serves as the islands’ corporate transparency mascot.“The only way to shine a light on the dirty money flowing through British overseas territories like the BVI is to have full transparency over who owns the companies registered there,” said Powell.“It’s completely unacceptable that following the money is still so hard, and it is a flagrant breach of their agreement with the British government.”Brickell said the “eyes of the world” will be on the UK government when it hosts a summit on countering illicit finance this December.“Failure to get our own house in order by then would be an acute embarrassment,” he said.Hodge isn’t backing off either.Earlier this year, she indicated that Westminster could force crown dependencies to improve transparency. Guernsey’s top politician responded by bemoaning “outdated prejudices” about the island.Hodge fears that crown dependencies are now “hiding” behind a prolonged EU row over how corporate registers in the 27-nation bloc should look.She doesn’t want to wait to see how that process plays out.“With a new government in place under Andy Burnham, I would hope we will be able to review our approach and be effective,” she said.Spokespeople for the Cayman Islands and the BVI rejected the suggestion that public access to corporate ownership registers were an accepted international standard and pointed out that tax and criminal authorities already had full access.A BVI spokesperson said: “We are proud of our legitimate interest access (LIA) regime which has significantly strengthened the accuracy, security, and accessibility of beneficial ownership data.“The regime offers greater transparency alongside appropriate protections for individual privacy, while remaining aligned with international standards, including the EU’s sixth anti-money laundering directive.”Explore more on these topicsTax havensTax avoidanceCayman IslandsBritish Virgin IslandsAmericasCaribbeanFinancial sectorfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dolly Parton was a rare singer who proved herself to be an electric movie star | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: From 9 to 5 to Steel Magnolias to Joyful Noise, the late star had real big screen presence that was impossible to imitate
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: From 9 to 5 to Steel Magnolias to Joyful Noise, the late star had real big screen presence that was impossible to imitate
Content: Dolly Parton in Best Little Whorehouse in Texas.Photograph: THA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDolly Parton in Best Little Whorehouse in Texas.Photograph: THA/ShutterstockDolly PartonDolly Parton was a rare singer who proved herself to be an electric movie starJesse HassengerFrom 9 to 5 to Steel Magnolias to Joyful Noise, the late star had real big screen presence that was impossible to imitate‘I just give from my heart’: how Dolly Parton’s philanthropy focused most on helping childrenCelebrity tributes pour in for Dolly Parton: ‘a gift to the world’Wed 26 Aug 2026 10.33 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 10.53 EDTShareThere are an awful lot of singers who take a shot at movie stardom. Most of them start out playing singing ingenues and trail off a few movies later, after their limitations become clear, the novelty wears off or their interests wander back to music.Dolly Parton, who died on 25 August at the age of 80, had the barest outline of such a film career: She had a big hit out of the gate with 9 to 5, endured a sizable flop about a decade later with 1992’s Straight Talk signaling the end of her movie phase, and had a couple of minor postscripts in the years that followed – more cameos-as-herself than fully fleshed-out roles. (Presumably she was busy releasing over a dozen albums, making countless TV appearances, sending books to children, and funding vaccine research, among other endeavors.) Yet within a modest filmography consisting of just half a dozen leading roles in theatrical releases (and more than one widely regarded as a minor disaster), she showed more genuine screen presence than countless other multihyphenates.Dolly Parton’s peerless career turned country music cliches inside out | Alexis PetridisRead moreMaybe it helped that Parton introduced herself on screen in a non-musical role. Well, almost: 9 to 5, a 1980 workplace comedy where she starred alongside Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda, did yield a number one charting theme song, the Oscar-nominated tune of the same name. (The titular theme from Fame won, but which one still gets played on the radio more often?) The movie itself, where Parton plays an office secretary whose piggish boss (Dabney Coleman) lusts after her and whose co-workers (initially including Tomlin and Fonda) suspect, incorrectly, that she has given in to his desires, is a far more relatable comedy, sort of a neo-screwball-meets-women’s-picture with an additional early-‘80s feminist spin.View image in fullscreenDolly Parton acts in 9 to 5Photograph: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesThe trio of Tomlin, Fonda and Parton wind up bonding over their horrible boss – and eventually kidnapping him, with crowd-pleasing results. Another movie might have played the presence of the famously beautiful Parton around a workday office as something of a joke. But while 9 to 5 is quite funny, it has no choice but to take Parton’s character seriously, because her performance has such immediate, innate sweetness and sincerity. That’s not all there is to it, though; the introduction and establishment of her good-hearted patience is chased with a spitfire scene where she threatens to shoot Coleman in a way that would turn him “from a rooster into a hen”. She goes on to perform fine comic teamwork with Tomlin and Fonda. She has too much personality (and that distinctive twang) to let you entirely forget you’re watchingDolly Parton, but like a lot of more prominent movie stars, her work fuses her well-known public persona with the particular character at hand in a convincing, hooky way. If this had been her only movie, it would have been ample evidence of her big-screen worthiness.Parton ended the decade with another non-musical hit burnishing that reputation: the 1989 comedy-drama Steel Magnolias, which again placed her in an all-star cast, this time including Sally Field, Shirley MacLaine, Olympia Dukakis, Daryl Hannah, and a young Julia Roberts. It would be easy enough to assume, based on her two biggest movie successes, that her fortunes were lifted by acting alongside various luminaries. But the truth is, Parton rose to meet the level of her more experienced co-stars. Most of the movies that seemed more specifically designed to play to her strengths weren’t as successful, for her or others involved. Perhaps most prominently, The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas followed 9 to 5, and shared with it director Colin Higgins. Given that pedigree, and arriving during a decade light in lavish musicals, it seems like this one should have been a genre highlight that would solidify Parton’s film career. Instead, she described the making of the film, which teamed her with the ever-mercurial Burt Reynolds, as a “miserable, spirit-numbing ordeal” in one of her books.View image in fullscreenDaryl Hannah and Dolly Parton in Steel Magnolias.Photograph: Zade Rosenthal/Tri-Star/Kobal/REX/ShutterstockAt least misery doesn’t exactly come through on screen in the movie itself, which was reoriented from its Broadway origins to focus more on Parton, as the madame in charge of the film’s house of ill repute, and Reynolds, as the local sheriff who’s been secretly wooing her for years. Parton provides rays of good cheer amidst a lugubrious interpretation of what’s supposed to be light entertainment – a fusion of tediously reheated ‘50s-style big-musical spectacle and ‘70s-style smut-snickering.Celebrity tributes pour in for Dolly Parton: ‘a gift to the world’Read moreAgain Parton inhabits her character by feeling at least partially like herself; years later, she’s about the only element of the movie that feels timeless. It helps that she contributed two of her own songs to the movie version of the musical: the cute duet Sneakin’ Around, performed with Reynolds, and a new version of her classic I Will Always Love You, which became a signature movie song … but not from this movie. Instead, Whitney Houston’s cover was a smash hit from the soundtrack of her film The Bodyguard in 1992, the same year that Parton had her last starring vehicle for ages, the little-seen comedy Straight Talk. Parton might have consoled herself that at least that project didn’t involve her singing with Reynolds or Sylvester Stallone, who starred opposite her in the ill-fated 1984 musical romance Rhinestone.View image in fullscreenDolly Parton and Queen Latifah in Joyful NoisePhotograph: Van Redin/Publicity image from film companyParton’s best musical film came much later, and to less attention: The 2012 film Joyful Noise, where she was matched with another unusually successful musician-turned-actor. Queen Latifah plays a new choir director who reluctantly teams with the pastor’s recent widow (Parton) to kick their singers’ Christian-themed competitive singing up a notch. It’s pure formula stuff, but Latifah and Parton are fun to watch together – especially for the chance to see Parton sing again on screen, as a character who, despite her cartooniness, has a more human dimension than the embodiment of angelic presence, whether guardian or literally heavenly, that she tended to understandably inhabit for cameo parts.Joyful Noise was an outlier for the last three decades of Parton’s life – her first film lead in 20 years and her last to be released in theaters. (She had a Netflix movie, Dolly Parton’s Christmas on the Square, in 2020.) But from its inclusive version of Christian values to its playful jokes about her character’s plastic surgery, it represents Parton well even as it allows her some space to play a character distinctive from those in 9 to 5 or Steel Magnolias. She wasn’t a master of disguise; as a movie star, she certainly had a preferred character type. But while that type might have had elements of Marilyn Monroe comic bombshell, Doris Day sunniness, and young Barbra Streisand scrappiness, the end result, in movies good and bad, was pure Dolly: impossible to imitate, easy to love.Explore more on these topicsDolly PartoncommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I remember going: oh hello!’ Dara Ó Briain on comedy, coolness, cruelty and finding his birth parents | Dara O Briain | The Guardian
description: The standup has been the host of the panel show Mock the Week for more than two decades. As it returns to UK screens, he discusses its years as a macho bear pit, the dearth of jokes about Brexit – and why it’s important to punch up
Author: Sam Wollaston
Headline: The standup has been the host of the panel show Mock the Week for more than two decades. As it returns to UK screens, he discusses its years as a macho bear pit, the dearth of jokes about Brexit – and why it’s important to punch up
Content: ‘I think people are getting a bit tired of the Irish’ … Dara Ó Briain.Photograph: Pål Hansen/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I think people are getting a bit tired of the Irish’ … Dara Ó Briain.Photograph: Pål Hansen/The GuardianDara O BriainInterview‘I remember going: oh hello!’ Dara Ó Briain on comedy, coolness, cruelty and finding his birth parentsSam WollastonThe standup has been the host of the panel show Mock the Week for more than two decades. As it returns to UK screens, he discusses its years as a macho bear pit, the dearth of jokes about Brexit – and why it’s important to punch upWed 26 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 13.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDara Ó Briain is still having photos taken when I arrive at the studio in west London. A comedian requires comedy pictures, so Pål, the photographer, has him sitting on the floor holding up a scroll of the rust-coloured paper that he’s using as a backdrop. It looks as if the roof is falling in on Ó Briain. He calls over to me. “We can tailor the interview to match the pictures,” he says. “Starting with: do you ever feel like you’re trapped in a box?”Shoot over, he ditches his jacket and we walk up the road to find a quiet corner in a pub. There’s a new season of Mock the Week, the topical satirical panel show that ran for 17 years on BBC Two until 2022 and has now been reborn on the free-to-air channel TLC. A roster of comedians make up two teams and compete in a faux gameshow, ostensibly to answer questions about the previous week’s news, but really just to be funny.Ó Briain, 54, has hosted it since the start. In the first iteration, regular guests included Hugh Dennis, Frankie Boyle and Ed Byrne, but up-and-coming comics were often included too. “It became a kind of debutante’s ball for people who’ve gotten to the top at Edinburgh and are ready to go on screen,” Ó Briain explains, not without pride.When Mock the Week was on the BBC, there were accusations that the mockery was directed to the right from the left. Ó Briain, who describes himself as “centre left”, says that had a lot to do with what was going on in Westminster: “For the vast majority of that time, there was a Tory government – Conservative PM after Conservative PM – so obviously we were looking at them.” But he also admits there was probably something to those accusations. “I don’t think anyone put an argument in favour of Brexit during the whole thing; nobody on Mock the Week was going: ‘Well, maybe sovereignty or whatever …’”The show featured the right-leaning comedians Geoff Norcott and Simon Evans, but the right isn’t as well represented in British comedy. Ó Briain isn’t sure why – perhaps because “the direction in which you punch matters or people don’t warm to it”, he says. “I have seen comics do jokes about, say, nurses always asking for money, and the audience go: ‘No, I don’t think that, we’re not coming with you on that one.’” Don’t mock the weak. But equally, he suggests, audiences don’t like it if you’re too far the other way – “too happy-clappy”.View image in fullscreen‘It was generally seven men around the table: they were trying to find themselves, there were elbows’ … hosting Mock the Week.Photograph: BBCThe other accusation aimed at Mock the Week was that it was vicious, mean and male – a bear pit of a show on which macho comedians elbowed each other out of the way in order to get their jibe in. Jo Brand didn’t like it when she went on.Again, Ó Briain says the criticism was fair. “It was generally seven men around the table: they were trying to find themselves; there were elbows.” But he points out that the programme started more than two decades ago, when this was the culture of shows of this kind (see also Never Mind the Buzzcocks). Ó Briain says he wouldn’t have liked to be a contestant. “I would have found it too staccato; I like to build up a head of steam on a piece of bullshit. But now it has become a lot more conversational.”While there’s plenty to converse about in the average week, some topics are riper for mockery than others. Trump, for example, isn’t the gift you might assume he is. “Particularly Trump 2, darker Trump. There’s not even the funny mistakes going on. Now, it’s self-parody, so utterly ridiculous that maybe it’s normalised the ridiculousness, to a certain extent. And you know, the joke’s already there – what are we adding to it? It would be like doing jokes about the Simpsons.”What about Keir Starmer? “Awful. He did nothing and said very little.” He means as a topic of discussion, rather than as a politician, although he wasn’t impressed with the way he ran the country, either. He’s not sure about Andy Burnham yet – they are still to mock one of his weeks – but he is amused by the process by which he came to power. “Makerfield gets to pick the prime minister now, is that how it happens?”So what or who is a gift to Mock the Week?Peter Murrelland the SNP expenses scandal, he says: “Not quite a victimless crime, because I guess the people who made donations to the SNP were victims. But the details were so perfect: the number of video consoles,the £2,000 salt shaker[Murrell spent £2,618.16 on Lalique Feuilles pepper and salt grinders], the fact Nicola Sturgeon bent over backwards to act like she didn’t know her in-lawssuddenly had a 30ft camper van.” They got some good mileage from that in the last season – more mileage than the camper van, which drove onlyfrom the showroom to the in-laws’ drive.Now, freed from the shackles of public service impartiality and scrutiny, and with more women involved, includingSara Pascoe,Maisie Adam,Laura LexxandAngela Barnes, perhaps Mock the Week is a nicer place, even if it has many fewer viewers (a little more than 1 million when repeats are included) than the 3-million-plus it averaged in its BBC peak.Ó Briain wasn’t meant to be a comedian. He studied mathematics and theoretical physics at University College Dublin in the early 90s. He says he was a shy and self-conscious teenager, but pushed himself to join the debating society at UCD. During one debate, he told a joke: “It got a laugh, and a round of applause, and I remember this whoosh of adrenaline and me going: oh hello!”He still feels that whoosh, although the high isn’t so high and it might take a two-hour show, rather than one joke, to get there. But he loves the work and it takes him to cool places such as Athens, Barcelona and Stockholm (as well as Chatham, Dorking and Leicester). His two most recent tours have been less about the gags, more about the storytelling – and more personal.View image in fullscreen‘The direction in which you punch matters’ … playing Latitude festival in Suffolk, 2017.Photograph: Rob Ball/RedfernsBorn in Bray, County Wicklow, Ó Briain was adopted into whathe has describedas “a stable home” and had a happy childhood. A few years ago, he decided to find out about his biological parents. “The plan wasn’t that it should be a show, it was just this thing I should investigate, because of normal human emotions. I always knew there was this story waiting to be found out, and then the impetus was that none of us are getting younger. I know of people who have found parents and then met them in a nursing home and they’ve had Alzheimer’s.”He realised the story wasn’t only about him after seeingthe film Philomena. “I came out of the cinema with a sudden appreciation that this is actually not my story at all, I’m only a baby in it, but there’s a woman who got pregnant and went on this journey,” he says. “It’s her story and I should probably at the very least make contact in order to close that circle for her and let her know it was great and I found a lovely family and all that stuff.”It was hard – bureaucratically, emotionally – but he found her and they met up. It was awkward and strange. He got a bunch of new siblings. He told the story in his show So … Where Were We?, which won best tour at the Chortle awards in 2023.His next show, Re:Creation, which he’s been touring across Europe, tells the story of trying to track down his biological father. No spoilers (there are some dates left, plus it’s onAmazon Prime), but it contains less sadness and anger than the previous set. “It’s a bit of a romp, with a twist towards the end that is delightful to deliver. Not quite The Sixth Sense, but kind of a gasp moment.”The problem now is what to do next. “Both stories just kind of emerge in a very tellable form. There’s no way of doing a third, no trilogy. Even as I’m doing it, enjoying telling the story, my head is going: ‘Yeah, next time, you’re going to actually have to do some work, write some jokes, because you’re not going to be gifted another parent to find, there isn’t another great family reveal,’” he says.Well, there isonepossibility, surely. Maybe not a parent … He laughs. “Yes, the perfect thing would be a knock on the door and there’s a 25-year-old going: ‘I think …’ And I would go: ‘Thank you so much!’ Because this would be the only way you could extend the trilogy – if I was the father of a child given up for adoption.” It’s not going to happen, though. “I’ve done the audit, run it backwards in my head going: was there any situation that could have …?” He adds quickly: “I mean, I’ve had my checkered history. But I feel it’s all accounted for.”His TV career started as a children’s presenter on the Irish state broadcaster RTÉ, while he was doing his first standup gigs on the Irish comedy circuit. He came to prominence hosting the topical panel show Don’t Feed the Gondolas from 1997 to 2001. His big break on the other side of the Irish Sea came in 2003, when he hosted The Live Floor Show on BBC Two, which led to appearances on Have I Got News for You.Since making his debut as Mock the Week’s host in 2005, Ó Briain has presented just about everything on television. Alongside the panel shows and the comedy, his interest in maths and physics continued. He has presented Stargazing Live from Jodrell Bank observatory with Prof Brian Cox; his hobby is astrophotography, which he does from his garden in London (“you can filter out all the light”); and he’s had many pops at bad science (hello, Gillian McKeith!) in his comedy.Even when chatting, he’ll borrow analogies from science. He says X, formerly known as Twitter, has become a black hole: “It’s got sucked into this thing and created so much density that it’s actually going to collapse under its own gravity.” (He has abandoned the platform.) The popularity of panel shows? They have their moments. “It’s like this graph of an extinction event: it goes back down again, but it never fully eliminates a small number of hard‑shelled animals who survive each time – the cockroaches who are the comedians at the bottom, never fully eliminated because they’re cheap and people like them, so they’ll come back.”View image in fullscreen‘I know of people who have found parents and then met them in a nursing home and they’ve had Alzheimer’s.’Photograph: Pål Hansen/The GuardianHis own career, meanwhile, is more of a sine wave: “It goes up and down, but carries on.” Or is it a damped oscillation? “If you don’t pay attention, it gets smaller and smaller, asymptotically, until there’s only a tiny little vibration right at the very end and I’m sitting in an olive grove in Spain going: ‘Buenos dias.’”You’ll know, if you’ve seen him on stage or on TV, that Ó Briain’s delivery is superfast. Well, it doesn’t slow down over a quiet orange juice and lemonade. When he sets off on something, he’s like a rocket in space. I fire little thrusters (chip in with the odd question) in an attempt to steer the ship, but when something has that much momentum sometimes you just have to run with it.We go to many other places –solar eclipses, the World Cup, what to do if there’s a medical emergency in the audience,Arsenal’s transfer window, Blankety Blank, whether or not it’s cool to be Irish in London, but there isn’t space here … oh, go on then, just that last one. The answer is yes, but again it’s sinusoidal. “We are currently cool, but I think people are getting a bit tired of it, so probably it’s time for someone else to be cool for a while.”Whether he’s cool or not, 90 minutes with Dara Ó Briain is eye-opening, exhausting and delightful. He’s still talking when he gets into the car that has come to fetch him. It’s something about Melania Trump, although I’m not sure if it’s the documentary or the woman. And then it’s too late when I realise: I forgot to ask if he ever feels as if he’s trapped in a box.Mock the Week returns to TLC in the UK on 13 September at 9pm.
