title: With the end of physical media in sight, gamers have had enough | Games | The Guardian
description: An increasing tension between players and publishers about ownership of titles could lead to a divestment from the system the big companies are trying to enforce
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: An increasing tension between players and publishers about ownership of titles could lead to a divestment from the system the big companies are trying to enforce
Content: Gamers want ownership and that might mean going old school.Photograph: Sabrina Bracher/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGamers want ownership and that might mean going old school.Photograph: Sabrina Bracher/Getty ImagesPushing Buttons newsletterGamesWith the end of physical media in sight, gamers have had enoughAn increasing tension between players and publishers about ownership of titles could lead to a divestment from the system the big companies are trying to enforceKeith StuartWed 26 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 22.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the time of press, there is a well-publicised protest taking place in the video games community. PlayStation 5 owners are being encouraged to log off from their consoles between 23 and 30 August – no playing games, no downloading new titles. The motivating factor is Sony’s decision tocease physical game disc productionfrom January 2028. After that, games will only be released as digital products. In an act of poor timing or wilful defiance, Sony chose this week to send out a mass email reminding customers of their PS5 terms and conditions: “The software is licensed to you, not sold,” states the relevant clause. “You are granted a limited, non-exclusive, non-transferable, and personal license to play … ” It knows, of course, that most customers won’t open the email, let alone read it.There has always been a tension between game players and game publishers – an underlying sense of mutual mistrust. Players are wary of their favourite franchises being canned, or games being delayed or released with bugs. Publishers and manufacturers are wary of piracy and the capricious tastes of consumers. But now the atmosphere among many game players feels more starkly political than ever. Microsoft has been targeted by theBoycott, Divestment, Sanctionsmovement for itsties to the Israeli military; the consumer advocacy groupStop Killing Gamesis gaining support; players haveprotested overthe purchase of Electronic Arts by a Saudi-led consortium –boycotts have been proposedin part due to the possible ramifications regarding LGBTQ+ content in titles such as The Sims. As the games industry has grown and globalised, its impact on culture, society and politics has increased. Yet, on an individual level, gamers and consumers are feeling increasingly powerless.View image in fullscreenThe end of physical games … time to go retro.Photograph: ShutterstockIs it possible to divest from the mainstream games industrial complex as a player? Yes, but with obvious sacrifices. Your PS5 still runs physical discs (if it has an optical drive) and will also play almost all PS4 games, so you have enough single-player titles to see you out for several decades. You couldbuy a secondhandXbox, PlayStation or Nintendo machine from any era and find games that are still wildly pleasurable. Instead of playing online, you could rediscover couch co-op via evergreen titles such as Micro Machines and Worms. Alternatively, it’s possible to build a functional gaming PC for about £500, especially if you source secondhand components, that will let you play most current titles on lower graphics settings, while Steam, Itch.io or GOG all give you access to the vast, rich independent gaming scene.Short on cash? Love retro games? Apart from buying an old console, you could also invest in aRaspberry Pi4 or 5 mini computer. I bought thePi Hut’s starter kitfor £99, which gives you everything you need hardware-wise. Install the OS, download an emulator such as RetroPie, Batocera or Recalbox and, hey presto, instant retro gaming machine! (Although you’ll need to find a way to download game Roms). There is also a huge range of dedicated retro consoles and handhelds, including the lovelyEverCade(which lets you buy licensed, authentic versions of classic titles) and the pocket-sized Retroid, Ayaneo and Miyoo Mini devices.If none of this matters to you, that’s fine – keep enjoying the games you love. But for gamers truly worried about the impact of their consent and consumption, it may be time to think of video games in the same way we think of food: as something requiring ethical sacrifices. It is all too easy to succumb to a sense of powerlessness in the modern era – the systems seem to be stacked against us. But one thing games have always tried to teach us is that we have agency, we are imaginative creatures, we can challenge and beat the system in ways no one foresaw.As forPlayStation, it’s true that a huge majority of game sales are now digital (a point Sony has made in its defence) but this week has reminded us, in stark clarity, what convenience and compliance will cost us in the end.What to playView image in fullscreenMini metropolis ... Combolands.Photograph: Crux GamesAs a fan of games that combine different genres in interesting ways, I have just downloadedCombolands, an ingenious combination of roguelike deck builder and city-building sim. Here, you construct cute towns on procedurally generated islands by placing complementary building types next to each other, triggering combos that help grow your mini metropolis. The pixellated visuals recall the glory days of Sim City and Civilization, and I like how sessions last less than an hour before it’s time to rebuild. Oh, and it runs on a basic PC setup.Available on:PCEstimated playtime:10 hours plusWhat to readView image in fullscreenPlay it … one of the top adventure indie games of the 21st century, Night in the Woods.Photograph: Night in the WoodsI like it when war breaks out over a video game list feature – it reminds me of 90s games journalism when these thingsreallymattered. On 11 August, entertainment website Colliderposted its listof the10 best adventure games of the 21st century. Unimpressed by the choices, game designer Greg Costikyan and his team at Indie Gamer Reviewer got together and came up withan alternative selection. Read both and make up your own mind!TheGTAVIleaks are continuing, mostly via a hacker named Cyberleek, who has released a fresh batch of game clips – this time with some, let’s say, adult-themed content. Kotaku has been following thesituationclosely. Meanwhile Take-Two hasfiled subpoena requestsin federal district court to secure information from Microsoft and Discord about the online accounts involved.As he turned 63 this week,Hideo Kojimavowed to keep making games – a relief to those of us who have spent hundreds of hours in his life’s work, hiding in cardboard boxes, walking up long ladders and delivering packages to reclusive scientists in the Australian outback. Eurogamer hasmore detailson his social media promise. Keep on keeping on, Hideo.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to click‘A cognitive cacophony’: hands-on with the Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 beta testMarvel’s Wolverine: Spider-Man developers turn to a more cutthroat characterMy Arms Are Longer Now – comedy stealth game sends lawlessness into new territoryThe new Halloween video game has been banned in Australia – and not because of the violenceThe Duskbloods: the best of FromSoftware fights in a frantic multiplayer battlegroundStupid Never Dies – a zombie fights for the love of a frozen corpseMetal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2 – once more unto the mercenary breach | ★★★☆☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenA long and rich history … Pokémon Pokopia.Photograph: NintendoThis week, a question fromJohnny, via email:“I’ve just started getting into anime, working my way through classics likeAttack on Titanand Neon Genesis Evangelion, and newcomers such as Witch Hat Atelier and Tomb Raider King, and now I’m interested in trying an anime-based video game. Can you recommend any?”There is a very long and rich history of anime video games, going back to Taito’s Lupin III arcade cabinet in 1980. If you just want games based on specific shows, Namco’sDragon Ball FighterZ,Pokémon PokopiaandFairy Tail Dungeonsare my picks of the current crop. If you’re happy with gamesinspiredby anime, I’d recommend hardcore role-playing adventureMetaphor: ReFantazio, the Ghibli-co-createdNi No Kuni(which later received an anime tie-in),Nier: Automata(also now an anime) and the brilliantPersonaseries. My son, Zac, also recommendsEdens Zero. If you want to go on a retro hunt, there are classic games based on Neon Genesis Evangelion, Sword Art Online, Mobile Suit Gundam, JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure and my eternal favourite, Ranma 1/2 – check eBay or CEX for copies – andganbatte kudasai!If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletteremail us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterSonyPlayStation 5PlayStationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Vholume review – a headlong rush of parkour perfection in a brutalist wonderland | Games | The Guardian
description: Race across impossible dystopian cityscapes in this exhilarating game of wall-runs, death-chancing leaps and split-second improvisation
Author: Christian Donlan
Headline: Race across impossible dystopian cityscapes in this exhilarating game of wall-runs, death-chancing leaps and split-second improvisation
Content: Concrete jungle … Vholume.Photograph: Nathan Grange/Léonard Lemaitre/Niels Tiercelin/IronEqualView image in fullscreenConcrete jungle … Vholume.Photograph: Nathan Grange/Léonard Lemaitre/Niels Tiercelin/IronEqualGamesReviewVholume review – a headlong rush of parkour perfection in a brutalist wonderlandPC; Nathan Grange, Léonard Lemaitre, Niels Tiercelin, IronEqualRace across impossible dystopian cityscapes in this exhilarating game of wall-runs, death-chancing leaps and split-second improvisationChristian DonlanWed 26 Aug 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 08.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt first, Vholume seems like a quick rush through some smartly selected references. Has this breathless yet austere parkour game been designed or ingeniously curated? The urban gymnast moveset comes from Mirror’s Edge. Level names use terms like conapt, first coined by Philip K Dick. And the environments themselves are dystopian and surreal, Half-Life 2’s City 17 colliding with the blasted avenues and mute archways of de Chirico. Many games have influences. Vholume has actual taste.All the surface stuff fades away when the game is in motion, however. Vholume’s an on-foot racing game in which you hoof it through spectacularly odd environments, moving from one beam of concrete to the next. You’re clipping your wall-runs and power-slides together to bridge seemingly impossible gaps between buildings, forever in search of the next stretch of track, the next turn, the next jump that gets you to the level’s exit and the worldwide leaderboards. And once that’s done, you have a choice: onwards to another gauntlet, or back to the start of this one again to slice a few microseconds off your score? Or maybe you’d rather head over to multiplayer to race against the ghosts of others?View image in fullscreenRun for it … Vholume.Photograph: Nathan Grange/Léonard Lemaitre/Niels Tiercelin/IronEqualThis quickly becomes utterly compelling, and at the heart of it all is the realisation that Vholume is surprisingly accommodating to players of all abilities. Powered mainly by trigger squeezes that allow you to hop or duck, the game truly wants your wall-kicks and mantling to connect neatly and leave you feeling lithe and speedy. It’s also happy to let you find height-gaining exploits and kludge a save from falls that really should have killed you. This is ultimately confidence rather than indulgence. It’s the confidence of a game that knows it can let weaker players muddle through because, up in the thin, high-altitude air at the very top of the leaderboard, real beauty is unfolding.As you progress further into the game, simple full-ahead courses are interleaved with more complex levels that feel like puzzles, but in truth every level is a range of different potential routes depending on how quickly you’re travelling, how eager your reflexes are, and how far your fingers on the pad can get ahead of your own interrupting thoughts. If you’ve ever done the Couch to 5K, you’ll understand Vholume’s slightly cosmic suggestion that time is equivalent to distance when you’re wearing running shoes; the game’s endlessly eager to open up the number of paths forward at any moment depending on how fast you’re going. Welcome to the garden of forking PBs.As is often the case, I’m not sure Vholume always gets better as it gets busier, however. Jump pads, maze-like special levels and parts of the environment that move by themselves all start to play a role in the game as you progress. But while the intricate later levels are fascinating, the balance between the fun the designer is having and the fun the player is having is more even in its early stages, which are a twitchy headlong thrill.That’s what’s so perverse about this game. One of Vholume’s creators made their name with Babbdi and Straftat, two games that look like a product of the demoscene but actually zero in on deeply satisfying mechanics delivered with care. Vholume’s world is horrible, then, but your path through it is paved with joy and exhilaration. It understands that the only thing better than a game that wants to make you think is a game that wants to make sure you never think, even for a millisecond – because if the thinking brain gets itself involved, the whole beautiful thing will fall apart.Vholume is out now; £6.Explore more on these topicsGamesPCSports gamesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival – a game so grotesque it scares its own director | Games | The Guardian
description: With oversight from Clive Barker himself, and a role reprisal as Pinhead from actor Doug Bradley, Revival aims to introduce new audiences to the discomfort of Hellraiser
Author: Bex April May
Headline: With oversight from Clive Barker himself, and a role reprisal as Pinhead from actor Doug Bradley, Revival aims to introduce new audiences to the discomfort of Hellraiser
Content: A monk-like villain … Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival.Photograph: Saber InteractiveView image in fullscreenA monk-like villain … Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival.Photograph: Saber InteractiveGamesClive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival – a game so grotesque it scares its own directorWith oversight from Clive Barker himself, and a role reprisal as Pinhead from actor Doug Bradley, Revival aims to introduce new audiences to the discomfort of HellraiserBex April MayWed 26 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf a horror game gives its own director a physical reaction, it’s probably doing something right. While researching the images people find hardest to look at, game director Emil Esov discovered he hastrypophobia– a fear of clusters of small holes. Rather than tone the scary images down, he fed them straight into Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival.The forthcoming first-person action-horror game drops players into a new story in Barker’s universe. Aidan Lynch must use the Genesis Configuration puzzle box to rescue his girlfriend from the Labyrinth as Pinhead, his Cenobites and a cult close in. But Revival is not built around jump scares. The team at Mad HeadGamesbegan with one question: what should players feel? The answer was discomfort.“That’s a key emotion,” says Esov, “You know when you are looking at something, but you cannot look away?” Early in the game, players must push a hand inside a grotesque sculpture to retrieve an item – it’s all about feeling extreme unease. Even a stealth kill is drawn out rather than instant, he explains: “There is struggle. There is sweating, moaning. It’s really, really stressful.”View image in fullscreenExtreme unease … Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival.Photograph: Saber InteractiveThat does not mean simply filling every room with blood and bodies. Esov likens Pinhead to a monk rather than a traditional slasher villain: calm, imposing and “almost trolling you”. The horror comes from what he might do, but also the unnerving way he talks about doing it.Clive Barkerhimself helped shape the characters, themes and rules of the universe, before staying on as an adviser as the story became a game. His feedback could move from big questions to one wonderfully specific request, which Esov recalls as: “Can you make the sky more purple in the Labyrinth?” Esov loved that “level of detailed nit-picking”, which showed that Barker was still watching over the world he created.Doug Bradley also returns as Pinhead for the first time (except for a few lines in a time-limited chapter of Dead by Daylight) in the two decades since his last appearance in a Hellraiser film. Recording took place remotely, and Esov soon realised the actor needed little coaching. “You don’t have to direct him,” he says. “He actually is Pinhead!”As for the Cenobites, they get more individual roles and screen time, but won’t be ordinary targets; their undeniable power had to survive the move into an action game. “You cannot fight them,” Esov says, “They’re not a gameplay aspect that you get to beat.”Elsewhere, the first-person combat has drawn comparisons toResident Eviland BioShock, while Condemned influenced the unpredictable melee fights. Around a quarter of the game takes place in the Labyrinth, and the Genesis Configuration works as both a key part of the story and a tool for the player. The difficulty settings include a highest level named after Hellraiser itself, which is how Esov prefers to play. His hellish serving suggestion of sorts: “It should be discomforting even to play.”Esov hopes Revival will introduce a new audience to the mix of violence, sex, beauty and pain that sets Hellraiser apart. He wants a game “that doesn’t hold back”. If players come away disturbed, they will not be alone: Revival got under its own director’s skin before it ever had the chance to get under theirs.Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival comes to PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S on 8 OctoberExplore more on these topicsGamesClive BarkerHorror booksRole playing gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Wreck review – scuba drama about siblings under pressure | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Gabe Winsor’s inventively staged tale is charming and sweetly lo-fi, but the emotion never quite clicks
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Gabe Winsor’s inventively staged tale is charming and sweetly lo-fi, but the emotion never quite clicks
Content: A life aquatic … Morgan Beale as Eddie and Camilla Anvar as Ira, in The Wreck.Photograph: Alex BrennerView image in fullscreenA life aquatic … Morgan Beale as Eddie and Camilla Anvar as Ira, in The Wreck.Photograph: Alex BrennerEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewThe Wreck review – scuba drama about siblings under pressureSummerhall, EdinburghGabe Winsor’s inventively staged tale is charming and sweetly lo-fi, but the emotion never quite clicksChris WiegandWed 26 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDeep sea diving and plumbing the depths of family history make a decent parallel in this nimble multimedia production byBuzzcut, which has a sweetly eccentric air yet leaves a little too much beneath the surface.The premise is familiar, as Eddie (Morgan Beale) returns to the seaside town where his sister, Ira (Camilla Anvar), still lives in her childhood bedroom and runs the family pub now that their parents are gone. Guilt, resentment and jealousy bubble up as they squabble over which of them was their parents’ favourite and what to do with the business, while Ira shares her doubts about Eddie’s new husband.Written and directed by Gabe Winsor, The Wreck unfolds over the siblings’ daytime scuba dives and night-time dancing at the pub’s sparsely attended disco, presided over by DJ Sea Bass (you half expect to spot the electronic eel from Jaha Koo’s excellentHaribo Kimchi, playing across town). In a nice twist, they end up burying their own treasure – but you never fully invest in the characters’ relationships or their predicaments over the 50-minute duration.View image in fullscreenPuppeteer Beckett Gray and Camilla Anvar create an undersea scene.Photograph: Alex BrennerThat is partly because of the time spent realising the show’s inventive form. Live camera work and rod-and-string puppeteering (both by Beckett Gray) are used to animate the water-world – with puppet designs by Cat Rock and a fishtank model box by Tiffer Cundy, atmospherically lit by Han Sayles. All of this takes place behind a diaphanous sheet, so the behind-the-scenes activity becomes a secondary drama, and several different backdrops are used to change the scene. Surtitles and divers’ hand signals are used to make the show accessible and the tech is handled smoothly, yet retains a lo-fi air. Faye James plays her own compositions live, blending accordion and suitably aquatic-sounding electronica.The underwater action begins to drag and the conversations on dry land can also frustrate, although the characters’ reticence feels realistic (as does the siblings’ shared shorthand). But even if the drama is caught between the domestic and the deep blue sea, it’s a show with plenty of charm.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatrePuppetryEdinburgh festivalSummerhallreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Adam Riches: The Captain review – the extraordinary glory of a ‘half man, half fish’ Victorian hero | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: An endurance test for a standup already starring in a fringe hit, this show resurrects the man who drilled the first ever cross-Channel swimmer
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: An endurance test for a standup already starring in a fringe hit, this show resurrects the man who drilled the first ever cross-Channel swimmer
Content: Deep dive … Adam Riches: The Captain.Photograph: Matt StrongeView image in fullscreenDeep dive … Adam Riches: The Captain.Photograph: Matt StrongeEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewAdam Riches: The Captain review – the extraordinary glory of a ‘half man, half fish’ Victorian heroSummerhall, EdinburghAn endurance test for a standup already starring in a fringe hit, this show resurrects the man who drilled the first ever cross-Channel swimmerBrian LoganWed 26 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Who are these people that do what [the rest of us] cannot?”Adam Riches’ solo play The Captain teases at the daredevil spirit, incarnate here in Capt Matthew Webb, the first man to swim the Channel unaided. Riches plays Fred Beckwith, a swimming coach who trains the young Webb for his tilt at greatness. The show takes the form of a lecture-cum-eulogy to the “half man, half fish” Webb, whose body lies under a shroud on a table in the apt surroundings of Summerhall’s Anatomy theatre.A comedian by trade, Riches offers up a version of the true story here that’s as funny as his comedy elsewhere on the fringe,The Critic’s Way. The gentle sendup of Victorian values is droll. The swimming workshops and cheerleading of Webb’s channel crossing, to which the audience is co-opted with gusto (this is an Adam Riches show, after all), are stirring good fun. And there’s a real relish forthe story’s bizarre details– such as Beckwith’s “mystical fifth swimming technique”, the sidestroke. Or the American rival to Webb who completes the crossing before him, albeit in a rubber suit that strongly resembles a boat.‘Audiences ask to feel my calves!’ The endurance extremists pounding treadmills and pumping pedals at the fringeRead moreYou could argue that that comic instinct undermines the seriousness of Riches’ exploration of what drives some people to strive for the impossible – and what mark they leave on the rest of us. Riches can seldom resist a joke, and even at his most earnest – as Beckwith hymns the manly strength and firmness of his hero’s endeavours – you sense the next gag pregnant on his lips.But the sincerity of his interest shines through. Perhaps unsurprisingly for a man whose whole oeuvre has explored extreme masculinity, and whose every Edinburgh fringe (two shows this year, three next) is itself a heroic feat of stamina, Riches considers Webb’s grasp-exceeding reach, and the role glory plays in a life well lived, with real depth of feeling. Why swim 21 miles when you can swim 39? It might as well be Riches’ motto, and he makes an engaging case for it in this tribute to Victorian pluck and watery derring-do.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Adam RichesTheatreComedy (Stage)Swimming (Sport)Swimming (Life and style)Comedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sami Abu Wardeh Hates You review – a clown strides into the mainstream with style | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The comedian delivers a tour of his peripatetic childhood, with stops for risque gags and to ponder his resemblance to a ‘porn Super Mario’
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: The comedian delivers a tour of his peripatetic childhood, with stops for risque gags and to ponder his resemblance to a ‘porn Super Mario’
Content: Teasing at the boundaries of the permissible … Sami Abu Wardeh pictured outside Pleasance Courtyard.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTeasing at the boundaries of the permissible … Sami Abu Wardeh pictured outside Pleasance Courtyard.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewSami Abu Wardeh Hates You review – a clown strides into the mainstream with stylePleasance Courtyard, EdinburghThe comedian delivers a tour of his peripatetic childhood, with stops for risque gags and to ponder his resemblance to a ‘porn Super Mario’Brian LoganWed 26 Aug 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 10.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleComedy fans have seen Sami Abu Wardeh in several guises, from acapering clowncatching cherry tomatoes in his mouth, to teller (on last year’s fringe) of the historical stories behind the Gaza crisis. But we’ve never seen him deliver straight autobiographical standup – until now. The new direction, the 40-year-old tells us, is thanks to his agent, who’s told him that audiences need to get to know him better. And who may be concerned, Wardeh implies, by recent dust-ups between this “anti-fascist”/pro-Palestine performer and one or two audience members to whom that worldview was unwelcome.View image in fullscreenFar more than just chat … Sami Abu Wardeh.Photograph: Dylan WoodleySami Abu Wardeh Hates You (its title notwithstanding) presents us with a more palatable act, one effortlessly capable of delivering mainstream comedy. From the opening gag about walk-on music, to the tour of his peripatetic childhood (from Kuwait via southwest London to Dubai), to the risque gags about wanking and his resemblance to a “porn Super Mario”, the show might have been designed to demonstrate the Irish-Palestinian’s mastery of standup topics and techniques. But he gives them his own spin; whether that’s workshopping racist slurs with his bully, or orchestrating his Middle Eastern schoolmates in a rap-along to Will Smith’s Men in Black.All of this is greatly embellished by our host’s clowning skills, which ensure that most of those routines are far more than just chat. Body, vocals and gurning, leering face are all bent towards caricature here, as Wardeh brings to larger-than-life the demonic-seeming rituals of the Catholic church, say, or the sex appeal of his Arabic teacher. An anecdote about voicing an audiobook platforms his accent abilities, forever teasing at the boundaries of the permissible.Courtney Büchner: One of the Girls review – all aboard for a rollercoaster relationshipRead moreYou wait in vain for the show’s premise – “a chaotic exploration of the value of hate today” – to be fulfilled, but the subject is addressed just briefly. Only the later stages bring us into the present day, with a story about a comically ineffective protest he launched against racist policing. We get a veiled picture of who Sami Abu Wardeh is now, but a vivid and funny one of who he was while getting here.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalEdinburgh festival 2022FestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Kirsty Mann: Corpse review – a comedy so creepy you’ll fear the next revelation | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The comedian brings a calm authority to her tale of a haunted house and digs out maximum horror from a minimal staging
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: The comedian brings a calm authority to her tale of a haunted house and digs out maximum horror from a minimal staging
Content: Powerful presence … Kirsty Mann in Corpse at Summerhall, Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPowerful presence … Kirsty Mann in Corpse at Summerhall, Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewKirsty Mann: Corpse review – a comedy so creepy you’ll fear the next revelationSummerhall, EdinburghThe comedian brings a calm authority to her tale of a haunted house and digs out maximum horror from a minimal stagingChris WiegandWed 26 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome shows work their magic on you slowly but Kirsty Mann will have you hooked in under a minute. A thunderous sound effect, a flash of blood-red lighting and a DIY ghost costume is all it takes to get the audience strapped in for her comic tale of a haunting. “Are you a believer?” she asks us. Mann may not convince you of supernatural powers but she overwhelmingly proves the power of storytelling.It succeeds partly because our host is such a natural on stage and so rational, too. Mann quickly comes across as an ordinary neighbour, even while detailing the most uncommon events of moving into her new home. When she and her husband snapped up a semi in east London they knew it was a fixer-upper but it turns out the knotweed is the least of their problems. The previous resident died in the same bed in which they consummate their moving in and it gets creepier by the day. Why does the toilet seemingly flush itself? Are those scratch marks on the bedroom door? What the hell is going on under the apple tree?View image in fullscreenA natural … Kirsty Mann in Corpse.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianMann is a doctor as well as a comedian (“So when I’m not killing it on stage …”) and her spooked state begins to cause problems at work and test her marriage. She plays assorted characters including her often absent husband, who nicknames her Piglet – accentuating their tenderness yet also her increasingly jangled nerves. The story unfolds amid removal boxes to add an extra air of uncertainty. Once you’ve seen the previous owner’s paintings you will never unsee them.Soft Spot review – this wine-glass circus has a lot of bottleRead moreThere are sparing references to horror cinema and Mann operates with the knowledge, as proven by The Woman in Black, that less is more when scaring on stage. Her clinical examination to verify a patient’s death is breathtakingly done and there is a moment of darkness when you fear what you’ll discover when the lights go up. The scenes of comical hysteria, with her clambering amid the audience, are more run-of-the-mill. If the final flourish is not quite unsettling enough it is still a relief, leaving the venue after this afternoon show, to not walk home in the dark.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 30 August and atShedinburgh, Edinburgh, on 29 August. Then atSoho theatre, London, 2-13 February.All our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalHorror filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Miley Cyrus, Taylor Swift and more pay tribute to Dolly Parton: ‘her legacy will be everlasting’ | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: Lily Tomlin, Beyoncé, Céline Dion and Oprah Winfrey are among those remembering the queen of country after she died aged 80
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: Lily Tomlin, Beyoncé, Céline Dion and Oprah Winfrey are among those remembering the queen of country after she died aged 80
Content: Dolly Parton in 2025.Photograph: AFF-USA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDolly Parton in 2025.Photograph: AFF-USA/ShutterstockDolly PartonMiley Cyrus, Taylor Swift and more pay tribute to Dolly Parton: ‘her legacy will be everlasting’Lily Tomlin, Beyoncé, Céline Dion and Oprah Winfrey are among those remembering the queen of countryafter she died aged 80Alexis Petridis on Dolly Parton’s peerless career that turned country music cliches inside outDolly Parton – a life in picturesDolly Parton celebrated by kd lang, Peggy Seeger, Annie Lennox and moreOwen MyersandBenjamin LeeWed 26 Aug 2026 03.46 EDTFirst published on Tue 25 Aug 2026 15.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTributes have poured in forDolly Parton, the country singer, songwriter and actor, after her death aged 80.News of her deathwas shared by her nephewon social media. “Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus,” he said.Earlier this year, Parton had canceled a Las Vegas residency over health issues.“Our family and the team she has entrusted with her legacy will work diligently to ensure her spirit will live with us forever,” the official family statement said. “Dolly was a farmer, just like her Daddy. He farmed the soil; she farmed songs and happiness.”Dolly Parton’s peerless career turned country music cliches inside out | Alexis PetridisRead moreParton was known for hit songs such as Jolene and I Will Always Love You, starring in films such as 9 to 5 and Steel Magnolias, and her philanthropy work.Famous names who knew her or were fans of her work have been paying tribute.Céline DionCéline Dion posted a reminiscence on Instagram:“We will now be missing one of the most joyful voices this world has ever known. Thank you for the music, the laughter, and the love you gave us all. We will always love you.”Miley CyrusParton’s goddaughter wrote: “The feeling of losing my Aunt Dolly is beyond what feels right to share. Our most sacred moments were private and they’ll stay there behind the stage, beneath the glamour & between our hearts.”She added: “I will always love her and want to make her proud. My heart breaks for the world, her family and friends who will miss her deeply. We’re in this loss together and we will see her in all of the most beautiful things.”Oprah WinfreyWinfrey shared a photo of one of her “fondest memories” with Parton, “having a hoot and a holler while wearing Bob Mackie gowns on her show Dolly”. She continued:“This girl from the Smoky Mountains of Tennessee dreamed a life and then lived a life bigger than she could have ever imagined, giving so generously to others in ways we saw and ways we didn’t.“No one like her. She brought the light, and we are all better because she was here.God bless you, Dolly – you earned your wings.”Taylor SwiftIn a statement released to press, Swift said:“A world without Dolly doesn’t feel possible, real or right. But because of the eternally generous way she spent her time on this earth and the countless lives she changed for the better, her legacy will be an everlasting one.“Somehow she was true grace and true grit, all in one dazzling person. She possessed the softest heart when it came to the struggles of others, and a backbone of steel to defend her own self-worth as an artist.“Along with her other fans, I am so grateful for all of it. For the melodies and lyrics she wrote that thawed even the coldest hearts. For the millions of books she provided children all over the world so that they might fall in love with stories the way she did. For the tightropes she walked so that young girls like me could grow up dreaming of joining the circus too. Dolly, I’ll think of you each step of the way.”BeyoncéThe singer, who collaborated with Parton on a new version of Jolene on her last album, paid tribute in a statement published to her website:“Dolly, you were the barometer. The north star. Bold and brilliant. Talented and tenacious. You taught so many lessons on how to be uniquely oneself. I am grateful for your art, your heart, your generosity, your humor, your entrepreneurship.“I’m honored that I had the privilege to work with you. I will treasure that forever. Thank you for your profound impact on the world. You are an angel who has made this world a happier place because of your joyful art. You are truly one of one. Rest peacefully.”Kacey Musgraves“The world feels a lot less sparkly all of a sudden,”wrotethe country star.View image in fullscreenDolly Parton, Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda arrive for the premiere of 9 To 5 in New York City, 1980.Photograph: Richard Drew/APJane FondaIn a lengthy and emotional Instagram post, Parton’s 9 to 5 co-star wrote: “I know that millions are mourning and I want to say this – more than anyone I have ever known, Dolly will always be with us because she was so present, so powerful, so generous and playful that she is woven into all our lives and hearts forever.” She also added that she was “the voluptuous embodiment of empathy”.Lily TomlinParton’s 9 to 5 co-starshareda picture of the singer on X, writing: “Friend. Songwriter. The Great Harmonizer of Humanity. Dolly. Dolly. Dolly. Forever Dolly.”Jamie Lee CurtisAlongside a photo on Instagram, the Oscar-winning actorwrote: “Thank you, Dolly. For all of it.”‘9 to 5? She was full-on round the clock!’ Dolly Parton celebrated by kd lang, Peggy Seeger, Annie Lennox and moreRead moreSabrina CarpenterThe singerremembered Parton as an “angel walking on the earth”.“I will cherish our laughter and conversations and I will keep your wisdom, your playful outlook on life, and perfect sense of humor in my pocket for the rainy days,” she wrote. “There will never be another you and how lucky are we all to have experienced your singular magic as well as your once in a lifetime voice, songs, and heart.”Elton JohnThe singer wrote that he was “shocked and devastated to hear of Dolly’s passing. A giant of an artist – unique and irreplaceable, with the kindest heart.”Paul McCartneyMcCartney, who collaborated with Parton and Ringo Starr on acover of Let It Beon her 2023 album Rockstar,sharedthis tribute on Instagram:“The magnificent starDolly Partonhas died and it is so sad. She was such a wonderful woman. I first met her in Nashville at the Grand Ole Opry where she had been playing with the country star Porter Wagoner and was about to start her solo career. She was so bubbly and full of life it is difficult to take in the news that she has passed.”“Her songwriting, her singing and her philanthropy were unrivaled in the world of country music and it is hard to imagine living in a world without Dolly. She was a very clever business woman who understood the value of her music and, most importantly, the effect that she had on the people of the world.“There was no greater honour for me than to have her sing my song Let It Be and, even though I only made a small contribution to it, I am so honoured that she did it. I am so proud to have known her and admire her unique talents.“Thanks Dolly for the beautiful music you gave me and the whole world. We will always love you, god bless and rest in peace. You were the best.”Bernie SandersIn a post on X, the Vermont senatorcalledher “one of the great entertainers of our era” but also “a lifelong philanthropist and advocate for literacy, education, LGBTQ+ rights, healthcare and disaster relief”.View image in fullscreenKeith Urban and Dolly Parton.Photograph: KeystoneUSA-Zuma/Rex FeaturesKeith UrbanIn an Instagram story, the country star wrote: “Heartbroken today. Honestly … I have no words right now.”Patti LaBelleThe singer and close friend of Parton said she was “deeply saddened by the loss of my dear friend who was loved by all”.“Dolly’s artistry, brilliance, and extraordinary life inspired so many people, including me,” LaBelle told CNN. “Her light will forever shine! I send my deepest condolences to all of her loved ones and fans all over the world!”View image in fullscreenDolly Parton and Julia Roberts attend the Steel Magnolias premiere in New York City in 1989.Photograph: Ron Galella, Ltd./WireImageJulia RobertsParton’s Steel Magnolias co-star shared a statement, saying: “Dolly was a magical and joyous human. I hold knowing her as a treasure in my life. The sun has dimmed today.”Dionne WarwickAlongside a picture of Parton and herself, the singerposted: “I will certainly miss her laughter, jokes and her being. Rest well and in total peace my friend. My heart is heavy.”From Jolene to Islands in the Stream: Dolly Parton’s 10 best recordingsRead moreBarack ObamaThe former US president wrote on X: “It’s hard to imagine many people having a bigger impact than Dolly Parton. Born in a one-room cabin, she earned 11 Grammys and an Emmy, built a business empire, helped millions of kids learn to read, and – as if that wasn’t enough – helped accelerate the research that led to the Moderna Covid vaccine. What a life. Michelle and I are thinking of Dolly’s family and her many, many fans.”EminemThe rapper shareda letter Parton sent to himafter he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. “Even though I don’t know a lot about rap music, I’ve come to know you are the very best of it,” Parton wrote to him, adding: “I have always felt some unexplained connection to you like I know you somehow … no matter how complex your world may be just know you are very special and touch people in ways you don’t even know.”“I’m sorry we never got a chance to meet, but getting this note from Dolly really had an impact on me,” Eminem wrote. “She definitely didn’t have to take the time to do it. Even for a kid who mostly listened to rap music, she was an icon. A superstar in every sense. Rest easy Dolly. And thank you for the kind words.”Octavia SpencerThe Oscar-winning actorshared a poston Instagram, writing: “Dolly you were a gift to the world, your voice, your philanthropic heart, and warmth made us a feel seen and that the world was a pretty decent place. We miss you.”Reba McEntireThe country starshareda picture of the pair on Instagram, adding: “Dolly, thank you for all the wonderful things you did for us here on earth. Your love, your music and you gave so much with your huge huge heart.”View image in fullscreenDolly Parton and Reba McEntire.Photograph: Matt Baron/ShutterstockTim CookThe Apple CEOcalledParton “a brilliant songwriter, cultural icon, and dedicated philanthropist” and praised her for helping to “instill a love of reading and learning in millions of children around the world”.Seth MacFarlaneThe actor and animator, who worked with Parton on sci-fi comedy series The Orville, wrote that the experience had been “extraordinary”. “Her kindness, generosity, and authenticity were evident from moment one, and the benign yet assured command she maintained over her empire was obvious from the genuine love and trust you could see from everyone who worked for her,” hepostedonline. “The world is a dimmer place today without her.”Dolly Parton’s flamboyant, fun style: ‘I’m not a fashion icon; I’m an eyesore’Read moreBret MichaelsThe Poison singer alsosharedon Facebook: “Sending my deepest thoughts, prayers and condolences on the loss of the incredible Dolly Parton to her close family and friends. Dolly, you have forever added so much to our world and will forever be loved.”Mick JaggerThe Rolling Stones frontman wrote on X: “What a wonderful songwriter and singer Dolly was. She brought so many people together, we will all miss her so much.”Belinda CarlisleThe singer-songwritercalledParton “a light in this world” and wrote that she was “heartbroken” by the news.13:53Dolly Parton: why the world loved the queen of country - The LatestExplore more on these topicsDolly PartonCountryCelebrityMiley CyrusTaylor SwiftBeyoncéOprah WinfreynewsShareReuse this content

title: Rupert Grint to reprise role of Ron Weasley in Harry Potter stage show | Harry Potter and the Cursed Child | The Guardian
description: Like co-star Tom Felton, Grint will once again play the role that made him famous, in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: Like co-star Tom Felton, Grint will once again play the role that made him famous, in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child
Content: ‘Ron Weasley has been a part of me since I was 11 years old and I can’t wait to meet him again in this stage of life,’ Rupert Grint said in a statement.Photograph: LyricView image in fullscreen‘Ron Weasley has been a part of me since I was 11 years old and I can’t wait to meet him again in this stage of life,’ Rupert Grint said in a statement.Photograph: LyricHarry Potter and the Cursed ChildRupert Grint to reprise role of Ron Weasley in Harry Potter stage showLike co-star Tom Felton, Grint will once again play the role that made him famous, in Harry Potter and the Cursed ChildBenjamin LeeWed 26 Aug 2026 10.49 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 16.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRupert Grintis set to reprise the role of Ron Weasley in theBroadwayhitHarry Potterand the Cursed Child.The actor will join the long-running stage show for 17 weeks starting in February 2027.“Ron Weasley has been a part of me since I was 11 years old and I can’t wait to meet him again in this stage of life,” Grint said in a statement. “There is something so full-circle and so special about stepping back into Ron’s shoes now when we are both fathers; it is somehow both very familiar and completely new. And the joy of being back onBroadway, this time in a role that defined so much of my life is truly exciting.”Producers Sonia Friedman and Colin Callender said that his return “creates a powerful bridge between the story audiences first fell in love with and the story of family, legacy and the passage of time thatHarry Potter and the Cursed Childcarries forward”.View image in fullscreenRupert Grint in Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix.Photograph: Warner Bros/Sportsphoto/AllstarThe 38-year-old actor follows on from Tom Felton, who alsodecided to reprisethe role of Draco Malfoy on stage after playing him in the film series. Felton will continue to play the character until January.‘There’s so much magic!’: how we made Harry Potter and the Cursed ChildRead moreHarry Potter and the Cursed Child wasoriginallystagedin London in 2016, and across its many international incarnations it has sold more than 14m tickets. The New York production has made over $532m.Grint’s post-Potter films have included M Night Shyamalan’sKnock at the Cabinand romantic dramaCharlie Countryman. He was recently seen in horrorNightbornand will play Bob Cratchitopposite Johnny Deppin this November’s Ebenezer.He made his Broadway debut in 2014’sIt’s Only a Playfrom Terrence McNally alongside Nathan Lane.The star has previously chosen to distance himself from Harry Potter writerJK Rowling’s anti-trans views. “I firmly stand with the trans community and echo the sentiments expressed by many of my peers,”he said in 2020. “Trans women are women. Trans men are men. We should all be entitled to live with love and without judgment.”This year also sees the launch of HBO’s much-anticipated Harry Pottertelevision series.Explore more on these topicsHarry Potter and the Cursed ChildRupert GrintBroadwayUS theaterTheatreHarry PotternewsShareReuse this content

title: Janie Bradford obituary | Motown records | The Guardian
description: Songwriter who contributed to the first record made at Motown’s Detroit studio and co-wrote many of the label’s hits
Author: Richard Williams
Headline: Songwriter who contributed to the first record made at Motown’s Detroit studio and co-wrote many of the label’s hits
Content: Janie Bradford with members of the Oak Ridge Boys at the American Song festival, Sarasota Springs, Florida, in 1974.Photograph: ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJanie Bradford with members of the Oak Ridge Boys at the American Song festival, Sarasota Springs, Florida, in 1974.Photograph: ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content/Getty ImagesMotown recordsObituaryJanie Bradford obituarySongwriter who contributed to the first record made at Motown’s Detroit studio and co-wrote many of the label’s hitsRichard WilliamsWed 26 Aug 2026 10.50 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 10.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJanie Bradford was a poetry-loving receptionist, not yet out of her teens, when she provided her boss, Berry Gordy Jr, with the lines that helped him complete a song called Money (That’s What I Want). Gordy, then in the early stages of establishing Motown Records and searching for what would become the label’s signature sound, was sitting at the piano in the summer of 1959 when Bradford, who had been listening to him at work, came up with a couplet that drove home the song’s message: “Your love gives me such a thrill / But your love don’t pay my bills.”Money (That’s What I Want)was the first record to be made at Motown’s new Detroit studios, to be known as Hitsville USA. Sung by the 18-year-old Barrett Strong, it was released in the US in August 1959 and reached No 2 in the R&B charts and No 23 in the pop charts. In recognition of her contribution, Gordy added Bradford’s name to his own in the songwriting credits.The song’s simple 12-bar blues structure, thumping rhythm and general air of rowdiness – and an amusingly realistic lyric far removed from what would become Motown’s standard odes to young love in all its guises and shadings – soon endeared it to young British beat groups, who noted its enlivening effect on their audiences. When the Beatles included it on their second album in 1963 and the Rolling Stones released it on an EP, the publishing royalties significantly augmented the young receptionist’s wages.Bradford, who has died aged 87, was described by Smokey Robinson of the Miracles, Motown’s first million-selling act, as one of the company’s original six members of staff. She went on to co-write several more songs for Gordy’s artists, including Too Busy Thinking About My Baby, on which she shared the credits with Strong and the producer Norman Whitfield. First recorded by the Temptations in 1966, three years later it was picked as Marvin Gaye’s follow-up to his enormous hit with I Heard It Through the Grapevine.Born in Charleston, Missouri, Janie moved to Detroit with her family as a child, part of the great migration of African Americans from the rural south to the industrial cities of the north and the midwest. At school she learned to love poetry, with a particular fondness for the work of Robert Frost. She was introduced to Gordy by Jackie Wilson, the singer whose big hit of 1957, Reet Petite, had been co-written by the aspiring music mogul.According to Raynoma Singleton, Motown’s first vocal arranger, Gordy’s second wife and another of the original half-dozen Motown employees, Bradford had “a stupendous figure and a filthy mouth. Her mouth was so murderous that it could have had her arrested, but it also poured out sensational lyrics.”View image in fullscreenBradford at the 26th annual Heroes and Legends awards, Beverly Hills, California, in 2015.Photograph: Harmony Gerber/WireImageWhile contributing to songs recorded by such now-forgotten early Motown acts as Freddie Gorman, Debbie Dean and the Satintones, Bradford became one of those who could turn her hand to many tasks. “In those early days,” Gordy recalled, “everybody did what needed to be done, and Janie was no exception. She was smart and determined.”In 1961, when the decision was made to change the name of the newly signed Primettes, a young female vocal group from a Detroit housing project, it was Bradford who drew up a list including the name under which they became famous: the Supremes. During the long period when it seemed as though they would never make a commercial breakthrough, the B-side of a single called Let Me Go the Right Way featured a song titled Time Changes Things, which Bradford had co-written with Brian Holland and Lamont Dozier. It was Holland and Dozier, together with Brian’s brother Eddie, who wrote and produced the Supremes’ record-breaking run of 10 No 1s between 1964 and 1967.Bradford also collaborated with Dozier and Brian Holland on Contract on Love, the 12-year-old Little Stevie Wonder’s second single release, in 1962. A ballad titled Don’t Compare Me With Her, co-written with Dozier and Eddie Holland and originally intended for the Supremes, became the B-side of Kim Weston’s Take Me In Your Arms (Rock Me for a Little While), a hit in 1965.When Gordy moved the company to Los Angeles in 1970, she went with them, given the job of liaising with and developing the songwriters contracted to Gordy’s publishing company, Jobete Music. But when she left, at the end of that decade, after 20 years, it was without a pension and amid some bitterness. “I never felt the door would close on me,” she told Singleton, a similarly disenchanted involuntary exile.When she fell on hard times in the early 1980s, Diana Ross responded to a request to record one of her new songs, co-written with Freddie Gorman. Appearing on the B-side of Muscles, a top 10 hit, I Am Me brought in a significant sum. She went on to found the annual Heroes and Legends awards, honouring stars of the music industry and raising money to provide higher-education scholarships for young people.She is survived by her husband, Wardean Hobbs, whom she married in 1971, a son, Lance, a daughter, Nicole, and two grandchildren.Janie Bradford Hobbs, songwriter and music industry executive, born 2 June 1939; died 21 August 2026Explore more on these topicsMotown recordsPop and rockobituariesShareReuse this content

title: A Ugandan quarry worker carrying rocks on her head: Dan Nelken’s best photograph | Art and design | The Guardian
description: ‘Janet had eight children. Her husband drove a boda-boda taxi, but had lost a leg – so she had been working in her local quarry for 10 years. “I am now the husband in this home,” she said’
Author: Chris Broughton
Headline: ‘Janet had eight children. Her husband drove a boda-boda taxi, but had lost a leg – so she had been working in her local quarry for 10 years. “I am now the husband in this home,” she said’
Content: ‘Many of the women had small children or babies with them, yet most dressed as though they were going to market’ … Janet by Dan Nelken.Photograph: Dan NelkenView image in fullscreen‘Many of the women had small children or babies with them, yet most dressed as though they were going to market’ … Janet by Dan Nelken.Photograph: Dan NelkenMy best shotArt and designA Ugandan quarry worker carrying rocks on her head: Dan Nelken’s best photograph‘Janet had eight children. Her husband drove a boda-boda taxi, but had lost a leg – so she had been working in her local quarry for 10 years. “I am now the husband in this home,” she said’Interview byChris BroughtonWed 26 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2017, my wife, Adele Brown, was invited to spend three weeks at an NGO in Gulu,Uganda, teaching critical thinking skills to blind high school-age students. I was asked along to document the organisation’s activities. I became fascinated by the town’s main market, where vendors sold goods such as used clothes, fruit and firewood. I asked the Ugandan teachers how I might approach someone to take their portrait. They suggested I offer a modest “model fee” after seeking permission.One of the students – Emmanuel (Emma) – wanted to assist me. We would visit the market together. When I saw a vendor I wanted to photograph, Emma would approach and seek their consent. Most agreed, but after returning home to New York, I looked at the results and was disappointed. As with other well-intentioned projects, I thought that was the end of it.The images weren’t working because I felt the vendors were getting lost in their own environment – the backgrounds were too distracting. Adele and I were asked back to the NGO the following year, and this gave me the opportunity to resolve this issue. My eureka moment came when I decided the backdrop I needed was mosquito-netting. This allowed the women to stand out from their working environment while still letting their surroundings come through. The netting also added the symbolism of malaria, one of Uganda’s biggest health problems.double quotation markThe oldest woman I photographed at the quarry was 74. Another had lost an eye as a result of working thereMy wife and I noticed that women seemed to be doing nearly all the work, and that became the theme of my project. Emma mentioned a quarry about 10 miles outside town. The women who worked there were breaking rocks all day, reducing them to gravel size and being paid for each jerrycan they filled. Some had small children or babies with them, yet most dressed as though they were going to market – some even wore jewellery.I encouraged each woman to choose her own pose, giving her full control over how she wanted to be seen. The oldest woman I photographed at the quarry was 74. Another had lost an eye as a result of working there. But like all the women I photographed, they projected real dignity and a strong sense of self.I was keen to photograph as wide an economic spectrum as possible – women with their own businesses, as well as those at the bottom of the economic ladder. I wanted to know the women’s stories, too, so I collaborated with Ugandan author Beatrice Lamwaka, who interviewed each participant about her circumstances: what had led to her doing the work she did, her hopes and dreams for herself and her children. Northern Uganda is still dealing with the trauma of the civil war and this came through in several of the women’s narratives.This is Janet, who had been working in the quarry for 10 years when I photographed her. She had eight children to support and, like many of the women we spoke to, she was doing this alone. Her husband, who used to drive a type of motorbike-taxi called a boda boda, had been in an accident and lost a leg. “I am now the husband in this home,” she said, “and I have to do whatever I can to keep this house standing.” Many of the women had started working at the quarry as children because that’s what their mothers were doing. My portraits also included one of 10-year-old Jovia, who had been working there on weekends for four years to help pay her school fees – she wanted to become a doctor.I called the projectHeadStrongand was overwhelmed at how enthusiastic many of the women were when I went back to them with prints. I think photographers had sometimes shown interest before and then never been seen again. I am forever grateful to the 116 women who trusted me to take their portraits. They are the heroes of this project.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Dan NelkenDan Nelken’s CVBorn:1946, Tel AvivHighpoint:HeadStrongstands out as my most meaningful project. My hope is that the book will introduce readers to a group of remarkable women who, from their Ugandan perspectives, share a universal story of hope, often in the face of adversity, and aspire to build a better life for themselves and their children.Toptip:No matter what project you undertake, stay open-minded. Often, the direction I thought I was headed when I began new work deviated in unexpected ways that ultimately improved my original concept. And it often takes longer than you plan.See more atdannelken.comor on Instagram@headstrong_ugExplore more on these topicsArt and designMy best shotUgandaPhotographyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘My TikTok was flooded’: Suad Mooge on Ireland’s Rose of Tralee, navigating backlash and celebrating identity | Ireland | The Guardian
description: Dublin’s representative in the traditional festival defiantly reckons with xenophobia and balances Gaelic pride with her Somali heritage
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: Dublin’s representative in the traditional festival defiantly reckons with xenophobia and balances Gaelic pride with her Somali heritage
Content: Whirlwind affair … Dublin Rose, Suad Mooge.Photograph: Dublin Rose CentreView image in fullscreenWhirlwind affair … Dublin Rose, Suad Mooge.Photograph: Dublin Rose CentreThe Long WaveIrelandInterview‘My TikTok was flooded’: Suad Mooge on Ireland’s Rose of Tralee, navigating backlash and celebrating identityNesrine MalikDublin’s representative in the traditional festival defiantly reckons with xenophobia and balances Gaelic pride with her Somali heritageDon’t already get The Long Wave in your inbox? Sign up hereWed 26 Aug 2026 09.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 11.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast week marked the climax of Ireland’s Rose of Tralee festival, an annual celebration of Irish women, culture and the Irish diaspora. When Suad Mooge was chosen as Dublin’s participantin the festivalearlier this year, she quickly became a symbol of Ireland’s fraught conversation around immigration and what constitutes Irish identity.I caught up with Suad on a video call a week after the festival’s culmination, and found someone reflective and determined in the face of criticism.View image in fullscreen‘Why not?’… Suad Mooge submitted her own entry to the Rose of Tralee competition.Photograph: Fennell Photography/Dublin Rose CentreSuad is a wellspring of energy. Personable, open and radiating so much charm. More than anything, though, there is a sort of sororal girlhood about her. One can immediately see why she was chosen as Dublin’s Rose from among 39 competitors, and therefore the city’s representative in the wider Rose of Tralee festival. I asked Suad what prompted her to enter. Why not, she thought, after seeing an Instagram ad that made her realise you can simply nominate yourself. She applied then forgot all about it, until she received a notification that she had been selected. She went on to be named the Dublin Rose, and proceeded to the nationwide stage.The 10 days before the overall winner is crowned at the culmination of the festival are a whirlwind affair, Suad tells me. All the roses go on a tour ofIreland, meeting with the public, attending cultural events – Irish dancing, singing and sports – until they finally arrive in Tralee for the televised events and the finale. Everywhere they went, Suad tells me, they received a “huge welcome”.A viralbacklashView image in fullscreen‘Some bits were fun … people commenting online was a bit mad’ – Suad on her Dublin Rose experience.Photograph: Dublin Rose CentreBut that warm in-person reception came in tandem with a huge viral onslaught. “Even when I first got elected as Dublin Rose,” Mooge recalls, “In the first 24 hours there were 10,000 tweets. Then it was 20,000, 50,000.” Many of those comments and posts questioned Suad’s right to participate as someone of Somali heritage, and veered into racism and abuse. “My TikTok was completely flooded. Some bits were fun. I got to go on TV and do the Six O’Clock Show, but the incoming of people commenting online was a bit mad.” She had to lock her accounts and stay off her phone. Even rightwing USmedia picked up on the news, and dog-whistled about a “Somali Muslim” in the contest.Suad says it was “hard” to be at the centre of the backlash. The contest was already “physically and emotionally overwhelming”, with early starts and late nights, but the experience became even more difficult due to the discourse around her. But she remembers the other women with her – she was one of 32 – and how they helped and supported each other.An IrishculturalinstitutionView image in fullscreen‘There’s a lot of reclaiming’ … on the post-colonial resurgence of Irish culture.Photograph: Andres Poveda/RTÉ/Rose of TraleeThe Rose of Tralee, which culminates with a final in the titular town of Tralee, County Kerry, is a particularly unique Irish festival. In its 66th year, its purpose is “bringing back that Irish connection,” Suad says, between the Irish at home and the Irish diaspora abroad, and “celebrating it”, with Irish women at the core. When we start talking about Irish culture, how much she learned during the festival and the tour of Ireland, she brims with excitement. She quotes John B Keane, a famous dramatist and author from Kerry, who captured the beauty of the county that stunned her when she visited it; there are “two kingdoms — the Kingdom of Heaven and the Kingdom of Kerry”.She references how there has been arecent resurgence of pride in Irish culture, including traditional music and the Gaelic language, after hundreds of years of colonial erasure due to British occupation. “We were forced not to speak our language any more, but Irish is having such a comeback; everybody is doing Irish lessons. Irish culture is everywhere now; there’s a real pride in it, there’s a lot of reclaiming, we still came out on top and still have our culture. And people want to integrate and become part of this culture.”A sunny denialView image in fullscreen‘We need to face it’ … Suad on racism and xenophobia in Ireland.Photograph: Andres Poveda/RTÉ/Rose of TraleeOne of the problems of this positively inclined predisposition, Suad tells me, is that uncomfortable conversations are avoided. The response to racism and xenophobia is often: “‘Oh, it’s grand, it’s grand. It’s just a couple of eejits.’ We just brush things under the rug. A few things can be true at the same time. Yes, there is a lot of noise online and in person everyone is lovely. In the same breath, there is an issue. We need to face it. Otherwise these people will just continue sharing these ideas.”She notes that immigration to Ireland, when compared with immigration to the UK, for example, is a relatively recent phenomenon. Her family came to Ireland in the mid-90s and were the only Somali people in their area. Since then, the rate of immigration has increased drastically. “There was never that slow transition into it, and the country wasn’t necessarily equipped for that on a government level, and that trickles down to the people. They haven’t put proper systems to integrate systems and integrate people, as well as support the locals. It’s caused a divide.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe result is that “Ireland has become so much more diverse, but I don’t think people’s idea of Irishness has fully caught up. When I was elected as Dublin Rose, it tickled a lot of people’s feathers because it challenged their idea of what it means to be Irish. They don’t picture someone who looks like me. Representation and acceptance have not moved at the same pace.”Processing the experienceView image in fullscreen‘Nothing that could compare to what our parents went through’.Photograph: Mark Henderson/Against Racism Ireland/UNHCR Fair Play CupThe noise has died down now. Suad has taken a week off and tells me she is processing what happened, slowing down, staying off her devices and decompressing. But alongside the fatigue there is a determination that is at once steely and matter-of-fact. “My mam raised me not to let this stuff affect me,” she says. From a young age her mother would tell her “you’re going to get a lot of shit, but don’t back down. At the same time it was hard. But I’m at a healthy level of ‘don’t give power to these comments’.” What she has learned is to not “let people’s ideas of you limit you”.She ends, mentioning her mum again, and what she owes her and her generation. She “built me up,” Suad says. “A lot of our families have come from war. They crossed oceans to be here. There’s nothing that could compare to what our parents went through.”How can she let the criticism, when compared to the trials that her parents endured, get to her? “You can’t. Wallah, you can’t.”Tap inHow do you feel about the Rose of Tralee competition? What is the conversation missing? Share your thoughts by replying to this, or emailing us atthelongwave@theguardian.comand we may include your response in a future issue.Cartoon |Carnival across bordersView image in fullscreenHow carnival connects … a cartoon depicting multiple Caribbean nations celebrating.Illustration: Sarah AkinterinwaTo receive the complete version of The Long Wave in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.Explore more on these topicsIrelandThe Long WaveMigrationSomaliaWomenEuropenewslettersShareReuse this content

title: A moment that changed me: I sought out rejection. Instead, strangers met me with profound generosity | Life and style | The Guardian
description: As I turned 21, fear was holding me back. So I decided to face it headfirst. It taught me that courage leads to connection – and people who owe you nothing can be astonishingly kind
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As I turned 21, fear was holding me back. So I decided to face it headfirst. It taught me that courage leads to connection – and people who owe you nothing can be astonishingly kind
Content: ‘My first rejection challenge’ … making coffee in Warrington.Photograph: courtesy of Sophie JonesView image in fullscreen‘My first rejection challenge’ … making coffee in Warrington.Photograph: courtesy of Sophie JonesA moment that changed meLife and styleA moment that changed me: I sought out rejection. Instead, strangers met me with profound generosityAs I turned 21, fear was holding me back. So I decided to face it headfirst. It taught me that courage leads to connection – and people who owe you nothing can be astonishingly kindSophie JonesWed 26 Aug 2026 01.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn May 2024, I decided to spend 30 days getting rejected on purpose.At first, it sounded ridiculous. After all, most people spend their lives actively trying to avoid rejection – and I was deciding to walk, full force, towards it. But it had become obvious, as I turned 21, that my terror of being rejected was holding me back.‘An experiment in ritual humiliation’: would a month of rejection therapy make me fearless?Read moreFor over two years, I’d stayed in a relationship I knew wasn’t working, all too aware that the alternative – dating – would likely be riddled with rejection. On social occasions I often felt absent, focusing solely on not seeming weird or doing anything that might make others laugh at me. And in my first proper job, as a social media manager, I would talk myself out of opportunities that would put me in the spotlight and might have given me a chance to shine.So I promised myself I’d stop hiding from rejection for one month and see what happened. After a lifetime of worrying what people thought about me, I knew that only radical action would work.Later that week, on a sunny August afternoon, I found myself walking into a small independent coffee shop in my home town of Warrington, preparing for my first rejection challenge. I hesitated by the door for what felt like forever before finally plucking up the courage to walk to the counter.There, instead of placing my order, I forced myself to say the words, “I was wondering, if you showed me, could I make my own coffee please?”I had no reason for asking; I wasn’t especially particular about how my drink was made and I didn’t harbour grand ambitions of becoming a barista. I just wanted to see what would happen if I asked – and how I’d feel if they said no.View image in fullscreen‘They laughed with me, but never at me.’Photograph: courtesy of Sophie JonesI fully expected the staff to laugh at me or get annoyed for wasting their time, and I had a backup plan in place: I’d apologise, let them make my drink, apologise again and leave.But there was no anger, no interrogation. I explained my self-imposed “rejection challenge” and the barista seemed to see the funny side. “Why not?” he said.Less than five minutes later, I was behind the counter with an apron around my waist. My instructor walked me though the steps before letting me take the reins. He showed me how to steam milk without burning it, how to pull the perfect espresso shot, and reassured me every step of the way. We chatted about coffee, work, life – and I soon felt like I’d known him for a lot longer than just a few minutes.Walking out with my too-syrupy, slightly wonky latte, I felt a new admiration for baristas everywhere. I also began to suspect that my fear of rejection might actually be rooted in my own prejudice: the assumption that others were always judging me.As the challenge went on, I continued to be met with patience and generosity. I would approach people with unusual requests: asking strangers if I could join in their group photo, if they would film me singing, or if I could sit with them in my local cafe. I wore a wedding dress to do my supermarket shop. I even asked a packed commuter train for dating advice, turning what would have likely been another silent commute into a robust debate full of romance tips from across the whole carriage.When I began to run out of ideas, I asked friends to dream up outlandish scenarios for me to throw myself into, promising I’d do whatever they suggested.And time after time, I was exposed not to rejection, but the heartening kindness of humans who owed me nothing. Even when my strange requests were declined, the interactions were overwhelmingly positive – people were warm and curious about me, about my journey, and encouraged me to continue putting myself out there. They laughed with me, but never at me.View image in fullscreenWalking down the (supermarket) aisle in March 2025.Photograph: courtesy of Sophie JonesI had hoped my 30-day challenge would inoculate me against my fear of rejection, and it worked – but not in the way I was expecting. Instead of simply learning to cope with humiliation,I instead discovered rejection to be relatively rare; I’d been assuming the worst of others for years.After the month was up, I continued to incorporate this type of “rejection therapy” into my daily routine. I still make a point of doing things that push me out of my comfort zone, which often means striking up conversations with people I don’t know. Giving others the benefit of the doubt has opened up a world of happiness and opportunity. Courage, I’ve found, isn’t something that’s always rewarded with success, but it nearly always leads to connection.The Rejection Cure by Sophie Jones is published by Bloomsbury Tonic (£16.99).
