title: Nectar Classic memory foam mattress review: an outstanding budget buy | Sleep | The Guardian
description: With a genuinely impressive lifetime guarantee, Nectar’s mattress outperforms pricier rivals for comfort and motion isolation
Author: Jane Hoskyn
Headline: With a genuinely impressive lifetime guarantee, Nectar’s mattress outperforms pricier rivals for comfort and motion isolation
Content: Paws for thought: the Nectar Classic is a comfortable all-rounder.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPaws for thought: the Nectar Classic is a comfortable all-rounder.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterSleepReviewNectar Classic memory foam mattress review: an outstanding budget buyWith a genuinely impressive lifetime guarantee, Nectar’s mattress outperforms pricier rivals for comfort and motion isolationThe best mattresses, testedJane HoskynWed 26 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMemory foam has been calledthe Marmite of the bed industry. Nice soundbite, but I think it’s more like butter – because manymattressesnow include a “comfort layer” of this squishy material to make them more palatable. You wouldn’t eat a whole block of butter, though, and you probably wouldn’t want to sleep on a mattress made entirely from memory foam. Too much squish, too little support.The Nectar Classic memory foam, like so many of the best foam and hybrid (foam and springs) mattresses, tempers the marshmallowy feel of true memory foam by sandwiching it between other types of foam, namely breathable polyfoam and dense support foam. As I discovered when testing it, this creates a lovely balance of comfort and firmness that feels more like a hybrid mattress, only without the bounce.At £449 for a double, the Nectar Classic memory foam is also excellent value, especially as it comes witha lifetime guaranteethat genuinely deserves to be called “industry leading”. Here, I tear myself away from its cosy embrace to reveal why I loved it, despite wanting a fight with its washing label.View at NectarHow I testedThe Nectar is put through the all-important, industry-standard cat approval testI was sent a double-size Nectar Classic memory foam mattress in May, just as temperatures first punched past the 30C mark. Once I’d given the mattress a couple of days to expand to its full size and firmness, my family testing panel came over to rate it out of 10 for comfort, aesthetics and other subjective factors. They also helped me run lab-style experiments with heat pads, weights and wobbly cups of water to measure its sinkage, motion isolation, heat retention and edge support. Here’s more onour mattress-testing shenanigans– cats, bottoms and all.My husband, Alan, and I slept on the Nectar for six weeks in June and July, after positioning it on a slatted Ikea base and covering it with a mattress protector and cotton bedding. It was the worst of times for sleeping. The room temperature occasionally dropped below 28C with the help of anelectric fan, but for the most part it hovered around 32C. The fact that we managed to sleep on the Nectar, rather than just lie on it, shows how well it performed on temperature control.Delivery, sustainability and manoeuvrability are vital considerations every time I test a mattress. Quick delivery, plenty of text updates, helpful handlers and recyclable packaging are big green flags. Factors such as UK manufacture, low-carbon processes and mattress recycling schemes help boost the otherwise low sustainability ranking of foam.Then there’s price. Instead of looking for cheapness per se, I want value for money and durability, especially from a product that’s as difficult to dispose of as a memory foam mattress.What you need to know, from price to firmnessView image in fullscreenThe Nectar combines layers of foam of different densities.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianView at NectarThe Classic memory foam is Nectar’s most popular mattress, according to the brand, and part of a range that also includes another all-foam mattress (thePremier),two foam-and-spring hybrid mattresses, and akids’ mattress. The Classic memory foam is the most affordable of Nectar’s adult mattresses: £199 for a single, rising to £649 for a super-king. The double I tested costs £449. That’s cheaper than theTempur Ease– another all-foam mattress with a feel and performance similar to the Nectar.The Nectar Classic isn’t just a massive chunk of high-viscosity memory foam. As with most modern foam mattresses, it combines layers of foam of different densities. Immediately below the fabric cover is a top layer of breathable polyfoam to help regulate body temperature and add a little bounce, followed by a thick middle layer of memory foam for cushioning, then a base layer of dense foam for support and durability.Nectar rates the mattress as “6.5 out of 10 (medium-firm)”, but it feels firmer than that when you first sleep on it. My testing panel gave it an average 8/10, and then, after Alan and I had slept on it for a month, we rated it 7/10 (where 10 is firmest). This isn’t a fault: all foam mattresses soften after being slept on, then settle after a while to their intended tension level.The fabric sleep surface is made from synthetic fabric (9.5% low-density polyethylene and 90.5% polyester), while the bottom cover is 100% polyester. Nectar says the fabric is woven with “cooling fibres” and describes it as “menopause-friendly”, explaining that it “wicks heat away and encourages airflow”.The Nectar’s cover isn’t removable, despite having a giant zip that you can unzip all the way round to, yes, remove the cover (I agree, it makes no sense). When I unzipped it, partly to investigate the layers inside, I found a washing label that warned: “non-removable cover”, “do not wash”, “do not dry clean” and “zip for manufacturing use only”. So while youcanremove the cover, you’re not supposed to.Nectar’s warrantydoesn’t explicitly discuss this, but I’d play it safe and keep that zip zipped. While the headline warranty term is “forever”, which genuinely beats any other mattress guarantee I’ve seen (besidesDreamCloud, which shares a parent company with Nectar), limitations include any use “in violation of instructions” – such as removing the cover. If the mattress is defective within 10 years, you’ll get a replacement. From year 11, Nectar will completely repair and re-cover it.Nectar Classic memory foam mattress specificationsType:memory foamMaterials:polyurethane foam filling; polyester and polyethylene coverFirmness:advertised as medium-firm; panel rated as 8/10 after two days, then we rated as 7/10 after six weeksDepth:25cmCover:do not removeTurn or rotate:“rotate regularly”, according to label;rotate “every few months”, according to the Nectar blogTrial:365 nightsWarranty:forever, with limitationsOld mattress recycling:£60Sustainability credentials:mattresses are made in the UK using CertiPur- and Oeko-Tex-certified foam; Nectar works withClimatePartnerto reduce environmental footprint; returned mattresses are donated to the British Heart FoundationDeliveryView image in fullscreenThe box was small enough for one person to lug upstairs.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianNectar mattresses are shrink-wrapped into boxes and delivered byBJS Home Delivery, and the service was excellent in my experience. BJS kept me updated via text and WhatsApp, sending me a three-hour window on the day before delivery, and including a tracking link that proved useful and accurate.The two delivery drivers asked if I wanted them to carry the box upstairs and even remove the packaging, but I was happy for them to leave it in the hallway. At 32kg for a double, the Nectar Classic is one of the lighter mattresses I’ve tested, and the box was small enough for me to lug upstairs by myself – a rare treat in my life as a mattress reviewer.What we loveA glass of water puts the Nectar Classic’s motion isolation to the testThe first thing I loved was how blissfully easy this mattress was to carry up the stairs and unpack. I use double-size mattresses in my tests for the Filter because a king-size pocket-sprung mattress would get stuck in our narrow, angled stairwell. But the Nectar Classic memory foam is solight and tightly rolledthat even a super-king would have made it upstairs easily. Given the affordability and manoeuvrability of the Nectar Classic, I’d recommend buying the largest size your bedroom has space for.After giving the mattress a couple of days to expand, we invited our family over for their verdict. My sister Maeve, who identifies as a memory-foam sceptic, declared herself “really surprised” by howfirm and breathableit felt. Her husband, Ben, is easier to please (any bed works, as long as he can sleep in it immediately), but agreed: “this is better than the other foam mattresses [we’ve tested]. I can evensit on the edgeof this one without sinking.”When settling in for the sleep test, Alan and I also loved howflat, supportive and airythe mattress was. This is largely because the Nectar’s top layer is much less mouldable than theTempur Pro Plus SmartCooland thePanda bamboo mattress topper. The middle layer is more “sinky” and helps with pressure relief, but its top layersprings backmore quickly than pure memory foam when you press it, which makes it feel less cloying.I slept much better on the Nectar than I’d expected to, given the heat of June and July. Over the weeks, it softened slightly to cushion my pressure points, but itnever softened too much. When we ran our sinkage tests in the first week, the sleep surface sank 2cm under 7.5kg of weights. By the end of week four, it sank 2.7cm – less than theSimba Hybrid Pro. I was still measuring 2.7cm in week six, which suggests the softening had settled.The Nectar Classic’smotion isolationis outstanding, as is often the case with foam. While the “non-sinky” upper layer made it easy to turn in bed, the lower layer of adaptive foam seemed to absorb our movements so we never disturbed each other while fidgeting.What we don’t loveView image in fullscreenNo bounce means this mattress won’t be the first choice for those who love a springy bed.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianThe Nectar was more comfortable in the heatwave than I’d expected from a foam mattress with a polyester cover. That’s damning with faint praise, though. It only performed moderately well ontemperature control, and I suspect that my electric fan, cotton bedsheets and bamboo duvet (thesummer edition of the Panda Cloud, which topped mybest duvetstest) did a lot of heavy lifting to help me sleep.In my heat-retention test, the Nectar’s surface took marginally longer to fall back to ambient room temperature than Panda’s memory foam mattress topper, which I recently tested under similar balmy conditions. That said, I never experienced night sweats on the Nectar, unlike theOtty Bamboo topper, which I had to drag off our bed at 4am.The slight softening of the mattress over our weeks of sleeping was expected given its foam composition, but it never sagged. If you sleep on your back or your front, however, it may becometoo softfor you. If, on the other hand, you crave the sink-in pressure relief of memory foam, itmay feel too firm. There’s alsono bounce, so this probably won’t be your first choice if you love a springy bed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFoam and hybrid mattresses usually have fabric covers that you can unzip to wash in the machine, but the Nectar doesn’t (remember, ignore the zip!). This helps to keep its price down because there’s no inner lining to protect the foam when the cover is off. However, it does mean thatyou have to buy a mattress protectorand use it diligently to keep the mattress in good condition, especially during its one-year trial period.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenRolling out change: Nectar says it is working to cut the mattress’s environmental impact.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianMemory foam (viscoelastic polyurethane foam) is one of the least sustainable materials used in furnishings. It’s made using petroleum-derived chemicals including polyols and diisocyanates, and emits volatile organic compounds (VOCs) when removed from its shrink-wrapping at home. That’s what the “off-gassing” smell is.Nectar is working to limit the damage, though.It claims it has offset 43m kilograms of carbon to date, and has enlisted the help ofClimatePartnerto cut its footprint rather than just offset it. Among its plans are a switch away from polyurethane foam to a “low-emission alternative”, and “updates on plastic packaging”. Meanwhile, all its foam is CertiPur and Oeko-Tex certified, and its mattresses are made in Manchester and delivered in FSC-certified cardboard.Nectar charges £60 to collect your old mattress when you buy a new one from the company. Where a mattress can’t be resold, it’s donated to the British Heart Foundation (BHF). Nectar says this scheme has raised more than £1.2m for the BHF. Nectar’s lifetime warranty is also worth mentioning here because it will help you avoid having to dispose of your mattress for many years.Nectar Classic memory foam mattress: should I buy it?View image in fullscreenRoom for everyone: the Nectar Classic is an easy mattress to live with.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianThe Nectar Classic memory foam mattress is an outstanding buy. It’s one of the lightest and easiest-to-manoeuvre mattresses I’ve tested, beaten only by the budgetIkea Valevåg. This makes it an excellent choice for anyone moving house or setting up home – or indeed, anyone blessed with a tight stairwell like mine.It’s easy to sleep on, too. Side sleepers may initially find it too firm, but it adapts to cushion your pressure points and strike a lovely balance of comfort and support. Despite testing this mattress in a heatwave, I never woke up at 4am in a pool of sweat and misery, as I have with a few other memory foam products.I wouldn’t call it a “cooling” mattress, though. If overheating is a problem for you, I’d recommend a sprung or hybrid mattress instead. Sprung mattresses also tend to be a more sustainable choice.Those are the main reasons I gave this mattress four stars rather than five, although I’d give it four and a half if I could. It feels durable enough to last for many years, and its generous warranty backs this up.The Nectar is no Marmite mattress. You may love it, but you’re highly unlikely to hate it. It’ll appeal to a wide range of people, including side sleepers, back sleepers and couples, and it’s well worth its price.View at NectarNectar Classic mattressvs…Otty Original HybridView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianDouble, £540 with code FILTER10 at OttyThe firm-but-cosy feel of the Nectar Classic reminded me more of the brilliant Otty than any other mattress. The Nectar is cheaper, though (the Otty costs £599.99 for a double; currently £540 with the code FILTER10), and lighter, so it’s easier to move around. Why, then, did I give the Otty five stars, and the Nectar only four? The Otty, which contains springs as well as layers of foam, dissipated heat more quickly in my tests than the Nectar. It also felt more instantly comfortable, whereas the Nectar needed a couple of weeks to develop a bit of “give” under my pressure points. Its lower proportion of foam gives it the edge on sustainability, too. It won’t shout at you for removing and washing its cover, either.Read our fullOtty Original Hybrid mattress reviewTempur EaseView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianDouble, £699 at TempurThe Tempur Ease doesn’t hide its memory foam layer in the middle like the Nectar, but puts it immediately under the fabric cover (which you can unzip to wash, hooray). The overall effect is still reassuringly supportive, but it feels more yielding and may be a better choice for side sleepers. If you crave a marshmallowy memory foam surface, though – and can afford the investment – I’d recommend the medium edition ofTempur’s Pro SmartCool mattress. I found it too soft, but it makes you feel fully suspended in your bed and is fantastic for pain relief.Simba Hybrid ProView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianDouble, £909.30 at SimbaI had some of the best sleeps of my life on the Simba Hybrid Pro. The foam layers give it fantastic motion isolation and a sumptuous feel. It softened quite a lot over my months of testing, though, and it’s heavier than the Nectar. Its price is weighty, too, at £1,299 for a double at RRP (£909.30 at the time of writing in the brand’s bank holiday sale).Read our fullSimba Hybrid Pro mattress reviewFor more ways to sleep better with the Filter:The best mattresses, testedThe best mattress toppersThe best pillows, testedJane Hoskyn is a features journalist who’s spent three decades rearranging bookshelves and “testing” products while deadlines loom. She would always rather be in the woods, or napping, or napping in the woodsExplore more on these topicsSleepThe FilterHomesHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Stuck bundts? You need ‘cake goop’: Natalie Paull’s lime and yoghurt bundt – recipe  | Australian food and drink | The Guardian
description: The cookbook author and owner of Melbourne’s Beatrix Bakes shares a her ‘100% reliable’ formula for freeing bundts from tins
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The cookbook author and owner of Melbourne’s Beatrix Bakes shares a her ‘100% reliable’ formula for freeing bundts from tins
Content: Natalie Paull’s lime and yoghurt bundt cake. Stylist: Kirsten Jenkins. Home economist: Genene Dwyer and Sarah Watson.Photograph: Rochelle EagleView image in fullscreenNatalie Paull’s lime and yoghurt bundt cake. Stylist: Kirsten Jenkins. Home economist: Genene Dwyer and Sarah Watson.Photograph: Rochelle EagleAustralian food and drinkStuck bundts? You need ‘cake goop’: Natalie Paull’s lime and yoghurt bundt – recipeThe cookbook author and owner of Melbourne’s Beatrix Bakes shares a her ‘100% reliable’ formula for freeing bundts from tinsNatalie PaullWed 26 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 22.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen all the layer cakes are baked and iced, I will always love a slice of pretty patterned bundt. Especially one that is lightened with the perfect amount of baking powder (overly dense bundts are stodgy sadness) and brightened with limes and yoghurt.Cake goop – a mix of flour, oil and butter – is a gift of guaranteed cake release that I found on the internet, and it means no more stuck bundts. Bless the baker who invented it! Goop has it all – release, plus enough sticking power to hold the batter as it rises and cools, without slumping. Additionally, mixing the flour with oil means you don’t get that fine, white, dusty crust on the outside of the cooked cake. Goop is 100% reliable with a 100% untarnished release record in my kitchen.Pastry shops are displaying their buns uncovered – just don’t bite the merchandiseRead moreIf you do have a small stuck piece of cake, shimmy it out of the tin with an offset spatula and patch it back on to the cake while warm. Pretty easy! If a whole ring of cake has stuck, cut it into workable sections, prise each out and place back on the cake. Drench the bundt with icing sugar after its soak to hide the Franken-bundt’s monster appearance.The recipe calls for the eggs to be warmed before cracking. Warmer-than-room- temperature eggs emulsify into the creamed base better, and an emulsified mix means no “curdled” appearance. To do this, submerge the uncracked eggs in hot tap water for five minutes.The cake will keep for three days, covered, at room temperature. And it freezes perfectly for up to three months.Lime and yoghurt bundt cake – recipeMakes1 bundtor a 20cm round cakeTakes2-3 hoursFor the cake goop20gplainflour(10% protein)20gvegetable oil20gunsalted butter, squidgy soft, at 22CFor the cake batter6 juicy limes400gcastersugar280gunsalted butter, soft, at 20C5 eggs, warmed, but uncracked375g soft plain flour(8-9% protein)2 tsp baking powder¼ tsp fine sea salt240g plain yoghurt, at room temperature, or microwave in 30-second bursts, stirring in between, to de-chillFor the lime syrup250glime juice(from the limes used for the cake batter)300g icing sugar mixPreheat the oven to 170C/150C fan.Makethe cake goop by mixing the ingredients into a paste, then brush it into every nook and cranny of the bundt tin. Set the tin aside.Make the batter. Zest the limes, then in a bowl rub the zest into the sugar with your fingers to release maximum fragrant oil. In the bowl of a stand mixer with the paddle attachment, cream the butter and lime sugar on medium speed for around six to eight minutes until the mix is pale and fluffy. Stop and scrape the side down once or twice during the creaming. In a separate bowl, crack the eggs, whisk and weigh 250g, then add to the mixer bowl in three batches, beating after each addition, then beat for another five minutes on medium speed.Combine the flour, baking powder and salt together in a bowl.Remove the bowl from the mixer and push the batter off the paddle. Sift half the flour mix over the top and fold it in with a sturdy plastic spatula. When it is almost fully mixed in, fold in half the yoghurt. Repeat with the remaining flour, then the remaining yoghurt. Make sure the final mix is very thorough so no flour or yoghurt streaks remain. Scrape the batter into the bundt tin and carefully smooth the top with a spoon.Bake for 60 to 70 minutes until the cake has a fawn-coloured crust, the top has gently puffed and cracked, and a skewer inserted into the thickest part of the bundt comes out clean (internal temperature should be 95C).Make the syrup while the cake bakes. Place the icing sugar in a wide bowl and hand-whisk half the juice in. Then whisk in the remaining juice. (By making a thick paste first, then thinning with the remaining juice, you can avoid sifting the icing sugar.)Remove the cake from the oven. Using a metal skewer, poke lots of holes in the top of the cake, then slowly spoon half the syrup over the cake – it will attempt to run off the sides but concentrate most of the syrup on the open cracked ring of cake on the top. It’s quite mesmerising to watch it soak in. Leave for 10 minutes.Invert the cake on to a serving plate. With a skewer, poke a few fine holes on the top and inner ring wall and brush more syrup over. I have given you a little extra syrup if you want a super-soaked cake, but I brush on two coats, then dab it again as it cools. Cool for 30 minutes before cutting the first slice.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Murdoch BooksThis is an edited extract fromSweet Heartby Natalie Paull, with photography by Rochelle Eagle, available in Australia 1 September through Murdoch Books, $49.99Explore more on these topicsAustralian food and drinkCakeFoodBakingDessertAustralian lifestylerecipesShareReuse this content

title: How to turn the dregs of a ketchup bottle into a classic Marie Rose dressing – recipe | Sauces and gravies | The Guardian
description: Shake up the remnants of a bottle of ketchup with a splash of sprits, a heap of mayonnaise and a few other simple additions, and turn it into one of the culinary world’s most famous sauces
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Shake up the remnants of a bottle of ketchup with a splash of sprits, a heap of mayonnaise and a few other simple additions, and turn it into one of the culinary world’s most famous sauces
Content: Tom Hunt’s ketchup bottle Marie Rose sauce goes as well on lettuce wedges as in a prawn cocktail.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s ketchup bottle Marie Rose sauce goes as well on lettuce wedges as in a prawn cocktail.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notSauces and graviesHow to turn the dregs of a ketchup bottle into a classic Marie Rose dressing – recipeShake up the remnants of a bottle of ketchup with a splash of sprits, a heap of mayonnaise and a few other simple additions, and turn it into one of the culinary world’s most famous saucesTom HuntWed 26 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy new favourite preparation for sauces, marinades and dressings is in a near-empty jar, tub or bottle, so I can upcycle all the remains. Rather than washing it and putting it in the recycling, I instead add a few store-cupboard ingredients to create a dressing or sauce, often re-exploring classics such as a retro Marie Rose sauce or myyoghurt-pot chicken. It’s a convenient way to use up the last dregs of a ketchup bottle, for instance, which often seems to harbour exactly the right amount of sauce.My Marie Rose recipe is inspired by the one inSimon HopkinsonandLindsey Bareham’s 1997The Prawn Cocktail Years. It’s wonderfully simple, with the sophisticated addition of a dash of cognac, though other recipes use brandy. I had neither, however, but I did have some sweet vermouth left over, which worked exceptionally well, so feel free to experiment with whatever spirits you have to hand – vodka, for instance, works brilliantly, and gives the sauce a nice kick.Serve tossed with prawns, avocado, lettuce and cucumber in a classic prawn cocktail, or splat on to burger buns, or do as I did and serve drizzled over wedges of iceberg lettuce garnished with celery leaves and capers, and dusted with paprika. Glass or plastic bottles both work, though squeezy ones help to deliver a chef-like drizzle.Ketchup bottle Marie RoseWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appWhen I was a kid, I used to love ketchup on just about everything, so these days it seems a rather odd concept to mix it with mayonnaise and prawns. Even so, it is surprisingly good – well, of course it is – and a great way to use up the annoying last dregs in the bottom of the bottle. Besides the other dishes mentioned above, Marie Rose also goes really well withavocado fries, if you happen to also have an under-ripe avocado to hand.4-5 tbsp mayonnaise1 tsp sweet vermouth, or other spirit (vodka, cognac, brandy)1-3 tbsp sriracha, Tabasco or other chilli sauce, to taste1 small squeeze lemon juiceFlaky sea salt and black pepper1 part-empty ketchup bottle, with roughly 1-2 tbsp remainingPaprika, to finish, optionalUsing a funnel, if you have one, add the mayonnaise, vermouth, Tabasco (or other chilli sauce), lemon juice, a small pinch of sea salt and generous grind of black pepper to the near-empty ketchup bottle. Screw the lid back on and shake well. Taste, adjusting for seasoning, heat and acidity as required, then squeeze directly over your chosen dish. Finish with a pinch of paprika, if you like.Explore more on these topicsSauces and graviesWaste notFoodFood wasteShellfishfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A Tamil summer vegetarian feast: Cynthia Shanmugalingam’s cucumber yoghurt curry and gooseberry pickle  | Curry | The Guardian
description: Serve this cold curry with a hot, fenugreek-flavoured preserve for a seasonal refresher
Author: Cynthia Shanmugalingam
Headline: Serve this cold curry with a hot, fenugreek-flavoured preserve for a seasonal refresher
Content: Cynthia Shanmugalingam’s cucumber yoghurt curry with gooseberry pickle.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Liam Baker.View image in fullscreenCynthia Shanmugalingam’s cucumber yoghurt curry with gooseberry pickle.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Liam Baker.CurryA Tamil summer vegetarian feast: Cynthia Shanmugalingam’s cucumber yoghurt curry and gooseberry pickleServe this cold curry with a hot, fenugreek-flavoured preserve for a seasonal refresherCynthia ShanmugalingamWed 26 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis lovely summery “curry” is a cold, refreshing dish from Karnataka in India, and is eaten widely in Tamil Nadu, just 20 miles across the Palk Strait from my ancestral Tamil homeland in north and eastern Sri Lanka. Along with chefs Louis and Seb in our development kitchen, we decided that smacking the cucumbers helps give them a silky texture, and means the fragrant yoghurt base can get into all the nooks and crannies. It’s wonderful with plain rice and a side of fenugreek-heavy hot Tamil pickle, made with English gooseberries rather than superfood nelli, both of which are said to make your skin shine and hair bouncy.Hot gooseberry pickleWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenCynthia Shanmugalingam’s hot gooseberry pickle.Prep10 minCook10 minPickle10 minChill2 hr+Serves4250g gooseberries250ml apple cider vinegar1 tbsp caster sugar1 tsp salt1 tsp fenugreek seeds1 tbsp mustard seeds4 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed3 tbsp vegetable oil4 tbsp Kashmiri chilli powderSome saltWash the gooseberries well, then spread them out on a cloth and leave to dry.Put the vinegar, 250ml water, the sugar and salt in a saucepan and cook on a high heat until the sugar and salt have dissolved and the liquid is simmering. Add the gooseberries, turn off the heat and leave to pickle for 10 minutes.In a small frying pan, dry roast the fenugreek for about 60 seconds, until fragrant, then leave to cool. Tip the cooled fenugreek into a small spice grinder or mortar, add the mustard seeds and crushed garlic, then blitz or grind to a paste. Scrape the mix into a small bowl, add the drained gooseberries, the oil, chilli powder and salt, then cover and put in the fridge for at least two hours.Cucumber yoghurt curryWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenCynthia Shanmugalingam’s cucumber yoghurt curry.Prep15 minCook10 minServes42 cucumbers80g desiccated coconut (frozen or freshly grated), soaked in water for 15 minutes, then drained2 green chillies, roughly chopped4 garlic cloves, peeled and roughly chopped30g fresh coriander, stalks and leaves½ tsp black peppercorns2 tsp sesame seeds100g natural yoghurtSalt, to tasteBoiled white rice, to serveFor the temper4 tsp vegetable oil, or coconut oil10 fresh curry leaves1 tsp fenugreek seeds(optional)2 tsp mustard seeds2 tsp cumin seeds3 dried red chillies, ideally cascabelFirst, make a coconut-cucumber paste. Peel the cucumbers, reserving the skins. Wrap each cucumber in clingfilm, then bash them lightly with a rolling pin. Remove the clingfilm, keeping the seeds, and cut the flesh on a slight diagonal into 1cm slices. Put a few of the chopped cucumbers, the cucumber seeds and skins into a blender, add the drained coconut, green chillies, garlic, coriander, black peppercorns and sesame seeds, then blitz smooth.Put the yoghurt in a medium bowl, and whisk until smooth, then beat in enough water, if need be, to get it to a pouring consistency. Add salt to taste, stir in the cucumber paste and remaining chopped cucumber, then pour into a serving bowl and put in the fridge to chill.When you’re ready to eat, make the temper. Put the oil in a small frying pan on a highheat, add the curry leaves and, after about 30 seconds, when they’re sizzling, stir in the fenugreek (if using), mustard seeds, cumin seeds and red chillies – stand well back, because the spices will probably splutter. Pour the hot temper, oil and all, over the cucumber yoghurt curry and serve with plain boiled white rice.Cynthia Shanmugalingam is chef/proprietor ofRambutan, London SE1Explore more on these topicsCurryFoodMain courseSide dishesHerbs and spicesPickling, fermenting and preservingFruitrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Would you pay for an algorithm to pick your friends? New social apps spread across cities | Friendship | The Guardian
description: With many adults admitting they feel lonely, meetup platforms offer the chance to make new connections
Author: Kimi Chaddah
Headline: With many adults admitting they feel lonely, meetup platforms offer the chance to make new connections
Content: Paid social clubs are spreading across UK cities – typically charging anything from nothing at all to £20 a month.Photograph: Caia Image/Getty Images/Collection Mix: Subjects RFView image in fullscreenPaid social clubs are spreading across UK cities – typically charging anything from nothing at all to £20 a month.Photograph: Caia Image/Getty Images/Collection Mix: Subjects RFFriendshipWould you pay for an algorithm to pick your friends? New social apps spread across citiesWith many adults admitting they feel lonely, meetup platforms offer the chance to make new connectionsKimi ChaddahWed 26 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWould you pay £20 a month for the chance of making a friend, on the understanding that an algorithm – not you – gets to decide who you’ll meet?Driven by the decline of “third spaces” such as youth centres and pubs, an increase in remote working and rising loneliness – 40% of adults aged 16 to 29 feel lonely “always, often or some of the time”, according to the Office for National Statistics – paid social events are now in vogue.“There hasn’t been anything that feels authentic to helping people meet people,” says Nicola Gunby, a co-founder of Cliq, an online platform and app that aims “to bring people together through shared interests and real-world experiences”.“The first place people in their 20s and 30s turn to when trying to make friends is Facebook groups,” she says. “But they’ve ended up becoming a noticeboard for people who’ve, say, lost their dog or want to sell their bed.” For Gunby, these groups are “far too big and broad to be a genuine community”.Into this gap has stepped a new wave of what are effectively paid social clubs.View image in fullscreenThe way people decide on which social events to attend is starting to change.Photograph: ToucanStudios/Getty ImagesThe mechanics are fairly simple: platforms such as PLY (it stands for People Like You) and Agora match people using information such as their interests, lifestyle habits and profession. Then, typically, an algorithm decides which events a user should attend, as opposed to free alternatives, such as the Meetup platform, that leave that choice with members.The ideal outcome for participants is showing up, making some new connections and leaving with plans to meet up again.But as these clubs spread across UK cities – typically charging from nothing at all to £20 a month – the question for anyone considering joining, is the same as you would ask about any subscription: what are you actually paying for, and is it worth it?At PLY, memberships tend to start at £19.99 a month, giving members access to exclusive events and discounts with other businesses, falling to about £9.99 a month for longer commitments.“When you do things for free, people often don’t turn up,” says Karen Harris, the founder of PLY, of its membership model. “People need someone who’s committed, who’s looking to maintain friendships and taking it seriously.”View image in fullscreenYou can use Meetup without having to pay a fee.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto/ShutterstockAccording to Harris, the majority of PLY’s customers sign up for longer-term memberships – a reflection of both the lower cost and of how long a friendship takes to build. On average, she says, it takes three events “to find your person”.Other clubs offer a mix of pay-as-you-go and subscription options. This is Agora’s model as it makes things more accessible, argues its founder, Sahil Shirazee.In the two years since its launch, the club has hosted more than 300 events and claims to have helped form hundreds of friendships.For some of those looking to make new friends, flexibility is important. “A membership fee would make me feel pressured into attending so many events every month,” says Charlotte Johnson, 29, from Hertfordshire, who is a Cliq user.Paying per event “encourages me to go if I’ve paid for it” while leaving her free to not attend those that aren’t of interest to her.Johnson says that “what really surprised me was I got more than expected”. She highlights a recent brunch event that included things such as a take-home goodie bag. She has since signed up for a pottery event.“Everyone’s there for the same, if not similar, reasons,” she adds, “which takes a lot of the fear out of meeting strangers.” If participants don’t click with anyone within a month of joining, some of the platforms, including PLY, offer a money-back guarantee.View image in fullscreenCliq hosts run clubs.Photograph: CliqNot everyone is convinced that paying for friendship is something to celebrate.Shirazee admits he still gets asked why people should have to pay to meet each other at all. But, he says, if you want to solve problems such as loneliness, and create meaningful communities as quickly as possible, “you need to make sure the people who want to crack this issue are able to not only get compensated, but grow”.Harris rejects the idea that people are “paying for access to strangers”.double quotation markYou’re paying for a system, for structure, that makes connections much betterPLY founder Karen Harris“You’re paying for a system, for structure, that makes connections much better,” she says. Free socialisation, she argues, usually relies on the presence of a host or facilitator, whereas at PLY events, “interaction is peer-to-peer, without a facilitator moving you forward”.Free events haven’t disappeared, though – and continue to be the preferred option for some.“I tend to choose free events most of the time because I can’t always afford to pay for social activities,” says Giovanna Giusi, a primary school teacher.The 28-year-old says she appreciates having access to a mixture of free events, such as hikes or walks, and paid events. This allows her to “be part of a community even when money is tighter”.She says the paid events “make it possible to offer experiences that couldn’t realistically happen for free, such as workshops with instructors, private classes or activities that need a venue”.“People always say they want more community and more opportunities to meet others, but it’s easy to forget that organising those communities still takes time, work and money,” Giusi says.Whether paid socialisation becomes the norm is, for now, an open question.Despite it being the foundation of their business model, the organisers say they hope not. “In the long run, I don’t want Agora to exist,” Shirazee says, because “meeting people is so natural” it shouldn’t rely on an algorithm.But in the meantime, after establishing a “proper base” in London, he is already planning to expand to different cities next year.Explore more on these topicsFriendshipConsumer affairsSocial mediaTechnology sectorfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Walking on the edge: a three-day hike along Cumbria’s rugged, overlooked coast | Walking holidays | The Guardian
description: In the shadow of the crowded Lake District, this quiet coast path offers great views, breathtaking nature and a striking new hotel on the historic waterfront
Author: Chris Moss
Headline: In the shadow of the crowded Lake District, this quiet coast path offers great views, breathtaking nature and a striking new hotel on the historic waterfront
Content: The Edge Hotel, which opened last October in Whitehaven, was created as a base for coastal activities.View image in fullscreenThe Edge Hotel, which opened last October in Whitehaven, was created as a base for coastal activities.Walking holidaysWalking on the edge: a three-day hike along Cumbria’s rugged, overlooked coastIn the shadow of the crowded Lake District, this quiet coast path offers great views, breathtaking nature and a striking new hotel on the historic waterfrontChris MossWed 26 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 03.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat’s the edgiest region in the UK? I don’t mean in the sense of sketchy or fashionable, but where on the map of these four nations feels most at the margins of everywhere else? For my money, the north Cumbrian coast is a strong contender. Hemmed in by the Lake District fells on one side and the Solway Firth and Irish Sea on the other, this strip of towns and villages, farms and nature reserves, clinging to the low-lying littoral, has been battling nature, weather, geology and geography throughout its history.Coastal erosion is part of the challenge. Like the railway navvies before them, the planners and builders of theEngland Coast Path(ECP) have done sterling work at plotting a viable footpath and shoring it up. But there are and always will be sections that are compromised and even impassable. I chose a section that would take three days, walking southwards, and my final destination, St Bees, was only reachable via a diversion. It’s all part of the adventure, and we’re lucky to have the ECP as a national trail, as it means issues and obstacles on the English coast will usually be promptly addressed.View image in fullscreenThe harbour at Maryport.Photograph: John Morrison/AlamyI began my walk at Maryport, a natural choice as it’s where theCumbrian Coast Line, travelling south from Carlisle, meets the seashore. I resisted the urge to jump off the train and set off walking, instead taking time to look around. I’m glad I did. It’s a lovely place, in a ramshackle way, and quite fascinating. The Romans, who called it Alauna, built a fort here; theSenhouse museumboasts Britain’s largest collection of Roman altars and inscriptions found at a single site.AnLS Lowry trailtakes in places he painted. I followed it from the church beside the quay, up the steep town steps, and along some of the streets he worked into his compositions. Information panels celebrated less well-known, similarly gifted local painters:Sheila Fell, from nearby Aspatria, andPercy Kelly, born in Workington, known for his thick lines and dark landscapes, who played for Workington AFC under Bill Shanklyand, in later life, became Roberta Penelope.double quotation markThe Cumbria coast is more Morrissey lyric than Countryfile fantasyOut on the coast path, I took in my first views of Dumfriesshire to the north. There were few walkers on the empty strand. At Flimby, the “path” was just a line of kelp on a pebble beach, bordered by flowering sea kale. Clouds of cabbage white and small blue butterflies sprang up as I walked. West Cumbria is theonly areawhere the latter can be found in northern England. An unfamiliar call and a flutter of white wings sent me to my birder app. It was a pair of sandwich terns – an “amber” status bird on the RSPB website.There were patches of heather and rosehip, occasional dunes and a few birds. Swallows picked off flies. Herring gulls shouted. Black-headed gulls planed. Carrot-beaked oyster catchers fluted their alarm calls. On my left, above the marram grass, I could see industrial plants and old workers’ terraces. The Cumbria coast is more Morrissey lyric than Countryfile fantasy. Boulders have been arrayed to protect against storms. Two teenage girls bronzed (or pinked) themselves on rocks in the midday sun.View image in fullscreenSt Bees Lighthouse, near Whitehaven.Photograph: Alan Novelli/AlamyWorkington welcomed me, after seven miles. I’d been here before, for a “Where tourists seldom tread” feature for this newspaper, but it felt new arriving on foot and from the shore. Workington looks as its name sounds. Decades of industry have made the people steely and friendly. I spent the night above town at theHunday Manor hotel, which has superb views over the coast and back to the fells.The next day’s walk to Whitehaven was the longest at about 12 miles. The opening stretch, back down into Workington, was a pleasant surprise. From above town, I’d noted fuel silos, warehouses and industrial estates, but around the harbour the land was all grassy knolls. I could see Scafell Pike rising up to the south-east, and Scotland shimmering to the north. In the distance were cliffs and a wide inlet – my destination, Whitehaven.double quotation markWhitehaven is one of northern England’s loveliest towns, but it hasn’t sold its entire soul to tourismI undertook this walk during the the UK’s fifth heatwave, one of the driest, warmest periods in living memory in these parts. As the mercury rose, I climbed up on to the clifftops, pausing atthe Howe, a hill originally created from industrial slag, to gulp down water and look up at a 3-metresteel and wood crucifixput up by a local man in memory of his wife. From here, there was a messy section with scant waymarking, but I eventually came to Harrington, a bonny little suburban village, with kite flyers on the bluff and smart little terraces marching up the side streets. I ate lunch and watched trains come and go; they’re regular enough that you can always cut short a walk and hop on one.Up on the cliffs again, I passed a large windfarm, and approached the village of Parton on a bridleway that sliced through sheep fields. The air was filled with the hairy seeds of thorns, bursting in the heat.A path beneath dramatic sandstone cliffs guided me into Whitehaven. One of northern England’s loveliest towns, it has all the amenities a tired walker needs. But while it caters to visitors, it hasn’t sold its entire soul to tourism – which is the case with some Lakeland towns.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhitehaven used to be an industrial powerhouse, shipping tobacco, coal, ceramics, iron ore, limestone and textiles, and it was the fifth most active British port involved in the transatlantic slave trade. The older streets are lined with crumbling mansions. Victorian-era lighthouses and a chimney known asthe Candlestickare unmissable landmarks; between these are ghostly traces of tenements, coastal batteries and long-silenced engine houses. Silting and larger ships led to the town being eclipsed by the deepwater ports of Liverpool and Glasgow. Shipbuilding moved to Belfast. Nostalgia, grit, grandeur and decay all mingle in Whitehaven’s collective maritime memory.View image in fullscreenThe coastal path, with St Bees in the distance.Photograph: Simon Evans/AlamyI swotted up on Whitehaven’s layered history atThe Beacon, one of the UK’s finest and most rejuvenating town museums. Underneath the museum, theHowling Wolf Bakeryand cafe serves delicious cakes, toasties and coffee. There are great restaurants all over town – I can recommendThe Peddler, in the former bus station, andZeston the waterside – and every kind of pub, chippy and cafe.The Edgehotel, which opened last October, will bolster Whitehaven’s ambitions to compete with the Lake District. It was created as a base for coastal activities; theharbour commission, which owns the property, is committed to supporting walkers, cyclists, musicians and community groups. There are 16 ensuite rooms looking out over the marina – an attractive mix of historic quays and jetties (known as tongues), and modern add-ons. The Edge’s irregular polyhedral shape is striking and yet apt. Rust-coloured, it looks post-industrial but also like a storm barrier. Its air-source underfloor heating and solar panels are in keeping with a region famed for renewable energy.An alternative route was in place for the final leg, with erosion on the footpath forcing me inland. But I was too elated to be bothered by a minor diversion. My coast walk (23 miles direct, but considerably more with walks around towns and hikes to/from the Workington hotel) culminated at St Bees Head with views of spectacular coves, secret beaches and sheer cliffs.Where the ECP crossed paths with the recently inauguratedCoast to Coast National Trail, I met a few walkers, Aussies rather than Brits, all heading inland for Ennerdale and Helvellyn, there to encounter crowds and join queues. My only company was fulmars, cormorants, herring gulls, ravens and kestrels. When I came across a little colony of kittiwakes nesting on tiny ledges, I decided it was time to sit down too, and soak up the gentle sea breezes and the wide, all-encompassing silence.The trip was supported by Cumbria Tourism, Avanti, Northern and Stagecoach buses.Stagecoach has DayRider and 3-day Explorer passes. DoublesatThe Edgefrom£117B&B and atHunday Manor Country Househotel from£125 B&B.Explore more on these topicsWalking holidaysEngland holidaysWalkingLake District holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Is Natalie Portman really the subject of Rachel Cusk’s new novel? Nine things you need to know about the literary hoo-haa | Culture | The Guardian
description: Fiction sleuths are obsessed with the idea that the book, Life of M, is a flagrant riff on the actor’s life. And despite being a firm Cusk fan, Portman is reportedly not happy
Author: Elle Hunt
Headline: Fiction sleuths are obsessed with the idea that the book, Life of M, is a flagrant riff on the actor’s life. And despite being a firm Cusk fan, Portman is reportedly not happy
Content: Rachel Cusk and Natalie Portman.Composite: Guardian Design;Brian de Rivera Simon/Getty Images;Enric Fontcuberta/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRachel Cusk and Natalie Portman.Composite: Guardian Design;Brian de Rivera Simon/Getty Images;Enric Fontcuberta/ShutterstockCelebrity crib sheetCultureIs Natalie Portman really the subject of Rachel Cusk’s new novel? Nine things you need to know about the literary hoo-haaFiction sleuths are obsessed with the idea that the book, Life of M, is a flagrant riff on the actor’s life. And despite being a firm Cusk fan, Portman is reportedly not happyElle HuntWed 26 Aug 2026 07.07 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 08.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLife of M, the latest book by the critically acclaimed author Rachel Cusk, is being billed by its publisher, Faber, as a “blazing interrogation of fame, power, beauty and truth” – and openly alleged as a thinly veiled portrait ofNatalie Portman. For weeks before publication, speculation has swirled that its movie-star main character is based on Portman – to her reported displeasure.With the bookout this week, readers and critics alike are judging it as literature and gossip. Don’t want to read it yourself, but want to have an opinion? Here’s your crib sheet.Life of M by Rachel Cusk review – is this story of a film star based on Natalie Portman?Read more1. Yes, it’s (probably) about Natalie PortmanThere’s little reading between the lines with Cusk’s movie-star main character M, “one of the most recognisable faces of our time”, who is frequently identifiable as Portman in all but name. On page three, M describes her experiences as a child star, acting in a film that “immediately brought her childhood to an end”. Several details tally with Léon: The Professional, Portman’s first film role (she was cast at 11 and filmed until she was 13), most obviously its sexualised relationship between an adult man and a young girl. M also says her parents requested some scenes be cut from the script, and that she was bullied at school after the film came out – both details Portman has shared publicly.Later come references to M’s “starring role in a film about a young girl chosen for the starring role in a ballet” (describing Black Swan down to specific scenes).2. It’s also not about Portman at allIf you pick up Life of M expecting explosive revelations about one of Hollywood’s most private and put-together stars, you’ll be disappointed. More than recognisably Portman, the novel is essentially Cusk, with her trademark roaming, disembodied narration and clinical gaze – which, despite the title, only intermittently turns to M. Scenes from the fictional actor’s rarefied existence are interspersed with the narrator’s observations of modern urban life and dense descriptions of rooms, and the chairs within those rooms. A tell-all, it ain’t.3. Portman was at least once ‘really in awe’ of CuskBoth Cusk and Portman reside in Paris, seemingly the setting of Life of M, and have crossed paths. In a 2023 GQ interview, Portman said she was “starstruck” at meeting Cusk: “I get really in awe… writing beautifully is just, like, the greatest gift.” Portman has also selected Cusk’s novels for her book club twice, praising “the way she disrupts form and the conventions of storytelling”, and once declared her “of course, a genius”. But, in the lead-up to Life of M, sources have downplayed reports of a friendship, with a report in the Daily Mail stating that Cusk and Portman had only “seen each other a few times” around Paris, while sources told Vanity Fair they never had “much of a relationship”.4. Portman may now support more conventional storytellingM is frequently described as beautiful and charming, but her inner world is chilly; she is untouched by depression and love alike, incapable of “total sincerity” and impeded by celebrity. Indeed, M’s efforts to be “normal” seem contrived; at a dinner party thrown by non-famous friends, she wonders “how they survive in this minuscule space”. Journalist Leaf Arbuthnotwrote in the Telegraphthat: “The impression is of an author pulling the limbs off a person one by one, as a child might do to an insect.” Sources claiming to be close to Portman have expressed outrage on her behalf, saying she bears no resemblance to the out-of-touch, dispassionate M. Fromthe Mail: “She is far from a diva, she is a quiet bookworm … This is a gross violation of her code. She believes women’s bonds should be nurtured, and not manipulated for commerce.”5. Portman is a reluctant museView image in fullscreenTouchy subject … Portman in 2025.Photograph: Gilbert Flores/Variety/Getty ImagesThis would not be the first time Portman has been made a non-consenting muse. Back in 2014, the author Jonathan Safran Foer was widely speculated to have ended his marriage (to fellow author Nicole Krauss) over his crush on Portman, who allegedly rebuffed him. Two years later, theNew York Times’ T magazinepublished Portman and Safran Foer’sexcruciatingly self-consciousemails. Their correspondence became so legendary in the New York literary scene that it ended upinspiring a 2023 Off-Broadway play, about a Pulitzer-winning novelist who develops a crush on a glamorous actress (played by Katie Holmes). As Vanity Fair concluded, Portman has form in being “thrust into other people’s narratives”.6. Cusk remains tight-lippedOver weeks of gossip about Life of M, Cusk and her team have remained quiet, leading toaccusations that they were “certainly leaning in”to the speculation to help drive sales. But when Cusk was interviewed by the New York Times last week, she said she was finding it “very stressful”. She refused to comment on whether she had discussed the novel with Portman, and said that whether she was the inspiration for M was “not really the point”. “Once you start to pull on that thread, it would unravel the whole thing … The book explains itself and defends itself pretty comprehensively.”7. Cusk also has form hereView image in fullscreenDrama queen … Cusk.Photograph: GL Portrait/AlamyThis is far from Cusk’s first brush with controversy over drawing inspiration for her books from real life. The first print run of her 2009 novel The Last Supper: A Summer in Italy had to be withdrawn and pulped by its publisher after individuals recognised themselves in Cusk’s portrayal and threatened legal action. In 2017, artist Damian Barr claimed he was the basis for Julian, a character in Cusk’s novel Transit,writing on Facebook: “Cusk’s veil of fiction is thin. Thinner than a thin thing.”8. The reviews are in …The reviews are, as they say, “mixed”. The Guardian declared Life of M “a book to admire enormously, but not one to love”. The New York Times despaired at Cusk’s “ponderous pronouncements”, where the reader “might want to fling Life of M aside and instead fire up Life of Brian”. The New Yorkerdamned the “tedious” gossipy interest in the book, but also wasn’t a big fan of Cusk’s “unsubtle vehemence” and “dogged refusal of specificity”. On GoodReads, at the time of writing, it has a 3.72 rating from 80 reviews. One describes it as “the literary equivalent of vagueposting”.9. Was it all a dream?It’s still not known whether Portman ever collaborated with Cusk on Life of M, but the final pages describe a standoff between M and the narrator over their “autobiography” project. “I don’t like the way you portray me,” M says. “You’ve made it seem like I lack humanity.” Cusk told the New York Times that her intent was to disorient the reader and seed doubt: “It’s almost like the book that you’ve just read completely explodes and self-destructs at the end.” It may be, as has been speculated, that the drama is nothing but a marketing ploy, or even cooked up by Cusk and Portman together. Whatever the truth, it’s worked. Literary fiction hasn’t been of such mainstream interest sinceCat Person, prompting the question: could more gossip solve the reading crisis?Explore more on these topicsCultureCelebrity crib sheetRachel CuskNatalie PortmanCelebrityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: South African police arrest two Thai men for allegedly smuggling parrot eggs  | South Africa | The Guardian
description: Bird eggs intercepted in homemade incubators at Johannesburg airport as officials try to halt wildlife trafficking
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: Bird eggs intercepted in homemade incubators at Johannesburg airport as officials try to halt wildlife trafficking
Content: The National Zoological Garden in Pretoria is incubating the seized eggs and said some of the rescued parrot eggs had successfully hatched.Photograph: Ministry of Forestry, Fisheries and the EnvironmentThe National Zoological Garden in Pretoria is incubating the seized eggs and said some of the rescued parrot eggs had successfully hatched.Photograph: Ministry of Forestry, Fisheries and the EnvironmentSouth AfricaSouth African police arrest two Thai men for allegedly smuggling parrot eggsBird eggs intercepted in homemade incubators at Johannesburg airport as officials try to halt wildlife traffickingRachel Savagein JohannesburgWed 26 Aug 2026 11.09 EDTFirst published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSouth African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents for allegedly attempting to smuggle endangered parrot eggs out of the country as authorities try to stem the tide of wildlife trafficking.A 50-year-old Thai national was arrested at OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg on 20 August, carrying 50 bird eggs in a homemade incubator in a hand-luggage bag, South Africa’s environment ministry said in astatement.View image in fullscreenThe seized parrot eggs.Photograph: Ministry of Forestry, Fisheries and the EnvironmentThe ministry said preliminary investigations indicated that the eggs were from parrot species listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites), which regulates international trade in wild animals and plants to ensure species do not become extinct. It did not specify which species.Another Thai national, a 23-year-old, was arrested at the same airport on 16 July, allegedly trying to smuggle 418 parrot eggs in two homemade incubator bags. Thailand’s embassy in South Africa did not immediately respond to a request for comment.South Africa is battling wildlife smuggling on several fronts, frompoached rhino hornsand the bones ofillegally farmed tigerstoabalone shellfishandsucculent plants.The environment ministry said: “The illegal collection and trafficking of parrot eggs pose a serious threat to wild bird populations and animal welfare. Eggs are often concealed in improvised incubation devices and transported under conditions that significantly compromise their viability and endanger the welfare of developing embryos and hatchlings.”Staff at the National Zoological Garden in Pretoria are incubating the seized eggs, the ministry said. “Several of the rescued eggs have successfully hatched and the chicks are receiving intensive veterinary and husbandry care to maximise their chances of survival,” the statement added.The ministry said the arrests were carried out after a “joint intelligence-driven operation” led by its Environmental Management Inspectorate, known as the “Green Scorpions”, and police intelligence, border and endangered species units.SouthAfricapunishes the illegal export of Cites-listed species with a fine of 10m rand (£460,000), up to 10 years in prison or both.Explore more on these topicsSouth AfricaBirdsWildlifeThailandEndangered speciesAfricaAnimalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mpox is back – and in new countries. How can this outbreak be contained? | Global health | The Guardian
description: The public health emergencies in 2022 and 2024 saw the virus reported in 145 countries, but in the new cases children appear particularly affected
Author: Kat Lay
Headline: The public health emergencies in 2022 and 2024 saw the virus reported in 145 countries, but in the new cases children appear particularly affected
Content: A man infected with mpox at a hospital in Burundi.Photograph: Tchandrou Nitanga/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA man infected with mpox at a hospital in Burundi.Photograph: Tchandrou Nitanga/AFP/Getty ImagesGlobal healthMpox is back – and in new countries. How can this outbreak be contained?The public health emergencies in 2022 and 2024 saw the virus reported in 145 countries, but in the new cases children appear particularly affectedSupported byAbout this contentKat LayGlobal health correspondentWed 26 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 11.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA fresh outbreak of mpoxin Guinea Bissau– the country’s first – means the virus formerly known as monkey pox is back in the headlines. So what has changed?Since 2022, there have beenalmost 190,000 lab-confirmed casesof mpox reported worldwide in 145 countries. Before then, outbreaks of mpox tended to be relatively small and in a handful of African countries, where the viral infection was known to be endemic.What is mpox?Mpox is an infectious disease that typically starts with flu-like symptoms, including fever, chills and aching muscles. These are followed by a distinctive rash, beginning as raised spots that turn into blisters filled with fluid before forming scabs.View image in fullscreenA colourised electron microscope image shows Mpox virus particles, represented in green, found within infected cultured cells, represented in blue. The virus particles are in various stages of maturity, which accounts for their differences in shape.Photograph: APIt used to be called monkeypox, because the virus was first discovered in captive monkeys in 1958. But during an international outbreak in 2022, there were concerns that the name was fuelling racist and stigmatising language on and offline, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to recommendchanging it to mpox.It is endemic to many parts of Africa, with outbreaks historically starting when people ate meat from infected wild animals. But in recent years it has spread beyond the usual areas, with sustained chains of human-to-human transmission. The Atlanta-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said this month that mpox wason course to become endemic in the US.Why is it spreading to new countries?There are, broadly, two types of mpox, known as “clades”. Clade I was once called the “Congo Basin clade” and clade II the “West African clade”.The latter sparked a major global outbreak in 2022 when it appeared to undergo some changes that allowed it to spread more efficiently from person to person. It is passed on via close contact – in that outbreak, mostly by sexual contact, with men who have sex with menat the highest risk.View image in fullscreenA Red Cross worker disinfects a tent in the Don Bosco camps for internally displaced people in Goma, in the Democratic Republic of Congo.Photograph: Moise Kasereka/EPAIn June 2024, researchersraised the alarmabout a new variant of clade I in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), which also appeared to be spreading more easily between people. That grew into another major international outbreak, which was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the WHO on 14 August 2024.“Emergence of mpox in more countries in west Africa is to be expected,” said Prof Michael Marks, of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine and University College London hospital. “Mpox outbreaks have now been declared in a number of countries in the region, including Guinea and Sierra Leone within the last 12 months.“Mpox spreads by close physical contact. This makes it suitable to spread in a variety of different contexts, such as in close sexual networks, as was seen during the 2022 global pandemic, or areas where many people are living closely together such as settings with refugees and internally displaced people, as was seen in the DRC outbreak over the last few years,” Marks said.What happened to those two big outbreaks?The 2022 outbreak was declared a public health emergency in July that year. After contact-tracing and mass vaccination programmes, the status was lifted in May 2023. There had been about 90,000 infections.View image in fullscreenA passenger passes mpox alerts at Chennai airport in India.Photograph: R Satish Babu/AFPThe 2024 outbreak had its international public health emergency statuslifted in September 2025, not because the disease had disappeared but because numbers of cases and deaths were declining and officials felt the situation had become better controlled.If genetic testing reveales a new variant, or surveillance suggested an outbreak was spreading particularly fast, making people particularly sick or proving more deadly, global health authorities would be likely to step in again.How worrying is the new outbreak?Cases had not been reported in Guinea Bissau before this outbreak. Unicef said it was concerned that of 46 suspected cases, 23 were children aged under 15 and most of those were aged under four.“The concern about children is that they are at the highest risk of severe disease and death from mpox,” said Dr Aula Abbara, a senior lecturer at Imperial College London and adviser to Médecins Sans Frontières UK. “Young children can become much sicker than healthy adults.”View image in fullscreenFuraha Elisabeth applies medication to the skin of her child, Sagesse Hakizimana, at a health centre near Goma, in the DRC.Photograph: Arlette Bashizi/ReutersHowever, she cautioned that the apparent over-representation of children in the outbreak data should be interpreted carefully. She said: “There may also be some bias in the data. Families are often more likely to seek healthcare for a sick child than for an adult, particularly in a resource-constrained setting with a fragile health system, such as Guinea-Bissau.”Marks added: “Children have close physical contact with their parents and with each other, and in settings such as Guinea-Bissau are often living in cramped conditions, which make close physical contact and transmission more likely.”Confirmed cases do not appear linked to each other, which suggests the virus is circulating more widely in the community and there are unidentified cases.Are there vaccines and treatments?The WHOrecommends two vaccines, which can be given to people at high risk or offered to people who have been in contact with a known case to prevent further spread. The question is where they are available.Marks said: “The major challenge remains that supplies of vaccines are best in high-income countries but worst in low-income settings, where the need and conditions for mpox transmission are highest.”A new global stockpile isdue to be launchedwithin weeks, which should mean vaccines can be deployed more rapidly to quell outbreaks. Officials also hope it will allow manufacturers to plan ahead and produce more of the jabs by providing a clear, concrete demand.View image in fullscreenA young mpox patient receives treatment at the Kavumu hospital in Karanrhada, in the Democratic Republic of Congo.Photograph: Michael Lunanga/EPAAn antiviral called tecovirimatdid not appear any better than a placebowhen tested on patients with mpox clade I in the DRC, although the question of whether it might help some immunocompromised patients – such as those living with HIV – remains open. That trial did show, however, that giving patients good, supportive care dramatically improved their chances of survival.While vaccines remained an important tool for outbreak control, basic supportive care could be lifesaving, Abbara said. She added that strengthening surveillance, testing, contact tracing and broader public health measures would be critical to understanding and containing the outbreak.“Vaccines are important, but outbreaks are not controlled by vaccines alone,” she said. “Early detection, contact tracing, supportive care and strong public health surveillance remain absolutely essential.”Explore more on these topicsGlobal healthMpoxGuinea-BissauInfectious diseasesWorld Health OrganizationHealthMicrobiologynewsShareReuse this content

title: Moringa lattes and tigernut kebabs: the Ghanaians ‘taking back the power’ of their food | Food security | The Guardian
description: In Ghana, a grassroots movement is championing nutritious, homegrown, climate-resilient produce, rather than western imports
Author: Kaamil Ahmed
Headline: In Ghana, a grassroots movement is championing nutritious, homegrown, climate-resilient produce, rather than western imports
Content: The Ghana Food Movement's cooking masterclasses offer local people the chance to learn more about traditional Ghanaian food.Photograph: Ghana Food MovementView image in fullscreenThe Ghana Food Movement's cooking masterclasses offer local people the chance to learn more about traditional Ghanaian food.Photograph: Ghana Food MovementFood securityMoringa lattes and tigernut kebabs: the Ghanaians ‘taking back the power’ of their foodIn Ghana, a grassroots movement is championing nutritious, homegrown, climate-resilient produce, rather than western importsSupported byAbout this contentKaamil AhmedWed 26 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 10.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter three years at catering school in Accra, Abiro Wisdom was certain of one thing – he did not want to go into catering. At least not the route that he might be expected to take. His course had prepared students for working in international hotels, focusing on French, Italian and Mexican cuisine. The nutritious, homegrown food that Wisdom had eaten while growing up in Bolgatanga, northernGhana, did not feature at all.“I didn’t see myself there,” he says of the big chain hotels. “I felt I wouldn’t be myself working there – I wouldn’t be able to talk about the food from where I come from.”View image in fullscreenAbiro Wisdom found that his catering course in Accra did not feature the nutritious, homegrown food that he had grown up eating.Photograph: Ghana Food MovementWisdom instead joined the GhanaFoodMovement (GFM), which was founded in 2019 – the year he graduated – and quickly became a champion for Indigenous foods. He says: “We’re a community of food lovers, of believers in the potential of Ghanaian food.”Ghana imports at leasthalf of its foodand is heavily influenced by foreign cuisine and ingredients, but Wisdom believes northern Ghana, the country’s agricultural heartland with its huge variety of nutritious and climate-resilient crops and vegetables, could be the secret to the country’s broken food system.The GFM was initially a network of volunteers interested in food systems – chefs, farmers, entrepreneurs and experts in food security. In the early days they met in cafes and set up events in whatever space they could find to deliver three-course meals highlighting a single crop and the diverse ways it can be used.“[Traditionally] we make tigernut milk, but you can make so many different things, for example tigernut burgers and tigernut kebabs,” says Aimee Wallin, the group’s Malian-Swedish co-managing director. “We want people to taste what we are about, not just talk about what we are about.”The group has been registered as a non-profit organisation for the past five years and now has its own kitchen where it brainstorms new recipes, many of them thought up by Wisdom. It runs monthly pop-ups and dine-and-dance nights, as well as panel discussions and recipe testing events for chefs and local businesses. Wisdom says: “We might brainstorm ideas around a single food, such as moringa leaves, to show how it’s possible to sell – and make a profit from – dishes and drinks using Indigenous ingredients.”View image in fullscreenThe Ghana Food Movement’s spice making workshop with Indigenous alligator pepper, egusi seeds and ginger shavings among other ingredients.Photograph: Ghana Food MovementThe GFM has started working with schools, helping children appreciate local ingredients.Wisdom hopes this multi-pronged approach will help instil more national pride in Ghanaian food. “My goal is that we have a generation of chefs who believe in Ghanaian food and its own identity,” he says.“I’ve come to understand how food contributes to politics, to the economy, how it contributes to self-identity. [Now I can] trace the impact of food on our society, on our land, to the sea, to the farmer, down to how the food gets to the market, then to our plates. As chefs, we have to be able to tell the story of the food.”This month the group won aChampions of Change titlein the 50 Best Restaurants Awards in recognition of the transformational work it is doing.View image in fullscreenThe Ghana Food Movement’s dine-and-dance night at The Kitchen, which it opened in Accra in 2024.Photograph: Kyei Baidoo/Ghana Food MovementForeign, colonial influence has played a heavy role onAfrican food systems, when ruling powers dictated land should be used forcash cropsfor export,such as cocoaor peanuts, at the expense of food for local consumption.At the same time, they put more value on imported ingredients such as rice, disrupting the sustainability of countries’ food systems. The impact has continued to modern times, making African countries heavily reliant on imports and vulnerable to price shocks when wars or other crises disrupt shipping.But, as Wisdom discovered at university, there is also a lingering cultural influence, with western food still taught in culinary institutes and sought after in restaurants.Africa’s small-scale revolution against big agriculture: five farmers talk greener, better foodRead more“The narrative has always been that our practices are wrong and the west’s practices are right. It’s just super-stupid. Why would you do that when you can just grow your own food?” says Wallin.“Part of the postcolonial agenda is for us to still have to depend on other countries. If it’s not to buy their products, to buy their vegetables, then at least we need to buy their seeds and their pesticides and their fertilisers,” says Wallin, who points out that many of the local ingredients they champion do not need extra agricultural inputs because they are adapted to the local environment.“The one who feeds us will control us and that’s how it is today. So, if we want to control ourselves, we also need to feed ourselves. It’s power. Taking back the power of our foods and using it to our advantage.”For younger Ghanaians there is a new international pull towards heavily advertised trends and social media fads such as matcha lattes, bubble tea and smash burgers.View image in fullscreenThe chefs often highlights one local ingredient in three or four different courses, such as plantain.Photograph: Kyei Baidoo/Ghana Food MovementWallin says that also offers a culinary opportunity – to earn the interest of young people, by offering alternatives, replacing matcha with moringa lattes or making shawarma out of tigernut instead of meat.Both Wallin and Wisdom believe that their movement has the urgent task of saving Ghana’s food heritage before knowledge is lost.“If we want to talk about what our future food system should look like,” says Wallin, “we need to talk to our grandmas, to our grandpas, to the farmers out in the communities because they sit on that knowledge. If we don’t talk to them now, it’s going to be too late. So it’s really now or never.”Explore more on these topicsFood securityGhanaFoodAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: How to lose Trump’s trade war: test Canada’s resolve with threats to hockey sticks | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: The US president expected Ottawa to bow to tariff demands, but Canada is striking back – and it could cost Americans
Author: Adam Gabbatt
Headline: The US president expected Ottawa to bow to tariff demands, but Canada is striking back – and it could cost Americans
Content: Donald Trump in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, on 21 August and Mark Carney in Quebec, Canada, on 24 August.Photograph: Saul Loeb,andrej Ivanov/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, on 21 August and Mark Carney in Quebec, Canada, on 24 August.Photograph: Saul Loeb,andrej Ivanov/AFP/Getty ImagesThis Week in TrumplandTrump tariffsAnalysisHow to lose Trump’s trade war: test Canada’s resolve with threats to hockey sticksAdam GabbattThe US president expected Ottawa to bow to tariff demands, but Canada is striking back – and it could cost AmericansThis was originally published in This Week in Trumpland.Sign up to receive it in your inbox every WednesdayWed 26 Aug 2026 14.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 14.49 EDTShareEarlier this year, a survey found thatCanada, along withSwitzerland, wasthe best-liked countryin the world. We all know this kind of polling is about as scientific as a high school popularity contest, but at least anecdotally, Canadians have a reputation for being friendly and welcoming, respectful and polite. Many people would find it difficult to dislike Canadians.But not Donald Trump, who in a “hold my beer” moment this week demonstrated that he, at least, finds it easy to resent Canadians.
