The US president called the country “difficult and unreasonable”, and in a particularly hysterical moment,threatened to rename a lake, after trade talks collapsed.Days earlier, Trump had claimed a deal withCanadawas imminent, which would avoid the new taxes.Wiped out: US faces surging toilet paper prices amid trade war with CanadaRead moreBut, in a development that surely galled the Art of the Deal author, there was no agreement.Instead, Trump and his team demonstrated the art of collapsing the deal, as trade talks fell apart due to what Canada said wereunreasonable, last-minute demandsfrom the US side.It meant that the US tariffs duly came in on Saturday, applied to various Canadian exports including hockey sticks and tongue depressors, but if Trump expected Canada to bow to his demands – the president was seeking more favorable terms on things like steel and aluminum – he was disappointed.Instead,Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister who has emerged as a rare world leader willing to stand up to Trump, said Canada had been “attacked”, and announced retaliatory tariffs on about $20bn worth of US goods, including steel, dairy products, appliances and farm equipment.All this means US consumers are seeing surging prices on all kinds of products – including toilet paper. My colleague Lauren Aratanireports that“the US accounts for more than 20% of global tissue consumption despite having only 4% of the world’s population”. And this outsize usage has grown more expensive. “Though American toilet paper and tissues are often made domestically, they heavily rely on lumber-rich Canada for raw materials,” she writes.It’s fair to say that Canada’s retaliation upset Trump, who famously loves to win. On Tuesday, he claimed the US “is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer” – we’ll see how that goes – and has dubbed Canadian negotiators“clowns”.Earlier this week, TrumpcomparedDoug Ford, the premier of Ontario, unfavorably to his deceased brother Rob, the scandal-plagued former mayor of Toronto, whose time in office saw himadmit to smoking crack cocaineand being “hammered” in public.And while Trump was flailing about, JD Vance was doing his best Scrappy Do, “lemme at ’em” impression, lobbing insults at Canadafrom the safety of a Republican rallyin Maine. Vance claimed that Canada and China are “the two worst countries when it comes to trade policy anywhere in the world”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis Week in TrumplandA deep dive into the policies, controversies and oddities surrounding the Trump administrationEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe added: “We have to remember, Canada is a state. Sorry. Freudian slip. That was actually an accident.” The satisfied look on his face didn’t make it seem like one.Vance went on to add that Canada “quite literally would get invaded by a foreign country were it not for the umbrella of protection provided by the United States of America”. It was an interesting take, given the only country that has mused about invading Canada is the US – as recently as last year Trump wasthreatening to annex the nation.So in a nutshell:Donald Trumphas led the US into an unsavory spat against the world’s most popular country, a scrap that could result in Americans – less than three months out from crucial midterm elections in which Republicans face an uphill battle – struggle to pay for a roll of toilet paper.Win!Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsThis Week in TrumplandDonald TrumpMark CarneyTariffsCanadaAmericasanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Wiped out: US faces surging toilet paper prices amid trade war with Canada | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: Paper products among hardest-hit sectors after trade negotiations broke down, with 25-50% tariffs estimated
Author: Lauren Aratani
Headline: Paper products among hardest-hit sectors after trade negotiations broke down, with 25-50% tariffs estimated
Content: A customer picks up a pack of toilet paper from a store shelf in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, on 2 March 2025.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA customer picks up a pack of toilet paper from a store shelf in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, on 2 March 2025.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesTrump tariffsWiped out: US faces surging toilet paper prices amid trade war with CanadaPaper products among hardest-hit sectors after trade negotiations broke down, with 25-50% tariffs estimatedAre you a Canadian boycotting US products? We’d like to hear from youLauren Arataniin New YorkWed 26 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUsing the bathroom or having a cry is about to become more expensive for North Americans as theUSandCanadaenter a full-fledged trade war that threatens to flush away decades of peaceful trading between the two nations.After trade negotiationsbroke downbetween the two countrieslast weekend, Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister,vowedto match US tariffs “dollar for dollar” andunveiledalistof nearly 900 American goods that will face 25% to 50% tariffs starting on 8 September.Paper products are among the hardest-hit sectors, withCanadathreatening to put tariffs of between 25% and 50% on “toilet paper or face tissue stock” from 8 September in retaliation for a 50% hike from Washington DC.Though American toilet paper and tissues are often made domestically, theyheavily relyon lumber-rich Canada for raw materials. Procter & Gamble, the owner of Charmin toilet paper,saidlast year that it would have to increase prices amid tariffs that were in place at the time.Canada announces retaliatory tariffs on wide range of US goodsRead moreThe US imported $328m worth of toilet paper from Canada in 2024, according to theWorld Bank, making it by far the largest exporter of the product to the US. Retailersincluding Costcosource much of their paper products from the country.The US accounts for more than 20% of global tissue consumption despite having only 4% of the world’s population. The average Americanuses 141 rollsof toilet paper per year, making them No 1 for No 2s globally, just ahead of Germans, each using an average of 134 rolls annually.It’s not just paper products that could rise in price. Thetrade warhighlights the deep economic ties shared between the two countries as consumers continue to worry about inflation on both sides of the border.US tariffsare specifically affecting Canadian liquor, including popular whiskey brands Crown Royal and Canadian Club, which are currently under a 50% tariff.While Canada has not introduced a tariff on American liquor, most Canadian provinces have introduced their own bans on American alcohol, in retaliation for earlier tariffs on Canadian products.Donald Trumpused these province-wide bans on American alcohol as part of hislegal justificationfor his new tariffs against Canada.Carney has asked province leaders to consider putting American liquor back on the shelves, though as the Nova Scotia premier Tim HoustontoldCBC News: “Whether Nova Scotians or Canadians will actually buy it when it’s back on the shelves, that’s a whole other discussion.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrump announces new 50% tariff on Canadian cars, trucks and steelRead moreTrump also said that his new tariffs are in retaliation for Canadian levies against theAmerican dairy industry. Heintroduceda 50% tariff on nearly all Canadian dairy products, with the exception of Canadian cheese.In response, Canada has a 50% tariff on American dairy products, along with a 25% tariff on American cheese.Canada also took a swing at the US fishing industry, with a 25% tariff on American fish and seafood, including frozen lobster. The move prompted Republican senator Susan Collins, facing a tough re-election battle in lobster-capital Maine, to call Trump’s latest move“a mistake”.A 25%tariff on Canadian cars and auto partsis set to affect the American auto industry, which relies heavily on Canadian parts for manufacturing. Trump has threatened todouble the tariffto 50% if a deal isn’t made by 1 January 2027.With negotiations down the drain, it’s unclear if or when the tariffs will be lifted. But the Trump administration is adamant that“there’s no possible way”the trade dispute with Canada will affect US consumers, according to Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative.“The fundamentals are good,” he said. “I don’t think this is going to affect anything.”Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsCanadaMark CarneyDonald TrumpAmericasTariffsTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Girl, 13, among missing British citizens after flash flood in Nepal | Nepal | The Guardian
description: More than 400 travellers are said to be missing after flood on Tibet border, including 33 Britons
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: More than 400 travellers are said to be missing after flood on Tibet border, including 33 Britons
Content: Damaged buildings after a flash flood at Trishuli, Nepal.Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/ReutersView image in fullscreenDamaged buildings after a flash flood at Trishuli, Nepal.Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/ReutersNepalGirl, 13, among missing British citizens after flash flood in NepalMore than 400 travellers are said to be missing after flood on Tibet border, including 33 BritonsFlash floods on Nepal-Tibet border – latest updatesCaroline DaviesandNadeem BadshahWed 26 Aug 2026 15.12 EDTFirst published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 10.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThirty-three British citizens including a 13-year-old girl are among more than 400 travellers missing after a flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border, according to Nepal’s tourism board.The sudden flood happened on the Tibetan side of the Bhote Koshi River at about 8.30am local time on Wednesday. The 33 UK citizens are among at least 341 foreign nationals unaccounted for.Earlier on Wednesday, the tour operator Alpine Eco Trek said a 13-year-old girl was among the missing British nationals, as well as two Irish citizens.Among the missing British nationals are three men aged 65, 64 and 52, and seven women aged 44, 47, 51, 60, 63, 63 and 65, according to travel logs.The firm, which offers guided tours and expeditions inNepal, confirmed four of its Nepali tour guides – aged 38, 35, 45 and 29 – are missing as well.Kumar Adhikari, the manager of Alpine Eco Trek, said on Wednesday: “I feel so sad. We are just thinking about what to do next.“We are in pain at the moment, deep pain.”Adhikari said the tour group, who were on a nine-day tour to Mount Kailash, were crossing into Tibet from Nepal when they became trapped at the border as the flash floods struck.He said he was in contact with his tour guides until 8.40am when their phones went offline, at which point the group would have been inside Tibet’s immigration office.“We were hoping that inside it was safe,” he said. “But later the video came from China’s government which (showed) even Tibet’s side was hit by the flood.”The tourist board said more than 100 of the missing people were yet to have a nationality confirmed.Police in Nepal said 157 bodies had been recovered and more than 40 people were injured and receiving treatment in hospital.View image in fullscreenA vehicle covered in mud in Trishuli, Nepal.Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/ReutersA wall of mud and rock appeared to have collapsed into the river on the Himalayan border of Nepal and Tibet, triggering catastrophic flooding on the Nepali side, Reuters reported. It said verified ​videos showed dozens of people being swept away at the border.Houses, roads and energy infrastructure were destroyed in Nepal, while officials in Tibet said they feared “major casualties”, with some people missing in the county of Gyirong after ⁠a mudslide hit a border land crossing.Mudslide submerges China-Nepal crossing point – videoInitial reports suggested an earthquake had triggered an avalanche and caused the floods, Shisir Khanal, Nepal’s foreign minister, told the country’s parliament.Eight South Koreans working on a hydropower plant ⁠were missing ⁠and ​10 others stranded, South Korea’s foreign ministry ⁠said.Local authorities said tourists in the Rasuwa district of Nepal and other areas along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers should “exercise extreme caution”, remain in safe areas and move to higher ground if required.Visitors were urged to stay in regular contact with hotels and travel agencies. People planning to travel to the affected areas in the coming days were warned to postpone their journeys.View image in fullscreenFamily members outside a trauma centre at Bir hospital in Kathmandu check a list of people who were injured.Photograph: Monika Malla/ReutersThe UK’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said: “I am deeply concerned to hear of the flash floods on the Nepal-China border. All my thoughts are with those affected and with British nationals in the area and their relatives here at home.”The British embassy in Kathmandu urged people in affected areas to follow local advice. A joint statement with the embassies of Australia, the EU, Finland, France, Norway and Switzerland said: “We are deeply saddened by the devastating flooding in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts and surrounding areas. Our thoughts are with all those affected by this disaster. We express our solidarity with the people of Nepal during this difficult time.“We encourage all those in affected areas to follow the guidance of local authorities and official safety advisories as the situation continues to evolve.”Explore more on these topicsNepalTibetFloodingChinaSouth and central AsiaAsia PacificNatural disastersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Flash floods on Nepal-Tibet border leave scores dead and hundreds missing | Nepal | The Guardian
description: At least 157 people dead and hundreds of tourists among missing after roads, bridges and power plants swept away
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: At least 157 people dead and hundreds of tourists among missing after roads, bridges and power plants swept away
Content: Aftermath of flash flooding in the Nuwakot district of Nepal.Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/APView image in fullscreenAftermath of flash flooding in the Nuwakot district of Nepal.Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/APNepalFlash floods on Nepal-Tibet border leave scores dead and hundreds missingAt least 157 people dead and hundreds of tourists among missing after roads, bridges and power plants swept awayNepal-Tibet flash floods – live updatesHannah Ellis-Petersenand agenciesWed 26 Aug 2026 14.28 EDTFirst published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 06.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 157 people have been killed and hundreds, including large numbers of foreign tourists, are missing after flash floods ⁠hit the Himalayan border areas of ⁠Nepal and Tibet inChina, police have said, with parts of India also at risk.The disaster was caused by a torrent of mud, water and debris that burst from the banks of a river that runs between China and Nepal. Homes, roads, bridges and power plants were swept away in Nepal, ⁠while officials inTibetsaid they feared “major casualties”.The US Geological Survey initially reported the event as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake, but additional analysis indicated the “seismic energy was instead generated by a glacial collapse and debris flow”.Authorities issued alerts urging residents in several districts to avoid the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers inNepal.Officials in Nepal said403 people, including 341 from foreign countries including India, the US, the UK, Australia, South Korea and Malaysia, had been reported missing in the country.Nepal’s tourism board said more than 100 of those missing were religious tourists from India and the Indian diaspora on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus. At least 62 missing Nepali citizens were among hundreds of locals trekking in Rasuwa, one of the worst hit districts.The board said that 47 of the missing tourists were from the United States, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 24 from Canada. UN Secretary-General António Guterres said UN teams and partners were mobilising supplies and personnel in Nepal to support communities affected by the disaster.In Tibet, China’s state broadcaster said at least three people were killed and 265 were missing.View image in fullscreenThe aftermath of the flash flood in the Nuwakot district of Nepal.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockOfficials said the flooding could get worse because parts of the river remained blocked by ice rocks and debris.Flood alerts were also issued in the Indian states of Bihar and Uttar ​Pradesh, which border Nepal and are downstream of the affected rivers.Police in Nepal said they were still unable to assess the full scale of the damage. Rescuers said helicopters could not land in affected areas of ⁠Syapru Besi and Timure in the mountainous district of Rasuwa until the river waters had receded. Rescue efforts were also hampered by heavy monsoon rains.Images of crumbled homes in ‌the flood waters, floating cars and a ‌metal bridge being washed away, and villages engulfed by water, mud and debris were broadcast on Nepali television.Footage shows scale of floods in Nepal“There could be heavy casualties or loss of property,” ‌said the district administrator, Narendra Pariyar, who urged those living on the banks of the Bhote Koshi to move to higher ground.“There is devastation everywhere we look,” said Tula Bahadur BK, a health worker in Rasuwa. “The settlements next to the river have been completely swept away. Five of my own relatives are missing.”Nepal’s energy ministry said the country’s electricity supplies had been significantly affected, mostly as a result of destroyed hydroelectric plants.Police and military officers joined in Nepal’s rescue effort, the country’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, said. “Instructions have ​been given … to move the people living in ​the lower areas to safer places. People along the river are advised to exercise extra caution ​and remain alert.”The Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, said he had spoken with Shah and offered Nepal “all possible types of humanitarian assistance”.China’s official Xinhua news agency said the ​flash flood occurred on the Nepal side of the border and cut roads, communications and power links in the Shigatse region.Chinese authorities were conducting large-scale search and rescue operations in the Tibetan border area of Gyirong, according to state broadcaster CCTV.View image in fullscreenRescuers use a digger to move a survivor of the flash flood to safety in the Nuwakot district of Nepal.Photograph: Prakash Mathema/AFP/Getty ImagesChina’s president, Xi Jinping, urged “all-out” search efforts for the missing and better monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary disasters.The Himalayan region, which spans Nepal, India, China and Bhutan, is particularly vulnerable to floods and landslides because it is warming faster than the rest of the world as a result of the climate crisis.Research shows that extreme weather events such as heatwaves and torrential rains have become more frequent. Nepal’s snow-capped mountains had lost close to one-third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global warming, the United Nations said in 2023. Experts have called for greater surveillance and early warning systems across the Himalayan region.Last year, a flood from the Bhote Koshi River killed nine people and washed away a “friendship bridge” linking Nepal and China, disrupting trade and transport for months.Researchers in Kathmandu also found earlier this year that glaciers across the Hindu Kush region were melting at an accelerating rate. Ice loss rates have doubled since 2000.Explore more on these topicsNepalTibetFloodingNatural disastersExtreme weatherSouth and central AsiaChinanewsShareReuse this content

title: Typhoon Narra: record flood waters submerge homes and force mass evacuations in China | China | The Guardian
description: Heavy rain expected in parts of Vietnam and southern ‌China, as another storm system, Typhoon Saudel, heads for Japan and Taiwan
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Heavy rain expected in parts of Vietnam and southern ‌China, as another storm system, Typhoon Saudel, heads for Japan and Taiwan
Content: An aerial view shows flooded areas in the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region of China, after heavy rainfall brought by Typhoon Narra.Photograph: China News Service/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn aerial view shows flooded areas in the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region of China, after heavy rainfall brought by Typhoon Narra.Photograph: China News Service/Getty ImagesChinaTyphoon Narra: record flood waters submerge homes and force mass evacuations in ChinaHeavy rain expected in parts of Vietnam and southern ‌China, as another storm system, Typhoon Saudel, heads for Japan and TaiwanReutersTue 25 Aug 2026 21.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 18.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWidespread flooding triggered by Typhoon Narra has submerged homes and forced mass evacuations in southern China, as another storm system tracked towards Japan andTaiwan.Authorities in Chongzuo, in China’s Guangxi region – famous for its giant waterfalls and karst limestone mountains – on Tuesday evacuated more than 15,000 people after water ⁠levels surpassed a record high set in 2008.Rising flood waters have prompted China to relocate a total of 54,000 people in Guangxi, state television said.Narra made landfall as a tropical storm on Tuesday evening ⁠in China’s southern island province of Hainan after lingering over the Beibu Gulf for ‌several days, dumping heavy rain on ‌Guangxi, Hainan and Guangdong.Heavy rain is expected to persist across parts of Vietnam and southern ‌China through Wednesday, with areas of Guangxi, Guangdong, Hainan and Fujian forecast to receive torrential rain, state media said.0:53Typhoon Narra floods cities in China’s Guangxi region – videoIn Chongzuo, river water overflowed into the city, with water levels reaching the rooftops of some buildings and power lines.A notice from Chongzuo authorities on Monday ordered all businesses and tourist operations to cease and urged evacuated residents not to return to high-risk areas.Meanwhile, medium-strength Typhoon Saudel moved towards southernJapanand northern Taiwan where ‌it is expected to bring sporadic heavy rain, as Taiwan reported one dead and four missing from a separate weather system over its south and east.Japan’s weather agency warned of destructive winds and high seas as Typhoon Saudel approached the south-western islands of Okinawa prefecture.Saudel is expected to pass to the north of Taiwan starting late Thursday and into Friday, though its intensity is forecast to gradually weaken, the island’s Central Weather Administration said.View image in fullscreenA resident wearing a raincoat wades through flood water inside an inundated home in Zihguan District, Kaohsiung, Taiwan.Photograph: Cheng-Chia Huang/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockHowever, there is uncertainty about ⁠the timing and extent of the typhoon’s rainfall impact, it added.In southern and eastern Taiwan, ​the government reported one person dead and ​four missing from a tropical depression ​that brought flooding in the cities of Tainan and Kaohsiung, home to more than 4 million people.During ​the three days from ‌Sunday to Tuesday, almost ​a metre (3.9 feet) of ​rain fell in Kaohsiung, which the government said exceeded rainfall during 2009’s devastating Typhoon Morakot that killed about 700 people and caused damage of up to $3bn.Saudel is forecast to hit the coast in the south-eastern Chinese province of Fujian from late Thursday to early Friday.Explore more on these topicsChinaExtreme weatherTaiwanJapanAsia PacificFloodingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Escape wizard’ who has broken out of four prisons is arrested in Spain | Spain | The Guardian
description: Albanian criminal has cut bars, descended sheets and even used human pyramid in escapes in Italy and Belgium
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Albanian criminal has cut bars, descended sheets and even used human pyramid in escapes in Italy and Belgium
Content: Toma Taulant, who was serving a prison sentence due to end in 2048, escaped from a maximum-security prison in Milan eight months ago.Photograph: SFM Press Reporter/AlamyView image in fullscreenToma Taulant, who was serving a prison sentence due to end in 2048, escaped from a maximum-security prison in Milan eight months ago.Photograph: SFM Press Reporter/AlamySpain‘Escape wizard’ who has broken out of four prisons is arrested in SpainAlbanian criminal has cut bars, descended sheets and even used human pyramid in escapes in Italy and BelgiumSam Jonesin MadridWed 26 Aug 2026 12.22 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 18.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice in Spain have arrested a dangerous Albanian criminal nicknamed the “escape wizard” who has managed to break out of four jails inItalyand Belgium by sawing through bars, clambering down knotted sheets and even using a human pyramid to breach prison walls.The fugitive, who has not been officially named, was arrested after officers from the Policía Nacional force discovered he was living in the north-eastern Spanish city of Tarragona. He was the subject of a European arrest warrant issued by the Italian authorities.Spanish police identified the man by the initials TT, which correspond to those of Toma Taulant, an Albanian national known in Italian media as the“mago della fuga”, or “escape wizard”.Before escaping from a maximum-security prison in Milan eight months ago, he was serving a prison sentence due to end in 2048 for a series of offences including violent robbery, theft and drug dealing, according to Italian media reports cited by Agence France-Presse.“It sounds like something out of a film, but sometimes reality is stranger than fiction,” the Policía Nacional said in a statement that described him as “the master of escapes”.“He escaped from a jail in [the Umbrian city of] Terni in 2009, from a jail in Parma in 2013 and from a Belgian prison that same year after using a human pyramid to climb over the wall,” the police said. “His latest escape, in December 2025, came after he managed to break out of a maximum-security prison in Italy after sawing through the bars and climbing out of the window down knotted sheets.”According to the statement, the “very dangerous” fugitive was arrested in Tarragona last Friday, putting up “strong and active resistance” as officers swooped.“The man was accompanied by a number of his compatriots who tried to stop him being arrested, including one man who struck and injured two officers,” the force said. Police are still looking for the assailant but have recovered a Sig Sauer pistol that was discarded by one of the suspect’s associates.Once in custody, the man was found to be in possession of fake identity documents, which revealed that he had a criminal record in the Catalan city of Girona for possession of weapons and explosives. He was also found to be carrying two €500 banknotes that are thought to have been counterfeited, which have been sent to the Bank ofSpainfor investigation.The suspect was denied bail and has been remanded in custody at a jail in Tarragona while he awaits extradition to Italy.Explore more on these topicsSpainItalyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ​W​hy are European leaders staying silent after our summer of climate shock? | World news | The Guardian
description: Lethal temperatures ​and wildfires have exposed a widening gulf between voters demanding ​action and politicians unwilling to confront the long-term choices global heating requires
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Lethal temperatures ​and wildfires have exposed a widening gulf between voters demanding ​action and politicians unwilling to confront the long-term choices global heating requires
Content: Spain's prime minister Pedro Sánchez is one of the few European leaders who seems to be taking the climate crisis seriously.Photograph: Chema Moya/EPAView image in fullscreenSpain's prime minister Pedro Sánchez is one of the few European leaders who seems to be taking the climate crisis seriously.Photograph: Chema Moya/EPAThis Is EuropeWorld news​W​hy are European leaders staying silent after our summer of climate shock?Lethal temperatures ​and wildfires have exposed a widening gulf between voters demanding ​action and politicians unwilling to confront the long-term choices global heating requiresDon’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereJon HenleyWed 26 Aug 2026 10.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 10.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe climate crisis means “we’re going to have to change everything – the way we live, the way we produce, the way we trade,” France’s veteran radical-left firebrand, Jean-Luc Mélenchon,told the summer congressof his France Insoumise party last weekend.The term “climate change”, said Mélenchon – the most likely rival to Marine Le Pen in next year’s presidential run-off,according to one poll this week– may sound “almost reassuring”, but its actual impact will feel like “landing on another planet whenever we leave home”.The speech is notable because despite the four heatwaves that have scorched Europe this summer,shattering temperature records,fanning unprecedented firesandcausing thousands of excess deaths, few politicians want to talk about climate action.Europe is the world’sfastest-warming continent, heating up twice as quickly as elsewhere. The consequences, as UN climate chief Simon Stiell puts it, are “reaching national emergency levels”.And yet major policy speeches by Europe’s political leaders addressing the climate crisis, making plain its causes, and laying out the changes that will be needed to live with it can be counted on the fingers of one hand.French voters have faced “silence from some politicians and inadequate pronouncements or demagoguery from others”, saidLe Monde in a stark editorial, warning that “decision-makers on both the right and the left are losing credibility”.People want “a political message that translates into action, and sheds light on the future”, it said. The gap between “citizens’ heightened awareness of the crisis and the lack of commitment from their elected officials to address it” will trigger mounting frustration and anger.A mid-July Ipsos pollfound environmental protection had jumped 12 points from June to become French voters’ fourth greatest concern, after what the pollster described as “a first real experience of what the hell of a significantly hotter world might look like”.In the UK too,Labour party activists worrythat despite the ever more visible impacts of the climate crisis, there has been no major political push from the government on the issue, even as voters become increasingly convinced of the need for action.And while Friedrich Merzsaid this weekaction was needed to “curb climate change and adapt to the consequences” (though not at a cost to German industry), he’sbeen accused all summerof ducking the issue for fear of boosting theclimate-sceptic, far-right AfD.There are, of course, exceptions. Spain’s outspoken prime minister, Pedro Sánchez (pictured top),has long warnedthat “climate change kills”, and recently stressed: “It’s not enough to address the consequences; what we have to do is reduce its causes.”A French centre-left presidential contender, Raphäel Glucksmann,spoke this weekof the need for an “ecological transformation” ending the use of fossil fuels, and pledged a 100-day “ecological revolution” if elected president (which looks extremely unlikely).But the silence from most mainstream politicians is deafening,says Jean Jouzel, a veteran French climatologist. The political class in general, he says, “have simply not yet engaged with the reality of global heating. They have to tackle it head-on.”The root of the problem, Jouzel suggests, is that “politicians live in the short-term. Their horizon is avoiding any damage during their period in office. For me, a real political leader … has the courage to look to the medium and the long-term.”Short-termism, political polarisation and cost-of-living fears have, in effect, silenced leaders across Europe, as populist and far-right partiessuccessfully frame green lawsas an “ideological mantra” and the elite’s punishment for “ordinary working people”.The reasoning is clear: voters suffering high energy bills, food inflation and stagnating wages are unlikely to hail demands for real financial and lifestyle sacrifices in pursuit of an ill-defined climate gain. Carbon taxes andboiler restrictionscarry electoral risk.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLocal over globalView image in fullscreenThe summer heatdome over Europe caused an unprecedented demand for air conditioners – for those who can afford them.Photograph: Cristina Quicler/AFP/Getty ImagesBut that reluctance to address the real issue hasshifted Europe’s climate debateaway from long-term carbon reduction towards more localised adaptation – which, perhaps inevitably, has itself now become a battleground in thecontinent’s culture wars.Air conditioningis a prime example, now loudly touted on Europe’s right as a vital symbol of personal freedom and technological comfort, but widely decried by the left as environmentally irresponsible and symptomatic of long-term planning failures.“If I am elected president, I will put into place a massive air-conditioning plan,”Le Pen trumpeted this summer, arguing the technology had little or no impact on global heating: “When environmentalists don’t want something, they twist the studies.”The risk in all this is that by focusing on necessary but essentially reactive coping measures, leaders wind up reducing the existential challenges of global heating to debates over consumer choice and comfort that can fit into an electoral cycle.Meanwhile, vital long-term carbon reduction gets pushed further and further into the background. As Dutch MEP,Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy, argues: “Nobody should feel guilty for wanting relief from extreme heat. Air conditioning saves lives.” However, he continues, neither should we “accept the cynical argument that the answer to rising temperatures is simply to install more air conditioning – while abandoning the very policies designed to tackle the causes of those rising temperatures”.Be that as it may, in the multiple European countries with national elections coming up over the next 18 months – including France, Italy and Spain – the climate emergency remains, for the time being at least, largely absent from the debate.And that’s regrettable, because as Jouzel says: “Global heating is no longer a scientific debate. It’s a very real political problem.”Grégoire Leménager, writing in the French weekly Le Nouvel Obs, agreed. “Looking the other way is no longer an option,” he said. Nothing is simple, but after the summer Europe has just endured, politicians who “refuse to make climate action a cornerstone of their manifestos” will, he continued, “be exposed for what they are: criminal accomplices to an inevitable defeat”.To receive the complete version of This Is Europe in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThis Is EuropeEuropeClimate crisisWildfiresDroughtnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Flight attendant’s breast cancer was occupational disease, court rules | Breast cancer | The Guardian
description: Sophie Lainault, who worked for Air France, wins legal case linking illness to more than 12,600 hours on flights
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Sophie Lainault, who worked for Air France, wins legal case linking illness to more than 12,600 hours on flights
Content: Sophie Lainault began working as a flight attendant for Air France in 1989.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSophie Lainault began working as a flight attendant for Air France in 1989.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto/ShutterstockBreast cancerFlight attendant’s breast cancer was occupational disease, court rulesSophie Lainault, who worked for Air France, wins legal case linking illness to more than 12,600 hours on flightsAgence France-Presse in ParisWed 26 Aug 2026 10.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 18.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA flight attendant inFrancehas succeeded in having her breast cancer recognised as an occupational disease, a first for the country’s aviation industry, her lawyer and a trade union said.The ruling, which recognised that Sophie Lainault, a former flight attendant forAir France, had frequently worked at night and been exposed to passive smoking, could pave the way for similar claims, the lawyer and the CFDT union said.Lainault, from Anglet in south-west France, told the news agency AFP that she hoped her legal victory could help other women.“It is truly my dearest wish that this opens the way for other women who might not have dared until now,” the 59-year-old said.Now in remission, Lainault said she worked for Air France, the country’s flagship carrier, between 1989 and 2019 as a flight attendant and later as a purser on long-haul flights, accumulating more than 12,600 flight hours, including more than 6,500 at night.PBS should fund drug to treat breast cancer, endometriosis and gender dysphoria, experts recommendRead moreThe ruling, seen by AFP, came from a court in the city of Bayonne in early July and recognised the occupational origin of Lainault’s cancer.The court highlighted the role of night work, exposure to ionising radiation and passive smoking. Smoking was permitted on Air France flights until 2000.Two regional committees responsible for recognising occupational diseases had previously concluded that no link had been established.Breast canceris not included in France’s official list of occupational diseases, meaning that obtaining recognition can be a lengthy and difficult ordeal for patients.Lainault said that she had fought for two-and-a-half years for the recognition, supported by CFDT activists. She said the ruling would allow her to take early retirement.Lainault’s lawyer, Elisabeth Leroux, said the court decision set a legal precedent. The ruling was final and no appeal had been lodged, she added.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSome studies have suggested that women who regularly work night shifts may face a higher risk of developing cancer.Air France said it “was not a party to the proceedings and has not been informed of the court’s reasoning”.The airline said: “The health and safety of employees at work is an absolute priority.”In 2023, a French nurse who had worked night shifts for 28 years and been exposed to radiation succeeded in havingher breast cancer recognisedas an occupational disease.With nearly 13,000 deaths each year, breast cancer is the deadliest cancer among women in France.Explore more on these topicsBreast cancerAir transportFranceWorkers' rightsWork & careersEuropeAir France/KLMnewsShareReuse this content

title: Devon man becomes first person to swim Switzerland’s 10 largest lakes | Swimming | The Guardian
description: Neil Gilson completes 230-mile challenge after a ‘tough’ 22-hour crossing of Lac Léman
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Neil Gilson completes 230-mile challenge after a ‘tough’ 22-hour crossing of Lac Léman
Content: Neil Gilson has become the first person to swim the 10 largest lakes in Switzerland, a total of about 230 miles.Photograph: Jamie HancockView image in fullscreenNeil Gilson has become the first person to swim the 10 largest lakes in Switzerland, a total of about 230 miles.Photograph: Jamie HancockSwimmingDevon man becomes first person to swim Switzerland’s 10 largest lakesNeil Gilson completes 230-mile challenge after a ‘tough’ 22-hour crossing of Lac LémanSteven MorrisWed 26 Aug 2026 09.58 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe staggered rather than sprang out of the lake but it wasn’t surprising.Neil Gilson, a former international athlete, could be forgiven for feeling a little wobbly, having become the first person to swim the 10 largest lakes in Switzerland, a total of about 230 miles (370km).Over the last two summers, Gilson, a father of three from Devon in the English West Country, has ticked the lakes off and on Wednesdayhe finished swimming the 45-mile lengthof Lac Léman (Lake Geneva), taking just over 22 hours.His 12-year-old daughter, Lily, and 10-year-old son, Jack, were in the water waiting as he neared the end to accompany him across the finishing line.“They swam the last 200m with me,” Gilson said. “There were tears in my goggles. For the whole challenge, I was envisioning that moment. It kept me going through some difficult times – lovely.”Gilson, 40, was once ranked second in Britain for the 1500-metre freestyle and after finishing race swimming,turned to endurance challenges.In 2024, he swam across Lac Léman in 22 hours and nine minutes, a world record. But it wasn’t enough. He decided to tackle 10 Swiss lakes.View image in fullscreenNeil Gilson, seen here on Sandy Cove beach, trained for his Swiss lakes challenge in the sea off North Devon.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianGilson put in countless hours in the pool at a leisure centre, the sea off the northDevoncoast and the gym to prepare.There have been blips. Gilson admits that a swim of about 40 miles in Lake Maggiore this summer almost broke him. It was colder than he anticipated and he had to swim more quickly to get his core temperature up, which meant he used more energy than planned. He had “nothing left” for the last few miles.Lake Thun proved surprisingly difficult as the pressure to complete the challenge – and the physical effort – caught up with him. After clambering out of the lake, he said: “My arms don’t like me and I feel shattered.”Gilson said he found swimming in lakes more demanding than the sea. “They’re more unpredictable. You can get some really choppy conditions because of the wind and you can hit walls of cold water.”He began Léman on Tuesday morning and finished on Wednesday lunchtime. He admitted that 18 hours into the swim, he thought of giving up. “It was so tough in the night – the current was strong. I felt really close to stopping but what kept me going was my family waiting there.”View image in fullscreenNeil Gilson’s support team said ‘the right things’ to keep him going, he said.Photograph: Jamie HancockGilson said his support team, which accompanied him in a boat, helped by giving him coffee – and saying “the right things”.He just missed out on beating his own world record for Léman, but is confidentGuinness World Recordswill recognise him as the first to complete what has been billed the Legend of the Lakes challenge – and in subsequent years, that other ultra-swimmers may try to do it more quickly.As well as doing the swim as an extraordinary challenge, Gilson is seeking to draw attention to a neuropsychiatric condition, Pandas, that affected his son at 18 months old. People withPans or Pandasexperience a variety of symptoms ranging from mental health symptoms to changes in behaviour and difficulties with movement.Jack was diagnosed with Pandas after catching tonsillitis. “He went to bed a happy, healthy little boy, and woke up as someone we didn’t recognise, gripped by aggression, OCD [obsessive-compulsive disorder], tics and intense fear; he refused to eat, wouldn’t leave the house or even speak. It was terrifying,” Gilson said.Jack is doing well – as shown by his joining his dad for the last leg of his swim – but Gilson said: “The challenge has always been about more than swimming. Every lake, every kilometre and every difficult moment has been about raising awareness of Pans and Pandas.“It’s a condition that isn’t rare but is rarely diagnosed. Raising awareness of it means more than anything.”Explore more on these topicsSwimmingSwitzerlandDevonEnglandEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Call to ban marmot hunting in France as campaigners say they are ‘killed for fun’ | France | The Guardian
description: Protests and petitions planned amid growing concerns over impact of climate crisis on numbers of Alpine rodent
Author: Kim Willsher
Headline: Protests and petitions planned amid growing concerns over impact of climate crisis on numbers of Alpine rodent
Content: Open season on the rodents, members of the squirrel and groundhog family, begins in September.Photograph: gillou70/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenOpen season on the rodents, members of the squirrel and groundhog family, begins in September.Photograph: gillou70/Getty Images/iStockphotoFranceCall to ban marmot hunting in France as campaigners say they are ‘killed for fun’Protests and petitions planned amid growing concerns over impact of climate crisis on numbers of Alpine rodentKim Willsherin ParisWed 26 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 10.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnimal rights campaigners are gearing up for protests and petitions aimed at persuading the French government to ban the hunting of Alpine marmots.Open season on the rodents, members of the squirrel and groundhog family, begins in September, a few weeks before they go into a long winter hibernation.Although the marmot is not a threatened species inFrance, its numbers are reportedly declining as a result of the climate emergency. Campaigners say they are opposed to them being hunted for fun.Pauline di Nicolantonio, the president of theAssociation for Justice for Savoie Animals (AJAS), which has launched protests against marmot hunting for the last two years, said: “The question is a moral one.“When you tell people that hunting marmots is allowed in France, they are shocked. The marmot is extremely popular and symbolic in the Savoie where we are based and elsewhere in the Alps. You only have to go into any tourist office to see it’s the main logo or emblem.”Plant-eating marmots are spread across mountainous areas ofEuropeand North America. Most live in family groups organised by one dominant couple; when threatened they emit a high-pitched signal. In late summer and into autumn their bodies swell to up to 8kg as they stock up on food for a five- to six-month hibernation.There are 15 marmot species in the world and as wild game they were traditionally hunted for their meat, fat and fur. Today, hunting is allowed in certain states in the US and Canada, and in France, Switzerland and Austria but banned in Italy and Germany. An average of 1,000 marmots are shot in France each year.For generations of French children the marmot has been celebrated as the subject of folk tales and poems –one by Goethe set to music by Beethoven– the mascot of Alpine ski resorts and the sympathetic star of a popular television advert for awell-known brand of milk chocolate.In fact, the rodents’ cuddly reputation belies a bloodier reality; much of its waking life is spent in a vicious battle for dominance and territory that often involves killing its parents or children.View image in fullscreenExperts say they are seeing the breaking up of social groups of marmots.Photograph: Jean Christophe Verhaegen/AFP/Getty ImagesChristophe Bonenfant, a scientist at France’sNational Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS)at the University of Lyon, studies marmots in theGrande Sassière alpine nature reserve. Evidence of the climate crisis in Europe is most evident in the Alps where rock faces are fissuring and glaciers shrinking at an unprecedented rate.Bonenfant and his colleague Rébecca Garcia have noticed the marmots’ domestic and territorial battles becoming increasingly brutal as the climate emergency destroys the animal’s “social stability”.They have also noted that while the animals are not listed as endangered, females are producing fewer marmot pups and a combination of the cycle of violence and smaller litters is leading to a steady drop in populations.“What we are seeing is the breaking up of social groups, which are lasting less long, and more rapid changes of dominant animals in those groups,” Bonenfant said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“As a herbivore the marmot is quite low down the food chain but its importance is as food for carnivores like eagles and foxes and from time to time badgers. It also makes galleried tunnels that contribute to the aeration of the soil. It’s not classified as a nuisance species.”He said of hunting: “It’s not a species that raises questions about conservation, so the root of the question is the morality of hunting animals, not just in France but everywhere, and why people enjoy killing animals for fun.”There are strict hunting regulations set by individual local authorities limiting the number of marmots that can be killed and the season dates, but AJAS wants a national ban similar to that introduced in Italy in 1992.French farmers claim the animals are a nuisance making holes in their fields causing damage to machinery. The National Hunters Federation says hunting marmots is “strictly supervised and regulated” and the open season lasts at most a month. “There is no justification for banning marmot hunting: the species is not threatened, there are no plans to classify it as a protected species and their numbers are on the rise.”Di Nicolantonio said: “We know they are affected by the climate crisis and the data is worrying. Hunters often commission scientific reports to say there are lots of marmots around to justify killing them.“Hunting them is cruel, absurd and unpopular but isn’t banned because it’s considered a tradition. In the past, we might have eaten marmots but now shooting them is simply recreational.”Explore more on these topicsFranceAnimalsHuntingWildlifeConservationEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: On scraps of land and under constant threat, Gaza farmers struggle to survive | Gaza | The Guardian
description: Efforts to rebuild domestic food production face severe challenges and have come at deadly cost
Author: Seham Tantesh
Headline: Efforts to rebuild domestic food production face severe challenges and have come at deadly cost
Content: Saqer Abu Rabee, 48, irrigates his few remaining seedlings that survived from the first months of war.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSaqer Abu Rabee, 48, irrigates his few remaining seedlings that survived from the first months of war.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianGazaOn scraps of land and under constant threat, Gaza farmers struggle to surviveEfforts to rebuild domestic food production face severe challenges and have come at deadly costSeham Tanteshin Gaza, andJulian BorgerWed 26 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs Gaza’s population of 2.1 million has been hemmed into an ever smaller slice of the territory, farmers are using every last remaining patch of unspoiled earth, no matter how tiny, in their struggle to survive.With severe shortages of water, fertiliser and pesticide, and with more than 80% of greenhouses ruined, it has taken inventiveness and determination to clear land of debris and coax new seedlings into life. Moreover, venturing out into the open to tend to plants can be deadly.Saqer Abu Rabee’s eldest son and brother were killed while at work growing food for their communities on their small agricultural plots in Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza. His son Yousef was 24 when he was killed by a drone-fired missile in October 2024. Abu Rabee was working in the fields 10 metres from his son when it happened.“The missile was aimed directly at him and I have no doubt that he was the intended target,” Abu Rabee said. Yousef was well known locally as the driving force behind a collective first called We’ll Plant It and now simply Our Land, which brought together volunteers and encouraged farmers to go back to the land to restore agriculture in the area.View image in fullscreenYousef at work in 2024. He was killed by a drone-fired missile that year aged 24.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian“They decided to target him directly,” said Abu Rabee, who stressed his son had no political affiliations. “Before his death, we received daily threats from the Israeli army. They shelled our area every day three or four times while I was working alongside the labourers.”Abu Rabee’s brother Bilal was killed on 2 July after he went to retrieve some agricultural supplies from a destroyed building. His death came nine months into a partial ceasefire during which Israeli forces have killed more than 1,200 Palestinians. Abu Rabee is convinced farmers have become prime targets because of their role in sustaining Palestinian communities among Gaza’s ruins.The Israel Defense Forces deny targeting farmers or any civilians, saying they have only responded to imminent threats from Hamas since the October ceasefire.Despite the risks, Abu Rabee, 48, is still at work every day cultivating a 1.4-hectare (3.4-acre) plot in Beit Lahiya that was an orchard of orange trees before the war. He said the orchard was bulldozed by the Israeli army.“We cleared it and rehabilitated it using only basic tools, manual labour and tremendous human effort. It took a great deal of time and hard work before it was ready for cultivation again,” he said.Saqer Abu Rabee works on his plants nursery in GazaOut of that scrap of land, Abu Rabee says his family have produced hundreds of thousands of aubergine, tomato and pepper seedlings. They raise cash by growing their own aubergines to sell to wholesale traders, while most of the seedlings are distributed to other farmers or to individual households to plant in patches of earth around their homes and tents.He says the supply has transformed the local food market. Aubergines now cost less than two shekels a kilogram, compared with 40 shekels a few months ago. Peppers and mulukhiyah, a dark green leafy vegetable, are now selling at a tenth of their market price earlier this year.“What has happened is that Beit Lahiya has regained a degree of self-sufficiency,” Abu Rabee said. “In my view, without Beit Lahiya, Gaza would face famine. Before the war, it was considered the food basket of Gaza Strip because of its fertile soil, fresh groundwater and light, productive land.”View image in fullscreenSaqer Abu Rabee checks the state of crops grown for the production of seeds.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianIncreased aid and commercial deliveries under the ceasefire have brought Gaza back from the abyss of last year’s famine conditions, butaccording to UN agenciesthere are still 1.4 million people – 67% of Gaza’s population – facing crisis levels of acute food insecurity or worse.Much of the commercial inflows of food are of poor nutritional quality. The director general of the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), Qu Dongyu, has said the limited recovery will remain fragile without domestic food production.“Food security in Gaza cannot recover unless local food production starts again and farmers, herders, fishers and other producers can rebuild their livelihoods,” Qu said in July.View image in fullscreenSaqer Abu Rabee harvesting aubergines.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianBased on satellite data, theFAO estimatesthat little more than a quarter of Gaza’s total prewar cropland, 4,100 hectares, remains accessible, and only about 3%, 450 hectares, is undamaged, free of debris and ready for immediate cultivation.Most of Gaza’s prewar farmland is under Israeli military occupation, and the proportion has grown as the army haspushed the “yellow line” steadily forwardover the course of the ceasefire.Map of agriculture in GazaUsing specialised satellite imagery, the human rights advocacy groupForensic Architecturecarried out a survey of flora across Gaza as a measurable proxy for cultivable land. It found that nearly 68% of the territory’s flora was on the Israeli side of the yellow line and another 5% was inside a buffer zone declared by the army, delineated on maps with an orange line, where it is extremely dangerous for Palestinians to venture.Bilal Abu Rabee, Saqer’s brother, was shot dead along with another man when they came within range of Israeli sniper positions. Their bodies were left out in the open for two days because it was too dangerous for their relatives to retrieve them.The family’s old farm is now under Israeli control, so after the ceasefire was declared they came to Beit Lahiya to try to start again from scratch on leased land. Since last October the army has pushed the yellow line forward, swallowing up nearby farms in west Beit Lahiya.“The expansion has had a devastating impact on the agricultural sector,” Abu Rabee said. “Fertile farmland that farmers had worked tirelessly to cultivate after spending everything they had or even borrowing money, simply it was seized just as it was ready for harvest, leaving them with nothing.”View image in fullscreenBilal Abu Rabee, Saqer’s brother, who was shot dead in July.Photograph: HandoutOn the remaining land, the challenges appear endless. With hardly any livestock left, there is little homegrown dung-based fertiliser, so the family are improvising by piling decaying vegetation under tarpaulins. Meanwhile, they are battling nematodes and other soil infestations and a chronic lack of water, all the time under the constant, unpredictable threat of death.Abu Rabee said: “Stray bullets frequently reach this area and strike many places around us. Many people have also been wounded in the streets as a result of indiscriminate attacks. I fear for my own life simply because I’m a farmer.”Explore more on these topicsGazaPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaIsrael-Gaza warfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Iran seeks to criminalise all contact with foreign media in ‘chilling’ crackdown | Iran | The Guardian
description: As photojournalist sentenced to 15 years, rights groups warn law would turn civic engagement into security crime
Author: Deepa Parent
Headline: As photojournalist sentenced to 15 years, rights groups warn law would turn civic engagement into security crime
Content: Donald Trump’s use without permission of Yalda Moaiery’s photo of a Tehran protester may have led to Moaiery being sentenced for covering the US-Israeli war on Iran.Photograph: Yalda MoaieryView image in fullscreenDonald Trump’s use without permission of Yalda Moaiery’s photo of a Tehran protester may have led to Moaiery being sentenced for covering the US-Israeli war on Iran.Photograph: Yalda MoaieryRights and freedomIranIran seeks to criminalise all contact with foreign media in ‘chilling’ crackdownAs photojournalist sentenced to 15 years, rights groups warn law would turn civic engagement into security crimeSupported byAbout this contentDeepa ParentWed 26 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIran has taken the first step towards criminalising contact with foreign media, in a move human rights groups have said attempts to “sever the entire Iranian society from the rest of the world”.For journalists, researchers and even ordinary citizens, the proposed law being discussed by Iranian lawmakers this month could make speaking to international audiences and groups a potential criminal act and restrict coverage of events such asJanuary’s mass anti-regime protests.Even social media platforms that the regime considers to be “financed” by another country, such as Instagram and X, would fall under the bill, said Moein Khazaeli, an Iranian human rights lawyer at Dadban, a legal counselling centre for Iranian activists.“It means any kind of interview, contact, or sending photographs to them [foreign media or organisations] could lead to six months to two years’ imprisonment. Not just the US and Israel, but any contact with foreign media in any country could be considered a crime if one doesn’t inform the intelligence ministry beforehand,” said Khazaeli.Among the recent examples of the risks facing Iranian journalists is the case of Yalda Moaiery, an acclaimed photographerwho was sentenced this month to 15 years in prison in Tehran for documenting the US-Israeli war on Iran.View image in fullscreenThe Iranian photojournalist Yalda Moaiery, who was sentenced in absentia to 15 years in prison for her work covering the US-Israeli war in Iran.Photograph: Santiago Mejia/San Francisco Chronicle/Polaris/eyevineAlthough Moaiery was charged under the espionage law introduced after last year’s12-day war between Iran and Israel, Khazaeli said the new bill signalled a broader effort to regulate and punish contact between Iranians and foreign media and institutions. “It could move [Iran] to a North Korea kind of situation,” he said.Moaiery, 44, has spent two decades covering the harsh realities faced by people in Iran, including the nationwide Woman, Life, Freedom protests in 2022 and the anti-regimeprotests that led to thousands being killedin January.She came to international prominence in 2019 aftercriticising Trump’s use of one of her photosof a woman at a demonstration near Tehran University, saying Trump’s sanctions were damaging Iranian lives, including those of her friends and family. “This image shows my people and is for my people, and shouldn’t be abused by these men in Washington,” she wrote.‘Blindfolded, I sat down slowly. Then the interrogation began’: Iranian Nobel laureate Narges Mohammadi on the torture of solitary confinementRead moreNow, in a cruel irony, Moaiery said she had been sentenced in absentia for her work covering the US-Israeli war in Iran and accused of media activity deemed to strengthen and aid Israel and the US.“I have been a critic of Israel and its policies all my life. I am not an Israel supporter, never, ever. And I have always been a critic of American politics. It was like something that you are against, and they want to stick it to you. So it’s hard. It’s super hard,” she told the Guardian.Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI), said the new law on media contact risked turning Iran into an “isolated black hole”.“It is not simply an attack on journalists and citizen journalists; it is an attempt to sever the entire Iranian society from the rest of the world by criminalising the free flow of information itself.“It sends a chilling message and threatens to turn ordinary academic, professional and civic engagement into a potential national security crime,” she said.View image in fullscreenCasualties in Tehran of an airstrike during the 40-day US-Israeli war on Iran, taken by Yalda Moaiery on 15 March.Photograph: Yalda Moaiery/ReutersMoaiery was arrested and sentenced to eight years in prison in 2022, but later received an amnesty. This time, however, she fears her sentence could be upheld and she might be jailed.“Of course, I am scared,” she said. “The only thing that I’m worried about is wasting my life if I have to be there for 15 years. When I get out, I’ll be 60 years old.”She also criticised foreign journalists who travelled to Tehran to cover the funeral in July of the latesupreme leader, Ali Khamenei.“I have one word for them: shameful. They just want to say, ‘We were in Tehran.’ OK, but what did you do? They didn’t go and ask people about the economic situation or talk to the families of the thousands who died in January. Why were you here? To participate in their propaganda?”Explore more on these topicsIranRights and freedomPress freedomNewspapers & magazinesMiddle East and north AfricaJournalist safetyProtestDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran faces strait of Hormuz paradox as strategic value of chokehold erodes | Iran | The Guardian
description: Internal calls to end war get louder as Gulf neighbours plan alternative pipelines to cut reliance on waterway
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Internal calls to end war get louder as Gulf neighbours plan alternative pipelines to cut reliance on waterway
Content: Vessels in the strait of Hormuz are visible near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersView image in fullscreenVessels in the strait of Hormuz are visible near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersIranAnalysisIran faces strait of Hormuz paradox as strategic value of chokehold erodesPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorInternal calls to end war get louder as Gulf neighbours plan alternative pipelines to cut reliance on waterwayWed 26 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 14.19 EDTShareIs the strait of Hormuz, recently cited by the office of the Iranian supreme leader as “the pillar of Iran’s new security order”, and as transformative as possessing a nuclear weapon, in reality becoming a fast-diminishing asset, leavingIranincreasingly vulnerable to the new planned US wave of economic sanctions?It is the key debate that is raging inside Iran, with many different conclusions being drawn for Tehran’s negotiating strategy. Those who warn the strait’s value as a chokehold on the world economy will erode, leaving the country without foreign exchange reserves, argue that Iran’s negotiators should seek a deal soon.One analysis written by Hamid Paktinat, the founder of the Forum of Economic Activists, suggests the construction of alternative pipelines and export routes by Iran’s Gulf neighbours will halve the strait’s strategic value within three years.Those who worry about wasting assets inevitably set store by the separate visits this week to Tehran of Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, and Pakistan’s army chief, Asim Munir. These two men are critical to renegotiating the terms for the reopening of the strait and the revival of the discardedmemorandum of understandingagreed by the US and Iran in June.‘Economic D-day’: how desperate is Trump to end Iran war? — The LatestRead moreThe Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, and the parliamentary speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, have both recently made unusually blunt comments about the need to end the war – and the economic consequence of continuing it. Ghalibaf said that regardless of how much military power Iran possessed, “if people are hungry” and there was no economic growth, the country could not endure. Security, he argued, could not be sustained without a functioning economy. He added that, as someone with a military background, “we know the value of peace better than those who talk about peace”.Pezeshkian was even more blunt: “The war must end at some point,” he said. His argument was that Iran should end the conflict now, while Tehran still believes it is negotiating from a position of strength, rather than wait until its position weakens.The Iranian central bank governor, Abdolnaser Hemmati, also recently went on TV to warn about the economic pressures. “We are facing four or five major challenges simultaneously, including maximum sanctions, blockade, cutting off oil exports, and a budget imbalance, each of which puts pressure on the economy,” he said. “One of the neighbouring countries told me that if one-fifth of what happened in your country happened in our country, we would not be able to govern the country.”What is driving these remarks is the pressure on ordinary people in Iran, and an acceptance that the strait cannot become a permanent security doctrine in itself.Hamid Asefi, a Tehran-based journalist specialising in geo-economics, is one of many warning that if Hormuz is to be played as Iran’s final card every time a crisis arises, this card will gradually lose its value. “A threat that is constantly repeated turns from ‘deterrence’ into a political habit; and a political habit, if not accompanied by concrete achievements, sooner or later leads to an inflation of threats,” he said.The main question is no longer: can Iran close the strait, he wrote, but if Iran closes Hormuz to the world, does it open the door to power for itself or lock part of its power behind that door?“This is the Hormuz paradox. In international politics, a lever that is constantly flaunted can become its own enemy because it forces others to plan to reduce their vulnerability […] the main question of Iranian policy in Hormuz must change from: ‘How can we make the passage difficult?’ to ‘How can we make the passage so safe and stable that everyone needs Iran to maintain this order?’”That does not imply the lever is valueless. Far from it.Graph showing daily transits through strait of HormuzAccording to data compiled by the ship tracker Kpler, only 112 oil and gas tankers went through the strait between 1 and 19 August. Almost 79% used unconfirmed routes, 19% used Iran’s preferred northern route and 2% used the Omani route. In reality many of the ships that used the unknown routes probably turned off their transponders and used US protection along the Oman route.It also appears that aided by the US government, Saudi, Emirati, Qatari and Kuwaiti oil companies have chartered a small group of oil tankers to take cargo through the southern route to the Gulf of Oman, where they then offload the oil to waiting tankers owned by their customers. Much of the risk is therefore transferred from shipping companies and oil customers to the more highly motivated state oil producers and to the US government. Iran has drawn up a blacklist of about 48 ships that it will try to ban or fine.8:57‘Economic D-day’: How desperate is Trump to end Iran war? - The LatestBut the US government is probably exaggerating the impact of these workarounds. Chris Wright, the US secretary of energy, claimed on 18 August the US navy had assisted in the transfer of more than 15m barrels of oil and other products. He also claimed the average daily transfer of oil through the strait was now more than 8m barrels, but even this figure is less than half the prewar average and is anyway seen as inflated. Most ship data trackers estimate the daily figure at closer to 6m barrels a day.Arsenio Dominguez, the secretary general of the International Maritime Organization, furthermore dismissed Donald Trump’s outlandish claim that the US navy had all but opened the strait, telling Bloomberg: “Given the very small number of ships that transit the strait of Hormuz, it is clear that this strait is, in practice, not open.” The US president has countered that all mines in the strait have been removed, leaving Iranian drone and naval attacks as the chief threat.But the fact that before the war the strait accounted for 20% of oil and oil-related products is serving as a catalyst for the restructuring of the global energy infrastructure. Countries in the Gulf are rapidly building a network of alternative pipelines, with the aim of protecting more than half of their prewar exports from the impact of Hormuz by the end of this decade.Paktinat has looked through the region at the capacity, length and cost of pipelines being prepared in six countries over the next one to four years. He concluded Saudi Arabia’s reliance on the strait of Hormuz would decrease from 70% to 15%. The UAE’s reliance would decrease from 50% to 15%, and Iraq’s dependence would fall from 100% to 30%.Kuwait and Qatar’s reliance would decrease from 100% to less than half. Bahrain’s reliance would fall from 100% to 15%, he assessed. Finally, Oman’s reliance would change from 0% to becoming a major coastal oil transfer hub for the entire region.Overall, he says, the strategic value of the strait of Hormuz will be halved within three years and almost lost within six years with the implementation of these projects. The narrow horseshoe waterway will remain, but its strategic importance – the centre of Iranian gravity – will have evaporated.In the meantime, the US will try to turn Trump’s premature boast that the Iranian economy has completely collapsed into reality. It will try once again to block the vital arteries of the Iranian government across five key sectors: gold, cryptocurrency, technology, shipping and aviation.Success is by no means guaranteed, as Trump must know from the failure to defeat Iran in his first term. But slowly chipping away at Iran’s economic resilience until the strait finally becomes an irrelevance may be Trump’s only remaining option.Explore more on these topicsIranStrait of HormuzMiddle East and north AfricaUS foreign policyanalysisShareReuse this content

title: At least 14 newborn babies die in fire at Pakistan hospital’s maternity ward | Pakistan | The Guardian
description: Authorities at biggest state hospital in Islamabad say 15 babies were in the ward when fire broke out
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Authorities at biggest state hospital in Islamabad say 15 babies were in the ward when fire broke out
Content: A man consoles a grieving father outside the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad.Photograph: Aamir Qureshi/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA man consoles a grieving father outside the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad.Photograph: Aamir Qureshi/AFP/Getty ImagesPakistanAt least 14 newborn babies die in fire at Pakistan hospital’s maternity wardAuthorities at biggest state hospital in Islamabad say 15 babies were in the ward when fire broke outShah Meer Balochin Islamabad andHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiWed 26 Aug 2026 03.05 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 14 newborn babies have died in a fire that broke out in the maternity ward at one of Pakistan’s most prominent state hospitals.The blaze began in the early hours of Wednesday and engulfed the ward at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences, the biggest state hospital in Islamabad.A statement by the hospital administration confirmed that 14 newborn babies in the intensive care unit (ICU) died in the fire.Dr Aneeza Jalil, a hospital spokesperson, told the Dawn newspaper that 15 babies were on the ward at the time and that one baby was saved by a doctor.Women who had just given birth had to run down several flights of stairs and climb out of windows and down ladders to escape.The health minister, Mustafa Kamal, said many of the babies were in incubators or on oxygen, and that the oxygen canisters made the fire worse.Investigators said the fire was started by a faulty air conditioning unit, which exploded inside the nursery where newborn infants under intensive care were sleeping.View image in fullscreenPolice officers peer through broken windows of the gynaecology ward after the fire.Photograph: MA Sheikh/APAmong the witnesses was Sardar Atti ur Rehman, 38, whose wife had given birth to a girl at the hospital the previous day. He had been sleeping at the hospital and rushed into the maternity ward as the fire was spreading, desperately looking for his wife and child.He described scenes of panic as thick smoke filled the ward. “I could not see my family including my newborn baby in the room but kept searching,” he said. “My heart was heavy.” He later discovered they had both escaped the fire alive.He said he saw a woman laid out on a stretcher and helped to drag her out of the ward, but other women refused to leave as they cried out for their babies.“I saw a mother who was crying and screaming for her child who was admitted inside the ICU,” he said. “I tried to enter the ICU but failed as the smoke was too thick. I could not see anything and I was facing issues to breathe. I begged her that you need to save yourself and we will look for the child later.”Rehman said there were few staff on the ward at the time of the fire and that the families were left to fend for themselves.One father at the scene, whose newborn son was among the dead, claimed that there had been a lock on the door of the nursery and that no staff had been present to unlock it. The windows of the nursery were smashed by rescuers as they tried to reach the babies.View image in fullscreenRelatives of the children who died in the fire gather at the hospital.Photograph: M Yousaf/APSohail Ashraf, the Islamabad chief commissioner, said the emergency call was made just before 7am and rescue and police teams quickly reached the scene.The hospital administration said: “The fire was immediately brought under control and the children were immediately shifted to the intensive care unit.”Alamzaib Khan, 26, was also among those who tried to run into the ward as it burned. His wife had given birth to a baby girl two days ago and she was still in the hospital recovering from a C-section, while his baby had already been taken home.“I was sleeping on the pavement when I heard people screaming and wailing,” he said. “I ran towards the ICU and children’s ward and I saw my wife while climbing down a ladder.”After checking on his wife, he tried to help with the rescue of others. “The moment I approached the children’s ward, I couldn’t see anything because the smoke was so thick,” he said. “I tried to go inside but it was not possible.”“People were crying, screaming and asking for help. Women from the operation room had to run for their lives,” he said. “Women were in pain themselves but crying and begging everyone to help them to rescue their children. It’s hard to describe this terrible moment.”The prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, directed authorities to conduct an ​immediate investigation into the incident, which was one of the deadliest hospital fires in years.“Such a situation involving children is irreparable,” Sharif said. “Those responsible should be identified, and the strictest action should be taken.”Pakistan’s president, Asif Ali Zardari, expressed condolences to the families of the newborn babies. In a statement, he said the loss of lives was heartbreaking.Fires in large buildings such as factories and shopping centres are frequent in Pakistan, often due to poor safety laws and lax enforcement of building codes.Explore more on these topicsPakistanSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: London neurosurgeons perform first successful AI-assisted operation to remove brain tumour | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Surgeons aided by real-time analysis of camera footage that identified critical anatomy in brain to be avoided
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Surgeons aided by real-time analysis of camera footage that identified critical anatomy in brain to be avoided
Content: Rhys Hibbert, right (with neurosurgeon Hani Marcus, left) was the first patient to have a brain tumour successfully removed in an AI-assisted operation. He was operated on at the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery in London.Photograph: UCLH/PAView image in fullscreenRhys Hibbert, right (with neurosurgeon Hani Marcus, left) was the first patient to have a brain tumour successfully removed in an AI-assisted operation. He was operated on at the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery in London.Photograph: UCLH/PAAI (artificial intelligence)London neurosurgeons perform first successful AI-assisted operation
