to remove brain tumourSurgeons aided by real-time analysis of camera footage that identified critical anatomy in brain to be avoidedAndrew GregoryHealth editorWed 26 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNeurosurgeons inLondonhave performed the world’s first successful AI-assisted operation to remove a brain tumour, saving the sight of a 48-year-old man, health officials have said.The surgery was performed in May at the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery (NHNN), part of University College London hospitals NHS foundation trust, but details were kept secret until Thursday while the patient, Rhys Hibbert, recovered.While the surgical team remained in full control, the AI system analysed live camera footage during the operation, helping identify key structures such as nerves and blood vessels that should be avoided near the 11mm (0.4in) tumour on Hibbert’s pituitary gland.“When I came round … I could see everything in the room clearly,” said Hibbert, who was able to walk independently without glasses or sticks within a week of the surgery.He has since returned to work as a customer service manager. “It feels like I’ve got a 360‑degree panoramic view of everything around me,” he said.The surgeons operated on Hibbert using new AI technology which helps to identify tiny anatomy in the brain by colour-coding important structures to help surgeons recognise them safely.The hospital had previously used the technology as a research tool but the operation was the first time it had been used on a patient.The pituitary gland, blood vessels and nerves controlling vision are tightly packed together, and “going a millimetre wrong can make a critical difference”, health officials said, potentially leading to blindness, stroke or death.Dr Sophia Bano, an associate professor in robotics and AI at UCL and the technical lead for the AI system, said: “By learning from hundreds of surgical videos, [the system] has been exposed to a breadth of surgical examples that would take a surgeon many years to encounter.“It is designed to help recognise critical anatomy, surgical instruments and tissue interactions in real time, supporting the surgeon during highly delicate procedures.”Initially managed without surgery, Hibbert’s symptoms had worsened since his diagnosis in 2024, and included severe hormone imbalance and vision problems. Without the operation, he faced going blind, health officials said.Hibbert, from Bedfordshire, said: “The NHNN was founded in 1859 … and was the world’s first dedicated neurosurgical hospital. So to me, it seems very fitting that the same hospital should also be the world’s first to carry out an AI-assisted neurosurgery.”Prof Mike Lewis, the scientific director for innovation at the National Institute forHealthand Care Research (NIHR), which funded the operation as part of a clinical trial, said the “pioneering surgery” highlighted the potential of advanced AI to support surgeons and improve patient care.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)HospitalsLondonUCL (University College London)NeuroscienceEnglandHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: No more UK energy bills support likely before price cap rise | Energy bills | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham stops short of pledging further help as gas and electricity prices due to increase by 4% in October
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Andy Burnham stops short of pledging further help as gas and electricity prices due to increase by 4% in October
Content: The government has already removed VAT from domestic electricity bills, in a move announced in Burnham’s first week in office.Photograph: Daisy-Daisy/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenThe government has already removed VAT from domestic electricity bills, in a move announced in Burnham’s first week in office.Photograph: Daisy-Daisy/Getty Images/iStockphotoEnergy billsNo more UK energy bills support likely before price cap riseAndy Burnham stops short of pledging further help as gas and electricity prices due to increase by 4% in OctoberJessica ElgotandJillian AmbroseWed 26 Aug 2026 17.42 EDTFirst published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 12.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHouseholds are unlikely to receive further energy bills support before the October price cap, though more targeted measures could be looked at if there is a further shock in January, government sources said.Gas and electricity prices will rise by 4% from Octoberunder the new cap. The government has already removed VAT from domestic electricity bills to save average households £45 a year, a move announced in Andy Burnham’s first week in office.Prices had climbed by 13% at the start of July to take account of global energy market price rises caused by the US war on Iran and the closure of the strait of Hormuz.Burnham said on Wednesday that rising energy bills were “difficult for people and I recognise that” but he stopped short of promising intervention beyond the VAT cut, saying the government “would continue to look as we go forward at how we get energy prices down in the long term”.Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said bills were being driven up by the Iran war and the government would “keep looking at what more we can do to protect families from unaffordable bills”.The chancellor, John Healey, said the government would look again towards the end of the year at whether more support was needed.“No government can stop the squeeze felt by families and businesses with a global shock of this magnitude. It’s being felt around the world. But we can keep close watch as we move towards the new year, and we remain focused on giving families a bit of breathing space with the cost of living,” he told the Sun.“We’re a government that will look for practical action – working to put our country on a more resilient footing so we can better weather these shocks in future.”Burnham will continue his summer tour of the UK on Thursday with a stop in south Wales, promising to win back the trust of voters after historic losses forLabourin the May Senedd elections.“The answers to the UK’s challenges will not come from an echo chamber. They will come from the places that know their own strengths, and from a government willing to listen and then act,” he said ahead of the visit.The prime minister will spend the morning speaking to workers and apprentices, including about the cost of living and reindustrialisation, and the cost of energy is likely to be a key part of discussions.The Resolution Foundation thinktank, which has close ties to the government, suggested there should be targeted support designed, costed and ready to switch on if needed from January, when bills have been forecast to rise again by up to 9%.It said this should go beyond those on benefits and target those earning less than £24,000 a year, reaching about 40% of households, with potential savings of £175 on average.The thinktank’s chief executive, Ruth Curtice, said: “The rise in energy bills in October has been tempered but not avoided by the government’s decision to reduce electricity bills for everyone through a VAT cut. With wholesale gas prices hitting new post-Iran highs in the past week, there is a real risk of further rises in January. Given the acute pressure on both family and government budgets, we need a better mechanism for targeted support ready to activate if needed.”The Trades Union Congress renewed its call for awindfall tax on bank profitsto pay for a cut to bills. Its general secretary, Paul Nowak, said the government should be looking at ways now to fund more support for households this winter.“The government is going to have to keep going on measures to boost living standards – starting with a tax on banks’ enormous profits to cut energy bills for the majority of households,” he said. “It’s the right thing to do. Banks are raking it in while many up and down the country are struggling to get by – they can well afford to pay more tax.”Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, was preparing targeted support for energy bills before Burnham became prime minister. She told the Commons in March she wanted to “ensure that we are in a position in the autumn to have a targeted approach”.Government sources suggested that any further support would be costed in the budget and officials would wait to see how the conflict in the Gulf developed over the coming months, including whether the strait of Hormuz could be reopened.Burnham has suggested he is open to allowing more drilling sites in the North Sea if a quasi-judicial process approves exploration of the Jackdaw and Rosebank fossil fuel sites.That is likely to cause a backlash from some Labour MPs, butin a interview with the FTBurnham pointed to the “pragmatic approach” taken by the green energy entrepreneur and climate campaigner Dale Vince, who recently backed both schemes on the BBC’s Newsnight programme.Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary and now foreign secretary, once called the Rosebank proposal “climate vandalism”, andclimate experts have warnedthat the environmental damage caused by developing the oil and gas fields would destroy any economic benefits.Explore more on these topicsEnergy billsHousehold billsUK cost of living crisisEnergy industryEconomic policyAndy BurnhamLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Work is good for you’: how UK scheme could help tackle youth mental health crisis | Youth unemployment | The Guardian
description: Paid employment can boost confidence and wellbeing, says Pat McFadden as jobs guarantee scheme gets under way
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Paid employment can boost confidence and wellbeing, says Pat McFadden as jobs guarantee scheme gets under way
Content: Pat McFadden and Juliet Campbell, MP for Broxtowe, with Saqib (right), a Boots warehouse employee in Nottingham.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAView image in fullscreenPat McFadden and Juliet Campbell, MP for Broxtowe, with Saqib (right), a Boots warehouse employee in Nottingham.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAYouth unemployment‘Work is good for you’: how UK scheme could help tackle youth mental health crisisPaid employment can boost confidence and wellbeing, says Pat McFadden as jobs guarantee scheme gets under wayHeather StewartWed 26 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWork must be “part of the answer” to the mental health crisis among young people, the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, has said as he met some of the first beneficiaries of Labour’syouth jobs guarantee scheme.He was speaking on a visit to Boots’s headquarters in Nottingham on Wednesday, where several 18- to 21-year-olds were taken on under the job guarantee – with their wages paid by the taxpayer for six months.Some of the recruits were packing and labelling boxes of products to be posted out to households, and others are in administrative roles. They told McFadden about long periods of fruitless jobhunting.“It was just amazing for me to hear their stories,” McFadden said of the recruits. “These are young people who have been out of work for one, two, up to four years. Most of them have been working here for a few weeks. And you can already see how it’s changed their confidence in themselves – their sense of belief in themselves.”A rise in cases of mental illness is widely cited as one cause for the increase in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) in recent years.But McFadden said the reasons could run the other way, too. “Work is part of the answer. Work is good for you. It’s bad for your mental health to be sitting at home, isolated.View image in fullscreenYoung people told Pat McFadden that their social lives had improved and they had clearer daily routines as a result of being in paid work.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA“I see this not only as an economic thing, but as a response to greater instances of mental health problems for young people. The last thing we want to see is a diagnosis of problems leading to a life on benefits.”At a roundtable discussion, McFadden asked each of the young people how they felt as a result of their move into paid work. They cited better social lives and clearer daily routines.“I’m so conscious, having done this job for almost exactly a year now, that belief and confidence is a big part of the picture,” McFadden told journalists afterwards. “We mustn’t blame young people for the challenges they are facing in the labour market.”The number of Neets in the UK recently topped 1 million – with the latest data due out on Thursday.Alan Milburn, the Blair-era cabinet minister reviewing youth inactivity for the government, has warned that the numbercould hit 1.25m by 2030, without intervention. His final report is due in the autumn.McFadden made clear that welfare reform would probably be part of the government’s response, criticising the “black and white” distinction in the current universal credit system.“There’s a design flaw in the universal credit system, which too readily separates people into ‘fit for work’ and ‘unfit for work’, and when they are unfit for work, leaves them without any support or any conditions,” he said. “That’s what I call the culture of ‘signed off and written off’. I think we need to change that.”He highlighted a recent initiative under which claimants with no obligation to look for work have been asked to attend voluntary interviews with work coaches at their local Jobcentre.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMcFadden had started the day at a branch of Sainsbury’s in London, stacking shelves in the bread aisle, alongside the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the London mayor, Sadiq Khan.View image in fullscreenPat McFadden, Sadiq Khan and Andy Burnham help to stack shelves at Sainsbury’s in Nine Elms, London.Photograph: Richard Pohle/ReutersThe trio were highlighting the fact that Sainsbury’s is offering 10,000 internships for young people.McFadden praised Boots and Sainsbury’s, and encouraged other big employers to play their part in what he called the “national cause” of tackling youth unemployment.Asked whether it was a good use of public money to be subsidising corporations to take on young people, he said: “I’m enthused when businesses like Boots or Sainsbury’s – or any business in the country – steps up and says: ‘I want to play my part here.’ And if there’s a bit of a financial incentive in it, that’s fine.”The jobs guarantee scheme will eventually be available to 18- to 24-year-olds in Great Britain who have been claiming universal credit and seeking work for at least 18 months, with the aim of creating 90,000 subsidised placements over the next three years.It is initially being piloted in six areas with high unemployment, including central and east Scotland, Birmingham and Solihull, and south-east and south-west Wales. The government intends it to be nationwide by November.Explore more on these topicsYouth unemploymentUnemploymentYoung peopleMental healthWork & careersBootsWelfarenewsShareReuse this content

title: Plug-in balcony solar panels to go on sale in UK for first time | Solar power | The Guardian
description: DIY system will be stocked by big retailers, starting with Argos, enabling more homes to lower bills by generating own electricity
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: DIY system will be stocked by big retailers, starting with Argos, enabling more homes to lower bills by generating own electricity
Content: The systems can be plugged into a standard wall socket to generate solar power from a balcony, terrace, shed roof or any other outdoor space.Photograph: Ronald Rampsch/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe systems can be plugged into a standard wall socket to generate solar power from a balcony, terrace, shed roof or any other outdoor space.Photograph: Ronald Rampsch/AlamySolar powerPlug-in balcony solar panels to go on sale in UK for first timeDIY system will be stocked by big retailers, starting with Argos, enabling more homes to lower bills by generating own electricityJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentWed 26 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlug-in solar panels will go on sale in the UK for the first time from Thursday, allowing households unable to use rooftop panels to also generate their own cheap electricity.Households across the country will be able to join the millions across mainland Europe who generate their own renewable electricity using “balcony solar panels”, which will be stocked by some of the UK’s biggest retailers.Argos will be the first to offer the DIY solar systems this week, helping people living in flats or rented homes without roof access to lower their billsby generating their own electricity.The rival retailers Amazon, Currys, B&Q and Screwfix are also expected to stock their shelves with plug-in panels within the coming weeks at prices starting from about £400 to £500 depending on the capacity of the system.The devices are already popular in Spain and Germany, wherethey are known asBalkonkraftwerk(balcony power plant) because they can be plugged into a standard wall socket to generate solar power from a balcony, terrace, shed roof or any other outdoor space.The solar power flows directly into the property’s electrical circuit to power appliances without needing to buy as much from the grid. Each solar system must be registered so Great Britain’s NationalEnergySystem Operator can gauge how the cumulative impact of these panels could cut the need for gas-fired power or imports.View image in fullscreenThe solar power flows directly into the property’s electrical circuit to power appliances without needing to buy as much from the grid.Photograph: Climate CentralIn the UK the 800-watt solar systems due to go on sale will be about a fifth of the size of a typical residential rooftop solar set-up, meaning they are unable to provide enough energy to power a home but they could save the average household up to £110 a year on their annual electricity bill.Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said: “Plug-in solar is a simple, affordable way for households to take control of their energy bills and start saving straight away.”Graham Biggart, the managing director for Argos, said: “By making this technology more accessible, we’re putting more power in the hands of our customers and helping them explore practical ways to manage energy use at home.”The savings possible from each solar system will depend on how much solar power is generated, which could be affected by the orientation of each solar panel and the weather on any given day.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSavings will also depend on whether the household is able to use the electricity while it is being generated – perhaps by running washing machines or dishwashers during sunny spells – because plug-in batteries were not included in thenew legislation allowing plug-in solar salesto begin.Emily Seymour, the energy editor at the Which? consumer group, said: “These smaller systems will generate less electricity than conventional rooftop solar and won’t be suitable for every home. People may need planning permission or the consent of the building owner before going ahead, so it will be important to check your own circumstances before making a purchase.“There are also important safety considerations, particularly around the suitability of older electrical systems, the safe mounting of panels and the potential for people to use products or equipment incorrectly.”Joanna O’Loan, a manager at Energy Saving Trust, said: “While the savings will vary from home to home, plug-in solar panels will give more people greater control over their energy use and costs. As these products become more widely available, access to clear and reliable information is essential to help people make informed choices that are right for their home and budget.”Explore more on these topicsSolar powerEnergy industryRenewable energyEnergy billsRetail industryEnergyConsumer affairsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham drops support for political funding cap aimed at curbing mega-donors | Party funding | The Guardian
description: PM said he would set bar at £500k, but trade unions say funding reforms could undermine their ability to donate to Labour
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: PM said he would set bar at £500k, but trade unions say funding reforms could undermine their ability to donate to Labour
Content: Labour MPs have urged Andy Burnham to strengthen ‘timid’ elections  bill with amendments.Photograph: Richard Pohle/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenLabour MPs have urged Andy Burnham to strengthen ‘timid’ elections  bill with amendments.Photograph: Richard Pohle/AFP/GettyParty fundingBurnham drops support for political funding cap aimed at curbing mega-donorsPM said he would set bar at £500k, but trade unions say funding reforms could undermine their ability to donate to LabourKiran StaceyPolicy editorWed 26 Aug 2026 15.08 EDTFirst published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 15.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has dropped his support for capping political donations, causing anger among activists and Labour MPs who have long campaigned for change to the way parties are funded.The prime minister has decided not to back amendments to the elections bill, which would cap the amount a person or an organisation can give in a single donation, according to government sources.The decision comes after alobbying campaignfrom Labour’s trade union backers, who said amendments to the bill, which returns to parliament for its remaining stages next week, could undermine their ability to donate to the party. It is also a retreat from the support Burnham gave to the idea just a few weeks ago, whenhe emailed a campaignerfor electoral reform to say he would support a donations cap of £500,000.Stella Creasy, one of the Labour backbenchers who has tabled an amendment calling for a donations cap, said: “Millionaires are increasingly treating British politics as their plaything – splashing the cash to get the outcome they want and the next election as their cup final.“The public won’t forgive us if we miss this chance to clean up Westminster because we are squabbling with each other.”Shaun Bowler, the campaigner to whom Burnham promised his support in May, said: “Andy Burnham promised me a proper cap on political donations and a ‘wholesale culture change’ in Westminster. If his government now refuses to back a donations cap, then he has broken the promise he made to me – and to voters.“I wanted to believe the positive message he gave me. I wanted to believe that someone was finally going to take on the culture that has left so many people feeling that their voices don’t matter and that wealthy people can buy influence over our government.“But words mean nothing if they disappear the moment power is won. Large political donations are not democratic. They create influence, whether politicians want to admit it or not. The prime minister has one chance to start rebuilding trust: therepresentation of the people act.“He told me he wanted change. Now he needs to keep his promise and act.”Darren Hughes, the chief executive of the Electoral Reform Society, said: “Huge donations have a corrosive effect on trust in politics as they leave the public wondering what donors expect in return for their money.“A donations cap is a crucial step to ending the impression that our politics is for sale to the highest bidder and rebuilding that trust, which is currently at record lows.”However, aLaboursource said: “The representation of the people [elections] bill has been designed to deliver our manifesto commitments on votes at 16 and strengthen political donation rules to guard against foreign interference and that’s what the government is prioritising.”The elections bill, which returns to the Commons next week, is one of the most hotly contested of Burnham’s first few months in office. The bill was intended to lower the voting age to 16 and limit donations by foreign donors, but many in the Labour party believe it should go further in a number of areas.Rushanara Ali, the Labour MP who helped write the bill when she was a minister in the communities department, recentlytold the Guardianthat she felt it was too “timid” and “incremental”, and urged Burnham to strengthen it with amendments.Some Labour MPs intend to use the next stage of the bill to try to introduce clauses banning cryptocurrency donations and cracking down on social media misinformation at election times.Others want Burnhamto back their ideaof a national commission on changing the voting system – something the former Greater Manchester mayor has repeatedly backed in the past.The government has already saidit intends to capdonations by British people living abroad at £100,000, but a big fight is now brewing over whether to apply a similar cap to domestic donations.In May, Burnham signalled he would back a £500,000 cap, telling Bowler over email that he thought a donations cap “would guard against the perception of any one party being unduly influenced or swayed by one person or organisation”.He added: “As to the level, I think that would have to be subject to wider review of political funding but my gut feeling would suggest somewhere in the region of £500k.”Once Burnham got into office however, some of Britain’s biggest trade unions mounted a campaign against the idea, urging MPs not to back an amendment by Creasy to cap donations at £100,000 or another by her backbench colleague Alex Sobel to set the bar at £1m.Last month,GMBwrote to 80 MPs who are members of the union warning: “We believe this amendment risks having significant unintended consequences. Trade unions are already subject to a level of statutory regulation over political expenditure that no other membership organisations face.”Creasy is now changing her amendment in a move to placate union worries, proposing a £500,000 cap that would be gradually reduced until ministers intervene to set it at a level with which they feel comfortable.She said: “Our new amendment would give British democracy the breathing space to get a donations cap right.”However, even this compromise does not appear to have done enough to win ministerial support, which is likely to be crucial for securing enough votes to pass.Those close to the process say capping donations is not a priority for Burnham and not a subject over which it would be worth triggering a fight with Labour’s biggest backers.Explore more on these topicsParty fundingAndy BurnhamLabourTrade unionsGMB unionElectoral reformStella CreasynewsShareReuse this content

title: Man in prison in New York advances in primary for Alaska’s US House seat | Alaska | The Guardian
description: Democrat Eric Hafner, to be released in 2036, also ran for seat in 2024, securing spot on that general election ballot
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Democrat Eric Hafner, to be released in 2036, also ran for seat in 2024, securing spot on that general election ballot
Content: Voters at city hall in Anchorage, Alaska, on 4 November 2024.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVoters at city hall in Anchorage, Alaska, on 4 November 2024.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesAlaskaMan in prison in New York advances in primary for Alaska’s US House seatDemocrat Eric Hafner, to be released in 2036, also ran for seat in 2024, securing spot on that general election ballotAssociated PressWed 26 Aug 2026 18.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 19.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man who is serving time in a federal prison inNew Yorkadvanced on Wednesday from the primary forAlaska’s loneUS Houseseat.Eric Hafner, a registered Democrat, also ran for the seat in 2024 and secured a spot on the general election ballot that November despite a challenge brought by theAlaskaDemocratic party.Hafner pleaded guilty in 2022 to charges of making threats against police officers, judges and others. He is set to be released in 2036.The leading candidates in the race are the incumbent, Republican Nick Begich, and independent Bill Hill, a commercial fisher and retired educator.Hafner’s success in the primary as one of the candidates moving on to the general election is almost certain to draw another legal challenge because the US constitution requires candidates to live in the state they will represent at the time of the election.In the candidate information he filed with the state, he listed the same Box Elder, South Dakota, mailing address andNew Yorkphone number as his mother, Carol Hafner. Neither has any apparent ties to Alaska.Carol Hafner also is a failed prior candidate and ran again this year, this time in the state’s US Senate primary.Under Alaska’s election system, the top four primary finishers advance to the general election regardless of party affiliation. Eric Hafner received 5,757 votes after 93% of ballots had been counted. That was far behind the third-place candidate, Democrat Matt Schultz. But Schultz withdrew from the general election and was ineligible to advance.It remained too early to call the fourth-place finisher.Explore more on these topicsAlaskaUS midterm elections 2026House of RepresentativesNew YorkUS CongressUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez rejoins DSA after membership lapse of seven years | Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez | The Guardian
description: Then House candidate joined Democratic Socialists of America in 2018 but didn’t renew membership after a year
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Then House candidate joined Democratic Socialists of America in 2018 but didn’t renew membership after a year
Content: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at the Munich Security Conference in Germany on 13 February 2026.Photograph: Liesa Johannssen/ReutersView image in fullscreenAlexandria Ocasio-Cortez at the Munich Security Conference in Germany on 13 February 2026.Photograph: Liesa Johannssen/ReutersAlexandria Ocasio-CortezAlexandria Ocasio-Cortez rejoins DSA after membership lapse of seven yearsThen House candidate joined Democratic Socialists of America in 2018 but didn’t renew membership after a yearMaya YangWed 26 Aug 2026 18.11 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 18.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlexandria Ocasio-Cortezhas rejoined the Democratic Socialists of America after not renewing her membership for seven years, amid speculation that she might run for president in 2028.The 36-year-oldNew Yorkrepresentative and one of the country’s most prominent democratic socialists renewed her membership in the group’s national organization afterreportsemerged earlier this month that it had lapsed. Ocasio-Cortez initially joined the group in 2018.In a statement on Tuesday night, the DSA announced: “Democratic Socialists of America confirms Rep Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is a member in good standing of our organization, having recently rejoined in August 2026,” according to areportin City & State New York.Is the US ready for President Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez?Read moreIt added: “Previously, the representative joined DSA in 2018 with a one-year membership, which DSA’s national leadership recently noticed had lapsed, in 2019. She has since renewed her membership as of this month.”The DSA said it decided to disclose Ocasio-Cortez’s membership details amid reports that she could run for president in the next election cycle.Interest in the congresswoman’s status comes as the organization has seen its ranksgrowexponentially across the country, following a string of election victories from New York toFlorida.“While it is atypical for DSA to address the membership status of individuals, ongoing discussions about the 2028 presidential campaign have prompted this release … With chapters and members campaigning to draft RepAlexandria Ocasio-Cortezas a potential Presidential Primary candidate, we believe that the status of her membership is essential information for members to have in their deliberations and discussions,” the statement said, City & State New York reported.The Guardian reached out to the DSA for additional comment, but the organization declined. The Guardian has also contacted Ocasio-Cortez’s office.According to City & StateNew York, annual DSA membership cost $60 when Ocasio-Cortez joined in 2018, with members required to manually renew their dues each year. The organization has since moved to automatic renewals and introduced a range of monthly membership options, with dues ranging from $5 to $50.Despite Ocasio-Cortez having been a lapsed member of the DSA over the last seven years, in November 2020 the DSAofferedits “congratulations to DSA member AOC on officially being re-elected to Congress” on X.Similarly, in March 2024, the DSAwrote on X: “We commend DSA members Rep @CoriBush and Rep @AOC for upholding our democratic values by voting against this authoritarian legislation,” referring to the now-former Missouri representative Cori Bush and Ocasio-Cortez voting against a TikTok ban.Earlier this month, in aninterviewon ABC, host Jonathan Karl asked Ocasio-Cortez whether she was still a member of DSA. She responded: “Of the New York City chapter.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Not the national chapter?” Karl asked, to which Ocasio-Cortez replied: “No.”Asked to elaborate on the distinction, Ocasio-Cortez said: “Every DSA chapter is formed locally. And so the New York City DSA chapter, those are folks that you know, it’s kind of like your local union chapter.”In July 2024, the DSA withdrew its endorsement of Ocasio-Cortez at the request of NYC-DSA, according to the organization, citing her decision to vote for a House resolution that described “denial of Israel’s right to exist” as an example of antisemitism, as well as her participation in a recent panel discussion on antisemitism.“A national DSA endorsement comes with a serious commitment to the movement for Palestine and our collective socialist project … To build a socialist movement that’s capable of defeating capitalism, we must demand more from leaders in our movement,” the DSAsaidat the time.It added: “AOC recently hosted a public panel with leaders from the Jewish Council for Public Affairs, lobbyists for the [International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance] definition of antisemitism. On this panel, anti-Zionism and antisemitism were conflated and boycotting Zionist institutions was condemned. This sponsorship is a deep betrayal to all those who’ve risked their welfare to fight Israeli apartheid and genocide through political and direct action in recent months, and in decades past.”Explore more on these topicsAlexandria Ocasio-CortezDemocratic socialismHouse of RepresentativesDemocratsUS CongressNew YorkUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Meta agrees to major changes to Facebook and Instagram as it settles US trial over teen addiction for up to $18bn | Meta | The Guardian
description: US tech giant agrees to establish further protections for teens such as daily usage limits and blocks on night-time use
Author: Blake Montgomery
Headline: US tech giant agrees to establish further protections for teens such as daily usage limits and blocks on night-time use
Content: Meta had denied all allegations throughout the proceedings, saying states were chasing an ‘outlandish payout’.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreenMeta had denied all allegations throughout the proceedings, saying states were chasing an ‘outlandish payout’.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersMetaMeta agrees to major changes to Facebook and Instagram as it settles US trial over teen addiction for up to $18bnUS tech giant agrees to establish further protections for teens such as daily usage limits and blocks on night-time useBlake MontgomeryandDara KerrWed 26 Aug 2026 16.30 EDTFirst published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 09.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMetaagreed to significant changes to itsInstagramandFacebookapps in a settlement that ended a landmark lawsuit on Wednesday. Dozens of US states had accused the tech giant of addicting and harming children with dangerous products.The agreement curtails amajor trialin California and will require the social mediacompany to pay up to $18bn. Meta agreed to establish safeguards for teenage users, including daily usage limits and blocks on night-time use nationwide in the US.This is the first time in the US thatMetahas been forced to change key features of the experience of everyday users.The jury trial, which took place in federal court in Oakland, California,began with opening statementsjust last week. California and 28 other US states sued the $1.36tn (£1tn) company over allegations that Meta deliberately designed addictive products that hooked young people, leading to mental health issues, including anxiety, depression and suicide. The states additionally claimed the social media company regularly collected data on children under the age of 13 without parental permission in violation of federal and state laws. As part of the settlement, the company denies wrongdoing.1:03Parent whose 16-year-old daughter died by suicide reacts to Meta settlement – videoHook, hold, harvest and hide: Meta’s alleged strategy laid out in first week of landmark trialRead more“Today, we have secured a settlement with Meta that will make social media less dangerous for our kids and make a world of a difference for children and their families,” Rob Bonta, the attorney general ofCalifornia, said in a statement. “Meta has agreed to make massive transformations that will reduce the risk of harm from its platforms – and will do it within months.”Bonta said those changes included time limits, stopping notifications during school, a block on the app during critical overnight hours, bans on plastic surgery filters and more.The $18bn settlement will be divided between the states over a period of 10 years, subject to court approval. California would receive between $1.5bn and $2.1bn and Colorado will get about $615m.“The relief we are getting in this settlement is very meaningful and well beyond what any court has ordered or is likely to order,” said Phil Weiser, the attorney general of Colorado, adding: “The focus of this case was to protect our kids.”Throughout the proceedings,Meta denied all allegations, saying states were chasing an “outlandish payout”. On Wednesday, the company’s chief legal officer, CJ Mahoney, said the settlement reached with the states would only work if all social media companies changed their platform designs.“Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution. We therefore call on our industry peers, TikTok, Snap, and YouTube, to implement this new framework, right away,” Mahoney said in a statement. “As a parent, I’m proud of both the work Meta has done to protect kids historically, and of this new groundbreaking agreement. But its success depends on all other social media platforms following Meta’s lead.”Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap face thousands more similar US lawsuits brought by families, individuals, school districts and other attorneys general. Meta and YouTube lost the first of those cases to go to trial in February,beingorderedto pay $6m to the young woman who brought the suit. (TikTok and Snap settled before the case went to trial.) Two more lawsuits that were slated to go to trial this summer,one federalandone in California state court, also settled for undisclosed sums.Metalosta separate suit, brought by the attorney general of New Mexico, where it was ordered topay nearly $1bnto the state for allowing child sexual exploitation on its platforms.The trial in Oakland was expected to last for several weeks with dozens of witnesses taking the stand. Instead, there were only four days of proceedings.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionInstagram CEO denies company hid low use of teen safety feature in Meta trialRead moreJurors firstheard from the states’ star witness, Arturo Béjar, a former Meta safety engineer turned whistleblower. He testified that the company had a “don’t ask, don’t tell” strategy when it comes to the safety of children on its platforms.Béjar said thatMark Zuckerberg, Meta’s CEO, was aware of the harms of Instagram and Facebook, but that the executive publicly touted the platforms’ safety.“I felt that he created a false and misleading impression of Facebook’s commitment to young people,” Béjar testified.Zuckerberg had been listed as a witness in the trial but did not testify before the settlement agreement was reached.On Tuesday,questioningof Adam Mosseri, the Instagram CEO, began with the lawyer for the states accusing the company of touting safety features for teens, but not being forthcoming that young people don’t use them.When the executive was faced with multiple questions about not disclosing those low user numbers, Mosseri brushed them aside, saying: “We don’t publish every single stat.”Explore more on these topicsMetaInstagramFacebookSocial mediaSocial networkingChildren's healthMental healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Wiped out: US faces surging toilet paper prices amid trade war with Canada | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: Paper products among hardest-hit sectors after trade negotiations broke down, with 25-50% tariffs estimated
Author: Lauren Aratani
Headline: Paper products among hardest-hit sectors after trade negotiations broke down, with 25-50% tariffs estimated
Content: A customer picks up a pack of toilet paper from a store shelf in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, on 2 March 2025.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA customer picks up a pack of toilet paper from a store shelf in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, on 2 March 2025.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesTrump tariffsWiped out: US faces surging toilet paper prices amid trade war with CanadaPaper products among hardest-hit sectors after trade negotiations broke down, with 25-50% tariffs estimatedAre you a Canadian boycotting US products? We’d like to hear from youLauren Arataniin New YorkWed 26 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUsing the bathroom or having a cry is about to become more expensive for North Americans as theUSandCanadaenter a full-fledged trade war that threatens to flush away decades of peaceful trading between the two nations.After trade negotiationsbroke downbetween the two countrieslast weekend, Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister,vowedto match US tariffs “dollar for dollar” andunveiledalistof nearly 900 American goods that will face 25% to 50% tariffs starting on 8 September.Paper products are among the hardest-hit sectors, withCanadathreatening to put tariffs of between 25% and 50% on “toilet paper or face tissue stock” from 8 September in retaliation for a 50% hike from Washington DC.Though American toilet paper and tissues are often made domestically, theyheavily relyon lumber-rich Canada for raw materials. Procter & Gamble, the owner of Charmin toilet paper,saidlast year that it would have to increase prices amid tariffs that were in place at the time.Canada announces retaliatory tariffs on wide range of US goodsRead moreThe US imported $328m worth of toilet paper from Canada in 2024, according to theWorld Bank, making it by far the largest exporter of the product to the US. Retailersincluding Costcosource much of their paper products from the country.The US accounts for more than 20% of global tissue consumption despite having only 4% of the world’s population. The average Americanuses 141 rollsof toilet paper per year, making them No 1 for No 2s globally, just ahead of Germans, each using an average of 134 rolls annually.It’s not just paper products that could rise in price. Thetrade warhighlights the deep economic ties shared between the two countries as consumers continue to worry about inflation on both sides of the border.US tariffsare specifically affecting Canadian liquor, including popular whiskey brands Crown Royal and Canadian Club, which are currently under a 50% tariff.While Canada has not introduced a tariff on American liquor, most Canadian provinces have introduced their own bans on American alcohol, in retaliation for earlier tariffs on Canadian products.Donald Trumpused these province-wide bans on American alcohol as part of hislegal justificationfor his new tariffs against Canada.Carney has asked province leaders to consider putting American liquor back on the shelves, though as the Nova Scotia premier Tim HoustontoldCBC News: “Whether Nova Scotians or Canadians will actually buy it when it’s back on the shelves, that’s a whole other discussion.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrump announces new 50% tariff on Canadian cars, trucks and steelRead moreTrump also said that his new tariffs are in retaliation for Canadian levies against theAmerican dairy industry. Heintroduceda 50% tariff on nearly all Canadian dairy products, with the exception of Canadian cheese.In response, Canada has a 50% tariff on American dairy products, along with a 25% tariff on American cheese.Canada also took a swing at the US fishing industry, with a 25% tariff on American fish and seafood, including frozen lobster. The move prompted Republican senator Susan Collins, facing a tough re-election battle in lobster-capital Maine, to call Trump’s latest move“a mistake”.A 25%tariff on Canadian cars and auto partsis set to affect the American auto industry, which relies heavily on Canadian parts for manufacturing. Trump has threatened todouble the tariffto 50% if a deal isn’t made by 1 January 2027.With negotiations down the drain, it’s unclear if or when the tariffs will be lifted. But the Trump administration is adamant that“there’s no possible way”the trade dispute with Canada will affect US consumers, according to Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative.“The fundamentals are good,” he said. “I don’t think this is going to affect anything.”Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsCanadaMark CarneyDonald TrumpAmericasTariffsTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bill Gates calls for ‘human-reserved’ jobs in face of AI takeover | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: In 6,000-word essay Microsoft co-founder also expresses concern governments not prepared for technology’s impact
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: In 6,000-word essay Microsoft co-founder also expresses concern governments not prepared for technology’s impact
Content: Bill Gates wrote ‘it is fair to wonder whether the world’s institutions are up to the task of designing and implementing this new architecture’.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenBill Gates wrote ‘it is fair to wonder whether the world’s institutions are up to the task of designing and implementing this new architecture’.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)Bill Gates calls for ‘human-reserved’ jobs in face of AI takeoverIn 6,000-word essay Microsoft co-founder also expresses concern governments not prepared for technology’s impactBusiness live – latest updatesMark SweneyWed 26 Aug 2026 06.33 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 15.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBill Gates has called for “human-reserved” jobs in certain sectors to prevent AI replacing them, and expressed concern that governments are not prepared for the impact the technology will have.In a 6,000 word essay titledThe turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make are critical, the billionaire Microsoft co-founder likened the need to spare roles from digital encroachment to how nature reserves operate to protect the environment.“Many jobs will disappear forever,” he said, in his first lengthy piece on AI in three years. “I believe that as AI and robots improve, we’ll set aside certain things for only people to do.“I’ve started calling this domain human reserved. I like the phrase human reserved because it makes me think of nature reserves – places where we could put buildings and roads, but we choose not to because the loss would be too great.”He cited examples including the health professionals who cared for his father, who died of Alzheimer’s disease six years ago.“Something in the care they gave my dad was irreplaceably human, no robot could or should have done it,” he said. “Imagine a robot giving you the awful news that you have an incurable disease. There’s no technical reason why it couldn’t. Yet it shouldn’t.”Wednesday’s essay is one of Gates’s first major public interventions since he became embroiled in the Jeffrey Epstein scandal. An external review commissioned by the Gates Foundation found last month that there had beenabout 30 meetingsbetween Epstein and foundation leaders and staff – including Gates – between 2011 and 2014.Gates, who has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s crimes, remains the chair of his $89bn (£65bn) charitable foundation and previously said he regretted “every minute” he spent with the sex offender.Gates warns in his essay that governments are not prepared for the scale of the impact of AI.“The highest priority is a monumental task: creating a domestic and international framework for dealing with AI,” he wrote. “After the attacks of 9/11 the US government went through its biggest reorganisation since World War II for the purpose of improving just one function, national security.“AI will require much, much more. It will affect national security as well as employment, education, taxation, energy, elections, air and water, public health, the financial system, law enforcement, transportation, public lands and IT systems.“It is fair to wonder whether the world’s institutions are up to the task of designing and implementing this new architecture.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGates also said that as part of a global effort “some cooperation between the US and China will be required”.His staff are working to set up a meeting with China’s president, Xi Jinping, in November to discuss global efforts to mitigate the growing risks posed by AI.Gates last met Xi three years ago, when he became the first foreign entrepreneur the Chinese president had hosted since the global Covid pandemic.The tech billionaire also expressed concern in his essay about the impact of AI on education.“Ironically, the same tool that will allow people to learn more than ever could also lead to many people learning less,” he wrote. “Onepreliminary surveysuggested that heavier AI use was associated with less critical thinking. The effect was stronger for young people.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Bill GatesComputingTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Fears grow for fourth rate hike after Australia sees higher-than-expected July inflation | Australia news | The Guardian
description: ABS says CPI was 3.5% in July, casting doubt on Reserve Bank meeting its 2.5% inflation target without further hike
Author: Patrick Commins
Headline: ABS says CPI was 3.5% in July, casting doubt on Reserve Bank meeting its 2.5% inflation target without further hike
Content: Consumer prices climbed by 3.5% through the year, down from 3.8% in the previous month, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenConsumer prices climbed by 3.5% through the year, down from 3.8% in the previous month, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesAustralia newsFears grow for fourth rate hike after Australia sees higher-than-expected July inflationBureau of Statistics says CPI was 3.5% in July, casting doubt on Reserve Bank meeting its 2.5% inflation target without further hikeFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastPatrick ComminsEconomics editorWed 26 Aug 2026 02.44 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 02.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFears are growing that the Reserve Bank will hit millions of mortgage holders with a fourth rate hike this year, after inflation eased in July but by far less than expected.Consumer prices climbed by 3.5% through the year, down from 3.8% in the previous month, according to theAustralian Bureau of Statistics.That compared unfavourably to the forecast 3.3% annual rate predicted by economists leading into the result.The Reserve Bank’s preferred underlying inflation measure, which removes the most volatile prices, had been expected to moderate but instead was stuck at 3.6%.Brendan Rynne, KPMG’s chief economist, said “today’s data supports the view that without policy action we may be in for a long, costly grind to get inflation under control”.“The Reserve Bank may have missed an opportunity at the last board meeting to get ahead of the game by raising rates,” Rynne said.Annual rate of inflation.The disappointing update comes a day after minutes from the most recent RBA meeting showed board members were unconvinced that they would be able to hit their 2.5% inflation target by the end of next year and would react to any evidence that price pressures were not easing as expected.While thedecision on 11 August to hold the cash rateat 4.35% was unanimous, a number of board members thought another hike this year was “quite possible”.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailEconomists, many of whom had ruled out further rate increases, said the latest ABS figures heightened the chance of a November hike, with NAB analysts declaring that theircall for no further rate hikes was “under review”.Think you have a handle on how Australia’s economy works? Take the RBA’s quiz and find outRead morePhil O’Donaghoe, chief economist at Deutsche Bank, said he now expected the RBA would move as early as the next meeting in September, describing the underlying price growth as “intolerably high”.“We think the July CPI [consumer price index] leaves little room for the RBA to do anything other than follow through on its hawkish posturing, and the earlier it does, the better,” O’Donaghoe said.As expected, the end of the fuel excise relief in July helped push up pump prices by 7.5% in the month after falling for three months in a row, the ABS figures showed.Market-implied chance of a Reserve Bank cash rate hike by the meeting date.But My Bui, an economist at AMP, said “housing remains Australia’s chronic issue”, as home building costs lifted by 5.7% in the year to July, and rents by 3.6%.Bui said she still predicted an RBA rate hike in November, but “a September hike is certainly plausible”.The ABS said that the increase in construction costs “was driven by project home builders raising base prices to pass through higher labour and materials costs over the year”.The price of takeaway and restaurant meal prices climbed by 4.5% through the year, driven by higher operating costs including ingredients and the increase in the minimum wage from 1 July, the ABS said.Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsInflationEconomicsBusiness (Australia news)Reserve Bank of AustraliaAustralian Bureau of StatisticsInterest ratesnewsShareReuse this content

title: London rollout of robotaxis delayed amid lack of guidance for firms to follow | Self-driving cars | The Guardian
description: Uber and Wayve had said they would start trips ‘later this summer’ but launch now looks unlikely this year
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Uber and Wayve had said they would start trips ‘later this summer’ but launch now looks unlikely this year
Content: A Wayve autonomous car. Wayve and Uber have said more than 100,000 Londoners are on their waiting list for self-driving taxis.Photograph: tim@timandrew.co.uk/WayveView image in fullscreenA Wayve autonomous car. Wayve and Uber have said more than 100,000 Londoners are on their waiting list for self-driving taxis.Photograph: tim@timandrew.co.uk/WayveSelf-driving carsLondon rollout of robotaxis delayed amid lack of guidance for firms to followUber and Wayve had said they would start trips ‘later this summer’ but launch now looks unlikely this yearBusiness live – latest updatesMark SweneyWed 26 Aug 2026 04.48 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe rollout of robotaxis on the streets ofLondonis unlikely to happen this year, as regulatory and technical hurdles push back the ambitious schedule set out by the UK government.Only weeks ago Uber and London-based Wayve were granted the first minicab licences in the capital to allow them to offer self-driving taxi rides to paying customers – but with a human safety driver in place, for now – and said they would start trips“later this summer” before a full public launch.In 2025, Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, accelerated the proposed timeline for commercial trials of fully driverless taxi services by a year, announcing that they would start in the spring of this year.However, progress has slowed in recent months and Transport for London (TfL) has still not published the guidance that companies wanting to offer services must follow to win its approval.Last month, Christina Calderato, TfL’s director of strategy, told the London assembly’s transport committee that the transit authority would not be in a position to start accepting applications “for some time”.She said: “I do not think we are in a rush to get [the guidelines] out. There is a huge amount of work going on behind the scenes.”Uber and Wayve have said that more than 100,000 Londoners were on their waiting list for self-driving taxis.They are racing against Google-owned Waymo and its Chinese equivalent, Baidu’s Apollo Go, to launch self-driving taxi services in London. Robotaxis are now available to hire in more than 20 cities across the US, China and the Middle East.Earlier this month Zagreb became the first European city to offer autonomous rides to the general public, through Uber, but the service still has a human driver for “onboard monitoring”.On Tuesday, Waymo announced that it plans to launch commercial operations in Munich, Germany, late next year.Ben Loewenstein, Waymo’s head of policy and government affairs for the UK and Europe, told the Financial Times that the company was currently “working through the safety approval process” with the transport department and was waiting on TfL’s guidance to gain consent.He added that Waymo was working towards launching a fully autonomous service “by the end of this year” but would not say whether the company would be able to offer paid rides to the general public in that timeframe.TfL has granted 15 private hire vehicle licences to Ford Mustang Mach-E vehicles equipped with Wayve’s artificial intelligence driving software, as well as surround cameras and radar.A TfL-licensed private hire driver will sit in the driver’s seat during trips to intervene if necessary, although the software is expected to control the car.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUber and Wayve plan to launch small-scale commercial pilots with a driver behind the wheel soon.For its fully driverless launch Wayve plans to switch to a new Nissan Leaf vehicle that is still in production and is due to launch later this year.Alex Kendall, Wayve’s chief executive, said the company never claimed it would have a fully driverless operation this year.“I don’t want to put a timeline on it because we want to make sure we pass through [the regulatory process],” he told the FT. “This work is continuing at pace. London is a significant step up in complexity compared to Phoenix or San Francisco.”Baidu only began testing vehicles in London at the end of last month and has said it plans to launch public rides next year.Operating taxis without a driver requires approval via a new process, known as an automated passenger services permit, with the government’s Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency. So far, no vehicles have been approved by the DVSA.TfL was contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsSelf-driving carsAutomotive industryLondonTfLUberTechnology sectorAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Jed York’s trailer park arrest exposed inequality in America | San Francisco 49ers | The Guardian
description: The San Francisco 49ers owner’s arrest in Ohio over the weekend was quickly put behind him. Others are not so lucky
Author: Lee Escobedo
Headline: The San Francisco 49ers owner’s arrest in Ohio over the weekend was quickly put behind him. Others are not so lucky
Content: Jed York was arrested in Ohio on Sunday.Photograph: Getty ImagesJed York was arrested in Ohio on Sunday.Photograph: Getty ImagesSan Francisco 49ersJed York’s trailer park arrest exposed inequality in AmericaLee EscobedoThe San Francisco 49ers owner’s arrest in Ohio over the weekend was quickly put behind him. Others are not so luckyWed 26 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 09.34 EDTShareThe Wheat Hill Mobile Home Community sits off state Route 170, on the edge of East Palestine, Ohio, a town most Americans only learned about because a train derailed there in February 2023 andreleased toxic chemicals into the creek. I grew up in a trailer park like this one, and know the sights. The grid of aluminum boxes in rows. Skirting the color of old teeth, some of it buckled, some patched with a piece of lattice. The window units huff and puff in August, dripping dark condensation on to the gravel.I’m sure there were drugs on my street. I’m sure somebody was selling sex. I never saw it. What I saw were families raising kids in 800 square feet and people the country had already written off, living next to each other and mostly getting along.That’s the kind of place where police arrestedSan Francisco 49ersowner Jed York on the morning of 23 August.From Showtime to Insurance Time: how the LA Lakers became a $12.5bn hedge fund playRead moreAgents with the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force posted an undercover ad on a website known for prostitution. York answered it and agreed to pay a woman just $160 for sex, according to court records. There was no woman waiting for York. Dan Haueter, an East Palestine detective on the taskforce,described the method to the Ohio attorney general’s office in 2024: post an advertisement for sex online, negotiate a price with a prospective customer and arrange to meet in East Palestine. The sting worked because it’s based on real life. York carried the glowing phone he used to set the bargain to the trailer park, where officerstook him into custody.Police booked York on two counts: engaging in prostitution – which was later reduced to disorderly conduct – and possessing criminal tools (in this case, his cellphone).York pleaded no contest to the charges and was sentenced to two days in jail to be served concurrently and fined $1,150.Ohio charges buying sex from an adult as afirst-degree misdemeanorand sends the buyer to an education program.Selling is a third-degree misdemeanor. So the statute is harder on the buyer. But it helps a buyer like York if he can pay a high-powered lawyer to work on his case. York ended uppleading the count down to disorderly conduct.York is not the first NFL owner to find themselves in a situation like this. Florida prosecutors charged New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft in 2019 with soliciting prostitution at the Orchids of Asia spa in Jupiter, part of what police billed as a major human trafficking investigation. His lawyers challenged the hidden-camera warrants and won, andthe state dropped the charges in September 2020. By then, an assistant state attorney had alreadytold the court the investigation turned up no human trafficking. Prosecutors pressed ahead against four Chinese women who worked at Orchids of Asia instead. The women didn’t receive the same breaks. Instead, they receivedcriminal records and about $45,000 in fines.Nationwide, women account fornearly 64% of adult prostitution arrests. Rebecca Pfeffer, assistant professor of criminal justice at the University of Houston – Downtown, studied about 23,000 prostitution cases in Harris County, Texas, and found thatpolice arrested and jailed men less often than women. The women who landed in jail stayed there longer.My mom could support us because nothing on her record stopped her. Put a prostitution conviction on a woman two lots down, and the background check keeps her unemployed and desperate.TheNFL’s personal conduct policyis blunt about how owners should conduct themselves. The policy claims to hold owners to a higher standard than anyone else in the league, with stiffer consequences to match. A league spokesperson says York’s case will bereviewed under that policy. Kraft drew no discipline from the NFL afterFlorida dropped his charges in 2020. Owners write the rules, and theNFL commissioner they hire and pay enforces them. A standard like that lasts exactly as long as the owners want it to.But expecting those owners to hold themselves accountable is wishful thinking. The York situation would be less absurd if the US decriminalized the entire transaction for all parties.The ACLU reviewed the empirical research on how criminalization affects sex workers and foundthat police are a bigger threatto sex workers than clients are. Additionally, researchers from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health surveyed 250 women and found that22% had suffered violence from a client in the previous three months, while 78% had endured at least one abusive encounter with police. The numbers cover different time spans, so they aren’t a clean comp. But they make the same point. The police sent to protect women are also a danger to them. In that same cohort of women,70% had been locked up for more than three days, an average of 15 incarcerations apiece.Kate Shannon, associate professor of medicine at the University of British Columbia, and her colleagues looked at 87 studies and concluded that over the course of a decade,decriminalization could prevent 33% to 46%of projected HIV infections among female sex workers.In 2018,Congress passed a lawto fight trafficking. The law made websites liable for ads that facilitate prostitution, so the sites that sex workers used to advertise and vet clients shut down. ActivistsDanielle Blunt and Ariel Wolf surveyed sex workers, and 99% said the law did not make them feel safer. The Government Accountability Office reported in 2021 thatprosecutors had brought a single case under the law’s criminal provision, and no victim had received restitution.The three approaches to decriminalizing sex work get confused constantly, but they differ significantly.Legalizationkeeps prostitution a crime but makes exceptions for workers who register, get licensed or work in a permitted zone. The Nordic model,which Sweden adopted in 1999 and Canada, France and Northern Ireland later copied, makes selling sex legal and buying it a crime. The theory is that you protect the seller and punish the buyer. In practice, it’s mostly women who still lose.Clients who face arrest demand that sex workers meet them somewhere hidden– and possibly dangerous. Full decriminalization removes criminal penalties on both sides and regulates the work through labor and health law, as the state would handle any other job. Trafficking and assault laws still apply, and they are obviously more effective when a woman can walk into a police station without getting arrested.Most sex workers are just trying to survive, just as my mom was as a cashier.Median household income in East Palestineruns about $49,000. Last year, the York family sold off a small piece of the 49ers, a 6.2% stakefor more than $500m. Meanwhile, York’s penalty for his offense over the weekend cost him $1,150 (and, of course, when you’re rich any additional legal fees are easy enough to cover).A woman in Columbiana county once told an undercover officer that “no girls wanna go” to East Palestinebecause of the prostitution stings in the area.The county later convicted her of promoting prostitution anyway. York was arrested under the same chapter of Ohio law, and he was back on the road by Monday afternoon.Explore more on these topicsSan Francisco 49ersNFLRangersLeeds UnitedUS sportscommentShareReuse this content

title: NFL finally calls time on beleaguered Pro Bowl after years of format changes | NFL | The Guardian
description: NFL will no longer stage an all-star game or skills competitions as league moves to restore exclusivity of Pro Bowl selections
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: NFL will no longer stage an all-star game or skills competitions as league moves to restore exclusivity of Pro Bowl selections
Content: The Pro Bowl ⁠moved away from longtime host Hawaii after the 2016 edition.Photograph: Jerry Driendl/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Pro Bowl ⁠moved away from longtime host Hawaii after the 2016 edition.Photograph: Jerry Driendl/Getty ImagesNFLNFL finally calls time on beleaguered Pro Bowl after years of format changesLeague ends flag football and skills competitionsOnly original 88 selections will earn Pro Bowl statusPlayers to be honored at Super Bowl week in LAAgenciesWed 26 Aug 2026 19.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheNFLis ending the Pro Bowl Games after repeated format changes to its annual all-star event.Beginning ⁠with the 2026 season, 88 Pro Bowlers will be selected but the NFL no longer plans to stage an ⁠AFC-NFC game, a ⁠flag-football matchup ​or an accompanying series of competitions. The players chosen will instead be invited to next year’s Super Bowl site in ⁠Los Angeles for an in-person celebration in February.The biggest change beyond eliminating the event itself involves alternates. Only the original 88 ⁠selections will be named Pro Bowlers and no alternates will be added, ending ​a system that expanded the list ‌when players withdrew because of ‌injuries, Super Bowl commitments or other reasons.Voting remains split with fans, players ‌and coaches accounting for one-third of the selection process.“The Pro Bowl has always been about recognizing the players who distinguish themselves as the very best in the NFL,” NFL executive vice president Peter O’Reilly said Wednesday. “A Pro Bowl selection will return to its original purpose, honoring the best of the ‌best. We want that distinction to carry even greater meaning for the players, their families, their clubs and our fans.“The NFL ​reworked the event through multiple iterations in recent years as interest in the traditional tackle all-star game declined. The AFC-NFC format was temporarily replaced by a fantasy football style draft in 2014 before later returning in 2017. The Pro Bowl ⁠moved away from longtime host Hawaii after the 2016 edition.A tackle ​football game was last ​played in 2022, and ​rebranded as the Pro Bowl Games for a 2023 debut with skills ​competitions and flag ‌football. This past season, ​the Pro ​Bowl Games were moved to the Tuesday before the Super Bowl in San Francisco.League officials said discussions with players helped drive the latest change, citing concerns that repeated selections for replacement had diluted an honor that can have contractual and legacy implications.Explore more on these topicsNFLUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: LIV Golf to lay off majority of staff amid ‘compressed timeline’ for new investors | LIV Golf Series | The Guardian
description: LIV Golf has informed the majority of its workforce on Wednesday four months after Saudi Arabia ended financial support
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: LIV Golf has informed the majority of its workforce on Wednesday four months after Saudi Arabia ended financial support
Content: The purse for the season-ending Indianapolis event was slashed nearly in half.Photograph: Justin Casterline/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe purse for the season-ending Indianapolis event was slashed nearly in half.Photograph: Justin Casterline/Getty ImagesLIV Golf SeriesLIV Golf to lay off majority of staff amid ‘compressed timeline’ for new investorsSaudi Arabia’s PIF have ended financial supportChief executive working on deal but needs players’ buy-inReutersWed 26 Aug 2026 13.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 13.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLIVGolfinformed the majority of its workforce on Wednesday that they will be laid off in the first week of September.The news ⁠comes three days after the 2026 season concluded in Indianapolis and four months after Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund announced it wasending its financial support ⁠of the leagueafter ⁠spending more than $5bn over the past five years.Wednesday’s announcement to staff was not unexpected after the tour notified workers in the US and the UK of ⁠potential layoffs.Sky Sports to extend US Open contract after boost in female audience figuresRead moreThe LIV Golf chief executive, Scott O’Neil, is working to finalise a deal with a new lead investor to fund a re-imagined LIV 2.0. However, the league faces an ⁠uncertain future, with the season-ending team championship in Michigan cancelled, the purse for the Indianapolis event slashed nearly in ​half, multiple vendors still awaiting payments and the ‌potential for bankruptcy looming.“The funding ‌commitment announced by PIF earlier this year will reach its conclusion. As a result, we are scaling back ‌operations as we transition to the next chapter of LIV Golf and work toward making LIV 2.0 a reality,” a LIV Golf spokesperson said in a statement. “This week, we informed many of our colleagues that their employment under LIV 1.0 will end in the first week of September.“We are grateful to our employees for their hard work and dedication in building LIV Golf, and we remain committed to ‌supporting those affected through this transition.“O’Neil acknowledged last week that LIV Golf has “a very compressed timeline” to finalise a deal with a new lead investor, and such an agreement ​will require buy-in from a majority of the current player roster.Ted Goldthorpe, the head of the investment firm BC Partners, is reported to be the new lead investor who has agreed to a term sheet with LIV. O’Neil said there is a deadline to get players on board with the deal, without elaborating on when or what type ⁠of deadline that is.“The whole focus is on transaction, transaction, transaction,” he said. “We’re spending ​all our time thinking about ​how we best land this plane ​and have it landed so we can take off again. All our focus is ​in that direction.”O’Neil, who ‌replaced Greg Norman as ​LIV’s chief executive in ​early 2025, vowed to “do right by” vendors and contractors that have sued the league for missed payments.The vision for LIV 2.0 includes 10 events for the 2027 season, including five in the US and five in international markets. O’Neil reportedly has been seeking an investment between $250m and $350m, with a goal of reaching profitability after three years.Explore more on these topicsLIV Golf SeriesGolfSaudi Arabia and sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sávio savours debut goal as Spurs coast to emphatic Carabao Cup win over Charlton | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: Sávio came off the bench to score Tottenham’s fourth goal in a 5-1 Carabao Cup win against Charlton, with Mikey Moore and Dominic Solanke also on target
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Sávio came off the bench to score Tottenham’s fourth goal in a 5-1 Carabao Cup win against Charlton, with Mikey Moore and Dominic Solanke also on target
Content: Sávio of Tottenham Hotspur celebrates after scoring his team’s fourth goal after coming off the bench.Photograph: Ashley Western/Colorsport/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSávio of Tottenham Hotspur celebrates after scoring his team’s fourth goal after coming off the bench.Photograph: Ashley Western/Colorsport/ShutterstockCarabao CupSávio savours debut goal as Spurs coast to emphatic Carabao Cup win over CharltonDavid Hytnerat the Tottenham Hotspur StadiumWed 26 Aug 2026 16.58 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 19.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA new season at the snazziest modern stadium in England and something extremely welcome for Tottenham. A home win over domestic opposition. There were only four of them last time out; three in the Premier League with the final one – over Everton on the last day – helping them to avoid relegation. Had they lost that, thisCarabao Cupfixture against Charlton would also have been played in the Championship.Spurs needed this tonic for another reason – to begin the clean-up operation after Saturday’sawful 3-0 defeat at Brentford.The season could not have started any worse. With no European football, a decent cup run or runs are imperative and Spurs got themselves up and running in this competition on a night when everything came together perfectly.Thierno Barry fires hat-trick as ruthless Everton sweep Preston asideRead moreFor a good while, it looked as though Mikey Moore was going to be the story.The homegrown 19-year-old broke the deadlock with a vicious drive from the edge of the area; it was the purity of the strike that made it. But then came Sávio.Spurs were 3-0 up with further goals from Dominic Solanke and the substitute, Kevin Danso, when Roberto De Zerbisent on his £75m signingfrom Manchester City for his debut. It was a devastating cameo from Sávio, something to wet the whistle for the bigger challenges ahead. “A perfect day for him,” De Zerbi said.It took Sávio just 11 minutes to score and it was a lovely goal – a glide inside from the right, his markers close and yet nowhere near, his control of the situation total before the fizzing low finish into the near corner. De Zerbi has said he wants end product from Sávio, especially goals and he challenged him afterwards to score 10-12 before the end of the season. This was a good start. There was more.Once again, it was Sávio on the right, cutting back, closer to goal this time. He put one would-be challenger down and skated around another. It was all about the composure. The shot hit his teammate, Ben Davies, and went in.
