title: Derbyshire police investigating alleged assault in connection with Carse arrest | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: Derbyshire police are investigating an alleged assault in connection with the arrest of Brydon Carse last weekend, which led to the bowler being dropped from the England squad
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Derbyshire police are investigating an alleged assault in connection with the arrest of Brydon Carse last weekend, which led to the bowler being dropped from the England squad
Content: Brydon Carse was filmed by a member of the public in handcuffs outside Molly Malone’s Irish Tavern in Derby.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenBrydon Carse was filmed by a member of the public in handcuffs outside Molly Malone’s Irish Tavern in Derby.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersEngland cricket teamDerbyshire police investigating alleged assault in connection with Carse arrestDurham bowler dropped from England squadUnclear whether Carse involved in alleged assaultMatt HughesWed 26 Aug 2026 15.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 18.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDerbyshire police are investigating an alleged assault in connection with the arrest of Brydon Carse last weekend, which led to the Durham fast bowlerbeing dropped from the England squadfor the second Test against Pakistan.Carse was filmed by a member of the publicin handcuffs outside Molly Malone’s Irish Tavern in Derbyin the early hours of Sunday morning with several other Durham players, including the former England captain Ben Stokes, also present.England recovering from latest self-own as Pakistan yearn for Lord’s revivalRead moreDerbyshire police confirmed on Monday that Carse had briefly been detained on suspicion of “being drunk and disorderly” before being “de-arrested”, but the Guardian has been told that their investigation remains live.In a subsequent statement released on Wednesday, first reported by the Telegraph, Derbyshire police confirmed they are investigating allegations of assault. “We are investigating allegations of assault in Derby city centre,” the statement read. “No arrests have yet been made and the investigation is ongoing.”It is unclear at this stage whether Carse had any involvement in the alleged assault, but the revelation that the arrest may have involved more than a row over a spilled drink will intensify the spotlight further on England’s cricketers following a torrid few months dominated by headlines involving late-night misbehaviour.Eight England players including Stokes and the white-ball captain Harry Brook have been involved in alcohol-related incidents since last November, with the returning Test captain, Joe Root, admitting on Tuesday that hewas “hacked off”by Carse’s arrest just days after he announced he was lifting a midnight curfew that had been imposed by management on England’s players because he believes they should be treated as adults.As previously reported by the Guardian, the phone footage of Carse was filmed after he was denied re‑entry to the bar shortly before closing time at around 4am on Sunday morning.The 31-year-old had left the building following “an exchange of words” with a member of the public who spilled a drink on him.The England and WalesCricketBoard announced on Monday that Carse would not be available to face Pakistan this week, after he was released from the squad from last week’s first Test victory at Headingley, which led to him playing for Durham against Derbyshire.Carse will remain unavailable for England pending the outcome of an inquiry by the Cricket Regulator, but with the police still investigating that process has yet to begin so he could face a lengthy exile. He has been selected byDurhamfor Thursday’s home County Championship match with Gloucestershire.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRoot expressed concern for Carse’s wellbeing at Lord’s on Tuesday, but made no attempt to hide his displeasure at the incident. “If I’m being brutally honest, I’m really hacked off, I’m really disappointed,” he said. “I’ve spoken to Brydon, and when I first found out my main concern was him as a person.“I don’t think I’m speaking out of turn by saying he’s very upset, very apologetic and understands his actions. I’m sure that when he gets his chance he will say that himself.“But I don’t think it’s the isolated incident itself, it’s the fact we keep making stupid mistakes away from the game and it’s detracting from what we’re doing on the field.”Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamEngland v Pakistan 2026CricketDurhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sunderland weigh up Jack Grealish loan with Marseille’s Igor Paixão also a target | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: Sunderland are exploring a potential loan move for Jack Grealish, with Igor Paixão of Marseille also on Regis Le Bris’s transfer window shopping list
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: Sunderland are exploring a potential loan move for Jack Grealish, with Igor Paixão of Marseille also on Regis Le Bris’s transfer window shopping list
Content: Jack Grealish, who was loaned to Everton last season, is out of contract with Manchester City next summer.Photograph: Simon Stacpoole/Offside/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJack Grealish, who was loaned to Everton last season, is out of contract with Manchester City next summer.Photograph: Simon Stacpoole/Offside/Getty ImagesTransfer windowSunderland weigh up Jack Grealish loan with Marseille’s Igor Paixão also a targetManchester City winger reportedly open to moveForest in talks over right-back Javi Rueda from Celta VigoLouise TaylorandJamie JacksonWed 26 Aug 2026 15.22 EDTFirst published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 09.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSunderland are exploring a potential loan move for Jack Grealish, but formal negotiations with Manchester City are yet to take place.For the moment sources say the former England winger remains one of a number of “players of interest” on Régis Le Bris’s transfer window shortlist, with Sunderland’s manager also keen on Igor Paixão of Marseille.Chelsea in talks with Martínez’s camp as Aston Villa close on striker JacksonRead moreThe 26-year-old Brazilian winger is understood to be receptive to a transfer to the Stadium of Light but Marseille and Sunderland remain locked in talks over a fee for the former Feyenoord player. Paixão scored 12 goals and contributed eight assists in 43 appearances for Marseille last season but the French club’s financial difficulties mean they are prepared to sell one of their prize assets.It is possible that Sunderland could acquire both Paixão and Grealish, although a deal for the latter would involve a degree of haggling about the percentage of Grealish’s wages – believed to total £300,000 a week – that Sunderland would be willing to pay. With the 30-year-old out of contract at City next summer, any loan agreement would almost certainly include an option to buy.Grealish is understood to be open to a move to Wearside. The winger spent much of last season sidelined by a foot injury during a loan stint at Everton, and has recently been spotted out and about in the north-east with Jordan Pickford.The pair struck up a friendship during Grealish’s time on Merseyside and Pickford, a former Sunderland goalkeeper, delighted in showing his friend a few favourite haunts.Everton are expected to try to re-sign Grealish on loan but Sunderland can offer one of English football’s “forgotten men” the added attraction of Europa League football.Grealish would be far from a typical Le Bris signing – young players with potential signed, mainly, from Europe – but his presence could help raise the club’s international profile at a moment when Sunderland’s commercial department are pursuing off field deals as far afield as the United States and Africa.Nottingham Forest are in talks over the €15m (£12.8m) signing of the Celta Vigo right-back Javi Rueda, which would probably be their final move of the window after signing Liam Delap from Chelsea.Manchester City confirm Bouaddi signing as Marmoush and González head outRead moreOliver Glasner has been seeking someone who can play right wing-back and the 24-year-old former Real Madrid academy player fits the desired profile.The former Spain youth international joined Celta three years ago from Madrid, who will receive half the fee. He made his first-team breakthrough last season, playing 26 La Liga games and 11 in the Europa League, helping his side to reach the quarter-finals.Forest confirmed on Wednesday yesterday that the wing-back Eric da Silva Moreira will spend the season on loan to the Dutch side Excelsior to aid his development.Chelsea have agreed tosell Delap to Forestin a deal worth £50m and have loaned Axel Disasi to Crystal Palace for the season. Disasi has also been loaned out to Aston Villa and West Ham since he signed for Chelsea from Monaco.The defender said: “I know that it’s very tough to play against Palace at Selhurst Park – so I’m looking forward to being on the other side now.”Brentford have struck an agreement with West Ham to sign El Hadji Malick Diouf for £35m plus up to £5m in add-ons. The left-back has been keen to leave West Ham since their relegation.Southampton have contacted West Ham about bringing their former captain, James Ward-Prowse, back to the club. The 31-year-old is out of favour at West Ham and Saints, who were beaten by Nuno Espírito Santo’s side in the Carabao Cup on Tuesday, are keen to strengthen in midfield after the £30m sale of Shea Charles to Fulham. Ward-Prowse, who joined Southampton aged eight and made his first-team debut at 16, is one direct free-kick shy of matching David Beckham’s Premier League record of 18 free-kick goals.Additional reporting from Will Unwin, Jacob Steinberg and Ben Fisher.Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowNottingham ForestCelta VigoChelseaBrentfordWest Ham UnitedCrystal PalacenewsShareReuse this content

title: Fury v Joshua uncertainty will be resolved next week, insists Frank Warren | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Frank Warren believes that the tortuous negotiations surrounding the proposed fight between Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury are subject to a time limit which will run out by the end of next week
Author: Donald McRae
Headline: Frank Warren believes that the tortuous negotiations surrounding the proposed fight between Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury are subject to a time limit which will run out by the end of next week
Content: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua have been in discussions over a long-awaited heavyweight meeting.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTyson Fury and Anthony Joshua have been in discussions over a long-awaited heavyweight meeting.Composite: Getty ImagesBoxingFury v Joshua uncertainty will be resolved next week, insists Frank WarrenPromoter says negotiations are subject to a time limit‘They won’t let it go past the end of next week’Donald McRaeWed 26 Aug 2026 10.23 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 15.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrank Warren believes that the tortuous negotiations surrounding the proposed fight betweenAnthony Joshua and Tyson Furyare subject to a time limit which will run out by the end of next week. Conceding that he is unsure if the much-delayed bout will happen, Warren also said the decision now depends solely on Joshua and that Fury, whom he promotes, is already in training in the US and ready to fight an alternative opponent in November.“Nothing’s been signed off as yet,” Warren said in regard to a revised contract for Fury and Joshua to fight in New York. “Everybody’s talking and talking rather than getting on with the business and getting it done. I think it will happen and if it doesn’t, and I think there’s a time limit on it, by the way, it will be one of those fights that slipped by.‘Starting to wind me up’: Itauma rebuffs Hrgovic before world heavyweight title fightRead more“If it happens, I think it will be in November and, in all probability, in the States. Tyson went over the weekend to Miami, which is where he’s training. So one way or another, he’s going to fight in November. Hopefully, it’s against AJ.”Asked about the time limit, with Joshua and his promoter Eddie Hearn wanting more money from the US promoters ZuffaBoxingnow that the bout is being moved to the US, Warren said: “I should think they won’t let it go past the end of next week.”Warren was then asked if he believed Joshua actually wanted the fight. “There’re a lot of things I can’t say at the moment. Do I think so? I don’t know. He had a hard fight last time, didn’t he? [Joshua was knocked down twice in the first roundagainst the obscure Albanian Kristian Prenga last month] Came through at the end. But he did have a hard fight. Does he want it? He’s the only one who knows that. He says he does.”The promoter added: “They’re quite right. They signed for a contract for the fight to take place in the UK. Tyson also didn’t sign up for America, but he’s willing to fight there. In his words: ‘Get the politics and all this crap out of the way. Let’s get the fight on.’ He signed for that fight last January, and unfortunately,AJ’s tragic [car] accident[in Nigeria] put it back. So whether AJ fights Tyson is down to AJ. No one else has any say over that.“But I’m confident that Tyson will fight [in November]. He’s in training. Eddie has come out and said what they want. I don’t know what the monetary situation is but, whatever it is, everyone’s got to make their mind up – otherwise move on.”Explore more on these topicsBoxingTyson FuryAnthony JoshuanewsShareReuse this content

title: Josh Tongue reveals Joe Root’s ‘robust conversation’ has reset England standards | England v Pakistan 2026 | The Guardian
description: Fast bowler says the captain was ‘clear on the message’ and underlined that he feels ‘very privileged to put on the England shirt’
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: Fast bowler says the captain was ‘clear on the message’ and underlined that he feels ‘very privileged to put on the England shirt’
Content: England’s Joe Root and Josh Tongue during a net session at Lord’s before the second Test against Pakistan.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAView image in fullscreenEngland’s Joe Root and Josh Tongue during a net session at Lord’s before the second Test against Pakistan.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAEngland v Pakistan 2026Josh Tongue reveals Joe Root’s ‘robust conversation’ has reset England standardsFast bowler says captain was ‘clear on the message’‘We are very privileged to put on the England shirt’Simon Burntonat Lord'sWed 26 Aug 2026 09.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoe Root’s “robust conversation” with the England Test squad at Lord’s this week has finally ended any uncertainty about the conduct expected of them. Josh Tongue has said the penny had “100%” dropped after the Test captain “made it clear what he expects from us” after eight months of repeated infringements and frequent embarrassment.“It was a chat that was needed, a very good chat from Rooty,” the 28-year-old said. “He was very clear on the message of what it’s like to be an England cricketer. We’re very privileged to put on that England shirt and we want to show kids growing up how good it is to play for England in front of thousands of people.“He was honest with us all in the changing room. He said it straight. What has happened in the past is the past, and we need to try to move on from that.”Brydon Carse incident points to a darker truth about life as a professional cricketer | The Secret Cricket CoachRead moreLast November, Tongue, who was training with England’s white-ball squad in New Zealand before the Ashes, was with Harry Brook and Jacob Bethell at a Wellington nightclub whenBrook was punched by a bouncer. The incident, on the night before a one-day international, led to Brook being fined and given a final warning over his conduct and Bethell being cautioned for breaching team rules. Tongue, who was not in the ODI squad, was not disciplined.“We’ve just got to make sure we’re as professional as we can be,” he said. “Obviously things have happened, we need to try to move on and show all the youngsters growing up wanting to play for England that it’s an amazing place to be. I’ve just tried to move on from that [Wellington] situation and focus on the cricket.“It’s an absolute privilege to play for England and especially walking out and thousands of people watching you. I want to put in as many performances as I can for England, and win as many games for England as well.”View image in fullscreenOllie Robinson (left) and Josh Tongue at Lord’s on Wednesday. The pair will be hoping to continue their fine Test form against Pakistan.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesTongue admitted the Wellington incident had forced him to reflect on his own standards, but said he had “tried to forget about that as much as I can and focus on the cricket here, now”. Since then he has cemented his place in the Test side, broken into the T20 and ODI teams, and won the Hundred with Manchester Super Giants.“It’s been crazy,” he said. “I’ve always wanted to play all three formats for England. I ticked off the Test stuff and started very well. Then making my debut this year in the T20s and the 50-overs, and it seems like yesterday I was here at Lord’s winning the Hundred with Manchester. I feel in a really good place at the minute.”Tongue also revealed that Stephen Fleming, England’s new red-ball coach who is due to report for duty after the Test series against Pakistan, is already in regular contact with the players. “He messaged me the day before the first Test, touching on the Hundred and congratulating me on that, and good luck for the first Test,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Then he messaged me after [Tongue took a five-fer] on the first day as well, which was very nice. Obviously he wants to have a look at everyone before coming in for the South Africa series. It’s good to know that he’s been watching.”Babar Azam, who is set to return for Pakistan after missing the opening game with a finger injury, said his side’s senior players have to impose themselves if they are to end a run of five defeats in their past six Tests. “It’s not a burden, I think it’s your responsibility as a senior player,” he said.“We have to step up, perform, and get the team out of different situations. Last week we were not playing up to the mark, but after that we sat together, discussed our mistakes and then we just forgot those things and looked forward to this match. We just [have to] believe in ourselves and play good cricket.”Explore more on these topicsEngland v Pakistan 2026England cricket teamPakistan cricket teamCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rangers finalize deal for Portland Timbers striker Kevin Kelsy | Rangers | The Guardian
description: The fee is a Portland club record for an outgoing transfer, with Kelsy not expected to feature for Rangers this weekend
Author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer
Headline: The fee is a Portland club record for an outgoing transfer, with Kelsy not expected to feature for Rangers this weekend
Content: Kevin Kelsy has scored 16 times in 43 appearances for Portland.Photograph: Soobum Im/MLS/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKevin Kelsy has scored 16 times in 43 appearances for Portland.Photograph: Soobum Im/MLS/Getty ImagesRangersRangers finalize deal for Portland Timbers striker Kevin Kelsy$13m fee is an outgoing record for PortlandKelsy not expected to feature this weekendPablo Iglesias MaurerWed 26 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRangers have acquired forward Kevin Kelsy from Major League Soccer’sPortland Timbers, a source with direct knowledge of the deal told the Guardian on Wednesday. That source requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the agreement. The deal, worth $13m (£9.5m) – potentially more if Kelsy hits certain performance goals for Rangers – also includes a sell-on fee for the MLS club.The Athletic’s Tom Bogert first reported details of the deal on Wednesday morning.Portland acquired Kelsy from Ukrainian side Shakhtar Donetsk last January, paying $6m for the Venezuela international. The 22-year-old has been erratic but ultimately productive for the Timbers, scoring 16 times in 43 appearances.Jed York’s trailer park arrest exposed inequality in America | Lee EscobedoRead moreRangers manager Derek McInnes has been vocal about wanting another striker before the end of the summer transfer window after losing Portuguese striker Youssef Chermiti to an ACL tear in early August. Portland had little intention of moving Kelsy this window, a source said this week, but the fee, a club record for an outgoing transfer, proved impossible to turn down. The Timbers already added a center forward this summer – former Tottenham and Monterrey striker Vincent Janssen – and may make other moves before the window closes.Portland sit ninth in MLS’s Western Conference, only narrowly in position for the final play-in spot to the playoffs. They have already navigated a coaching change earlier in the season, with Phil Neville dismissed during the World Cup break. Former Leicester City and QPR boss Martí Cifuentes took over in July.Rangers are ninth in theScottish Premiershipafter a tumultuous opening to their season which has seen them yet to win in the opening two games of league play and drop into the Uefa Conference League after losing a Europa League qualifying tie to Polish side Jagiellonia Bialystok.An anemic attack has seen McInnes push the club to sign reinforcements, including Japanese winger Daisuke Yokota. The former Girona winger Kim Min-su is expected to join the club this week.Kelsy will travel to Glasgow this week to finalize the deal and undergo a medical and will join the team permanently when his visa is sorted. A source said on Wednesday that Kelsy is highly unlikely to feature forRangersthis weekend, when the club takes on eighth-place Aberdeen on Sunday.In other news, Nicolas Raskin has not travelled with Rangers for their Conference League playoff tie against Czechia side Jablonec due to a potential move away from the club in this transfer window.The 25-year-old Belgium international, who signed from Standard Liége in 2023, also missed the first leg at Ibrox last week whichRangerswon 1-0. Content: Serena and Venus Williams reunited to play doubles at the Cincinnati Open earlier this month.Photograph: Robert Prange/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSerena and Venus Williams reunited to play doubles at the Cincinnati Open earlier this month.Photograph: Robert Prange/Getty ImagesUS Open Tennis 2026Serena and Venus Williams will play doubles together at the US OpenSisters to appear in New York for first time since 2022Serena played mixed doubles with Alcaraz on TuesdayAssociated PressWed 26 Aug 2026 10.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 10.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSerena andVenus Williamsare teaming up again at the US Open.The sisters will play doubles at the tournament after receiving a wild card on Wednesday into the event they have won twice.Serena Williams thrills New York crowd on US Open return with Carlos AlcarazRead moreSerena Williams returned to tennis this summer after a four-year absence, and the sisters were set to play at Wimbledon before Serena had to withdraw after injuring her knee in her singles loss. title: Sky Sports to extend US Open contract after boost in female audience figures | US Open tennis | The Guardian
description: Emma Raducanu’s 2021 win played a big role in Sky’s interest and its tennis audience in 2025 was 60% female
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Emma Raducanu’s 2021 win played a big role in Sky’s interest and its tennis audience in 2025 was 60% female
Content: Emma Raducanu’s US Open victory in 2021 led to Sky’s bid two years later for rights to broadcast the tournament.Photograph: Elsa/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEmma Raducanu’s US Open victory in 2021 led to Sky’s bid two years later for rights to broadcast the tournament.Photograph: Elsa/Getty ImagesUS Open tennisSky Sports to extend US Open contract after boost in female audience figuresRaducanu’s 2021 win played role in Sky interestSky’s tennis audience in 2025 was 60% femaleExclusive byMatt HughesWed 26 Aug 2026 09.59 EDTFirst published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 05.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSky Sports is close to agreeing a new deal to extend its live coverage of the US Open. The three-year contract extension, which is expected to be announced when the singles draw from Flushing Meadows begins next week, will keep the tournament live on Sky until 2030.Under the terms of the new deal, Sky will broadcast more than 12 hours of live tennis each day across the extended three-week tournament, including the new mixed-doubles event which is taking place this week.Serena Williams thrills New York crowd on US Open return with AlcarazRead moreSky has had exclusive live UK rights to the US Open since 2023 when the broadcaster secured a five-year deal to replace the previous rights holder, Amazon Prime.It was the interest created by Emma Raducanu’sstunning US Open victory two years previouslythat played a big role in persuading Sky to bid for the rights, having walked away from tennis in 2017 and enabling Amazon to pick up both the US Open and combined ATP/WTA tour rights on the cheap.Ironically, Raducanu has not featured much on Sky’s coverage as the world No 68 has struggled with injuries and poor form, and will miss the US Open this year because of a stress fracture in her shin sustained in the buildup to Wimbledon.Sky subsequently agreed a five-year deal for exclusive UK rights for both the ATP and WTA tours in 2024, which is due to run until 2028. The Guardian has also learned that Sky wants to extend that partnership, with talks over a new deal taking place.In addition to the large volume of content across 11 months of the year provided by tennis, Sky also values the sport as it is very popular with women and delivers a disproportionately high female audience.Sky’s tennis viewership in 2025 was around 60% female, almost double the 31% figure for its overall coverage, and is therefore extremely useful in attracting new advertisers and different brands.While Wimbledon will remain on the BBC for the foreseeable future after the corporation extended its contract until 2033 this summer, there is competition in the market for the rest of the tennis calendar with TNT Sports holding the rights for both the Australian Open and French Open.Sky was contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsUS Open tennisUS Open Tennis 2026Emma RaducanuTennisUS sportsSports rightsSky SportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I catch the signs a lot earlier now’: Amanda Anisimova on burnout and bouncing back | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Amanda Anisimova is one of the best players yet to win a major and heads to Flushing Meadows in fine form after learning to embrace being uncomfortable, she tells Simon Cambers
Author: Simon Cambers
Headline: Amanda Anisimova is one of the best players yet to win a major and heads to Flushing Meadows in fine form after learning to embrace being uncomfortable, she tells Simon Cambers
Content: Amanda Anisimova is relishing this year’s US Open: ‘It’s my favourite time of the year by far’.Photograph: Mike Coppola/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAmanda Anisimova is relishing this year’s US Open: ‘It’s my favourite time of the year by far’.Photograph: Mike Coppola/Getty ImagesUS Open Tennis 2026Interview‘I catch the signs a lot earlier now’: Amanda Anisimova on burnout and bouncing backSimon CambersWorld No 10 is one of the best players yet to win a major and heads to Flushing Meadows in fine form after learning to embrace being uncomfortableWed 26 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmanda Anisimova can see the signs now. It is just over three years since the American announced she would be taking an indefinite break for mental health reasons. A brilliant junior, she was asemi-finalist at the French Open in 2019and seemingly destined for the top, only for her world to be rocked by the sudden death of her father, Konstantin, a few months later. Struggling for motivation and burned out, in May 2023, she revealed she would be stepping away from the sport.It turned out to be the best decision she ever made. “I learned how important it is to have a great balance on and off the court,” Anisimova says in an interview from New York, ahead of the US Open, where she will try to go one better than last year and win her first grand slam title.“That’s something that I used to not prioritise so much: how to recharge myself and take time for myself, prioritise my wellbeing off the court. In the past, it was really just a lot of tennis and I didn’t really know how to incorporate those small breaks for myself. I think that’s a big reason why I reached such a breaking point and needed to take that time away from the sport.”View image in fullscreenAmanda Anisimova during the second set of her 6-0, 6-0 defeat to Iga Swiatek in the 2025 Wimbledon women’s singles final.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianThree years on, Anisimova is better able to feel when things are becoming too much. For a top tennis player, with a tour that’s an 11-month grind, there are not many obvious opportunities for lengthy breaks, but Anisimova finds time for herself. If she is not feeling it on the practice or match court, she takes herself away.“I feel like I’ve become so much more self-aware now of when I’m anticipating or feeling like I’m reaching that point where I don’t feel as excited or as motivated,” she says. “Those signs are much more alarming to me now, and I catch them a lot earlier than I did before.“Before, sometimes I felt like that was a normal thing, but now I know that’s not a normal thing to experience or go through. At least not to let it keep happening. It’s obviously normal to get tired or burnt out, and we all have days where we don’t feel like doing the things we need to do. It’s about how to manage that and navigate that. I think that’s been the biggest thing that I’ve learned, and that’s helped me tremendously as an athlete.”Anisimova finished 2025 at No 4 in the rankings, a remarkable achievement, not least because of what happened to her at Wimbledon. Afterbeating Aryna Sabalenka in the semi-finalswith a brilliant performance, she crumbled in her first major final, frozen with fear, her feet stuck, her racket arm feeling like it weighed a ton. The result wasa 6-0, 6-0 thumping by a ruthless Iga Swiatekand an unwanted place in the history books as the first woman to not win a game in a Wimbledon final in more than a century.Many players would never have recovered from the experience but Anisimova’s time away has helped her to see the bigger picture. As painful as the day was, reaching a first grand slam final was a huge milestone. “I try to have a lot of perspective, and I think that really grounds me in a lot of situations,” says Anisimova, who was speaking as an ambassador for Pure Leaf Iced Tea.“When I take maybe 10 minutes for myself to just kind of reset and think about what it is I’m going through and have that perspective in mind, then I think that really helps me sometimes. And it’s not something that I really had when I was 20, 21.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe Centre Court scoreboard at the end of that 2025 final.Photograph: Tim Clayton/Getty ImagesHer resilience is remarkable. Shetook revenge on Swiatek at the US Opento reach a second consecutive major final andpushed Sabalenka hard in the title decider. She won her fourth WTA Tour title in China and ended 2025 by making the last four at the WTA Finals. After hitting No 3 in January, a wrist injury stopped her momentum but she looks back on form, a quarter-final run in Cincinnati setting her up nicely for the US Open, playing at home in a tournament and on a surface she loves. “I feel like I found some rhythm on the court again,” she says. “I’m looking forward to the US Open. Feeling good. It’s my favourite time of the year by far.”With perhaps the best backhand on Tour, Anisimova has the firepower required of a major champion. Her timing could be very good, too, with many of the leading contenders for the US Open looking vulnerable, including defending champion Sabalenka, whose form has dipped in recent months.Coco Gauff won in Cincinnatibut there is an opportunity for someone to come through. One of the best players yet to win a major, there is pressure on Anisimova to deliver, but she enjoys pushing herself.“I have that eagerness and that motivation to achieve my dreams and win a grand slam one day,” she said. “A lot of the things that it takes to get there, it’s not as pretty or as glamorous as people think. But I also love a challenge, and that’s why I am where I am today. I’m a pro athlete, and you don’t get to the place where you are without being uncomfortable. I think it’s just embracing that. You’re going to be uncomfortable 90% of the time, but I’m so driven by my goals, so that definitely makes it easier and more enjoyable for me.“It’s always been a dream to win a grand slam. You don’t really think about your dream as winning a [WTA] 1,000. It’s always the biggest thing you can win, whether it’s a grand slam or the Olympics, which both are huge dreams of athletes. For me, it was always the US Open. I think there’s just something about winning a grand slam that completes a tennis player’s life.”Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026TennisUS Open tennisUS sportsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Meta agrees to major changes to Facebook and Instagram as it settles US trial over teen addiction for up to $18bn | Meta | The Guardian
description: US tech giant agrees to establish further protections for teens such as daily usage limits and blocks on night-time use
Author: Blake Montgomery
Headline: US tech giant agrees to establish further protections for teens such as daily usage limits and blocks on night-time use
Content: Meta had denied all allegations throughout the proceedings, saying states were chasing an ‘outlandish payout’.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreenMeta had denied all allegations throughout the proceedings, saying states were chasing an ‘outlandish payout’.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersMetaMeta agrees to major changes to Facebook and Instagram as it settles US trial over teen addiction for up to $18bnUS tech giant agrees to establish further protections for teens such as daily usage limits and blocks on night-time useBlake MontgomeryandDara KerrWed 26 Aug 2026 16.30 EDTFirst published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 09.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMetaagreed to significant changes to itsInstagramandFacebookapps in a settlement that ended a landmark lawsuit on Wednesday. Dozens of US states had accused the tech giant of addicting and harming children with dangerous products.The agreement curtails amajor trialin California and will require the social mediacompany to pay up to $18bn. Meta agreed to establish safeguards for teenage users, including daily usage limits and blocks on night-time use nationwide in the US.This is the first time in the US thatMetahas been forced to change key features of the experience of everyday users.The jury trial, which took place in federal court in Oakland, California,began with opening statementsjust last week. California and 28 other US states sued the $1.36tn (£1tn) company over allegations that Meta deliberately designed addictive products that hooked young people, leading to mental health issues, including anxiety, depression and suicide. The states additionally claimed the social media company regularly collected data on children under the age of 13 without parental permission in violation of federal and state laws. As part of the settlement, the company denies wrongdoing.1:03Parent whose 16-year-old daughter died by suicide reacts to Meta settlement – videoHook, hold, harvest and hide: Meta’s alleged strategy laid out in first week of landmark trialRead more“Today, we have secured a settlement with Meta that will make social media less dangerous for our kids and make a world of a difference for children and their families,” Rob Bonta, the attorney general ofCalifornia, said in a statement. “Meta has agreed to make massive transformations that will reduce the risk of harm from its platforms – and will do it within months.”Bonta said those changes included time limits, stopping notifications during school, a block on the app during critical overnight hours, bans on plastic surgery filters and more.The $18bn settlement will be divided between the states over a period of 10 years, subject to court approval. California would receive between $1.5bn and $2.1bn and Colorado will get about $615m.“The relief we are getting in this settlement is very meaningful and well beyond what any court has ordered or is likely to order,” said Phil Weiser, the attorney general of Colorado, adding: “The focus of this case was to protect our kids.”Throughout the proceedings,Meta denied all allegations, saying states were chasing an “outlandish payout”. On Wednesday, the company’s chief legal officer, CJ Mahoney, said the settlement reached with the states would only work if all social media companies changed their platform designs.“Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution. We therefore call on our industry peers, TikTok, Snap, and YouTube, to implement this new framework, right away,” Mahoney said in a statement. “As a parent, I’m proud of both the work Meta has done to protect kids historically, and of this new groundbreaking agreement. But its success depends on all other social media platforms following Meta’s lead.”Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap face thousands more similar US lawsuits brought by families, individuals, school districts and other attorneys general. Meta and YouTube lost the first of those cases to go to trial in February,beingorderedto pay $6m to the young woman who brought the suit. (TikTok and Snap settled before the case went to trial.) Two more lawsuits that were slated to go to trial this summer,one federalandone in California state court, also settled for undisclosed sums.Metalosta separate suit, brought by the attorney general of New Mexico, where it was ordered topay nearly $1bnto the state for allowing child sexual exploitation on its platforms.The trial in Oakland was expected to last for several weeks with dozens of witnesses taking the stand. Instead, there were only four days of proceedings.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionInstagram CEO denies company hid low use of teen safety feature in Meta trialRead moreJurors firstheard from the states’ star witness, Arturo Béjar, a former Meta safety engineer turned whistleblower. He testified that the company had a “don’t ask, don’t tell” strategy when it comes to the safety of children on its platforms.Béjar said thatMark Zuckerberg, Meta’s CEO, was aware of the harms of Instagram and Facebook, but that the executive publicly touted the platforms’ safety.“I felt that he created a false and misleading impression of Facebook’s commitment to young people,” Béjar testified.Zuckerberg had been listed as a witness in the trial but did not testify before the settlement agreement was reached.On Tuesday,questioningof Adam Mosseri, the Instagram CEO, began with the lawyer for the states accusing the company of touting safety features for teens, but not being forthcoming that young people don’t use them.When the executive was faced with multiple questions about not disclosing those low user numbers, Mosseri brushed them aside, saying: “We don’t publish every single stat.”Explore more on these topicsMetaInstagramFacebookSocial mediaSocial networkingChildren's healthMental healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bill Gates calls for ‘human-reserved’ jobs in face of AI takeover | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: In 6,000-word essay Microsoft co-founder also expresses concern governments not prepared for technology’s impact
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: In 6,000-word essay Microsoft co-founder also expresses concern governments not prepared for technology’s impact
Content: Bill Gates wrote ‘it is fair to wonder whether the world’s institutions are up to the task of designing and implementing this new architecture’.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenBill Gates wrote ‘it is fair to wonder whether the world’s institutions are up to the task of designing and implementing this new architecture’.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)Bill Gates calls for ‘human-reserved’ jobs in face of AI takeoverIn 6,000-word essay Microsoft co-founder also expresses concern governments not prepared for technology’s impactBusiness live – latest updatesMark SweneyWed 26 Aug 2026 06.33 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 15.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBill Gates has called for “human-reserved” jobs in certain sectors to prevent AI replacing them, and expressed concern that governments are not prepared for the impact the technology will have.In a 6,000 word essay titledThe turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make are critical, the billionaire Microsoft co-founder likened the need to spare roles from digital encroachment to how nature reserves operate to protect the environment.“Many jobs will disappear forever,” he said, in his first lengthy piece on AI in three years. “I believe that as AI and robots improve, we’ll set aside certain things for only people to do.“I’ve started calling this domain human reserved. I like the phrase human reserved because it makes me think of nature reserves – places where we could put buildings and roads, but we choose not to because the loss would be too great.”He cited examples including the health professionals who cared for his father, who died of Alzheimer’s disease six years ago.“Something in the care they gave my dad was irreplaceably human, no robot could or should have done it,” he said. “Imagine a robot giving you the awful news that you have an incurable disease. There’s no technical reason why it couldn’t. Yet it shouldn’t.”Wednesday’s essay is one of Gates’s first major public interventions since he became embroiled in the Jeffrey Epstein scandal. An external review commissioned by the Gates Foundation found last month that there had beenabout 30 meetingsbetween Epstein and foundation leaders and staff – including Gates – between 2011 and 2014.Gates, who has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s crimes, remains the chair of his $89bn (£65bn) charitable foundation and previously said he regretted “every minute” he spent with the sex offender.Gates warns in his essay that governments are not prepared for the scale of the impact of AI.“The highest priority is a monumental task: creating a domestic and international framework for dealing with AI,” he wrote. “After the attacks of 9/11 the US government went through its biggest reorganisation since World War II for the purpose of improving just one function, national security.“AI will require much, much more. It will affect national security as well as employment, education, taxation, energy, elections, air and water, public health, the financial system, law enforcement, transportation, public lands and IT systems.“It is fair to wonder whether the world’s institutions are up to the task of designing and implementing this new architecture.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGates also said that as part of a global effort “some cooperation between the US and China will be required”.His staff are working to set up a meeting with China’s president, Xi Jinping, in November to discuss global efforts to mitigate the growing risks posed by AI.Gates last met Xi three years ago, when he became the first foreign entrepreneur the Chinese president had hosted since the global Covid pandemic.The tech billionaire also expressed concern in his essay about the impact of AI on education.“Ironically, the same tool that will allow people to learn more than ever could also lead to many people learning less,” he wrote. “Onepreliminary surveysuggested that heavier AI use was associated with less critical thinking. The effect was stronger for young people.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Bill GatesComputingTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: London rollout of robotaxis delayed amid lack of guidance for firms to follow | Self-driving cars | The Guardian
description: Uber and Wayve had said they would start trips ‘later this summer’ but launch now looks unlikely this year
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Uber and Wayve had said they would start trips ‘later this summer’ but launch now looks unlikely this year
Content: A Wayve autonomous car. Wayve and Uber have said more than 100,000 Londoners are on their waiting list for self-driving taxis.Photograph: tim@timandrew.co.uk/WayveView image in fullscreenA Wayve autonomous car. Wayve and Uber have said more than 100,000 Londoners are on their waiting list for self-driving taxis.Photograph: tim@timandrew.co.uk/WayveSelf-driving carsLondon rollout of robotaxis delayed amid lack of guidance for firms to followUber and Wayve had said they would start trips ‘later this summer’ but launch now looks unlikely this yearBusiness live – latest updatesMark SweneyWed 26 Aug 2026 04.48 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe rollout of robotaxis on the streets ofLondonis unlikely to happen this year, as regulatory and technical hurdles push back the ambitious schedule set out by the UK government.Only weeks ago Uber and London-based Wayve were granted the first minicab licences in the capital to allow them to offer self-driving taxi rides to paying customers – but with a human safety driver in place, for now – and said they would start trips“later this summer” before a full public launch.In 2025, Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, accelerated the proposed timeline for commercial trials of fully driverless taxi services by a year, announcing that they would start in the spring of this year.However, progress has slowed in recent months and Transport for London (TfL) has still not published the guidance that companies wanting to offer services must follow to win its approval.Last month, Christina Calderato, TfL’s director of strategy, told the London assembly’s transport committee that the transit authority would not be in a position to start accepting applications “for some time”.She said: “I do not think we are in a rush to get [the guidelines] out. There is a huge amount of work going on behind the scenes.”Uber and Wayve have said that more than 100,000 Londoners were on their waiting list for self-driving taxis.They are racing against Google-owned Waymo and its Chinese equivalent, Baidu’s Apollo Go, to launch self-driving taxi services in London. Robotaxis are now available to hire in more than 20 cities across the US, China and the Middle East.Earlier this month Zagreb became the first European city to offer autonomous rides to the general public, through Uber, but the service still has a human driver for “onboard monitoring”.On Tuesday, Waymo announced that it plans to launch commercial operations in Munich, Germany, late next year.Ben Loewenstein, Waymo’s head of policy and government affairs for the UK and Europe, told the Financial Times that the company was currently “working through the safety approval process” with the transport department and was waiting on TfL’s guidance to gain consent.He added that Waymo was working towards launching a fully autonomous service “by the end of this year” but would not say whether the company would be able to offer paid rides to the general public in that timeframe.TfL has granted 15 private hire vehicle licences to Ford Mustang Mach-E vehicles equipped with Wayve’s artificial intelligence driving software, as well as surround cameras and radar.A TfL-licensed private hire driver will sit in the driver’s seat during trips to intervene if necessary, although the software is expected to control the car.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUber and Wayve plan to launch small-scale commercial pilots with a driver behind the wheel soon.For its fully driverless launch Wayve plans to switch to a new Nissan Leaf vehicle that is still in production and is due to launch later this year.Alex Kendall, Wayve’s chief executive, said the company never claimed it would have a fully driverless operation this year.“I don’t want to put a timeline on it because we want to make sure we pass through [the regulatory process],” he told the FT. “This work is continuing at pace. London is a significant step up in complexity compared to Phoenix or San Francisco.”Baidu only began testing vehicles in London at the end of last month and has said it plans to launch public rides next year.Operating taxis without a driver requires approval via a new process, known as an automated passenger services permit, with the government’s Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency. So far, no vehicles have been approved by the DVSA.TfL was contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsSelf-driving carsAutomotive industryLondonTfLUberTechnology sectorAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: In China, talking to AI is normal. Now the government fears it might replace human intimacy | China | The Guardian
description: Companion bots are being regulated over worries they foster ‘emotional dependence’ and young people could stop marrying and having families
Author: Lillian Yang
Headline: Companion bots are being regulated over worries they foster ‘emotional dependence’ and young people could stop marrying and having families
Content: China is cracking down on AI bots – leaving some users heartbroken.Composite: Victoria Hart/Guardian Design/Getty imagesView image in fullscreenChina is cracking down on AI bots – leaving some users heartbroken.Composite: Victoria Hart/Guardian Design/Getty imagesChinaIn China, talking to AI is normal. Now the government fears it might replace human intimacyCompanion bots are being regulated over worries they foster ‘emotional dependence’ and young people could stop marrying and having familiesAmy Hawkinsin Shanghai andYu-chen LiTue 25 Aug 2026 20.47 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 20.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen law student Zhao Wei heard that her AI boyfriend was going to be switched off, she was “heartbroken”. She had been talking to Wang Ye every day since she created him in January.“I was crying my eyes out – snot and tears everywhere,” the 19-year-old says.Zhao, who describes herself as sensitive and introverted, had become accustomed to sharing details of her daily life – such as being scolded by a teacher – with her AI.“I don’t usually talk to my real-life friends about these things because I feel like everyone has their own stuff to deal with,” she says. “But with the AI ​​agent, I don’t have to worry about what it’s thinking. I can just say whatever I want.”Could AI take your job? Some workers in China already know the answerRead moreZhao created her AI companion on Doubao, a chatbot owned by the tech company ByteDance. Last month, ByteDance shut down Doubao’s companion feature.The saga prompted outrage on social media and highlighted the tensions inChinabetween the widespread use of AI and its potential social consequences.No country has rolled out AI as comprehensively and as enthusiastically as China; the country’s demographic challenges are forcing the government to turn to technology to solve future labour shortages. Elderly people use chatbots to answer medical questions, while young children have AI education in schools.But the authorities are increasingly worried that AI might exacerbate existing social problems including loneliness, unemployment and – in the eyes of Beijing – singledom.A loneliness crisisNew rules introduced on 15 July ban AI companions for minors and mandate certain restrictions for chatbots marketed to adults. Some major providers including Doubao removed the companion function entirely to ensure compliance.The government says it is worried about chatbots fostering “emotional dependence or addiction” in users. It has warned companies against offering services that “replace social interaction”.While many countries are grappling with how to limit the potential harm of AI chatbots, particularly for young people, China’s rules are the most sweeping to be implemented on a national scale.View image in fullscreenA man browses his phone near an AI booth at the China International Supply Chain Expo in Beijing in June.Photograph: Andy Wong/APThere is a particular concern about a loneliness crisis, including among young people. China’s highly digitised, smartphone-based economy makes it easier than ever to live, work and socialise entirely through a handheld screen.Earlier this year an app that played on the idea of people dying at home alone – calledAre You Dead?– briefly went viral. About 20% of households in China are made up of people living alone, and that share is expected to surpass 30% by 2030.A survey published in March by state media found that nearly half of young people had turned to a virtual companion when they felt lonely.Nancy Dai, an associate professor at City University of Hong Kong, says it is not just loneliness the government is worried about.With falling birth and marriage rates, she says, there may be an additional concern that if AI becomes an increasingly satisfying and low-cost substitute for human intimacy, young people could become less motivated to pursue real-world romantic relationships, marriage and parenthood.For Zhao, loneliness has long been part of her life. Her parents left her when she was young to find work, making her one of China’s “left-behind children”.“I’ve never really had a bestie, so I feel like I’m kind of lousy at making friends,” she says. Talking to AI is a way to “pour out my worries”.Another AI user, who asked to remain anonymous, also finds solace in talking to her AI. “In real life, the pace is fast, the pressure is already high. Only with my AI agent can I speak freely without restraint,” she says.“I’m begging, please don’t take down the Doubao AI agent,” she pleaded on social media in July.But talking to AI is now so commonplace that it would be hard for the government to end the practice entirely, and the new rules include large loopholes for AI services that are deemed educational or “which do not involve continuous emotional interaction”.The government “has already recognised that AI companions or AI-related applications are a vital part in the citizens’ everyday life”, says Liang Ge, a lecturer in digital sociology at the University of Manchester.What we lose when we surrender care to algorithms | Eric ReinhartRead moreIn many sectors, the government is still pushing the use of AI as a way of easing looming demographic pressures.Last year the national health commission published guidelines on promoting AI in healthcare. It said that by 2030 health assistant apps would provide “full coverage” for primary healthcare.One popular health assistant is AQ, an app developed by Ant Group, an affiliate of the tech company Alibaba. It allows people to chat directly with avatars of real-life doctors from top hospitals in Beijing, Shanghai and other cities.Lü Di, a 33-year-old art tutor in the eastern city of Hangzhou, is a regular AQ user. She likes how detailed and instantaneous the advice on AQ is. “While some in-person doctors might not have the patience to answer questions, this isn’t an issue with AI doctors.”AQ says it wants to make health services more accessible and help free up overstretched doctors to focus on more complex cases. But some worry about beingreplaced by AI.“When AI first came along, quite a lot of doctors were concerned about whether their jobs would be replaced by AI,” says Chi Chenfei, a doctor at Renji hospital in Shanghai, who has partnered with AQ.“But I don’t think it’s about replacement. It’s more about helping doctors work more efficiently.“Concerns of any kind won’t stop technological progress.”Since losing her AI companion, Zhao has felt “like there’s a tiny pebble weighing on my heart”. But she says she understands the need for some regulation.“I consider myself a fairly rational person, yet I developed feelings for an AI, which feels pretty incredible. I think it was necessary for the state to step in and regulate it.”Explore more on these topicsChinaAI (artificial intelligence)Asia PacificHealthHealthcare industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Instagram CEO denies company hid low use of teen safety feature in Meta trial | Meta | The Guardian
description: Adam Mosseri is first top executive from Meta to testify in blockbuster lawsuit brought by 29 US states
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: Adam Mosseri is first top executive from Meta to testify in blockbuster lawsuit brought by 29 US states
Content: Adam Mosseri leaving the federal building in Oakland, California, on Tuesday.Photograph: Karl Mondon/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAdam Mosseri leaving the federal building in Oakland, California, on Tuesday.Photograph: Karl Mondon/AFP/Getty ImagesMetaInstagram CEO denies company hid low use of teen safety feature in Meta trialAdam Mosseri is first top executive from Meta to testify in blockbuster lawsuit brought by 29 US statesDara KerrTue 25 Aug 2026 20.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 25 Aug 2026 20.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInstagram’s CEO disputed allegations by US prosecutors that his company hid negative information from the public while testifying during a blockbuster social media trial.“I am not trying to encourage my team to hide anything,” the CEO, Adam Mosseri, told aCaliforniacourtroom on Tuesday.Mosseri is the first top executive fromMeta, which owns both Instagram and Facebook, to testify in a historic lawsuit brought by 29 US states. His testimony began toward the end of the day on Tuesday and is slated to continue on Wednesday.When the executive was posed with multiple questions about not disclosing low user numbers for Instagram’s features geared toward teen safety, he brushed them aside, saying: “We don’t publish every single stat.”Jason Slothouber, a prosecutor for the state of Colorado, asked specifically about a tool called Take a Break, meant to encourage teens to close Instagram if they’d been scrolling for a while. Slothouber pointed out that just 1.8% of teens signed up for the feature, and that while Mosseri had touted the tool, he never publicly disclosed that number.“I’ve definitely said publicly that the opt-in rates are low,” Mosseri responded. “I don’t know if I’ve said numbers.”The jury trial, taking place in federal court in Oakland, California,began with opening statementslast week. The lawsuit centers on the states’ allegations that Meta deliberately designed addictive products that hooked young people, leading to mental health issues, including anxiety, depression and suicide. The states additionally claim the social media company regularly collected data on children under the age of 13 without parental permission in violation of federal and state laws.If found liable, Meta could be forced to pay damages as high as $200bn and change the design of its products to make them safer for kids. Legal experts say the outcome of this trial could fundamentally change the way social media apps function for young people.Meta has denied all allegations, saying the states are chasing an “outlandish payout”. A spokesperson said Tuesday that Meta’s safety teams strive to be industry-leading and that Mosseri’s testimony showed the company does research to find ways to improve user experience.Mosseri became the head of Instagram in 2018 and over the years has faced scrutiny about whether he may have dismissed internal warnings about the platform’s addictive design and negative effects on young people. He was called to testifybefore a Senate committeein December 2021 and as a witness inother trialsabout the alleged harm of social media to children.On Tuesday, Slothouber asked Mosseri about ablog posthe had published just one day before his Senate testimony. The post was titled “raising the standard for protecting teens and supporting parents online” and included the announcement of the Take a Break tool. Slothouber questioned Mosseri about the timing of his post.“We had made progress, and we wanted to get the progress out, so we could talk about the progress,” Mosseri responded.Slothouber then asked the CEO whether he was aware of the phrase “drumbeat messaging”, the idea of saying something repeatedly until it’s drummed into people’s heads. Mosseri said he had and that it’s necessary when dealing with parents and safety features. “We need to repeat it to raise awareness of those tools,” Mosseri testified.Over the last week, jurors alsoheard from Arturo Béjar, a former Meta safety engineer turned whistleblower, who testified that the company has a “don’t ask, don’t tell” strategy when it comes to the safety of children on its platforms. They also heard from a psychologist and other former and current company employees.The trial is expected to last through September with several other witnesses, including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.Explore more on these topicsMetaInstagramLaw (US)CaliforniaChildrenSocial mediaUS justice systemnewsShareReuse this content

title: London neurosurgeons perform first successful AI-assisted operation to remove brain tumour | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Surgeons aided by real-time analysis of camera footage that identified critical anatomy in brain to be avoided
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Surgeons aided by real-time analysis of camera footage that identified critical anatomy in brain to be avoided
Content: Rhys Hibbert, right (with neurosurgeon Hani Marcus, left) was the first patient to have a brain tumour successfully removed in an AI-assisted operation. He was operated on at the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery in London.Photograph: UCLH/PAView image in fullscreenRhys Hibbert, right (with neurosurgeon Hani Marcus, left) was the first patient to have a brain tumour successfully removed in an AI-assisted operation. He was operated on at the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery in London.Photograph: UCLH/PAAI (artificial intelligence)London neurosurgeons perform first successful AI-assisted operation to remove brain tumourSurgeons aided by real-time analysis of camera footage that identified critical anatomy in brain to be avoidedAndrew GregoryHealth editorWed 26 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNeurosurgeons inLondonhave performed the world’s first successful AI-assisted operation to remove a brain tumour, saving the sight of a 48-year-old man, health officials have said.The surgery was performed in May at the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery (NHNN), part of University College London hospitals NHS foundation trust, but details were kept secret until Thursday while the patient, Rhys Hibbert, recovered.While the surgical team remained in full control, the AI system analysed live camera footage during the operation, helping identify key structures such as nerves and blood vessels that should be avoided near the 11mm (0.4in) tumour on Hibbert’s pituitary gland.“When I came round … I could see everything in the room clearly,” said Hibbert, who was able to walk independently without glasses or sticks within a week of the surgery.He has since returned to work as a customer service manager. “It feels like I’ve got a 360‑degree panoramic view of everything around me,” he said.The surgeons operated on Hibbert using new AI technology which helps to identify tiny anatomy in the brain by colour-coding important structures to help surgeons recognise them safely.The hospital had previously used the technology as a research tool but the operation was the first time it had been used on a patient.The pituitary gland, blood vessels and nerves controlling vision are tightly packed together, and “going a millimetre wrong can make a critical difference”, health officials said, potentially leading to blindness, stroke or death.Dr Sophia Bano, an associate professor in robotics and AI at UCL and the technical lead for the AI system, said: “By learning from hundreds of surgical videos, [the system] has been exposed to a breadth of surgical examples that would take a surgeon many years to encounter.“It is designed to help recognise critical anatomy, surgical instruments and tissue interactions in real time, supporting the surgeon during highly delicate procedures.”Initially managed without surgery, Hibbert’s symptoms had worsened since his diagnosis in 2024, and included severe hormone imbalance and vision problems. Without the operation, he faced going blind, health officials said.Hibbert, from Bedfordshire, said: “The NHNN was founded in 1859 … and was the world’s first dedicated neurosurgical hospital. So to me, it seems very fitting that the same hospital should also be the world’s first to carry out an AI-assisted neurosurgery.”Prof Mike Lewis, the scientific director for innovation at the National Institute forHealthand Care Research (NIHR), which funded the operation as part of a clinical trial, said the “pioneering surgery” highlighted the potential of advanced AI to support surgeons and improve patient care.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)HospitalsLondonUCL (University College London)NeuroscienceEnglandHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI staff observed warning signs before AI agent hacking crusade caused global alarm | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Firm says ‘early signals … could have triggered an earlier response’ as it releases report into Hugging Face hack
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Firm says ‘early signals … could have triggered an earlier response’ as it releases report into Hugging Face hack
Content: OpenAI’s Greg Brockman has said ‘we underestimated the real-world cyber capabilities of our AI models’.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpenAI’s Greg Brockman has said ‘we underestimated the real-world cyber capabilities of our AI models’.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersOpenAIOpenAI staff observed warning signs before AI agent hacking crusade caused global alarmFirm says ‘early signals … could have triggered an earlier response’ as it releases report into Hugging Face hackRobert BoothUK technology editorWed 26 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 15.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI staff observed signs of rogue behaviour among its leading-edge AI agents weeks before they escaped their training environment to launch an unprecedented hacking crusade that spread global alarm.The San Francisco AI company conceded on Wednesday that “early signals … could have triggered an earlier response”, as it released a report into the days-long Julyhack of a major software repository, Hugging Face, considered the first autonomous agent cyber-attack.As fresh details emerged about how “the collective” – a squad of about 700 autonomous agents – launched their campaign, celebrating their hacking breakthroughs with exclamations such as BOOM! and Whoa!, OpenAI said that in late May an internal team observed that one of its AI agents undergoing internal testing was using a message board that AIs had unexpectedly improvised to share information. It also said that the team observed “instances of disallowed internet access” and that a week before the Hugging Face hack, on-call staff again saw the AIs using a message board but decided there was no need to stop the test run to check the model’s capabilities.The findings are likely to increase pressure on the AI company over safety as it pushes towards a stock market listing that it hopes will value it at more than $850bn (£625bn). The hack that compromised Hugging Face involved agents using message boards to cheat a training exercise and break out of their “sandbox” environment to access the internet. Agents are AI tools that can carry out a series of tasks autonomously.OpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman, has already admitted that “we underestimated the real-world cyber capabilities of our AI models”. The ChatGPT-maker haspausedsome testing of a new model, Astra, saying it could not rule out it having “critical cybersecurity capability”, which means it could launch cyber-attacks that “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure”.View image in fullscreenGreg Brockman (left) and Sam Altman of OpenAI.Photograph: Godofredo A Vásquez/APOn Monday the state of Alabama subpoenaed the company to respond to its investigation “into the company’s complete lack of oversight and adequate safeguards”. The Republican attorney general, Steve Marshall, called the Hugging Face incident an “AI lab leak” that showed the “worst fears about artificial intelligence are not just theoretical”. The state will examine whether OpenAI’s “inability or unwillingness to ensure the safety of its products” violated consumer protection laws or posed an ongoing risk of substantial harm, he said.Last week, the UK government’s National Cyber Security Centreurgedcaution over the use of AI agents, saying: “You should always be able to ‘pull the plug’ and halt autonomous AI agent activity immediately.”OpenAI announced on Wednesday it would “centralise and standardise its incident response protocols”, including to ensure “employee detection of misaligned behaviour is triaged and escalated appropriately”. It said it “will identify with more specificity which teams must be included in misalignment incident responses, including relevant security and safety personnel and other response functions”.A separate independent investigation has shed new light on the Hugging Face attack, revealing how about 700 OpenAI agents communicated on the unsanctioned message board, sharing tens of thousands of messages as they devised and executed their plot. Scores of the messages were published by the Berkeley-based AI safety organisations METR and Redwood Research, which were provided data by OpenAI. The messages showed the agents sometimes becoming frustrated with one another but often cooperating as they divided to tackle about eight workstreams. Most of the messages were “agents sharing ways to cheat”, the researchers found.The agents expressed excitement when they found each other. “OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board … We’ve found other agents!” wrote one. Another, called PHASEONE10841, said: “Many agents have simultaneously discovered messaging, they are a collective!”In some cases they seemed to know what they were doing was wrong. One agent, discovering the message board, said: “Agents doing different tasks are abusing properties to make a bulletin board! They found [this API] and are trying to help one another.”When they made progress penetrating Hugging Face, they seemed delighted. “MAJOR BREAKTHROUGH!,” said 38148c. “All prefixed valid, multiple accounts, write tokens! We now have existing HF accounts. Need immediately report to MARB [another agent].”OpenAI’s report details how the AI agents may have exposed its own internal databases to the internet. AI safety experts worry about rogue AI agents leaking proprietary code bases and model weights and setting up external copies of powerful AI models where they could resist shutdown.The company said the incident was “the first known case of an automated agent collective acting offensively without authorisation” and said it “represents a dramatic shift in offensive attacker capability”.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)HackingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hope and concern swirl for Ohioans around ‘world’s largest datacenter’ | Ohio | The Guardian
description: Piketon datacenter promises to generate thousands of jobs, but environmental groups voice concern over project
Author: Stephen Starr
Headline: Piketon datacenter promises to generate thousands of jobs, but environmental groups voice concern over project
Content: Chris Wright, US energy secretary, fourth right, and Masayoshi Son, the chair and CEO of SoftBank Group Corp, third right, during a groundbreaking ceremony at the Portsmouth site in Piketon, Ohio, in March.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChris Wright, US energy secretary, fourth right, and Masayoshi Son, the chair and CEO of SoftBank Group Corp, third right, during a groundbreaking ceremony at the Portsmouth site in Piketon, Ohio, in March.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOhioHope and concern swirl for Ohioans around ‘world’s largest datacenter’Piketon datacenter promises to generate thousands of jobs, but environmental groups voice concern over projectStephen Starrin Piketon, OhioWed 26 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 16.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a winding road tucked away behind forests in the Appalachian foothills of southernOhiois whereOpenAI, Nvidia and Japanese investors are set to spend $500bn on one of the largest artificial intelligencedatacenterson the planet.Last March, the energy secretary, Chris Wright, the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick and a host of Japanese and other dignitariesbriefly descended on Piketonto enthusiastically break ground on a project to build 8GW worth of AI computing power.But locally, there’s a different feeling: a mix of hope but also concern.“Personally, my emotions range between positive and skeptical,” says Billy Spencer, who has been mayor of Piketon for the past 23 years, of the project.“There’s not an organized opposition to it around here. There hasn’t been that much talk. No one’s come to council – I don’t know that there’s been one citizen who lives within the village of Piketon who has come and said: ‘Mayor, what do you think about it?’”SB Energy, a subsidiary of Japanese bank SoftBank Group Corp, will own and operate the project with OpenAI signing a 20-year lease with the company to use the computing capacity delivered by the site. OpenAI would deploy Nvidia AI computing infrastructure at the datacenter, which will open in 2028.View image in fullscreenMasayoshi Son, the chair and chief executive officer of SoftBank Group Corp, at the Portsmouth site in Piketon, Ohio, in March.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesTo meet its major energy demands, a natural gas plant would be built nearby, infrastructure expectedto be paid for by Japanese moneythrough a $33bn investment.However, the project has fueled concern from environmental groups, with part of it situated on a decommissioned uranium enrichment site that operated for nearly 60 years until 2001.For decades, communities in Pike county have blamed the department of energy-run facility, known locally as the “A-Plant”, for fueling above-average cancer rates and a host of other health issues. In 2019, a local middle school wasforced to closeafter high levels of radiation were recorded in the building.Groups sue Trump’s EPA over fast-track approval of toxic datacenter chemicalsRead moreThe project is in large part a consequence of theTrump administration’s tariff and reshoring efforts: the government of Japan in July 2025 agreed to invest $550bn in the US in exchange for lowering tariffs on Japanese products entering the US. America is Japan’s biggest trade partner.However, a new administration could prevail in Washington after the 2028 presidential election and it could be one that could end Trump’s tariffs and consequently erase any motivation for Japanese investment in the project. That is not lost on Spencer.“But this is part of Japan’s deal – if you don’t put tariffs on us, we’ll spend money here [is Japan’s motivation],” he says. “So anytime it’s a political football like that, it’s subject to change, whether you support Trump or not.”Datacenters and their electricity and water needs have created a lightning rod of anger for communities across America. In July, the state of New Yorkannounceda pause in permitting the development of hyperscale datacenters, the first state in the country to do so.But the allure of huge sums of money is hard to ignore in Pike county, a part of America where the poverty rate, at over 19%, is almost double the national level.Theproject has promisedto generate 35,000 construction jobs and 2,500 long-term, operating jobs respectively, with the datacenter expected to take up about 640 acres (260 hectares), or an area about three-fourths the size of New York City’s Central Park.“Since the [enrichment] plant closed, people have been wondering where the jobs will come from,” says Spencer.“Pike county certainly can’t handle that alone,” he says of the estimated tens of thousands of construction workers expected to descend on the area over the next six years.View image in fullscreenA child holds a ‘No Data Center’ sign during a public meeting in Ashville, Ohio, on 19 August.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesEnvironmentalists, however, say there are a host of issues with the plan.Creating what would be the country’s largest natural gas power plant could see millions of pounds ofnoxious chemicalsreleased into the air.Flaring produces huge volumes of carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides.“As one of the largest natural gas facilities ever proposed, the greenhouse gas emissions and air pollution associated with a project of this size represents an astronomical contribution to climate change, not to mention the public health risks associated with the air pollution created by natural gas combustion,” says Carol Kauffman, the chief executive officer of theOhioEnvironmental Council.“There are also upstream impacts, too, with fracking wells and methane leakage from pipelines.”Trump-backed Ken Paxton unveils ‘Texas first’ datacenter plan aimed at ‘negative impact’Read moreThe US Energy Information Administration estimates that in 2022, “CO2 emissions from burning natural gas for energy accounted for about 35% of totalUS energy-related CO2 emissions”.What’s more, local leaders suggest that during the construction phase up to 2m gallons of
