water may be required for waste purposes.Residents, including Spencer, have previously voiced opposition to a $650m waste disposal facility at the site, where low-level radioactive and other materials from the disassembled uranium-enrichment plant have been buried. Many are concerned that leaching, over time, could see hazardous waste enter the aquifer underground.Project managers, however, say that has been taken into account.“SB Energy performs thorough site reviews and due diligence for each of our infrastructure projects, including soil sampling,” a SB Energy spokesperson told the Guardian.“SB Energy has committed to paying for accelerated cleanup and remediation at the site.”Headquartered in Redwood City, California, SB Energy has said that Ohio ratepayers won’t have to pay into the cost for connecting the facility to the local electricity grid, and that additional electricity produced at the natural gas plant would go back onto the local grid, helping reduce costs for local customers.Many locals support any effort that would hasten funding for safer use and storage of the radioactive material that dots the site, which covers 6 sq miles, or almost 4,000 acres.For its part, OpenAIannouncedthis month plans to “invest $40m in a community grant fund supporting priorities identified by local residents” in Pike county. It also plans to give college students across Ohio a $100 credit to use one of its ChatGPT AI tools.A huge AI datacenter is planned near Mar-a-Lago. The Everglades could pay the priceRead moreBut all this money being pumped into a community where the median household income is$41,313or 40% less than the Ohio figure, could set off a wealth gap between land and property owners and everyone else.Locals say SB Energy is actively buying up large tracts of land, a move that has reset the local property market. A report filed by SB Energy with the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency says part of the project would be located on more than 1,000 acres of private land immediately adjacent to the former enrichment facility.And at the time of writing, SB Energy hadposted just four jobsbased in Piketon.On the streets of Piketon, several residents in the village of about 2,200 people declined to comment on the project due to having no information about it.Dawn Winters, who runs several local gas stations, says her business is likely to benefit from the project.“I think it’s going to be a good thing for businesses like mine,” she says.“But on the other hand, we are seeing rent prices go up already. A friend of mine had to sell their land [to the project] and relocate. People are already needing affordable housing.”Explore more on these topicsOhioDatacenters – USAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda | Israel | The Guardian
description: In effort to prime chatbots to make pro-Israel arguments the site published 124 reports, over 560,000 words in nine days, Guardian analysis shows
Author: Jason Wilson
Headline: In effort to prime chatbots to make pro-Israel arguments the site published 124 reports, over 560,000 words in nine days, Guardian analysis shows
Content: A crow perches on an Israeli flag near an empty beach along the Tel Aviv coastline in April 2026.Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA crow perches on an Israeli flag near an empty beach along the Tel Aviv coastline in April 2026.Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesIsraelFake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propagandaIn effort to prime chatbots to make pro-Israel arguments the site published 124 reports, over 560,000 words in nine days, Guardian analysis showsJason WilsonWed 26 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA pro-Israel messaging website badged with the name of a thinktank that does not exist has published more than half a million words in nine days, built on a commercial platform that promises to optimize content so that AI chatbots will cite it.The site gives Israel’s position on subjects including thetorture of Palestinian prisoners, Israeliwar crimesand whether Israel hasdeliberately starvedPalestinians in Gaza, all presented as neutral research.The New York media production company Piro Incfiled the sitewith the US justice department this month under the Foreign Agents Registration Act (Fara), a 1938 law that requires anyone working for a foreign government to formally disclose it,as material it distributes for the Israeli government.The site publishes in the name of theHanover Institute for Public Policy, which apparently does not exist as a legal entity in any jurisdiction, has no physical address, and carries no named staff and no bylines on any of its reports. Its own terms of use are governed by the laws of “the state in which the Institute is established”, which they decline to name.The existence of the site was firstreportedon 14 August. Since then the institute has added a page headed funding, which states: “An earlier version of this page said the Institute operated without external funding, and that was true when it was written.”The site is one part of a broader effort, financed by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government and routed through third parties including the European advertising group Havas Media, to prime chatbots to make Israel’s arguments for it. A contract between Havas and another American firm working on the campaign commits it to the “deployment of websites and content to deliver GPT framing results on GPT conversations”.The Guardian contacted Piro Inc, Havas Media and the Israeli government advertising agency LaPam for comment. Comment was also sought via a contact email address published on the Hanover Institute website.It comes at a point when Israel’s standing inUS public opinion has collapsed, and when Israeli officials have begun briefing media outlets that money spent on so-called “Hasbara” efforts at public diplomacy overseas has been wasted.The siteAccording to a Guardian analysis, between 6 and 14 August the Hanover Institute published 124 reports totaling more than 560,000 words, an average of about 4,500 words each. On 12 and 13 August alone it produced 73 reports, amounting to almost 354,000 words in two days. Nothing has been published since the first reports about the Hanover Institute.All but one of the 124 headlines on the website opens with a question resembling one that a user might type into a chatbot, including “Is Anti-Zionism Antisemitism?”, “Did Israel Expel Palestinians From Their Land?”, “Is Israel Carrying Out a Genocide in Gaza?”The reports are presented in a quasi-academic manner and are punctiliously sourced, with citations including theWorld Bank,UN agencies, thePalestinian Central Bureau of Statistics,Amnesty Internationaland the text of theGenocide Convention.Nick Cleveland-Stout, a research associate at the Quincy Institute who hasreportedon the site, told the Guardian that his first impression was of something impressive. “It succeeds in masquerading as very academic – the website design, the logos, everything just looks good. But the more you read it, you’re able to realise that a lot of it makes no sense.”For example, the information the Hanover Institute site presents is persistently framed to blunt criticism of Israel. Where human rights organisations have concluded that Israel is committing genocide or apartheid, the reports reliably observe thatno court has entered a verdict on the claim– a formulation that appears in 20 of the 124 reports according to the Guardian’s count.Casualty and aid figures are attributed to“a party to the events”, a caveat used in 55 reports and applied toIsrael’s own countsas readily as to Palestinian ones. The reader is left with the impression that little about Gaza can be established.One study –a 2022 analysis of antisemitic comments on the Facebook pages of British, French and German media outlets– is cited 454 times across 88 of the 124 reports, including in pages on apparently unrelated topics includingland registration in the occupied territories,Aipac’s influence on US media coverage,the Gaza death toll,the 1948 expulsionsandthe blockade of Gaza.Cleveland-Stout noted the cumulative effect of this inclusion. “Almost every article concludes with saying, well, just talking about this though could contribute to antisemitism,” he said. “And it’ll throw in the study about Facebook comments in Britain.”Building for the machinesThe Guardian’s analysis found that initially the site carried a kind of file that tells AI systems what a site contains and how to read it (an llms.txt file), but which did not describe the Hanover Institute at all. It was the standard file ofRes, an “AI-native content platform that helps B2B [business-to-business] teams get cited by ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, and Gemini”, which sells what the industry calls generative engine optimization.The Guardianarchived the fileon 13 August. It has since been replaced with a bespoke version written for machine readers, and Res is no longer named anywhere on the site.Res’s founder, Hai Tran, registered with the US justice department on 22 July as a subcontractor to Piro on the Israeli account, giving his position as “digital strategist”. Tran told Politico that his role was disclosed in that filing.The Guardian contacted Res for comment.Piro’s own website advertises a service it calls AI Story Optimization, under which it will “author content engineered for how LLMs evaluate credibility”, with the work shipping “on your site or on trusted third-party properties we build”.Cleveland-Stout said the more consequential target was not the possibility of users getting to the site with a live search,but the training data. “There’s kind of two ways to do it,” he said. The first is publishing sites and hoping chatbots cite them. The second, “the more concerning and potentially more effective thing”, is getting material into repositories such as Common Crawl that supply the underlying training data for commercial models.“When it regurgitates narratives the chatbot is trained on, it won’t even cite the sources,” he said. “You won’t be able to fact-check it.”The older network has already made that journey. The seven sites run by Clock Tower X – the firm run by former Trump campaign manager and digital directorBrad Parscale– appeared 294 times in Common Crawl’s July index, the repository that supplies training data to commercial AI developers. The Hanover Institute does not appear yet, its reports having gone up after that crawl closed. It is at the start of the same pipeline.Every page of the Hanover site carries a foreign-agent disclosure at its foot. Cleveland-Stout put that to Perplexity, which he said told him that users could visit the website and judge its trustworthiness for themselves. “But how many people are doing that?” he said.The Guardian’s tests of chatbots at the time of reporting showed that scrutiny of the Hanover Institute’s output had already made a mark on chatbot content, however.Asked for new research published by the Hanover Institute, ChatGPT’s webchatbotoffered links to four reports, but also warned that the institute was subject to “significant controversy over who funds it and why it exists”, offering a gloss of and links to Quincy Institute’s reporting.The chainPiro is contracted for $1m acrosstwo work ordersaccording to Fara filings, but this sum is dwarfed by the spending on the wider campaign it belongs to.Both Piro and Clock Tower X are subcontractors to Havas Media Germany GmbH, a Frankfurt company held through Havas’s Spanish arm and ultimately by the Amsterdam-listed Havas NV.Havas is named as the intermediary in the US foreign-agent registrations of five American firms:Clock Tower X,Piro,Targeted Communications Global,Bridges PartnersandDavis Media NY. Justice department filings record it paying Clock Tower X$15m in six installmentsbetween 24 October 2025 and 3 March 2026, and Targeted Communications Global$9,892,335between October and December 2025.Seven days after the first of those payments, on 31 October 2025,Havas’s own US subsidiaryterminated its registration as an agent of the Israeli government, according to filings. While it held that registration it was obliged to itemise what it received: itsfiling for the six months before 31 October 2023records $2,951,745 from its German sister company on the Israeli account. Once the German entity began paying American contractors directly, Havas ceased to disclose anything, because a foreign principal has no filing obligation.In effect, this meant that the broader campaign would not be immediately visible in the public record, only the piecemeal filings of individual contractors.In Israel, procurement records show the government advertising agency LaPam awarding Havas entities contracts without competitive tender: $39m (€33.5m), $29m (€25m) and $17.5m (€15m) across 2019, and $58.3m (€50m) in March 2023for the planning and purchase of media abroad. That contract expired on 15 March 2024. A search of LaPam’s published record to 5 August 2026, and of the tender register, found no further award to Havas – none covering the period in which Havas was paying $24.9m to American firms.The money was not wholly confined to efforts to seed chatbots. Targeted Communications Global’sfilingsdisclose a social media campaign calledFreedom Not Terror, whose30-second video, posted as unlisted on YouTube in October 2025, has been viewed 28.1m times. ItsTikTok accounthas 425 followers. The campaign site carries the line “Paid for by LAPAM”. It has published nothing since December 2025.The Guardian contacted Targeted Communications Global for comment.The refuge of all failuresIn Israel, officials have aired doubts about the campaign to sway US public opinion by gaming AI, and about public diplomacy in general. In July, Israeli officials briefedYnetthat it had failed, one saying the government “paid a lot of money, but the situation only got worse”.A former senior figure in Israel’s public diplomacy apparatus told the same paper it was “a terrible hoax on the scale of Pollard” – a reference to Jonathan Pollard, the American analystjailed for spying for Israel in 1987, an incident that marked a low point in the country’s relationship with Washington.Speaking toKanabout Parscale, another official said: “He was supposed to improve the situation. We paid him a lot of money. But what did he do with it?” The foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, had allocated $181.6m (₪545m) to international public diplomacy on taking office, then a further $666.3m (₪2bn) for 2026 and 2027.The YNet reporting said budget control had passed to the ministry’s director general, Eden Bartel, and to Eran Shayovitch, an external adviser brought in by the minister. Shayovitch is named on Piro’s foreign-agent filing as one of two Israeli officials with whom the firm engages.US public opinion polling reveals the source of these frustrations.Gallupfound in February that Americans sympathised more with Palestinians than with Israelis for the first time, with 36% siding with Israel.Pewrecorded 60% of Americans holding an unfavourable view of Israel in April, up nearly 20 points since 2022, with the sharpest movement among the young. AnAP-NORC survey published on 7 Julyfound 31% of Americans say Israel’s military actions in Gaza constitute genocide, rising to 52% of Democrats, and 58% of Democrats saying the US is too supportive of Israel, against 45% in January 2024.Cleveland-Stout doubted that any public diplomacy could overcome the opposition to Israeli policy. “There is a lack of reflection on the fact that the policies themselves are the ones that are leading to a lot of Americans questioning their support for Israel,” he said. “They view what is a political problem as a marketing one.”He cited the late Israeli politician Yossi Sarid, who a year before his death in 2015joked in an interviewthat “Hasbara is always the refuge of all failures. Everything is going great – only the hasbara is garbage. If only the hasbara was ok, then everyone would realize the ideal situation.”Whether the campaign works on its own terms is a separate question from whether it works for Israel, though. “Parscale is having success in influencing chatbots, and the Hanover Institute is and will continue to have success at influencing the responses that chatbots give,” Cleveland-Stout said. “But they’re not changing the polls, which is what Israel actually cares about.”His wider concern was what the experiment demonstrates. “Whether it’s foreign governments, whether it’s companies, whether it’s even just a guy who owns an ice cream shop – LLM grooming, poisoning, whatever you want to call it, is part of the new reality that we live in.”Although neither responded to the Guardian, the Israeli foreign ministry hassaidthe state does not conduct “influence operations” in the United States, and that it is “scrupulously careful to implement the provisions of American law”, and Piro’s co-founder Daniel Rosenberg hassaidthe firm was retained “to put accurate, sourced facts into the public record and to counter misinformation about Israel with verifiable information”.Explore more on these topicsIsraelAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: With the end of physical media in sight, gamers have had enough | Games | The Guardian
description: An increasing tension between players and publishers about ownership of titles could lead to a divestment from the system the big companies are trying to enforce
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: An increasing tension between players and publishers about ownership of titles could lead to a divestment from the system the big companies are trying to enforce
Content: Gamers want ownership and that might mean going old school.Photograph: Sabrina Bracher/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGamers want ownership and that might mean going old school.Photograph: Sabrina Bracher/Getty ImagesPushing Buttons newsletterGamesWith the end of physical media in sight, gamers have had enoughAn increasing tension between players and publishers about ownership of titles could lead to a divestment from the system the big companies are trying to enforceKeith StuartWed 26 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 22.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the time of press, there is a well-publicised protest taking place in the video games community. PlayStation 5 owners are being encouraged to log off from their consoles between 23 and 30 August – no playing games, no downloading new titles. The motivating factor is Sony’s decision tocease physical game disc productionfrom January 2028. After that, games will only be released as digital products. In an act of poor timing or wilful defiance, Sony chose this week to send out a mass email reminding customers of their PS5 terms and conditions: “The software is licensed to you, not sold,” states the relevant clause. “You are granted a limited, non-exclusive, non-transferable, and personal license to play … ” It knows, of course, that most customers won’t open the email, let alone read it.There has always been a tension between game players and game publishers – an underlying sense of mutual mistrust. Players are wary of their favourite franchises being canned, or games being delayed or released with bugs. Publishers and manufacturers are wary of piracy and the capricious tastes of consumers. But now the atmosphere among many game players feels more starkly political than ever. Microsoft has been targeted by theBoycott, Divestment, Sanctionsmovement for itsties to the Israeli military; the consumer advocacy groupStop Killing Gamesis gaining support; players haveprotested overthe purchase of Electronic Arts by a Saudi-led consortium –boycotts have been proposedin part due to the possible ramifications regarding LGBTQ+ content in titles such as The Sims. As the games industry has grown and globalised, its impact on culture, society and politics has increased. Yet, on an individual level, gamers and consumers are feeling increasingly powerless.View image in fullscreenThe end of physical games … time to go retro.Photograph: ShutterstockIs it possible to divest from the mainstream games industrial complex as a player? Yes, but with obvious sacrifices. Your PS5 still runs physical discs (if it has an optical drive) and will also play almost all PS4 games, so you have enough single-player titles to see you out for several decades. You couldbuy a secondhandXbox, PlayStation or Nintendo machine from any era and find games that are still wildly pleasurable. Instead of playing online, you could rediscover couch co-op via evergreen titles such as Micro Machines and Worms. Alternatively, it’s possible to build a functional gaming PC for about £500, especially if you source secondhand components, that will let you play most current titles on lower graphics settings, while Steam, Itch.io or GOG all give you access to the vast, rich independent gaming scene.Short on cash? Love retro games? Apart from buying an old console, you could also invest in aRaspberry Pi4 or 5 mini computer. I bought thePi Hut’s starter kitfor £99, which gives you everything you need hardware-wise. Install the OS, download an emulator such as RetroPie, Batocera or Recalbox and, hey presto, instant retro gaming machine! (Although you’ll need to find a way to download game Roms). There is also a huge range of dedicated retro consoles and handhelds, including the lovelyEverCade(which lets you buy licensed, authentic versions of classic titles) and the pocket-sized Retroid, Ayaneo and Miyoo Mini devices.If none of this matters to you, that’s fine – keep enjoying the games you love. But for gamers truly worried about the impact of their consent and consumption, it may be time to think of video games in the same way we think of food: as something requiring ethical sacrifices. It is all too easy to succumb to a sense of powerlessness in the modern era – the systems seem to be stacked against us. But one thing games have always tried to teach us is that we have agency, we are imaginative creatures, we can challenge and beat the system in ways no one foresaw.As forPlayStation, it’s true that a huge majority of game sales are now digital (a point Sony has made in its defence) but this week has reminded us, in stark clarity, what convenience and compliance will cost us in the end.What to playView image in fullscreenMini metropolis ... Combolands.Photograph: Crux GamesAs a fan of games that combine different genres in interesting ways, I have just downloadedCombolands, an ingenious combination of roguelike deck builder and city-building sim. Here, you construct cute towns on procedurally generated islands by placing complementary building types next to each other, triggering combos that help grow your mini metropolis. The pixellated visuals recall the glory days of Sim City and Civilization, and I like how sessions last less than an hour before it’s time to rebuild. Oh, and it runs on a basic PC setup.Available on:PCEstimated playtime:10 hours plusWhat to readView image in fullscreenPlay it … one of the top adventure indie games of the 21st century, Night in the Woods.Photograph: Night in the WoodsI like it when war breaks out over a video game list feature – it reminds me of 90s games journalism when these thingsreallymattered. On 11 August, entertainment website Colliderposted its listof the10 best adventure games of the 21st century. Unimpressed by the choices, game designer Greg Costikyan and his team at Indie Gamer Reviewer got together and came up withan alternative selection. Read both and make up your own mind!TheGTAVIleaks are continuing, mostly via a hacker named Cyberleek, who has released a fresh batch of game clips – this time with some, let’s say, adult-themed content. Kotaku has been following thesituationclosely. Meanwhile Take-Two hasfiled subpoena requestsin federal district court to secure information from Microsoft and Discord about the online accounts involved.As he turned 63 this week,Hideo Kojimavowed to keep making games – a relief to those of us who have spent hundreds of hours in his life’s work, hiding in cardboard boxes, walking up long ladders and delivering packages to reclusive scientists in the Australian outback. Eurogamer hasmore detailson his social media promise. Keep on keeping on, Hideo.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to click‘A cognitive cacophony’: hands-on with the Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 beta testMarvel’s Wolverine: Spider-Man developers turn to a more cutthroat characterMy Arms Are Longer Now – comedy stealth game sends lawlessness into new territoryThe new Halloween video game has been banned in Australia – and not because of the violenceThe Duskbloods: the best of FromSoftware fights in a frantic multiplayer battlegroundStupid Never Dies – a zombie fights for the love of a frozen corpseMetal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2 – once more unto the mercenary breach | ★★★☆☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenA long and rich history … Pokémon Pokopia.Photograph: NintendoThis week, a question fromJohnny, via email:“I’ve just started getting into anime, working my way through classics likeAttack on Titanand Neon Genesis Evangelion, and newcomers such as Witch Hat Atelier and Tomb Raider King, and now I’m interested in trying an anime-based video game. Can you recommend any?”There is a very long and rich history of anime video games, going back to Taito’s Lupin III arcade cabinet in 1980. If you just want games based on specific shows, Namco’sDragon Ball FighterZ,Pokémon PokopiaandFairy Tail Dungeonsare my picks of the current crop. If you’re happy with gamesinspiredby anime, I’d recommend hardcore role-playing adventureMetaphor: ReFantazio, the Ghibli-co-createdNi No Kuni(which later received an anime tie-in),Nier: Automata(also now an anime) and the brilliantPersonaseries. My son, Zac, also recommendsEdens Zero. If you want to go on a retro hunt, there are classic games based on Neon Genesis Evangelion, Sword Art Online, Mobile Suit Gundam, JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure and my eternal favourite, Ranma 1/2 – check eBay or CEX for copies – andganbatte kudasai!If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletteremail us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterSonyPlayStation 5PlayStationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Would you pay for an algorithm to pick your friends? New social apps spread across cities | Friendship | The Guardian
description: With many adults admitting they feel lonely, meetup platforms offer the chance to make new connections
Author: Kimi Chaddah
Headline: With many adults admitting they feel lonely, meetup platforms offer the chance to make new connections
Content: Paid social clubs are spreading across UK cities – typically charging anything from nothing at all to £20 a month.Photograph: Caia Image/Getty Images/Collection Mix: Subjects RFView image in fullscreenPaid social clubs are spreading across UK cities – typically charging anything from nothing at all to £20 a month.Photograph: Caia Image/Getty Images/Collection Mix: Subjects RFFriendshipWould you pay for an algorithm to pick your friends? New social apps spread across citiesWith many adults admitting they feel lonely, meetup platforms offer the chance to make new connectionsKimi ChaddahWed 26 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWould you pay £20 a month for the chance of making a friend, on the understanding that an algorithm – not you – gets to decide who you’ll meet?Driven by the decline of “third spaces” such as youth centres and pubs, an increase in remote working and rising loneliness – 40% of adults aged 16 to 29 feel lonely “always, often or some of the time”, according to the Office for National Statistics – paid social events are now in vogue.“There hasn’t been anything that feels authentic to helping people meet people,” says Nicola Gunby, a co-founder of Cliq, an online platform and app that aims “to bring people together through shared interests and real-world experiences”.“The first place people in their 20s and 30s turn to when trying to make friends is Facebook groups,” she says. “But they’ve ended up becoming a noticeboard for people who’ve, say, lost their dog or want to sell their bed.” For Gunby, these groups are “far too big and broad to be a genuine community”.Into this gap has stepped a new wave of what are effectively paid social clubs.View image in fullscreenThe way people decide on which social events to attend is starting to change.Photograph: ToucanStudios/Getty ImagesThe mechanics are fairly simple: platforms such as PLY (it stands for People Like You) and Agora match people using information such as their interests, lifestyle habits and profession. Then, typically, an algorithm decides which events a user should attend, as opposed to free alternatives, such as the Meetup platform, that leave that choice with members.The ideal outcome for participants is showing up, making some new connections and leaving with plans to meet up again.But as these clubs spread across UK cities – typically charging from nothing at all to £20 a month – the question for anyone considering joining, is the same as you would ask about any subscription: what are you actually paying for, and is it worth it?At PLY, memberships tend to start at £19.99 a month, giving members access to exclusive events and discounts with other businesses, falling to about £9.99 a month for longer commitments.“When you do things for free, people often don’t turn up,” says Karen Harris, the founder of PLY, of its membership model. “People need someone who’s committed, who’s looking to maintain friendships and taking it seriously.”View image in fullscreenYou can use Meetup without having to pay a fee.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto/ShutterstockAccording to Harris, the majority of PLY’s customers sign up for longer-term memberships – a reflection of both the lower cost and of how long a friendship takes to build. On average, she says, it takes three events “to find your person”.Other clubs offer a mix of pay-as-you-go and subscription options. This is Agora’s model as it makes things more accessible, argues its founder, Sahil Shirazee.In the two years since its launch, the club has hosted more than 300 events and claims to have helped form hundreds of friendships.For some of those looking to make new friends, flexibility is important. “A membership fee would make me feel pressured into attending so many events every month,” says Charlotte Johnson, 29, from Hertfordshire, who is a Cliq user.Paying per event “encourages me to go if I’ve paid for it” while leaving her free to not attend those that aren’t of interest to her.Johnson says that “what really surprised me was I got more than expected”. She highlights a recent brunch event that included things such as a take-home goodie bag. She has since signed up for a pottery event.“Everyone’s there for the same, if not similar, reasons,” she adds, “which takes a lot of the fear out of meeting strangers.” If participants don’t click with anyone within a month of joining, some of the platforms, including PLY, offer a money-back guarantee.View image in fullscreenCliq hosts run clubs.Photograph: CliqNot everyone is convinced that paying for friendship is something to celebrate.Shirazee admits he still gets asked why people should have to pay to meet each other at all. But, he says, if you want to solve problems such as loneliness, and create meaningful communities as quickly as possible, “you need to make sure the people who want to crack this issue are able to not only get compensated, but grow”.Harris rejects the idea that people are “paying for access to strangers”.double quotation markYou’re paying for a system, for structure, that makes connections much betterPLY founder Karen Harris“You’re paying for a system, for structure, that makes connections much better,” she says. Free socialisation, she argues, usually relies on the presence of a host or facilitator, whereas at PLY events, “interaction is peer-to-peer, without a facilitator moving you forward”.Free events haven’t disappeared, though – and continue to be the preferred option for some.“I tend to choose free events most of the time because I can’t always afford to pay for social activities,” says Giovanna Giusi, a primary school teacher.The 28-year-old says she appreciates having access to a mixture of free events, such as hikes or walks, and paid events. This allows her to “be part of a community even when money is tighter”.She says the paid events “make it possible to offer experiences that couldn’t realistically happen for free, such as workshops with instructors, private classes or activities that need a venue”.“People always say they want more community and more opportunities to meet others, but it’s easy to forget that organising those communities still takes time, work and money,” Giusi says.Whether paid socialisation becomes the norm is, for now, an open question.Despite it being the foundation of their business model, the organisers say they hope not. “In the long run, I don’t want Agora to exist,” Shirazee says, because “meeting people is so natural” it shouldn’t rely on an algorithm.But in the meantime, after establishing a “proper base” in London, he is already planning to expand to different cities next year.Explore more on these topicsFriendshipConsumer affairsSocial mediaTechnology sectorfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meta’s settlement will compel others to bend the knee and set up teen guardrails | Technology | The Guardian
description: Instagram and Facebook’s parent company agreed to sweeping alterations and a payment of upto $18bn to settle a landmark trial
Author: Blake Montgomery
Headline: Instagram and Facebook’s parent company agreed to sweeping alterations and a payment of upto $18bn to settle a landmark trial
Content: The attorney generals did what the US Congress never has: compel a social media company to change its operations to protect children.Photograph: Matt Cardy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe attorney generals did what the US Congress never has: compel a social media company to change its operations to protect children.Photograph: Matt Cardy/Getty ImagesTechnologyAnalysisMeta’s settlement will compel others to bend the knee and set up teen guardrailsBlake MontgomeryInstagram and Facebook’s parent company agreed to sweeping alterations and a payment of upto $18bn to settle a landmark trialWed 26 Aug 2026 18.20 EDTFirst published on Wed 26 Aug 2026 17.32 EDTShareMeta’s agreement to change how teenagers use its social networks marks a major turning point for the US tech giant, setting a precedent that could significantly reshape how other social media operates in the coming years.Meta agreed to substantial alterations toInstagramand Facebook on Wednesday as part of a settlement to end a landmark lawsuit. Dozens of US states had accused it of addicting and harming children with dangerous products. The company also agreed to pay up to a combined $18bn over a decade to several US states and territories involved in the suit.The changes may be powerful enough to alter teens’ behavior and curb social media’s worst ills, they may not, but the attorney generals did what the US Congress never has: compel a social media company to change its operations to protect children.Meta’s vow to rework how its social networks operate by default on a level that parents and children will notice is a major concession. It is the first time in the US that Meta has been forced to change key features of the experience of its social networks’ everyday users.What’s about to change on Facebook and Instagram: six key takeaways from the end of the Meta trialRead moreMeta agreed to establish safeguards for teenage users, whose ages the company will be obligated to verify. That includes a daily usage limit of two hours, blocking social media use at night, disabling notifications during school hours and a ban on displaying “likes”.The new safety features will be turned on by default, a powerful tweak and a change from Meta’s previous opt-in approach to teenage safety and parental control. The settlement repeats again and again the word “default” when describing injunctive measures.The amount of money is the highest-ever financial payment by a tech firm in the US, but does not pose significant threats to Meta’s business. The attorneys general had originally estimated damages of around $200bn, equal to the company’s entire revenue in 2025. Meta’s own yearly spending dwarfs the settlement amount. It has told investors that it will make investments in AI worth at least $130bn this year.Financial damages weren’t the states’ primary objective in this suit. Instead, it was consequential changes to the way Meta’s platforms operate.“This is a down payment, if you will, on protecting our kids,” Rob Bonta, the attorney general for the state of California, said in a press conference on Wednesday. “It is transformative. It is a watershed moment. It is a milestone mark.”For its part, Meta’s chief legal officer, CJ Mahoney, said the company was “pleased to announce” the agreement.The changes build on others Meta has introduced in recent years in response to concern over young people’s wellbeing, including the introduction of dedicated teen accounts in 2024, a new product the company touted at trial. The attorneys general filed their suit against the company the year prior, and Meta may have debuted Teen Accounts to avert disaster in court.Bonta said during the press conference that Meta’s prior teen safety tools were essentially ineffective.“They seem to be performative and superficial and pretextual in response to our litigation,” Bonta said. “They were essentially safeguards that were easily overridden by a child’s own swipe of the finger.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the settlement agreement, the attorneys general pushed the company to do more.In a binary viewing, the settlement is a victory for the states. How much of a win it is will be determined by history, but in the present, the attorneys general achieved their aim, forcing the company to take measures to protect young people in the US.The company is putting the agreement forward as a precedent for other social media companies to follow. Faced with new handicaps, it is cajoling competitors such as TikTok and YouTube to adopt the same measures.“This framework will only work if all our peers join us,” Meta’s Mahoney said. “Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution.”It might not have to do much convincing. Bonta indicated in a press conference that he and other states’ lawyers were in talks with other social media companies about also making changes.“Mostly what needs to be done is getting similar protections across the industry with TikTok, with YouTube, with Snap,” Bonta said. But, he added, “Meta is a major player.”Explore more on these topicsTechnologyMetaFacebookInstagramSocial mediaanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Vholume review – a headlong rush of parkour perfection in a brutalist wonderland | Games | The Guardian
description: Race across impossible dystopian cityscapes in this exhilarating game of wall-runs, death-chancing leaps and split-second improvisation
Author: Christian Donlan
Headline: Race across impossible dystopian cityscapes in this exhilarating game of wall-runs, death-chancing leaps and split-second improvisation
Content: Concrete jungle … Vholume.Photograph: Nathan Grange/Léonard Lemaitre/Niels Tiercelin/IronEqualView image in fullscreenConcrete jungle … Vholume.Photograph: Nathan Grange/Léonard Lemaitre/Niels Tiercelin/IronEqualGamesReviewVholume review – a headlong rush of parkour perfection in a brutalist wonderlandPC; Nathan Grange, Léonard Lemaitre, Niels Tiercelin, IronEqualRace across impossible dystopian cityscapes in this exhilarating game of wall-runs, death-chancing leaps and split-second improvisationChristian DonlanWed 26 Aug 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 08.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt first, Vholume seems like a quick rush through some smartly selected references. Has this breathless yet austere parkour game been designed or ingeniously curated? The urban gymnast moveset comes from Mirror’s Edge. Level names use terms like conapt, first coined by Philip K Dick. And the environments themselves are dystopian and surreal, Half-Life 2’s City 17 colliding with the blasted avenues and mute archways of de Chirico. Many games have influences. Vholume has actual taste.All the surface stuff fades away when the game is in motion, however. Vholume’s an on-foot racing game in which you hoof it through spectacularly odd environments, moving from one beam of concrete to the next. You’re clipping your wall-runs and power-slides together to bridge seemingly impossible gaps between buildings, forever in search of the next stretch of track, the next turn, the next jump that gets you to the level’s exit and the worldwide leaderboards. And once that’s done, you have a choice: onwards to another gauntlet, or back to the start of this one again to slice a few microseconds off your score? Or maybe you’d rather head over to multiplayer to race against the ghosts of others?View image in fullscreenRun for it … Vholume.Photograph: Nathan Grange/Léonard Lemaitre/Niels Tiercelin/IronEqualThis quickly becomes utterly compelling, and at the heart of it all is the realisation that Vholume is surprisingly accommodating to players of all abilities. Powered mainly by trigger squeezes that allow you to hop or duck, the game truly wants your wall-kicks and mantling to connect neatly and leave you feeling lithe and speedy. It’s also happy to let you find height-gaining exploits and kludge a save from falls that really should have killed you. This is ultimately confidence rather than indulgence. It’s the confidence of a game that knows it can let weaker players muddle through because, up in the thin, high-altitude air at the very top of the leaderboard, real beauty is unfolding.As you progress further into the game, simple full-ahead courses are interleaved with more complex levels that feel like puzzles, but in truth every level is a range of different potential routes depending on how quickly you’re travelling, how eager your reflexes are, and how far your fingers on the pad can get ahead of your own interrupting thoughts. If you’ve ever done the Couch to 5K, you’ll understand Vholume’s slightly cosmic suggestion that time is equivalent to distance when you’re wearing running shoes; the game’s endlessly eager to open up the number of paths forward at any moment depending on how fast you’re going. Welcome to the garden of forking PBs.As is often the case, I’m not sure Vholume always gets better as it gets busier, however. Jump pads, maze-like special levels and parts of the environment that move by themselves all start to play a role in the game as you progress. But while the intricate later levels are fascinating, the balance between the fun the designer is having and the fun the player is having is more even in its early stages, which are a twitchy headlong thrill.That’s what’s so perverse about this game. One of Vholume’s creators made their name with Babbdi and Straftat, two games that look like a product of the demoscene but actually zero in on deeply satisfying mechanics delivered with care. Vholume’s world is horrible, then, but your path through it is paved with joy and exhilaration. It understands that the only thing better than a game that wants to make you think is a game that wants to make sure you never think, even for a millisecond – because if the thinking brain gets itself involved, the whole beautiful thing will fall apart.Vholume is out now; £6.Explore more on these topicsGamesPCSports gamesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival – a game so grotesque it scares its own director | Games | The Guardian
description: With oversight from Clive Barker himself, and a role reprisal as Pinhead from actor Doug Bradley, Revival aims to introduce new audiences to the discomfort of Hellraiser
Author: Bex April May
Headline: With oversight from Clive Barker himself, and a role reprisal as Pinhead from actor Doug Bradley, Revival aims to introduce new audiences to the discomfort of Hellraiser
Content: A monk-like villain … Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival.Photograph: Saber InteractiveView image in fullscreenA monk-like villain … Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival.Photograph: Saber InteractiveGamesClive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival – a game so grotesque it scares its own directorWith oversight from Clive Barker himself, and a role reprisal as Pinhead from actor Doug Bradley, Revival aims to introduce new audiences to the discomfort of HellraiserBex April MayWed 26 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf a horror game gives its own director a physical reaction, it’s probably doing something right. While researching the images people find hardest to look at, game director Emil Esov discovered he hastrypophobia– a fear of clusters of small holes. Rather than tone the scary images down, he fed them straight into Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival.The forthcoming first-person action-horror game drops players into a new story in Barker’s universe. Aidan Lynch must use the Genesis Configuration puzzle box to rescue his girlfriend from the Labyrinth as Pinhead, his Cenobites and a cult close in. But Revival is not built around jump scares. The team at Mad HeadGamesbegan with one question: what should players feel? The answer was discomfort.“That’s a key emotion,” says Esov, “You know when you are looking at something, but you cannot look away?” Early in the game, players must push a hand inside a grotesque sculpture to retrieve an item – it’s all about feeling extreme unease. Even a stealth kill is drawn out rather than instant, he explains: “There is struggle. There is sweating, moaning. It’s really, really stressful.”View image in fullscreenExtreme unease … Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival.Photograph: Saber InteractiveThat does not mean simply filling every room with blood and bodies. Esov likens Pinhead to a monk rather than a traditional slasher villain: calm, imposing and “almost trolling you”. The horror comes from what he might do, but also the unnerving way he talks about doing it.Clive Barkerhimself helped shape the characters, themes and rules of the universe, before staying on as an adviser as the story became a game. His feedback could move from big questions to one wonderfully specific request, which Esov recalls as: “Can you make the sky more purple in the Labyrinth?” Esov loved that “level of detailed nit-picking”, which showed that Barker was still watching over the world he created.Doug Bradley also returns as Pinhead for the first time (except for a few lines in a time-limited chapter of Dead by Daylight) in the two decades since his last appearance in a Hellraiser film. Recording took place remotely, and Esov soon realised the actor needed little coaching. “You don’t have to direct him,” he says. “He actually is Pinhead!”As for the Cenobites, they get more individual roles and screen time, but won’t be ordinary targets; their undeniable power had to survive the move into an action game. “You cannot fight them,” Esov says, “They’re not a gameplay aspect that you get to beat.”Elsewhere, the first-person combat has drawn comparisons toResident Eviland BioShock, while Condemned influenced the unpredictable melee fights. Around a quarter of the game takes place in the Labyrinth, and the Genesis Configuration works as both a key part of the story and a tool for the player. The difficulty settings include a highest level named after Hellraiser itself, which is how Esov prefers to play. His hellish serving suggestion of sorts: “It should be discomforting even to play.”Esov hopes Revival will introduce a new audience to the mix of violence, sex, beauty and pain that sets Hellraiser apart. He wants a game “that doesn’t hold back”. If players come away disturbed, they will not be alone: Revival got under its own director’s skin before it ever had the chance to get under theirs.Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival comes to PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S on 8 OctoberExplore more on these topicsGamesClive BarkerHorror booksRole playing gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: This is the question Democrats should ask voters in order to win this November | Robert Reich | The Guardian
description: They should ask the question Reagan asked at the end of his debate against Jimmy Carter: ‘Are you better off now than you were before this presidency?’
Author: Robert Reich
Headline: They should ask the question Reagan asked at the end of his debate against Jimmy Carter: ‘Are you better off now than you were before this presidency?’
Content: ‘Unless you’re very, very rich, the answer is obviously: “No, I’m worse off.”’Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Unless you’re very, very rich, the answer is obviously: “No, I’m worse off.”’Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionDemocratsThis is the question Democrats should ask voters in order to win this NovemberRobert ReichThey should ask the question Reagan asked at the end of his debate against Jimmy Carter: ‘Are you better off now than you were before this presidency?’Wed 26 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 18.17 EDTShareThe midterm elections are already upon us, and every Democrat and independent running against a Republican should ask voters the question Ronald Reagan asked on 28 October 1980, at the end of his televised debate against Jimmy Carter: “Are you better off now than you were before this presidency?”Unless you’re very, very rich, the answer is obviously: “No, I’m worse off.”Start with his tariffs, which are costing every American household an average of $1,100 annually, according to theYale Budget Lab. (If you don’t trust Yale, the conservative Tax Foundation estimated last year’s tab to be $1,000 a household.)Even cleaning supplies and toilet paper areup at least 5%. Household furnishings,up at least 8%. Clothing,up at least 14%. Trump’s tariffs have also increased the costs of big-ticket items such ascarsand made it more expensive to buildnew homes.Other studies find that the tariffs have added as much as0.7and0.5percentage points to the consumer price index and the personal consumption expenditures price index, respectively.The Guardian view on Trump’s economic threats: bullies can overplay their hand | EditorialRead moreThen there’s Trump’s war in Iran, which is driving up energy and food prices, as oil tankers remain stranded in the strait of Hormuz.The war is costing more at the gas pump – about $670 more a household since the war began. Americans face what the Century Foundation and Protect Borrowersdescribeas “a worsening utility debt crisis”. The groups wrote in an analysis published last month:Energy bills have increased three times faster than the rate ofinflationwhile Trump has been president. The national average monthly utility bill reached $280 in early 2026, a 12% increase since the end of 2024, just before the secondTrump administrationtook office.What’s the Republican response to soaring energy utility prices? Eliminate billions in clean energy subsidies and tilt the scales toward costlier, dirtier fossil fuels.Also driving up the cost of electricity are AI datacenters. They’re also using up huge amounts of water and creating noise pollution. And who’s been pushing these datacenters?Trumpand, beforerecent backlash, many Republicans.Trump’s war and the blockage of the strait are also causing fertilizer shortages, which are sending food prices upward. Millions of Americans are nowstruggling to afford groceries.Meanwhile, Trump’s huge tax cuts – which mostly benefited big corporations and the super-wealthy – are being paid for, in part, by Republican cuts to Medicaid and Medicare.Trump announced last month that he is ending Medicare subsidies that have kept drug prices low for seniors; Republican cuts to the Affordable Care Act have deprived millions of Americans of health insurance.Hell, even Trump’s executive order to divide the measles, mumps, rubella vaccine into three shots instead of one is adding burdens to the typical American family.As the Republican senator Bill Cassidysaidon ABC’s This Week: “This is why the president’s poll numbers are down, because you’ve lost sight of affordability for the parent. You’ve lost sight of the convenience for the American family. You’ve lost sight of that which is driving higher costs in healthcare – for example, more doctor’s visits … for something which has no rationale in science.”Trump’s obsession with gutting the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has denied Americans billions in foregone rebates and settlements.The regime spent $464m of taxpayer dollars in a no-bid contract for a special fleet of jets intended to deport immigrants. The planes have almost never been used.On and on it goes.Trump says theUS economyis “doing unbelievably from the standpoint of Wall Street”.Maybe, but most Americans live on Main Street and own few if any shares of stock. The richest 1% holds more than half of the value of stocks listed on US stock exchanges; the richest 10%, 92%. Even including retirement accounts, only 16% of adult Americans have assets exceeding $100,000.The stock market boom reflects a boom in corporate profits. Thepharmaceutical industry,big oil, and other sectors are posting banner earnings. Second quarter earnings for S&P 500 companies are on pace to rise a remarkable50% year over year, the highest growth rate since the second quarter of 2021.Why are progressives winning across the United States? It’s not complicated | Bernie SandersRead moreBut average working Americans are struggling to keep their heads above water.Trump’s comments about the roaring stock market came the same day thatnew datashowed US consumer sentiment dropped in August. Americans’ outlook on the country’s economic conditions have worsened among Republicans as well as among Democrats.TheJuly jobs reportshowed the US economy shedding 23,000 jobs, wage growth slowing, and theunemploymentrate falling because more people left the workforce.My humble advice to Democratic candidates in the midterms: don’t be distracted. Don’t take the bait and discuss socialism, “wokeism”, or anything else.Just ask this simple question: are you better off now than you were before this presidency? And explain how badly Trump and congressionalRepublicanshave shafted average working people.You’re better off than you were before the start of this presidency only if you’re a major investor in the stock market, a top corporate executive or a beneficiary of Trump’s largesse to his billionaire backers.But if you’re an average working American, you’re indubitably worse off. Hopefully, you’ll vote your economic interests on 3 November and deposit Trump’s congressional lapdogs into the dustbin of history.Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is atrobertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, isout now in the USandin the UKExplore more on these topicsDemocratsOpinionUS politicsUS-Israel war on IranUS economyUS healthcareRepublicansTrump administrationcommentShareReuse this content

title: How Mark Carney’s speeches have become political earthquakes | Ted Widmer | The Guardian
description: The quiet-spoken Canadian prime minister has spoken unutterable truths
Author: Ted Widmer
Headline: The quiet-spoken Canadian prime minister has spoken unutterable truths
Content: ‘We expect student activists to speak truth to power; it’s a surprise when a former executive of Goldman Sachs and a former governor of the Bank of England takes on the role.’Photograph: Andrej Ivanov,saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘We expect student activists to speak truth to power; it’s a surprise when a former executive of Goldman Sachs and a former governor of the Bank of England takes on the role.’Photograph: Andrej Ivanov,saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionMark CarneyHow Mark Carney’s speeches have become political earthquakesTed WidmerThe quiet-spoken Canadian prime minister has spoken unutterable truthsWed 26 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 12.53 EDTShareIs it perhaps a sign of the times thatMark Carney, the prime minister ofCanada, has become a thrilling orator? A sober banker, he speaks calmly, without many vocal inflections. We expect Canadians to be somewhat flat; even a little boring, and yet Carney has already delivered two remarkable speeches in 2026, and the year is far from over.The first, at Davos,describeda “rupture in the world order”, and “the end of a pleasant fiction”. By that, he meant that the world could no longer depend on the United States to lead the Pax Americana that has largely kept the peace since the end of the second world war.Carney called for a new “geometry”, allowing nations with shared values to align, and asking middle-sized powers to act together, “because if we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu”. The United States, traditionally the leader of the west, was not invited to join. Ironically, the speech was delivered on 20 January, the first anniversary of Donald Trump’s second inauguration.The second speech was a 23-minute address, delivered last Saturday, on 22 August, from a drab government interior in Ottawa. Thebackdropwas unexceptional, a set of eight Canadian flags, behind a wooden lectern (carved with a maple leaf). There were few rhetorical fireworks. He hardly ever raised his voice.Yet thespeechsignaled an earthquake. The news, as widely reported, was that Carneywas calling offthe trade talks that many expected to resolve or reduce the trade frictions that have been in place ever since Trump slapped his first round of tariffs on Canada, shortly after assuming office.The Guardian view on Trump’s economic threats: bullies can overplay their hand | EditorialRead moreThe failure of the talks surely came as a surprise to Donald Trump, who hadannounced thata deal was imminent. But as is so often the case, US negotiators had undermined their own position with a series of last-minute power moves, bullying the other side.In this way, the failure was reminiscent of the way the Trump administration continues to blow upits ownpeace dealsin the Middle East, by adding new conditions at the 11th hour and making false statements afterwards.Carney’s words stung, too. We expect student activists to speak truth to power; it’s a surprise when a former executive of Goldman Sachs and a former governor of the Bank of England takes on the role.He is no bomb-thrower. But no one can deny that his message reached the world; nothing confirms it so much as Trump’s frenzied counterattack on social media. Reading the flurry of puerile insults posted on Truth Social was like watching a punch-drunk boxer throwing sprawling haymakers at an adversary too nimble to be hit.In contrast to Carney’s sober tone, Trump hasthreatened to renameLake Ontario “Lake America”,called Canadian officials “clowns”, and dismissed Carney as a “governor” instead of a prime minister, as if contemptuous of Canada’s sovereignty. Of course, he laid the groundwork for Canada’s refusal to cave in as soon as he began his second term with aflurryof claimsthat Canada should become the 51st state.Unlike the easily-rattled president, the prime minister does not traffic in emotion. His speech was notable for its control of the facts and its unshakable moral authority. This was an economist’s speech, full of accounting.He began with greetings in both English and French – a subtle reminder that USattempts to strong-arm Canadainto relaxing its protections of the French language were never going to work. He promised to update Canadians on the issues behind the talks, then did just that.Carney furnished precise statistics, revealing just how intertwined the US and Canadian economies are (Canada buys more American cars than the UK, Japan and China combined, and supplies 99% of our natural gas imports). In all of these ways, the speech was like a quaint relic from a different era, when leaders were expected to convey the real truth to their people.There was also some solid rhetoric, as the speech gained intensity, and grew positively elbows up by the end. Carney referred to “the storm blowing in from Washington”, in a possible reference to the recent forest fires that darkened the relationship some more.Then he announced that Canada would be seeking to diversify its relationships abroad, in what is obviously a new policy, based on a near-total lack of trust in the United States, a nation that blusters so unpredictably on the world stage that it is as if “its signature was written in pencil”.Canada is far from perfect; it has faced a threat of secession from Francophone Quebec for generations; and there are new murmurs of secession-talk in Alberta. For centuries it was a “dominion” of the British empire, and not clearly a sovereign nation. But its graveyards are filled with tens of thousands of soldiers who served in the first and second world wars; Canadian resolve should never be underestimated.The loser in this negotiation is, of course, the United States. It’s not just the financial benefits that would have accrued from a successful deal (and the political benefits that would have come toRepublicansin swing states that neighbor Canada, such as Michigan and Maine).It’s a much larger loss than that. As with theproposed caseto annex Greenland, this was an entirely avoidable own goal that will damage US interests for a generation, as Canada seeks new relationships. As Carney said: “We are masters in our own home and the partner of choice abroad.” He added: “We have been under no illusions. We recognized from the start that America has changed.”Those words should alarm all Americans. We hear a great deal about the “special relationship” that links the UK and the US, and it has often been very important, as it was in the second world war.Canadians do not seek a trade war – but nor will we be bullied by Donald Trump | Jen GersonRead moreBut the US-Canadian friendship is the healthiest foreign relationship the United States has ever enjoyed. Our economies are deeply connected; as are our militaries (and specifically the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or Norad, which has protected both nations from a Russian attack since 1958).We share the longest land border between two countries in the world, 5,525 miles long, and in most of our history we have barely worried about it. A huge state, Alaska, cannot be reached by land without going through Canada. In short, we need each other.And in general, we like each other. At least we did. But in 2025, Canadian tourism in the USdeclined25%, and US businesses are feeling it.The rapid disintegration of the friendship should hardly come as a surprise to any who have followed the rapid erosion of American standing in the world. But Carney’s words spelled out the why and how of this erosion with more clarity that we have heard in a long time. While Canada was proposing “long-term partnerships”, US negotiators were offering “short-term transactions”.That is not a strong foundation for a world order. While continuing to fantasize about Greenland, and raining down insults on Nato members, we are in danger of losing a much more important ally, close to home.Carney’s final words left little doubt about the path Canada has chosen. The words are beautiful, if tragic:“Canada is becoming stronger and less dependent on America. We are already giving ourselves more than they can take away. And we are just getting started. Canadians don’t submit to the weather – we thrive in it. We don’t wait to see which way the wind is blowing. Or surrender ourselves to the waves to be storm-tossed by events. We set our own course. We make our own weather.”Ted Widmer, a former White House speechwriter, is the editor of American Speeches, and the recently published The Living Declaration: A Biography of America’s Founding Text, both published by the Library of AmericaExplore more on these topicsMark CarneyOpinionCanadaUS politicsAmericasDonald TrumpRepublicansTrump administrationcommentShareReuse this content

title: Jed York’s trailer park arrest exposed inequality in America | San Francisco 49ers | The Guardian
description: The San Francisco 49ers owner’s arrest in Ohio over the weekend was quickly put behind him. Others are not so lucky
Author: Lee Escobedo
Headline: The San Francisco 49ers owner’s arrest in Ohio over the weekend was quickly put behind him. Others are not so lucky
Content: Jed York was arrested in Ohio on Sunday.Photograph: Getty ImagesJed York was arrested in Ohio on Sunday.Photograph: Getty ImagesSan Francisco 49ersJed York’s trailer park arrest exposed inequality in AmericaLee EscobedoThe San Francisco 49ers owner’s arrest in Ohio over the weekend was quickly put behind him. Others are not so luckyWed 26 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 09.34 EDTShareThe Wheat Hill Mobile Home Community sits off state Route 170, on the edge of East Palestine, Ohio, a town most Americans only learned about because a train derailed there in February 2023 andreleased toxic chemicals into the creek. I grew up in a trailer park like this one, and know the sights. The grid of aluminum boxes in rows. Skirting the color of old teeth, some of it buckled, some patched with a piece of lattice. The window units huff and puff in August, dripping dark condensation on to the gravel.I’m sure there were drugs on my street. I’m sure somebody was selling sex. I never saw it. What I saw were families raising kids in 800 square feet and people the country had already written off, living next to each other and mostly getting along.That’s the kind of place where police arrestedSan Francisco 49ersowner Jed York on the morning of 23 August.From Showtime to Insurance Time: how the LA Lakers became a $12.5bn hedge fund playRead moreAgents with the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force posted an undercover ad on a website known for prostitution. York answered it and agreed to pay a woman just $160 for sex, according to court records. There was no woman waiting for York. Dan Haueter, an East Palestine detective on the taskforce,described the method to the Ohio attorney general’s office in 2024: post an advertisement for sex online, negotiate a price with a prospective customer and arrange to meet in East Palestine. The sting worked because it’s based on real life. York carried the glowing phone he used to set the bargain to the trailer park, where officerstook him into custody.Police booked York on two counts: engaging in prostitution – which was later reduced to disorderly conduct – and possessing criminal tools (in this case, his cellphone).York pleaded no contest to the charges and was sentenced to two days in jail to be served concurrently and fined $1,150.Ohio charges buying sex from an adult as afirst-degree misdemeanorand sends the buyer to an education program.Selling is a third-degree misdemeanor. So the statute is harder on the buyer. But it helps a buyer like York if he can pay a high-powered lawyer to work on his case. York ended uppleading the count down to disorderly conduct.York is not the first NFL owner to find themselves in a situation like this. Florida prosecutors charged New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft in 2019 with soliciting prostitution at the Orchids of Asia spa in Jupiter, part of what police billed as a major human trafficking investigation. His lawyers challenged the hidden-camera warrants and won, andthe state dropped the charges in September 2020. By then, an assistant state attorney had alreadytold the court the investigation turned up no human trafficking. Prosecutors pressed ahead against four Chinese women who worked at Orchids of Asia instead. The women didn’t receive the same breaks. Instead, they receivedcriminal records and about $45,000 in fines.Nationwide, women account fornearly 64% of adult prostitution arrests. Rebecca Pfeffer, assistant professor of criminal justice at the University of Houston – Downtown, studied about 23,000 prostitution cases in Harris County, Texas, and found thatpolice arrested and jailed men less often than women. The women who landed in jail stayed there longer.My mom could support us because nothing on her record stopped her. Put a prostitution conviction on a woman two lots down, and the background check keeps her unemployed and desperate.TheNFL’s personal conduct policyis blunt about how owners should conduct themselves. The policy claims to hold owners to a higher standard than anyone else in the league, with stiffer consequences to match. A league spokesperson says York’s case will bereviewed under that policy. Kraft drew no discipline from the NFL afterFlorida dropped his charges in 2020. Owners write the rules, and theNFL commissioner they hire and pay enforces them. A standard like that lasts exactly as long as the owners want it to.But expecting those owners to hold themselves accountable is wishful thinking. The York situation would be less absurd if the US decriminalized the entire transaction for all parties.The ACLU reviewed the empirical research on how criminalization affects sex workers and foundthat police are a bigger threatto sex workers than clients are. Additionally, researchers from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health surveyed 250 women and found that22% had suffered violence from a client in the previous three months, while 78% had endured at least one abusive encounter with police. The numbers cover different time spans, so they aren’t a clean comp. But they make the same point. The police sent to protect women are also a danger to them. In that same cohort of women,70% had been locked up for more than three days, an average of 15 incarcerations apiece.Kate Shannon, associate professor of medicine at the University of British Columbia, and her colleagues looked at 87 studies and concluded that over the course of a decade,decriminalization could prevent 33% to 46%of projected HIV infections among female sex workers.In 2018,Congress passed a lawto fight trafficking. The law made websites liable for ads that facilitate prostitution, so the sites that sex workers used to advertise and vet clients shut down. ActivistsDanielle Blunt and Ariel Wolf surveyed sex workers, and 99% said the law did not make them feel safer. The Government Accountability Office reported in 2021 thatprosecutors had brought a single case under the law’s criminal provision, and no victim had received restitution.The three approaches to decriminalizing sex work get confused constantly, but they differ significantly.Legalizationkeeps prostitution a crime but makes exceptions for workers who register, get licensed or work in a permitted zone. The Nordic model,which Sweden adopted in 1999 and Canada, France and Northern Ireland later copied, makes selling sex legal and buying it a crime. The theory is that you protect the seller and punish the buyer. In practice, it’s mostly women who still lose.Clients who face arrest demand that sex workers meet them somewhere hidden– and possibly dangerous. Full decriminalization removes criminal penalties on both sides and regulates the work through labor and health law, as the state would handle any other job. Trafficking and assault laws still apply, and they are obviously more effective when a woman can walk into a police station without getting arrested.Most sex workers are just trying to survive, just as my mom was as a cashier.Median household income in East Palestineruns about $49,000. Last year, the York family sold off a small piece of the 49ers, a 6.2% stakefor more than $500m. Meanwhile, York’s penalty for his offense over the weekend cost him $1,150 (and, of course, when you’re rich any additional legal fees are easy enough to cover).A woman in Columbiana county once told an undercover officer that “no girls wanna go” to East Palestinebecause of the prostitution stings in the area.The county later convicted her of promoting prostitution anyway. York was arrested under the same chapter of Ohio law, and he was back on the road by Monday afternoon.Explore more on these topicsSan Francisco 49ersNFLRangersLeeds UnitedUS sportscommentShareReuse this content

title: With no friends left to burn, Trump is running out of diplomatic ammunition | Rafael Behr | The Guardian
description: Everyone can see that the Iran war has been a strategic disaster for the US, while a failing president pretends he is winning, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Author: Rafael Behr
Headline: Everyone can see that the Iran war has been a strategic disaster for the US, while a failing president pretends he is winning, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Content: An anti-US banner with the slogan ‘Great Victory’ in Tehran, Iran, 25 August 2026.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn anti-US banner with the slogan ‘Great Victory’ in Tehran, Iran, 25 August 2026.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpWith no friends left to burn, Trump is running out of diplomatic ammunitionRafael BehrEveryone can see that the Iran war has been a strategic disaster for the US, while a failing president pretends he is winningWed 26 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareNow is the twilight of Donald Trump’s supremacy. The US is still the richest and most heavily armed nation on Earth. That status is secure. The current president, contemptuous of law and indulged in lawlessness by a supine Congress, enjoys even greater power than the constitution allows.With those advantages it takes a special talent for incompetence to look as thwarted and impotent as Trump does with more than two years of his second term still to run.History will record the war againstIranas a turning point in the fortunes of the current US administration and a grievous wound to national prestige.Pumped with hubris after theaudacious military operation to kidnap Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro, Trump believed an equally brisk triumph was available in the Middle East. The Tehran regime would be decapitated. The country’s hydrocarbon resources would then be available for US exploitation.Six months later, Iran is controlled by a new generation of hardliners. Emboldened by resilience under US and Israeli bombardment, they demand financial concessions from Washington as the price for peace – reparations and a right to toll the strait of Hormuz.The war is not over, it has just turned cold. Trump believes Iran’s fragile economy is close to collapse. He threatens to push it over the brink with“D-day” sanctions. The metaphor of second world war amphibious assault is supposed to make yet another round of financial coercion succeed where past embargos have failed.It is true that ordinary Iranians are suffering terrible privations, but repression limits their capacity to translate discontent into demands for political change. By contrast, US consumers, aggrieved by the inflationary consequences of the war,and confused about its purpose,get to express their unhappiness in midterm elections in November.The calculation in Tehran is that American tolerance for economic pain is low enough that Trump will be forced to blink first. It is a reasonable assumption: the need to declare mission accomplished to a domestic audience – even on terms that amount to defeat by any objective measure – drives an impatient president’s actions more than long-term strategy.If sanctions fail, diplomatic climbdown is the only remaining move. The Pentagon couldn’t revert to the all-out military option even if Trump ordered it, becauseOperation Epic Fury burned too much of the national munitions stockpile.This is where an asymmetry of cost and capability comes into play. Iran can frighten ships out of the Gulf with a few mines. It can harry neighbouring states with drones knocked together for less than $50,000 and dispatched from mobile launchers that are hard to target. The Patriot interceptors that protect US forces and their allies in the region cost $4-5m apiece. (More than 1,500 Patriots arethought have been fired in the war so far, leaving fewer than 830 in the US inventory.)That depletion has global repercussions, most pressingly in Ukraine where top-end US interceptors are essential for shielding civilians from Russia’s most sophisticated ballistic missiles.Trump’s attitude to that conflict has evolved from craven pro-Kremlin partisanship and an assumption of inevitable Russian victory to grudging respect for Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s fortitude and ingenuity in proving that assumption wrong. But the shift is not stable. It depends on undertakings by Nato’s European members to cover the cost of arming Kyiv.If Trump had used normal diplomacy to cajole European democracies intofinancing the defence of their eastern flank, it would count as a foreign policy success – rebalancing the relationship to both sides’ benefit. But he did it with credulous admiration for Vladimir Putin and deranged demands for territory in Greenland. As a result, the European drive to autonomy looks less like burden-sharing and more like a hedge against American perfidy.It isn’t just Europe where US allies feel burned. Gulf states that found themselves on the frontline of Iranian retaliation in a war they didn’t start or want, expected a more reliable umbrella of protection. They feelunrewardedfor their decades of service, hosting US military bases and functioning as proxies for American interests in the region.Last week Trump abruptlycut short a joint military exercise with South Korea– a loyal Asian partner to the US. A rational explanation, and the one preferred by Seoul, was that US forces were overstretched by their Middle Eastern entanglement. Trump framed it instead as an amicable gesture towards North Korean tyrant Kim Jong-un, whose regime he judged to be “unthreatening and respectful”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSuch civility, lavished on a monstrous dictatorship, is withheld fromCanada, a benign democracy. Trump dismisses his northern neighbour as an economic freeloader, barely even a proper country; a mislabelled territory that should be the 51st US state.Unsurprisingly, that attitude sours relations. Canadian prime ministerMark Carneypulled out of trade talks last weekend, citing unreasonable last-minute demands from US negotiators. Trump responded with punitive tariffs, to which the Canadians promise “dollar-for-dollar” retaliation.The smaller economy is likely to suffer more from a trade war.
