But for Carney the cost in reduced commerce had to be weighed against the political damage he may incur if seen tocapitulate to Trump’s bullying. He knows the US president takes concessions as an invitation to come back with yet more demands. He also knows that November’s midterm elections are likely to flip the House of Representatives to Democratic party control, and possibly the Senate too.Trump cannot be chastened by unwelcome election results. He would rather deny their validity. But irrefutable evidence of failure at the ballot box may at least stir some Republicans out of stupefied obedience to a commander-in-chief whose way of governing has made their party less popular and left their country friendless.Even if the constitutional mechanisms that are supposed to keep a president in check are only partly rehabilitated, the spell of impunity is broken. The cult of personality that once made Trump look like an irrepressible force of nature has shrunk to a sycophantic sect. An administration that styled itself as a national revolution looks more like a kleptocratic junta, using the privileges of office to pilfer what it can as the clock runs down.The president still has followers across the country. A hardcore bring unshakable devotion to the cause. But even some of them can surely sense the decay of purpose and whiff of panic in a man running out of ammunition.Trump’s reign is far from over. With his hands on the levers of American power he can still do a lot of damage. But the rest of the world has learned to read his lurches, anticipate his spasms, manoeuvre around him. The phase of deference is past. Now is the time of planning for whatever comes next in the dimming light of a waning star.Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionIranUS-Israel war on IranUS foreign policyMiddle East and north AfricaCanadaMark CarneycommentShareReuse this content

title: Is the Trump Treasury panicking over the level of US debt? | Kenneth Rogoff | The Guardian
description: With the federal deficit near 6% of GDP and the national debt over $40tn, America’s fiscal position looks increasingly precarious
Author: Kenneth Rogoff
Headline: With the federal deficit near 6% of GDP and the national debt over $40tn, America’s fiscal position looks increasingly precarious
Content: ‘Scott Bessent’s ham-fisted attempt to control the bond market undermines his hard-earned credibility as the safest pair of hands on the Trump 2.0 economic team.’Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Scott Bessent’s ham-fisted attempt to control the bond market undermines his hard-earned credibility as the safest pair of hands on the Trump 2.0 economic team.’Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesProject Syndicate economistsUS Government borrowingIs the Trump Treasury panicking over the level of US debt?Kenneth RogoffWith the federal deficit near 6% of GDP and the national debt over $40tn, America’s fiscal position looks increasingly precariousBessent ‘will lose’ battle with bond markets, ex-mentor warnsWed 26 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareAre we seeing the first signs of panic in Donald Trump’s Treasury? The US is by far the world’s biggest debtor, and the steady rise in global long-term interest rates – which I havelong arguedwas inevitable – is starting to cause real pain.Until now, the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has dismissed concerns about US debt, which recentlysurpassed $40tn, as a big nothingburger. Growth, in his telling, will be so spectacular the US will easily be able to meet its interest obligations without any significant tax rises or spending cuts, while the rest of the world will happily keep feeding it money. But if Bessent really believes that, why is he trying to strong-arm the bond market byfiddling with the maturity structureof government debt?The obvious first move, and the one the markets are looking for, is to address the underlying problem by reining in America’s massive federal deficit, which is now running atroughly 6% of GDP. Bessent has repeatedly assured markets that the Trump administration’s voracious borrowing is temporary, and that AI-led growth will generate an abundance of tax revenues that will soon bring the deficit down to a somewhat more manageable 3% of GDP.Trump’s hypocritical new tariffs are a chance for the world to fight back | Joseph StiglitzRead moreThat could happen, but there aremany reasonsto think that pain-free budget consolidation is wishful thinking, not least because AI profits are likely to prove much harder to tax than labour income. In the near term, the costs of supporting an ageing population, paying for what appears to be aninevitable surgein military spending and caving to intense populist pressure for more public spending will probably rise at least as fast as revenues.Making matters worse, the premium on long-term US treasuries – a major part of the dollar’s “exorbitant privilege” as the global reserve currency – has largely evaporated. US debtno longertrades as a special safe asset relative to that of other advanced economies. The value of dollar dominance is thus fading even under the best of circumstances. And if budget pressures eventually trigger a crisis, the result could be a rapid loss of the dollar’s global market share that mightotherwise take decades.What, then, should the US Treasury do? The textbook answer, as Bessent well knows, is to take steps toward major budget consolidation, and not the blundering, heavy-handed random cuts that Elon Musk and his Doge acolytes pursued in 2025. Bessent’s problem is that his boss, Trump, understands that American taxpayers are not prepared for any kind of genuine austerity.That is why Bessent’s turn toward bond buyback gimmicks is worrying. In effect, Bessent is promising to take long-term debt out of the system and replace it with short-term debt, much as theFederal Reservedoes when it engages in quantitative easing. Such an approach can make sense in a panic, when there is a good chance long-term rates will come back down, but there is little evidence that the market is the one panicking right now.In fact, global long-term real interest rates are rising everywhere, suggesting that US exceptionalism no longer applies, at least not to the same degree. Bessent has argued for some time that long-term rates are too high, favouring short-term borrowing as a way to wait out the spike that he believes will soon subside.He may be right. Plenty of prominent economists, particularly those who have long insisted that interest rates would remain ultra-low for ever, still cling to the view that today’s elevated rates are an aberration. Unfortunately, studies based on historical data suggest that the recent increase is better thought of as anormalisationand that over the long term rates are more likely to rise than to fall.With the national debt now exceeding $40tn, this is not the time to tell investors that there is “nothing magic” about that number. Taken with the growing fiscal deficit, higher long-term interest rates and mounting spending pressures, America’s debt burden is a very real concern.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMore troubling still, Bessent’s ham-fisted attempt to control the bond market undermines his hard-earned credibility as the safest pair of hands on the Trump 2.0 economic team. Until now, Bessent has managed to steer Trump away from some – albeit not all – of his most damaging impulses, whether on tariffs or the appointment of the Fed chair. Of course, he has to toe the line on hot-button issues near and dear to Trump’s heart, insisting that the US has in effect defeated Iran and that nothing will benefit working Americans more than upending the international trade order. Otherwise, he would be fired immediately. But bond markets are not so easily pushed around.Bessent, the former bond trader and hedge fund manager, scored a major win when he supported the Argentinian peso last autumn, and he probably did not do too much damage by unexpectedly backing the Japanese yen over the summer, even if the effects faded fairly quickly. By contrast, his attempt at a Treasury-led quantitative easing has done little to stem the rise in long-term yields. Given that there is not going to be any meaningful debt reduction before November’s midterm elections, bond markets have good reason to remain deeply sceptical of America’s fiscal trajectory.Kenneth Rogoff is a professor of economics and public policy at Harvard University. He was the IMF’s chief economist from 2001 to 2003.©Project SyndicateExplore more on these topicsUS Government borrowingProject Syndicate economistsUS economyInflationEconomicsGlobal economyUS debt ceilingBondscommentShareReuse this content

title: What will we get out of the AI boom? The data suggests lots of noisy, energy-hungry datacentres and not much else  | Greg Jericho | The Guardian
description: Booms in investment usually lead to economic growth. But this one looks unlikely to translate into better living standards for Australians
Author: Greg Jericho
Headline: Booms in investment usually lead to economic growth. But this one looks unlikely to translate into better living standards for Australians
Content: Non-residential construction (which includes datacentres) has increased, but it is not at booming levels and wages have not been taking off.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersView image in fullscreenNon-residential construction (which includes datacentres) has increased, but it is not at booming levels and wages have not been taking off.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersGrogonomicsDatacentres - AustraliaWhat will we get out of the AI boom? The data suggests lots of noisy, energy-hungry datacentres and not much elseGreg JerichoBooms in investment usually lead to economic growth. But this one looks unlikely to translate into better living standards for AustraliansFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastWed 26 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 20.20 EDTShareThe debate around AI and datacentres is such that, to paraphrase Paul Keating, if you walked into any pet shop in Australia, the resident galah will be talking about it.I am on the record as being a sceptic of AI productivity booms, or the need to do all we can to make sure we are at the forefront of the AI revolution.Sure, there will be benefits in medical and scientific research. Does that require building datacentres in every vacant block of land in the country? And will medical and scientific research be the overarching use of these datacentres?Doubt it.Despite this, the one thing we are told is that it should lead to more economic growth. After all, that is just what happens when there is a boom in investment.Mega datacentre planned for outer Melbourne will be six times bigger than a large shopping centreRead moreExcept, as I noted whenthe March GDPfigures were released, the AI boom is not translating into anything that is leading to better living standards.I am not alone in being sceptical about this. TheAustralian Financial Reviewearlier this week asked: “We’re told business investment is key to boosting productivity, but what if the spending involves importing computer equipment?”This is the problem with the AI boom. The “investment” involves importing things like data processing chips, and any profits from the investment (should that even occur) flow overseas. Leaving us with … a lot of ugly, noisy, energy-hungry buildings?This is pertinent now because the June quarter GDP figures will be released next week. On Thursday we will get new investment figures, and government spending and trade figures will come next week.But the first set of GDP-related datawas the June quarter construction figuresreleased on Wednesday. In the quarter, overall construction fell 2.1% driven by a fall in engineering construction:If the graph does not display click hereAnd while non-residential building work (which includes datacentres) increased, it was not enough in the three months of the June quarter to cancel out the fall in engineering work.This suggests that total construction activity will detract about 0.3% pts from the June quarter GDP figures, whereas it contributed about 0.5% to the March quarter.The good news is that, because the construction and building work at the end of last year and early part of this year was big enough, overall construction work is still having a positive impact on the annual growth of the economy:If the graph does not display click hereBut these figures suggest that if there is going to be an increase in GDP in June it will not come from construction work, but will likely again have to come from “machinery and equipment” as was the case in March.That machinery and equipment is mostly those computer chips and air conditioners and other things going into the datacentres which are imported and which once installed generate little in the way of jobs or income for households.Australia’s drop in real wages is a disaster. But the profits of major corporations are doing just fine | GrogonomicsRead moreAnd yet the Reserve Bank of Australia has expressed concern that such investment is causing capacity constraints – that there is too much activity going on and inflation will go up as a result.You can understand them thinking that when we look at the total level of construction work (as opposed to the growth). In volume terms it is now higher than it was at the height of the mining boom:If the graph does not display click hereSuch a level would suggest Australia’s construction sector is bursting at the seams and the RBA is right to raise rates to try to slow down all the investment in new buildings – especially residential ones.Were that the case, however, you would expect wages for construction workers to be absolutely taking off (as happened in 2004-2006). But that is not the case. In the June quarter the average wage of construction workers in the private sector rose at an annual rate of just 3.3% – barely above the overall average for the private sector of 3.2%:If the graph does not display click hereOne reason, aside from the reality that despite what you might read workers don’t get whatever pay rise they demand, is that the level of construction work does not look as high when you compare it with the overall size of the economy:If the graph does not display click hereYes, the non-residential building work is at relatively high levels, but we are nowhere near the type of boom we saw in the 2000s:If the graph does not display click hereAnd so for now it appears the main economic impact of the AI boom will be computer chips bought from somewhere else, and we shall have to continue to wonder what really is the benefit from ever more datacentres and whether it will ever translate to wages and improved living standards.Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia InstituteExplore more on these topicsDatacentres - AustraliaGrogonomicsBusinessConstruction industryAustralian economyAI (artificial intelligence)commentShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham should rip up our undemocratic first past the post system – even if some in Labour disagree | Neal Lawson | The Guardian
description: Rearguard reactionaries may try to block the idea of a national commission into proportional representation, but we should want more not less democracy, says Neal Lawson, director of Compass
Author: Neal Lawson
Headline: Rearguard reactionaries may try to block the idea of a national commission into proportional representation, but we should want more not less democracy, says Neal Lawson, director of Compass
Content: Burnham speaking after his victory in the Makerfield byelection in June. The prime minister is a longstanding supporter of electoral reform.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBurnham speaking after his victory in the Makerfield byelection in June. The prime minister is a longstanding supporter of electoral reform.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesOpinionElectoral reformAndy Burnham should rip up our undemocratic first past the post system – even if some in Labour disagreeNeal LawsonRearguard reactionaries may try to block the idea of a national commission into proportional representation, but we should want more not less democracyWed 26 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 13.36 EDTShareApoll in the Mail on Sunday at the end of June was remarkable. It had not just Reform as low as 21%, but alsoLabourand the Tories. It was remarkable because it starkly demonstrated the fragmented landscape of the UK’s electoral terrain, as well as the electoral weakness of its main players.Polls since have varied, not least with the Burnham bounce, butthis week’s YouGov voting intention figuresput Reform, Labour and the Tories on 23%, 22% and 20% respectively (although it almost no longer matters which exact figure applies to which party). Add in the Greens and the Liberal Democrats on 13% apiece, the SNP dominating Scotland and Plaid Cymru Wales, then Restore UK and independent candidates and you have an unprecedented variety of options laid out before the British electorate.And all this despite the first past the post (FPTP) electoral system, which has for so long upheld two-party politics. It does so by punishing any party outside the duopoly by refusing to match votes to seats. If this unprecedented level of fragmentation exists in the face of a voting system that coerces people to back only their least bad option, then how diverse would this landscape be if people could vote with their heart and know that their vote really counted?This now complete mismatch between what voters want and what they get is the root cause of the governing crisis destabilising British politics. Labour won two-thirds of the seats in the Commons in 2024 on just a third of the vote, and its leadership assumed that this result conferred it legitimacy in the eyes of the public. But governments increasingly find that a Commons majority upheld by an unrepresentative voting system is more vulnerable to voter backlash. In this context, support quickly melts away, as Keir Starmer and Morgan McSweeney found out.If Britain continues under FPTP, then this governing chaos will deepen, and the only beneficiaries will be anti-democratic extremists.But now there is a golden chance to change all this. Next Wednesday, the representation of the people bill will come before parliament for its final stages. An amendment has been tabled to set up a national commission to look at which system of proportional representation (PR), which does match votes to seats, would best suit our country. It has huge backing in the Commons,in the Labour partyand among the public. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, is also alongstanding supporterof electoral reform. The political conditions have never been more favourable to begin making changes to the voting system. What could possibly go wrong?This: a minority but powerful view within the upper reaches of the Labour party, the cabinet and the party bureaucracy is vehemently opposed to PR and the plural politics of cooperation it demands. According to this tribal view, only Labour, governing alone, can represent the interests of “their voters”. And so it is preferable to lose all power than to share it. Labour winning – however tiny its share of the vote – is more important than democracy working. At best, those with this view may calculate whether PR or FPTP delivers the most Labour MPs, equating self-interest with the national interest.But all their paternalistic calculations miss the very big point: democracy should not be designed around what is best for Labour – or any party – but around what works best for the country.Labour’s rearguard reactionaries will try to block the idea of a national commission, water it down or kick it bureaucratically into touch. They will say only the cost of living matters, and that no one brings up PR on the doorstep. But it is precisely our rotten voting system that denies the changes people want, because it prioritises the cautious views of a few swing voters in a few swing seats and impels Labour to pander to them.The game is over for this old top-down, command-and-control politics. The myth of strong government from FPTP is dead. It is time for change, to do what Willy Brandt, the fabled leader of the German Social Democrats, implored the left to do in 1969, and “dare more democracy”. That means finally embracing multiparty government, and ensuring everyone’s vote is counted equally: it is the only way to end the cycle of chaos.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRadical Manchesterism beats in our prime minister’s heart. There, he made big changes happen by listening to voices beyond Labour and working cross-party to build a long-term consensus to transform a region. Next week, by backing himself and his best instincts on PR, he can transform the country.Neal Lawson is director of the cross-party campaign organisation CompassExplore more on these topicsElectoral reformOpinionLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: In Poland, compassion for Ukrainians has turned to contempt. The consequences could be dramatic | Mateusz Mazzini | The Guardian
description: Warsaw failed to anticipate that refugees would build new lives and Kyiv would demand an equal place at the European table, says Polish journalist Mateusz Mazzini
Author: Mateusz Mazzini
Headline: Warsaw failed to anticipate that refugees would build new lives and Kyiv would demand an equal place at the European table, says Polish journalist Mateusz Mazzini
Content: A protest against xenophobic attacks on Ukrainians at Szczepanski Square in Krakow, Poland, 9 August 2026.Photograph: Klaudia Radecka/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA protest against xenophobic attacks on Ukrainians at Szczepanski Square in Krakow, Poland, 9 August 2026.Photograph: Klaudia Radecka/NurPhoto/ShutterstockOpinionPolandIn Poland, compassion for Ukrainians has turned to contempt. The consequences could be dramaticMateusz MazziniWarsaw failed to anticipate that refugees would build new lives and Kyiv would demand an equal place at the European tableWed 26 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 03.16 EDTShareOne of the unintended consequences of Russia’s full-scale war againstUkrainewas that it gave Poland a rare slice of geopolitical stardom. When Russian tanks started their ultimately unsuccessful cavalcade towards the Ukrainian capital, ordinary Poles rushed to help millions of people fleeing the looming conflict. As Polish people opened their doors to civilians running from Russian bombs, even the then ruling populist Law and Justice party had to follow suit.It seemed that Poland and Ukraine were bound for an iron-clad alliance, unprecedented in their shared history. Polandadvocated for the Ukrainian cause in the west, with some success. Ukrainian leaders, in turn, praised Poles for their generosity and the government in Warsaw for contributing weapons and money to the war effort. Given that recent history between the two countries had been marked by accusations of second world war-era genocide, border shifts and postwar displacements of millions of people, it was a remarkable change.But it has not lasted. According to aan opinion poll by CBOS, Poland’s largest polling institution last month, 52% of Poles now oppose their country accepting Ukrainian refugees. A steadily growing number are becoming weary of supporting Kyiv, with many rightwingers arguing that weapons transfershave depleted Poland’s own capacityto defend against a potential Russian incursion.Memory politics has unhelpfully reared its head after Volodymyr Zelenskyy named a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a branch of which massacred about 100,000 Poles in 1943. The Polish right responded in kind, and the president, Karol Nawrocki,revoked Zelenskyy’s Order of the White Eagle, the highest state honour available to non-Poles. Both sides refused to back down, returning further honours and pretty much freezing mutual relations.This is all great fodder for the Russian propaganda thatruns amok on Polish social media. Misinformation about Ukrainian “welfare queens” claiming benefits at the expense of hard-working local people is fuelling tensions that, increasingly, turn to violence. A particularly vicious incident took place on 26 July,when a young Ukrainian couple was attackedoutside a grocery store in Wrocław. The suspected attackers allegedly shouted, “go away to war”. Headlines trickle out almost daily about Ukrainian citizens being verbally abused or physically attacked in Polish streets.Personal spats between leaders, historical disputes, Russian influence – these are some of the many reasons why the honeymoon is over. But another dimension of this deteriorating relationship keeps being overlooked. In dealing with the urgent fallout of the conflict, neither country had done enough to understand each other beyond the war. That failure is now coming back to haunt them.To put it bluntly, Poland had failed to fully realise that Ukrainians were not just helpless victims of Vladimir Putin, but actual people with agency. As soon as they could, many Ukrainian refugees moved out of their hosts’ living rooms and rented or bought apartments.They set up businesses, many of which are now flourishing, and created a robust community, often engaging in direct competition with local people. They refused to behave as grateful or passive recipients of Polish charity. This is an understandable, indeed desirable progression, but as a result, compassion ceased to be the currency of the relationship between Poles and Ukrainians. For Poland, a country nearly entirely ethnically homogenous since its postwar years, such a change became difficult, if not impossible, to handle.But Ukraine is of course, a country like any other, with a large economy and national interests beyond its resistance to Putin’s war of aggression. It has evolved from passive recipient of western aid in the aftermath of the full-scale invasion in 2022, to a global exporter of new military technology and knowhow. Accustomed to direct talks with US and western European leaders, Ukranians do not need an “advocate”, certainly not in Warsaw. Zelenskyy can run his own show.What emerges, therefore, is contempt in place of cooperation, and hate in place of hope. The initial enthusiasm was bound eventually to disappear, and both governments should have prepared for that. Instead, they allowed a vacuum to be filled by Russian misinformation aimed at pulling the two countries further apart, thus weakening Europe’s support for Ukraine. Such an outcome could and should have been avoided, especially by Donald Tusk’s liberal governing coalition.It failed to recognise Ukraine’s growing ambitions and continued to feed the myth that Warsaw was destined to play a Promethean role in Kyiv’s future. It did not prepare its own people for accepting refugees as fully fledged members of society. And it fostered the delusion that it wasPolandthat, somehow, had a decisive vote on whether Ukraine enters democratic Europe.Poland’s shortsightedness is a cautionary tale. Whatever happens in the next few years, it seems certain that Ukraine will be drawn closer to Europe, and Ukrainians closer to the European economies. They will become business competitors to the French and Germans, just as they have been to the Poles. Ukrainian leaders will come to Brussels, Paris and Berlin, asking not for free bullets and money, but for an equal voice, arguing that their defence of the continent against Russian barbarism has earned them a seat at the table.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNone of this should come as a surprise: Ukrainians are more than victims, and Ukraine is more than a country at war. Poland’s failure to take this into account has already had dramatic consequences. The rest of Europe still has time to prepare for that obvious reality.Mateusz Mazzini is a Warsaw-based journalist writing on global affairs for Poland’s Gazeta Wyborcza and PolitykaDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsPolandOpinionUkraineRussiaVolodymyr ZelenskyyKarol NawrockiDonald TuskEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: It shouldn’t be a secret who the prime minister has dinner with, and what was discussed. Australians deserve to know | Geoffrey Watson | The Guardian
description: Any money being paid to dine with Anthony Albanese should be a matter of public record
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Any money being paid to dine with Anthony Albanese should be a matter of public record
Content: ‘I agree with Anthony Albanese – we need urgently to restore faith in the system. Maybe we could start by cutting out the dinners with billionaires,’ writes Geoffrey Watson.Photograph: Matt Jelonek/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I agree with Anthony Albanese – we need urgently to restore faith in the system. Maybe we could start by cutting out the dinners with billionaires,’ writes Geoffrey Watson.Photograph: Matt Jelonek/Getty ImagesOpinionAnthony AlbaneseIt shouldn’t be a secret who the prime minister has dinner with, and what was discussed. Australians deserve to knowGeoffrey WatsonAny money being paid to dine with Anthony Albanese should be a matter of public recordFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTue 25 Aug 2026 23.24 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 02.13 EDTShareOur prime minister was quite right when he recently pointed out that diminishing public trust in our politicians and political system is a matter of pressing public importance. We all know this to be true: there is a sense that politicians are inaccessible and remote from our everyday problems, whether it is cost of living or housing. The perception is that the politicians are not listening to us.So I’m wondering, did Anthony Albanese raise these issues when dining at themultimillion-dollar home of a billionaire’s son? Or at either of the recent dinners, held inmansions in Adelaide and Perth, where a select group reportedly paid $10,000 each to dine alongside him?I guess not.double quotation markThese dinners are all about getting access to the decision-makersNot that we will ever know – because these were private dinners and what was said, what was discussed, is also private, only to be known by those who could afford to be invited. Albanese made that clear – “I don’t talk about private dinners,” he said.There are so many problems with this.No one pays money unless there is some value to be gained from paying it. Any motive cannot be waved away by suggesting that these were people interested in supporting democracy – if they were, they could have made a direct donation. No, these dinners are all about getting access to the decision-makers.The major parties had several chances to meet the moment. Instead they chose to safeguard their collective mediocrity | Zoe DanielRead moreSome of the attendees were reportedly from public companies and may owe a fiduciary duty to shareholders to get value for money. Presumably national matters of planning and policy were under discussion – potentially valuable information to the public. Perhaps there was a chance to persuade the prime minister toward a certain point of view. Whatever happened, this is all very wrong: there should be no occasions when information of general public importance is shared by our politicians with a select audience – if that group can know, then we are all entitled to know.It is also problematic that the price of participating is apparently so high. Only the powerful are welcome; only the rich are permitted to play.It is also unfair to smaller parties and to independents. Only the major parties can hold these sorts of fundraising events; only those who can make the big decisions can attract the big money. The funding system is already skewed to favour the major parties – so why not tip the scales further with a serving of caviar?The current system is flawed. The disclosure rules surrounding political donations are inadequate. When asked to provide the details of one of the dinners – eg how much money changed hands – the response from government frontbenchers was “that is a matter for the party”. What does that even mean? How is that an excuse for not immediately revealing the details on a matter of public interest? Any money being paid to dine with the PM should be a matter of public record – why is it a secret?It seems our system, which has always bent toward the rich and the powerful, is now being bent to breaking point. Unrestrained spending backed by unrestricted donations is not working. Elections, ideally, are a contest of ideas; they are increasingly becoming a contest of bank accounts. Right now in Australia billionaires seem to be vying to own their own political parties.double quotation markElections, ideally, are a contest of ideas; they are increasingly becoming a contest of bank accountsI agree with Albanese – we need urgently to restore faith in the system. Maybe we could start by cutting out the dinners with billionaires. It might be difficult to get both sides to agree to that, but one might think that the ALP – as the party claiming to represent ordinary Australians – could make such a concession.It is time to break the donation/spending cycle. A package of federal reforms has passed, but they are hopelessly biased in favour of the major parties – a rare instance of bipartisan policymaking. The most slanted components of the package have been challenged in the high court for infringing of the implied freedom of political communication and it is unclear as to whether, if the challenge succeeds, the balance of the reforms will proceed. We need to do something and I fear, given their inherent conflict of interest, that politicians cannot be trusted to do it properly.Albanese helpfully explains away his recent dinners with an airy “elections cost money” claim. Well that is true – but what is the true cost? Should the involvement of money in our election system come at the cost of the integrity of the whole system?Geoffrey Watson SC is a board member at the Centre for Public IntegrityExplore more on these topicsAnthony AlbaneseOpinionLabor partyAustralian politicsBusinesscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on child marriage: girls should not be wives | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: There’s growing agreement that under-18s need to be protected – but international turmoil is pushing many towards wedlock
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: There’s growing agreement that under-18s need to be protected – but international turmoil is pushing many towards wedlock
Content: A billboard features the president and first lady in Sierra Leone, which raised the minimum marriage age to 18 in 2024.Photograph: Saidu Bah/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA billboard features the president and first lady in Sierra Leone, which raised the minimum marriage age to 18 in 2024.Photograph: Saidu Bah/The GuardianOpinionChild marriageThe Guardian view on child marriage: girls should not be wivesEditorialThere’s growing agreement that under-18s need to be protected – but international turmoil is pushing many towards wedlockWed 26 Aug 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareEvery minute, 23 girls around the world wed, according to theGirls Not Bridescampaign, a coalition of more than 1,000 organisations across 100 countries. No child should be married. But girls are far more likely to be affected than boys, accounting for nine in 10 of those wed before 18, and their spouses are often much older men. The consequences, beyond the immediate threat of sexual violence, include the shortening of their education, increased risks of poverty and domestic abuse, and poor health, including high rates of maternal mortality. In spring, the Center for Global Development thinktankestimatedthat child marriage costs $175bn annually in lost productivity and increased health risks.The good news is that the last decade has seen a drop in rates; last year alone, Grenada, Bolivia, Burkina Faso, Kuwait and Portugal introduced bans. But there are disturbing signs of regression elsewhere. In May, the Talibanissued a new judicial codeenabling child marriage below the previous minimum age of 16, and preventing wives from ending marriages they entered as children if their husbands object. Previous protections were inadequate and often poorly enforced; now even those have been swept away. Activists say forced and early marriages have soared since the Taliban returned to power in 2021, thanks to the ban on secondary education and the state of the economy.Child marriage is almost double the global average in countries experiencing conflict or other crises, with more than one in three girls marrying before they turn 18, Girls Not Bridesreports. The breakdown of economic and support systems, and the exacerbation of factors driving child marriage, such as patriarchal values, can leave families seeing marriage as the only way to protect their daughters – even though they frequently face violence from their husbands. In Gaza, the rate of child marriages dropped from more than 28% in 2009 to just under 18% in 2022. The war has reversed that progress, says the UN Population Fund, with case workers reporting steeply rising rates.Yet child marriage happens in the developing world too. Under-18s could marry in all 50 states of the US until 2018; 17 states have now passed bans, but three – New Mexico, California and Mississippi –still have no age floor. England and Wales raised the minimum age to 18 in 2023; in Northern Ireland, those aged 16 and older can marry with parental consent, and in Scotland they can marry without it. In Australia, 16- and 17-year-oldsmay marry“in exceptional circumstances”.There is still cause for optimism. Although laws are often evaded – sometimes through corruption, more frequently because marriages are not officially registered – they still send an important message. In Sierra Leone, which raised the minimum marriage age to 18 in 2024,the first trial has begunover the forcible marriage of a 17-year-old. Four men, including the girl’s father and alleged groom, face jail sentences of at least 15 years or fines. The new law allows even guests at the wedding of a child to be imprisoned.Advocacy targeting girls as well as their communities is essential, helping some to resist marriage. Cuts to overseas aid now threaten such work.Child marriagewill not end until girls also have educational and economic opportunities, reproductive healthcare and some measure of security. This must be a priority.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsChild marriageOpinionViolence against women and girlsWomen's rights and gender equalityReproductive rightsTalibanSierra LeoneAfghanistaneditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Tim Curry, star of The Rocky Horror Picture Show and Stephen King’s It, dies aged 80 | Movies | The Guardian
description: A prolific performer across stage, screen and TV, the actor starred in Legend, Clue and It, but will always be associated with the flamboyantly camp rock’n’roll musical in which he made his breakthrough
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: A prolific performer across stage, screen and TV, the actor starred in Legend, Clue and It, but will always be associated with the flamboyantly camp rock’n’roll musical in which he made his breakthrough
Content: Mr versatility ... Tim Curry in 2008Photograph: Michael Tran/FilmMagicView image in fullscreenMr versatility ... Tim Curry in 2008Photograph: Michael Tran/FilmMagicMoviesTim Curry, star of The Rocky Horror Picture Show and Stephen King’s It, dies aged 80A prolific performer across stage, screen and TV, the actor starred in Legend, Clue and It, but will always be associated with the flamboyantly camp rock’n’roll musical in which he made his breakthroughTim Curry on sexuality, surviving a stroke – and 50 years of stardomFarewell, Dr Frank N Furter: why Tim Curry’s Rocky Horror Show will go onClowns, corsets and kings: Tim Curry – a life in picturesAndrew PulverWed 26 Aug 2026 11.47 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 17.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTim Curry, the versatile performer of screen and stage, who made his name as the flamboyant Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Show, has died aged 80.Reports sayCurry died at his home in Los Angeles.Farewell, Dr Frank N Furter: why Tim Curry’s Rocky Horror Show will go onRead moreThe actor’s manager confirmed to Variety that he died peacefully. No cause of death is known as yet.Ironically, Curry’s best-known roles all required a considerable physical transformation, to the extent that he was unrecognisable in all of them. Frank-N-Furter, Rocky Horror’s deranged scientist, saw him daubed in garish makeup and wearing stockings and suspenders, for the stage show (which debuted in 1973) and the film adaptation (released in 1975). In the Ridley Scott-directed fantasy Legend (1985), he was equipped with giant horns and scarlet skin as the Lord of Darkness. And in 1990, Curry was transformed with full-face clown pancake to play Pennywise in the TV miniseries It, based on theStephen Kingnovel.View image in fullscreen… Tim Curry in The Rocky Horror Picture Show.Photograph: PRAlongside these show-stopping incarnations, Curry enjoyed a successful parallel career in film, TV and theatre. Born in 1946, he earned a degree in drama and English from the University of Birmingham in 1968 and embarked on a stage career. His first significant role was in the original cast for the first West End production of the controversial musical Hair, in 1968 – where he met Richard O’Brien, who would go on to cast him in his own musical, TheRocky Horror Show. Curry went on to play Tristan Tzara in Tom Stoppard’s Travesties (taking over the role from John Hurt and Robert Powell), and Mozart in the Broadway transfer of Amadeus in 1980. Later highlights included King Arthur in the Broadway run of the Monty Python musical Spamalot.‘Risky is the best way to be’: Tim Curry on sexuality, surviving a stroke – and 50 years of stardomRead moreCurry worked regularly in film, in roles including that of Robert Graves in Jerzy Skolimowski’s sinister The Shout, and later as Jeremy in the Ian McEwan-scripted political drama The Ploughman’s Lunch. Later, Curry found himself working largely in comedies – including Home Alone 2: Lost in New York, Muppet Treasure Island, Scary Movie 2, and McHale’s Navy – before providing voiceovers for numerous animated films, such as Garfield: A Tail of Two Kitties, A Turtle’s Tale: Sammy’s Adventures and Ribbit.View image in fullscreenPennywise for them … Tim Curry as the killer clown in It.Photograph: Allstar/Cinetext/Lorimar TelevisionCurry was also a regular presence on TV for more than four decades, playingWilliam Shakespearein John Mortimer’s six-part biography of the playwright in 1978, Bill Sikes in the 1982 US TV adaptation of Oliver Twist, and the wizard Trymon in the adaptation of Terry Pratchett’s The Colour of Magic in 2008. He voiced a stream of animated series (Duckman, Sonic the Hedgehog, The Mask and Star Wars: The Clone Wars) and was cast in many guest roles in established series, including Psych, Poirot and Criminal Minds.“I’ve had the opportunities,” he said to theGuardian in 2025, “and I’m still showing up. You know? I think that’s what you have to do. You have to keep showing up.”Clowns, corsets and kings: Tim Curry – a life in picturesRead moreIn 2012, Curry had a stroke while receiving a massage and received brain surgery. He was left with mobility issues and his short-term memory was also affected. “It was an odd thing, because my father had a stroke and died very soon afterwards,” he said. “I knew I had to force myself to relax and just take the opportunity to float a little.”In 2025, he released his memoir Vagabond.“I’m very aware that I’m lucky,” Curry said last year. “I’m astonished actually at how ambitious I’ve been. I didn’t think of myself as ambitious at all.”Luke Evans, who played the role of Dr Frank-N-Furter in the recent Broadway production of The Rocky Horror Show, paid tribute onInstagram. The actor called him “a force, a bright fierce flame” and “an inspiration”. He added: “There will only be one Tim Curry.”Rocky Horror Picture Show co-star Susan Sarandoncalledhim a “funny sexy original” in an online post. “Even wheelchair bound he continued to be so sweet and generous with his fans,” she wrote. “Thank you Tim for meaning so much to so many people.”Carol Burnett, who starred with Curry in Annie, also paid tributeonline. “Nobody could play lovable villains better than he could,” she wrote. “He was a dear friend. I was blessed to know him.”Curry’s Clue co-star Michael McKeansharedon X: “My last conversation with Tim Curry was about life and love and laughter. The grim physical state he found himself in has now ended, a blessing. Our blessing was that we had Tim Curry in our lives. RIP, my friend.”Explore more on these topicsFilmTim CurryRocky Horror ShowLegendStephen KingFilm adaptationsTelevisionShareReuse this content

title: A Ugandan quarry worker carrying rocks on her head: Dan Nelken’s best photograph | Art and design | The Guardian
description: ‘Janet had eight children. Her husband drove a boda-boda taxi, but had lost a leg – so she had been working in her local quarry for 10 years. “I am now the husband in this home,” she said’
Author: Chris Broughton
Headline: ‘Janet had eight children. Her husband drove a boda-boda taxi, but had lost a leg – so she had been working in her local quarry for 10 years. “I am now the husband in this home,” she said’
Content: ‘Many of the women had small children or babies with them, yet most dressed as though they were going to market’ … Janet by Dan Nelken.Photograph: Dan NelkenView image in fullscreen‘Many of the women had small children or babies with them, yet most dressed as though they were going to market’ … Janet by Dan Nelken.Photograph: Dan NelkenMy best shotArt and designA Ugandan quarry worker carrying rocks on her head: Dan Nelken’s best photograph‘Janet had eight children. Her husband drove a boda-boda taxi, but had lost a leg – so she had been working in her local quarry for 10 years. “I am now the husband in this home,” she said’Interview byChris BroughtonWed 26 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2017, my wife, Adele Brown, was invited to spend three weeks at an NGO in Gulu,Uganda, teaching critical thinking skills to blind high school-age students. I was asked along to document the organisation’s activities. I became fascinated by the town’s main market, where vendors sold goods such as used clothes, fruit and firewood. I asked the Ugandan teachers how I might approach someone to take their portrait. They suggested I offer a modest “model fee” after seeking permission.One of the students – Emmanuel (Emma) – wanted to assist me. We would visit the market together. When I saw a vendor I wanted to photograph, Emma would approach and seek their consent. Most agreed, but after returning home to New York, I looked at the results and was disappointed. As with other well-intentioned projects, I thought that was the end of it.The images weren’t working because I felt the vendors were getting lost in their own environment – the backgrounds were too distracting. Adele and I were asked back to the NGO the following year, and this gave me the opportunity to resolve this issue. My eureka moment came when I decided the backdrop I needed was mosquito-netting. This allowed the women to stand out from their working environment while still letting their surroundings come through. The netting also added the symbolism of malaria, one of Uganda’s biggest health problems.double quotation markThe oldest woman I photographed at the quarry was 74. Another had lost an eye as a result of working thereMy wife and I noticed that women seemed to be doing nearly all the work, and that became the theme of my project. Emma mentioned a quarry about 10 miles outside town. The women who worked there were breaking rocks all day, reducing them to gravel size and being paid for each jerrycan they filled. Some had small children or babies with them, yet most dressed as though they were going to market – some even wore jewellery.I encouraged each woman to choose her own pose, giving her full control over how she wanted to be seen. The oldest woman I photographed at the quarry was 74. Another had lost an eye as a result of working there. But like all the women I photographed, they projected real dignity and a strong sense of self.I was keen to photograph as wide an economic spectrum as possible – women with their own businesses, as well as those at the bottom of the economic ladder. I wanted to know the women’s stories, too, so I collaborated with Ugandan author Beatrice Lamwaka, who interviewed each participant about her circumstances: what had led to her doing the work she did, her hopes and dreams for herself and her children. Northern Uganda is still dealing with the trauma of the civil war and this came through in several of the women’s narratives.This is Janet, who had been working in the quarry for 10 years when I photographed her. She had eight children to support and, like many of the women we spoke to, she was doing this alone. Her husband, who used to drive a type of motorbike-taxi called a boda boda, had been in an accident and lost a leg. “I am now the husband in this home,” she said, “and I have to do whatever I can to keep this house standing.” Many of the women had started working at the quarry as children because that’s what their mothers were doing. My portraits also included one of 10-year-old Jovia, who had been working there on weekends for four years to help pay her school fees – she wanted to become a doctor.I called the projectHeadStrongand was overwhelmed at how enthusiastic many of the women were when I went back to them with prints. I think photographers had sometimes shown interest before and then never been seen again. I am forever grateful to the 116 women who trusted me to take their portraits. They are the heroes of this project.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Dan NelkenDan Nelken’s CVBorn:1946, Tel AvivHighpoint:HeadStrongstands out as my most meaningful project. My hope is that the book will introduce readers to a group of remarkable women who, from their Ugandan perspectives, share a universal story of hope, often in the face of adversity, and aspire to build a better life for themselves and their children.Toptip:No matter what project you undertake, stay open-minded. Often, the direction I thought I was headed when I began new work deviated in unexpected ways that ultimately improved my original concept. And it often takes longer than you plan.See more atdannelken.comor on Instagram@headstrong_ugExplore more on these topicsArt and designMy best shotUgandaPhotographyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘9 to 5? She was full-on round the clock!’ Dolly Parton celebrated by kd lang, Peggy Seeger, Annie Lennox and more | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: Musicians and performers pay tribute to the country legend who managed to be a generational talent, a formidable entrepreneur, a dedicated philanthropist and a truly kind person
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: Musicians and performers pay tribute to the country legend who managed to be a generational talent, a formidable entrepreneur, a dedicated philanthropist and a truly kind person
Content: ‘She was in a class of her own’ … Dolly Parton in 1978.Photograph: Richard E Aaron/RedfernsView image in fullscreen‘She was in a class of her own’ … Dolly Parton in 1978.Photograph: Richard E Aaron/RedfernsDolly Parton‘9 to 5? She was full-on round the clock!’ Dolly Parton celebrated by kd lang, Peggy Seeger, Annie Lennox and moreMusicians and performers pay tribute to the country legend who managed to be a generational talent, a formidable entrepreneur, a dedicated philanthropist and a truly kind personAs told toDave SimpsonandOwen MyersWed 26 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 22.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Not just a big-bosomed singer of great songs’Shirley Collins, singer-songwriterI don’t really follow pop music or country and western very much, butDolly Partonwas always something special – separate from it all, in a way. She seemed absolutely indomitable. Coming from a large family in a mountain home and being brought up in poverty, she broke through to have this incredible career and you couldn’t help feeling fond of her. How she did it I don’t know, but nothing seemed to faze her.I was always impressed by her perception of things. Like in Jolene, the carelessness of someone taking someone’s husband “just because [she] can” is really clever. Dolly could see stuff and then write about it in ways that nobody else could.A few years ago, someone sent me a book called The Pack Horse Library, about women in the Appalachians in the 1930s who rode pack horses or mules in this wilderness country and took library books to all the isolated cabins with huge families, who wouldn’t normally get near a library. In modern times, Dolly has done exactly the same thing, but on such a massive scale,posting books to children around the world. She wasn’t just a big-bosomed singer of great songs – and she wrote so, so many great songs – but a fabulous human being. I think we’re all really rather privileged to have been able to see her.I wouldn’t talk like this about any other pop singer, but as a singer and a person she was in a class of her own. It’s a sad, sad day, but people will always think of her and smile.‘She embodied the ideal of live and let live’kd lang, singer-songwriterView image in fullscreenkd lang.Photograph: Carolyn Contino/BEI/ShutterstockShe was a plain-clothed prophet. She transcended all misconceptions of what a Christian is, what an American is, what an artist is or what an ally is. She came from a southern, Christian, country and western place and she never wavered inher support of the LGBTQ+ communityor the Black community – all those that have suffered at the hands of those with a far-right mentality.I believe in the divine timing of things and I think that, in her departure, there’s a gift, too, because I can’t think of anyone who had a more cohesive effect on people than Dolly Parton. Her exaggerated physical presence – her hair and her boobs and her hips and her clothes – was a caricature, one we sometimes laughed at. But the joke was on us, because she embraced who she was and never judged anyone else. She truly embodied that way of being – just live and let live.Of all her songs, I really likeCoat of Many Colors. I’m not a Christian, but there’s something so down-home about that. I truly believe that it is a story from Dolly’s life. She used the tools she was given and one of them was being from a large country family that was raised Christian. She took the very essence of the teachings and illuminated them to the highest degree. May she have a swift rebirth.‘She sent me a big, home-cooked meal’Joan Osborne, singer-songwriterView image in fullscreenJoan Osborne in London, 2024.Photograph: Robin Little/RedfernsI had the honour of singing her songDo I Ever Cross Your Mind?for a Dolly compilation called Just Because I’m a Woman in the early 00s. During the recording session, she sent over a big, home-cooked meal, that she had made herself, to give to the musicians and me so we wouldn’t get hungry while we worked. When the album was done, she sent me a very gracious handwritten letter, saying that my version of her song had made her cry. I wish I could lay my hands on that letter right now. It’s buried somewhere in my archives. But I do remember it very well and someday I’ll unearth it and frame it for my studio.I always admired the way that Dolly hid in plain sight. She was an immensely talented songwriter and beautiful singer, a serious artist and a brilliant businesswoman, but she wrapped herself in the disguise of a comic blond bombshell. Her presentation was probably a result, at least in part, of her desire to fulfil the fantasies of a little girl who grew up in poverty, but it was also a very smart career strategy.‘She was honest, brash, daring and way ahead of her time’Peggy Seeger, singer-songwriterDolly was a one-off – and I mean off the wall. Honest, brash, daring and way ahead of her time, yet very present in her own time. She wasn’t a 9 to 5 woman; she was full-on round the clock. I followed her career throughout and adored everything she did. She’s left us way too soon, yet left us so much.‘Her presence could fill 10 football stadiums’Annie Lennox, singer-songwriterView image in fullscreenAnnie Lennox(far right)at the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony with Dolly Parton(centre).Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for The Rock and Roll Hall of FameOn 5 November 2022, Eurythmics had the unforgettable experience of performing Jolene with the legendary Dolly Parton, joining alongside an exceptional mix of musical acolytes, representing a cross-section of musicians who were all being inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. When we arrived for the dress rehearsal, there she was, standing centre stage, a surprisingly tiny figure in vertiginous high-heeled boots and full rocker regalia, dressed head to toe in a figure-hugging outfit of black skintight PVC, adorned with suspended pendants of silver chains. As tiny as she was, her presence was big enough to fill 10 football stadiums.She was warm and personable, with a tremendously dry sense of humour. We all felt extremely favoured to be part of that song performance. It was a special moment with no pedestals in sight … except for the one we placed her upon that night.Rest in power, Dolly Parton … the REAL deal.‘She came along like Attack of the 50 Foot Woman’Billy Bragg, singer-songwriterView image in fullscreenBilly Bragg.Photograph: Guitarist Magazine/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesWe’ve lost someone who was an embodiment of a type of American exceptionalism that has been eclipsed by the Trump carnival of people who say: “Empathy is toxic.” She was the opposite of that. Her faith was based on the idea that, as she once said: “I just want everybody to be treated good.” That quote came from someoneasking her about anti-trans legislationin her home state of Tennessee. She didn’t hedge it. She went on to say: “We are all God’s children and how we are is who we are.” She didn’t stop at trans people, or American people, or white people. She extended that to everybody.When people are saying empathy is toxic, you need someone like Dolly Parton to come along like the Attack of the 50 Foot Woman and put them back in their box. Everyone talks about a divided America, but her superpower was to bring people together. She completely transcended her role and became a universal figure, a bit like the queen, and similarly the reaction to her passing has been exceptional.Obviously, as a songwriter, she was incredible. Everyone knows about the great songs that have been all over the radio in the last 24 hours, but for me her artistry also lies in the more obscure songs such as Do I Ever Cross Your Mind? – the chord changes are to die for – orDown from Dover, a heartbreaking song where a young woman is pregnant and waiting for her boyfriend to come back. He doesn’t come and the baby dies. It’s a heart-rending song that doesn’t just put the position of unwed young women at the centre; it also plumbs into that great Appalachian tradition of tragedy songs, which she heard when she was growing up and will have seen first-hand.She was tougher than any man. Her second album was called Just Because I’m a Woman. She was saying: don’t be messing with me, because I see through your pernicious attitudes towards me as a woman and I’m gonna turn that back on you. And she was incredibly powerful at doing that. She had kindness and empathy, but she wasn’t like a little flower. She had the strength to broadcast her empathy to the world. She was the epitome of that rhinestone, vaudeville, bouffant, over-the-top America that I’ve always been attracted to, but also the best of humanity. She really was the best of us.‘She silenced the crowd at Glastonbury’Jonny Woo, drag performerView image in fullscreenJonny Woo’s troupe at Glastonbury in 2014.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverEveryone loved Dolly. How could you not? She was the archetype of joy and beauty and generosity – and the music was amazing. The first time she came into my psyche was watching her in9 to 5and she’s the best person I’ve seen at Glastonbury in 20 years of going. When she was talking, just in her normal voice, the crowd were absolutely silent. Her voice was immaculate. Her storytelling was just joyous. I think there were more people watching her than the Rolling Stones.So, of course, my drag troupe and I all dressed up as her. That image is so joyous. It’s not derogatory to call her a camp icon. Like Céline Dion or Cher, she was very aware of the pleasure of her visual appeal. They’re celebratory and stylish, using their femininity and sexuality to lift your mood.9 to 5 review – Dolly Parton’s quietly radical office revenge satireRead moreShe said: “It costs a lot of money to look this cheap.” But on stage she was like a diamond: her music shone, her voice shone and her image shone. It’s just hard not to smile when you think of her.Because she came from such an extraordinarily poor background, she could connect with the working-class experience around the world. She was interested in people: “Tell me where you come from. What’s your life about?” I don’t know how much country music embraces queer culture – possibly not much – but she was hugely supportive of us.She was the kind of person who got on with it: did the job, got her money and helped people out, rather than making a big song and dance about it. She was strong without being aggressive and would rebut people without being unkind, which is a great skill. You just knew she had the back, not just of queer people, but of all people who face shit in their lives. She was looking out for you and singing for you. She’ll be hugely missed, but thinking of her immediately fills us with joy, rather than sadness.‘She could wrap anyone in warmth and love’KT Tunstall, singer-songwriterDolly was beyond the greatest. She was a world-leveller, in her immeasurable talent and in her ability to wrap anyone and everyone together in warmth and love. She’ll for ever be one of the best examples of how to spend a life on Earth.‘She represented anyone down on their luck’Kelly O’Brien, ‘the world’s No 1Dolly Parton tribute’View image in fullscreenKelly O’Brien with Dolly Parton.Photograph: Courtesy of Kelly O’BrienI don’t think I’ve had time to properly process Dolly’s passing. Every time I hear a bit of a song, it gets me started. I grew up in Australia. My parents would play her records and I’d go to sleep listening toLove Is Like a Butterflyand Jolene. As you get older, you think: “Wow, this woman’s clever. She’s no dumb blonde. She knows exactly what she’s doing.” Talking to interviewers, she would make fun of herself before anybody else could. From her entrepreneurism and humanitarianism to her philanthropy, she was a very clued-up woman.I started mucking around being Dolly 30 years ago. Being Dolly takes a lot of practice. I really studied her voice a lot, because I wanted to represent her in the best way possible. That meant going on a very strict diet, learning the accent, learning all the songs, her mannerisms. The costumes had to be right and the wigs had to be perfect. I based my work on her perfection.She means a lot to so many people in a world that’s gone a little bit mad. She’s this constant, kind, big-hearted, wholesome girl. She represented not only women, but anybody down on their luck, singing about unwedded women back in the early 70s and aworld on fire. She reached a whole new younger generation of admirerswhen she performed at Glastonbury in 2014, because she was Miley Cyrus’s godmother and so glamorous.She didn’t really approach politics, but then I think with her Rockstar album in 2023 she probably got a bit fed up and so became even more outspoken about LGBTQ+ rights and things like that. She used to have gay days at Dollywood and I think she used to get death threats, but she stood her ground. She’d go: “No, this is who these people are. They’re born this way. God accepts them and you have to do the same.” She brought some badass ideas to the deep south.I met her in 2011, backstage at the O2. I was dressed as her – unexpectedly, we had matching gold outfits! – and we were the same height. It was terrifying, because I was going to meet my idol, but she said she loved what I did and loved all the drag queens and Dolly impersonators everywhere. It was just magical, which she was.‘She wrote what she knew with great eloquence and skill’Paul Jepson, director of themusical 9 to 5View image in fullscreenPaul Jepson.Photograph: Andy Casey Upright MediaShe was an extraordinary person and very talented. We wanted to honour her extraordinary spirit. Our show’s music supervisor, Mark Crossland, and choreographer got to know Dolly. She had a lot of involvement in the development of the musical. Obviously, it’s her songs [and was originally a Broadway production, based on the 1980 movie], but everyone commented on how incredibly generous she was. She recorded herself singing, and bits of speaking, and sent them down the line from the US. Afterwards, she would ask if we needed to make any changes or needed anything else. She was the consummate pro. People often make this stuff up, but she was genuinely lovely and everybody loved her.One of the numbers in the show is Backwoods Barbie, which Karla Tracey – as Doralee – does exceptionally well. It’s actually a confession: she’s talking about where she comes from and she’s upset, because everyone has been horrible to her. Dolly got that: she was writing about something she knew very well with great eloquence and skill. A lot of people don’t know that the 9 to 5 song and movie was based on a real organisation, 9to5,that still existsand is still fighting discrimination and pushing for workers’ rights.I’m very glad the show has been touring in places such as Worthing, Bridlington and Darlington, which aren’t known as primary dates for this level of attention. They’re places that haven’t always been shown a lot of love – a bit downtrodden, if you will – and we wanted to stand up for them. I’d like to think that Dolly would have approved. It seemed a very Dolly thing to do.‘She dedicated much of her life to helping children’The Wiggles, children’s music groupWe are heartbroken to hear of the passing of Dolly Parton. Dolly brought so much joy, kindness and music into this world and we feel incredibly lucky to have spent time with her and to have called her our friend.Her extraordinary legacy goes far beyond the songs we all know and love. Dolly dedicated so much of her life to helping children dream big, including through herImagination Library,which has put millions of books into the hands of children around the world.Getting to make music with Dolly was something we will treasure for ever. But even more special was experiencing the warmth, generosity and joy that made her so deeply loved by generations of families. Thank you for the music, the laughter, the stories and everything you did for children everywhere. We will always be friends. We love you, Dolly. Rest peacefully.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
