title: ‘We met Princess Margaret and she was paralytic!’ My wild life onboard the Adam and the Ants Antmania rollercoaster | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: With their twangy sound, madcap outfits, lusty yodelling and pirouetting pirate frontman, the band became global superstars almost overnight. But, as their guitarist Marco Pirroni recalls, the thrill ride soon hit the buffers
Author: Sylvia Patterson
Headline: With their twangy sound, madcap outfits, lusty yodelling and pirouetting pirate frontman, the band became global superstars almost overnight. But, as their guitarist Marco Pirroni recalls, the thrill ride soon hit the buffers
Content: ‘Dress up, go mad, scream your head off’ … Pirroni, left, on stage with Adam Ant.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Dress up, go mad, scream your head off’ … Pirroni, left, on stage with Adam Ant.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyPop and rockInterview‘We met Princess Margaret and she was paralytic!’ My wild life onboard the Adam and the Ants Antmania rollercoasterSylvia PattersonWith their twangy sound, madcap outfits, lusty yodelling and pirouetting pirate frontman, the band became global superstars almost overnight. But, as their guitarist Marco Pirroni recalls, the thrill ride soon hit the buffersWed 26 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 13.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘The essence of pop is, one, brilliant fucking songs – and the rest is sex, subversion, style and humour. And that wasus.” SoAdam Anttold me in 1995, describing the reconstructed Adam and the Ants, which formed in early 1980 with the arrival of guitarist/songwriter Marco Pirroni, who was sitting next to him. “We’re responsible for bringing back dressing up, going mad and screaming your head off.”“That’s it!” grins Pirroni when I remind him of this, as we sit in the shabby-chic lounge of London’s 21Soho venue. Back then, I didn’t tell them I was 15 in 1980, forever sprinting across dancefloors pretending tobeAdam Ant, chiffon scarves tied to knees, limbs flailing like a whirling Cossack. Pirroni hears this today and laughs. “That’s what it’s all about,” he hoots. “When I was 13, watching Bowie, Roxy, T Rex, you just go, ‘I wanna dothat.’It’s exciting, sexy, about looking good, Top of the Pops. I can’t imagine anyone saying, ‘Wow, I desperately want to be in Cabaret Voltaire. They must be earning no money, look boring and nobody likes them – that’s the band for me!’”double quotation markThe pirate ship that seemingly took us up the Hudson? It was this stupid Playmobil cartoon boatPirroni, 67, is a winningly wry character, his sardonic eye enlivening his rollicking memoir, Your Money or Your Life: From Punk to Prince Charming. The book leads us, in forensic detail, through his teen years in mid-to-late 70s London. He was involved in every aspect of punk, every character, clothes shop, incident, ludicrous look and iconic gig. He was also a friend and bandmate of Sid Vicious, temporary guitarist with Siouxsie and the Banshees – and was obsessed with Roxy Music, John Barry and the spaghetti western soundtrack thrills of Ennio Morricone.View image in fullscreen‘You’d have to pay me millions to go back on the road’ … Pirroni.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianThese were the sensibilities he brought to the newly adrift Adam Ant in late 1979, after three original Ants were stolen by estranged manager Malcolm McLaren for new proteges Bow Wow Wow. They informed the Ants’ landmark second album, Kings of the Wild Frontier, released in November 1980 and mostly written in Pirroni’s bedroom in his parents’ home in Harrow, London. The pair conjured a feat of audacious imagination, a call-to-arms cacophony of twangy guitars, lusty yodelling, voodoo incantations, comedy gunshots and euphoric, communal chanting.Underpinning everything was their pioneering, two-drummer, Burundi beat sound. This was first suggested by McLaren, as was Native American imagery, and the result was a band that looked like a charging tribe of invincible warriors thundering over the horizon, fronted by a pirouetting pirate in feathers-and-frills, an “Apache” white stripe slashed across his nose.The impact was rapid, global and era-defining: Kings of the Wild Frontier wasn’t just No 1 in the album charts for 12 weeks, the band’s singles and narrative videos – storyboarded by Ant – laid the theatrical, visual-pop foundations for MTV in the US in 1981. They were dastardly, suggestive and definitely grownup, but they nonetheless ignited primal stirrings in even preteens, who saw in Ant a supernaturally attractive superhero, even before his turns as glossy-lipped Dandy Highwayman and pompadoured Prince Charming.View image in fullscreen‘We had three huge wardrobe trunks – and one was just my stuff!’ … Pirroni in his polka-dotted pomp.Photograph: Ilpo Musto/ShutterstockAnt wore glasses: thick-lensed, National Health whoppers. The first night Pirroni saw him without them on, wearing that white nose stripe and dressed in the 19th-century, gold-braided Hussar jacket from the film The Charge of the Light Brigade, his appeal was obvious. “It was like Clark Kent becoming Superman,” says Pirroni, who cultivated his own look, fond of polka dots and skull and crossbones. The band travelled with three huge wardrobe trunks. “And one was just my stuff!” says Pirroni.Today, the Ants’ Native American leanings would ignite accusations of cultural appropriation. But Pirroni rejects this. “Culture belongs to the human race,” he asserts. “It’s not even stealing. It’s ideas – they’refree. It’sart. We tried to do it well. We didn’t take the piss! Well, I’m going to be dead soon so it doesn’t really matter what I think. You go off and create your own thing. Or steal somebody else’s thing orwhatever the fuck you want.”For 18 months of Antmania, life moved at cosmic speed, a flip book of TV shows, hotels and airports, a heady era for deadly, disparate pop rivals. Pirroni was friends or acquainted with an ostentation of peacocking characters: from his punk years (Billy Idol, Viv Albertine, Chrissie Hynde), his Blitz Club-going era (Steve Strange, Spandau Ballet), and the ones he’d bump into at airports (Culture Club, Duran Duran, the Stray Cats, Madness). “Lots of people I knew personally were on telly, getting successful,” he nods. “And we’re probablyallthinking, ‘Those bastards!’ You’re young, you’re supposed to be competitive. I used to say in the press, ‘Their record’s shit!’ That’s the way bands are.”double quotation markAdam really thought Rod Hull and Emu were going to attack himSoon life became absurd. The Ants were regulars on kids’ TV: Tiswas, Multi-Coloured Swap Shop, The Children’s Royal Variety Performance with Clive Dunn, Basil Brush, Rod Hull and Emu.“Adamreallythought Rod Hull and Emu were going to attack him,” he laughs. “Princess Margaret was completely paralytic,breathingon you. We found it all hilariously funny. The pirate ship that seemingly took us up the Hudson in New York? It wasn’t a magnificent pirate ship with skull and crossbones. It was this stupid Playmobil …cartoon.As much as we were trying to be a cartoon – but not like this!”They had dinner with Liza Minnelli, hung out backstage with Liberace. “I remember being in this great big James Bond-like hotel suite looking over Tokyo and saying to Adam, ‘How did we get here?’ Eighteen months before, we’d been in my bedroom in Harrow.”Their descent was equally rapid. By late 1981, the band had three managers and Ant’s erratic personality – prone to excessive drama, persistent paranoia and chart-success obsession – was increasingly problematic. “Adam isextremely difficult,” declares Pirroni. “It was always, ‘Oh God, whatnow?’ ‘The BBC’s banned our record.’ ‘No, they haven’t, they’re just not playing it.’”View image in fullscreen‘How did we get here?’ … Pirroni, behind, with Adam Ant.Photograph: Virginia Turbett/RedfernsBy the age of just 22, Pirroni was disillusioned. He hated performing, finding it “boring, repetitive” and felt exasperated over all the infighting and resentments. “Bands are not built to last,” he says. As the Prince Charming Revue tour ended in January 1982, a cynical quip from Ant finished Pirroni off.“He said, ‘No one cares what we sound like, they just want to see me dance about.’ I thought, ‘Well, fuck it, what am I doing here then?’ It did feel a bit like the Beatles – with a really,reallyyoung audience, young girls. We didn’t do that on purpose. Perhaps we were just completely infantile!”Their relationship endured after the split in March 1982, lasting throughout the 80s and 90s, with Pirroni also working with Sinéad O’Connor and Siobhan Fahey, the Bananarama founder who is now a close friend (they’ve holidayed together in Antigua).Adam Ant, who has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, still tours. As a young man, he had mental health issues, which Pirroni was aware of in the 80s but remained a little sceptical “because he does make things up”. During the 1990s, he fielded calls from Ant’s doctors, the police and his neighbours: “I didn’t blame him. He was sick.”He was with Ant the day of his infamous altercation in the Prince of Wales pub in Kentish Town in 2002, wielding a starting pistol at revellers who mocked his cowboy outfit. He was later charged with affray and sectioned. Beforehand, Pirroni and Ant had met up in a restaurant, but Ant bolted off to continue drinking, says Pirroni. In the 1980s, the singer had famously been a righteous teetotaller in a hedonistic era. His disciplined lifestyle was, explains Pirroni today, a reaction to his severely alcoholic father. “But he controlled it. Until the mania took over.”Pirroni, who now lives a rural life in Derbyshire, lost contact with Ant years ago and is no longer interested in creating music. “Records now,” he says, “are like a plastic animal you give away with cornflakes. Your album given away to get people to come and see you live. I’m not going back on the road. You’d have to pay memillions.”He’s done enough anyway, I assure him. For teenagers like me, what he did was magic.“I find thatreallyhard to accept,” he unexpectedly confesses. “When someone comes up to me and says, ‘Kings is my favourite album. It really affected me.’ If I think that our album, my album, affected them in the same way as, say, Roxy Music’s For Your Pleasureaffected me, then I’mscared.”Your Money or Your Life: From Punk to Prince Charming by Marco Pirroni is published by New Modern on 10 September.Explore more on these topicsPop and rockAdam AntinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Wreck review – scuba drama about siblings under pressure | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Gabe Winsor’s inventively staged tale is charming and sweetly lo-fi, but the emotion never quite clicks
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Gabe Winsor’s inventively staged tale is charming and sweetly lo-fi, but the emotion never quite clicks
Content: A life aquatic … Morgan Beale as Eddie and Camilla Anvar as Ira, in The Wreck.Photograph: Alex BrennerView image in fullscreenA life aquatic … Morgan Beale as Eddie and Camilla Anvar as Ira, in The Wreck.Photograph: Alex BrennerEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewThe Wreck review – scuba drama about siblings under pressureSummerhall, EdinburghGabe Winsor’s inventively staged tale is charming and sweetly lo-fi, but the emotion never quite clicksChris WiegandWed 26 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDeep sea diving and plumbing the depths of family history make a decent parallel in this nimble multimedia production byBuzzcut, which has a sweetly eccentric air yet leaves a little too much beneath the surface.The premise is familiar, as Eddie (Morgan Beale) returns to the seaside town where his sister, Ira (Camilla Anvar), still lives in her childhood bedroom and runs the family pub now that their parents are gone. Guilt, resentment and jealousy bubble up as they squabble over which of them was their parents’ favourite and what to do with the business, while Ira shares her doubts about Eddie’s new husband.Written and directed by Gabe Winsor, The Wreck unfolds over the siblings’ daytime scuba dives and night-time dancing at the pub’s sparsely attended disco, presided over by DJ Sea Bass (you half expect to spot the electronic eel from Jaha Koo’s excellentHaribo Kimchi, playing across town). In a nice twist, they end up burying their own treasure – but you never fully invest in the characters’ relationships or their predicaments over the 50-minute duration.View image in fullscreenPuppeteer Beckett Gray and Camilla Anvar create an undersea scene.Photograph: Alex BrennerThat is partly because of the time spent realising the show’s inventive form. Live camera work and rod-and-string puppeteering (both by Beckett Gray) are used to animate the water-world – with puppet designs by Cat Rock and a fishtank model box by Tiffer Cundy, atmospherically lit by Han Sayles. All of this takes place behind a diaphanous sheet, so the behind-the-scenes activity becomes a secondary drama, and several different backdrops are used to change the scene. Surtitles and divers’ hand signals are used to make the show accessible and the tech is handled smoothly, yet retains a lo-fi air. Faye James plays her own compositions live, blending accordion and suitably aquatic-sounding electronica.The underwater action begins to drag and the conversations on dry land can also frustrate, although the characters’ reticence feels realistic (as does the siblings’ shared shorthand). But even if the drama is caught between the domestic and the deep blue sea, it’s a show with plenty of charm.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatrePuppetryEdinburgh festivalSummerhallreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival – a game so grotesque it scares its own director | Games | The Guardian
description: With oversight from Clive Barker himself, and a role reprisal as Pinhead from actor Doug Bradley, Revival aims to introduce new audiences to the discomfort of Hellraiser
Author: Bex April May
Headline: With oversight from Clive Barker himself, and a role reprisal as Pinhead from actor Doug Bradley, Revival aims to introduce new audiences to the discomfort of Hellraiser
Content: A monk-like villain … Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival.Photograph: Saber InteractiveView image in fullscreenA monk-like villain … Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival.Photograph: Saber InteractiveGamesClive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival – a game so grotesque it scares its own directorWith oversight from Clive Barker himself, and a role reprisal as Pinhead from actor Doug Bradley, Revival aims to introduce new audiences to the discomfort of HellraiserBex April MayWed 26 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf a horror game gives its own director a physical reaction, it’s probably doing something right. While researching the images people find hardest to look at, game director Emil Esov discovered he hastrypophobia– a fear of clusters of small holes. Rather than tone the scary images down, he fed them straight into Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival.The forthcoming first-person action-horror game drops players into a new story in Barker’s universe. Aidan Lynch must use the Genesis Configuration puzzle box to rescue his girlfriend from the Labyrinth as Pinhead, his Cenobites and a cult close in. But Revival is not built around jump scares. The team at Mad HeadGamesbegan with one question: what should players feel? The answer was discomfort.“That’s a key emotion,” says Esov, “You know when you are looking at something, but you cannot look away?” Early in the game, players must push a hand inside a grotesque sculpture to retrieve an item – it’s all about feeling extreme unease. Even a stealth kill is drawn out rather than instant, he explains: “There is struggle. There is sweating, moaning. It’s really, really stressful.”View image in fullscreenExtreme unease … Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival.Photograph: Saber InteractiveThat does not mean simply filling every room with blood and bodies. Esov likens Pinhead to a monk rather than a traditional slasher villain: calm, imposing and “almost trolling you”. The horror comes from what he might do, but also the unnerving way he talks about doing it.Clive Barkerhimself helped shape the characters, themes and rules of the universe, before staying on as an adviser as the story became a game. His feedback could move from big questions to one wonderfully specific request, which Esov recalls as: “Can you make the sky more purple in the Labyrinth?” Esov loved that “level of detailed nit-picking”, which showed that Barker was still watching over the world he created.Doug Bradley also returns as Pinhead for the first time (except for a few lines in a time-limited chapter of Dead by Daylight) in the two decades since his last appearance in a Hellraiser film. Recording took place remotely, and Esov soon realised the actor needed little coaching. “You don’t have to direct him,” he says. “He actually is Pinhead!”As for the Cenobites, they get more individual roles and screen time, but won’t be ordinary targets; their undeniable power had to survive the move into an action game. “You cannot fight them,” Esov says, “They’re not a gameplay aspect that you get to beat.”Elsewhere, the first-person combat has drawn comparisons toResident Eviland BioShock, while Condemned influenced the unpredictable melee fights. Around a quarter of the game takes place in the Labyrinth, and the Genesis Configuration works as both a key part of the story and a tool for the player. The difficulty settings include a highest level named after Hellraiser itself, which is how Esov prefers to play. His hellish serving suggestion of sorts: “It should be discomforting even to play.”Esov hopes Revival will introduce a new audience to the mix of violence, sex, beauty and pain that sets Hellraiser apart. He wants a game “that doesn’t hold back”. If players come away disturbed, they will not be alone: Revival got under its own director’s skin before it ever had the chance to get under theirs.Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival comes to PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S on 8 OctoberExplore more on these topicsGamesClive BarkerHorror booksRole playing gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The rise of ‘biogossip’: Rachel Cusk’s Natalie Portman novel is the latest in a delicious literary lineage | Rachel Cusk | The Guardian
description: The much-discussed Life of M is the latest in a lineage of celebrity satire that spans from Virginia Woolf to The Devil Wears Prada
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The much-discussed Life of M is the latest in a lineage of celebrity satire that spans from Virginia Woolf to The Devil Wears Prada
Content: Left: Anna Wintour at The Met Gala in 2019. Center: Virginia Woolf c 1933. Right: Natalie Portman at the Golden Globe awards in 2014.Composite: Invision/AP, Central Press/Getty Images, NurPhoto/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLeft: Anna Wintour at The Met Gala in 2019. Center: Virginia Woolf c 1933. Right: Natalie Portman at the Golden Globe awards in 2014.Composite: Invision/AP, Central Press/Getty Images, NurPhoto/Rex/ShutterstockRachel CuskThe rise of ‘biogossip’: Rachel Cusk’s Natalie Portman novel is the latest in a delicious literary lineageThe much-discussed Life of M is the latest in a lineage of celebrity satire that spans from Virginia Woolf to The Devil Wears PradaGreta RainbowWed 26 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInRachel Cusk’s new novel,Life of M, the famous actor protagonist participates in an event at a book store after hours. The actor, M, is joined by “a writer of some renown” and a fashion model who possesses “some vague self-absorption”. A brand sponsored the affair. I spent literal hours trying to find the real-world equivalent of the opaque fictional passage. I scrolled through the backlogs of influencers I know to appear bookish in their content, who might have fallen prey toDior’s Ulysses tote bag droporMiu Miu’s “literary club”. I even stooped so low as to DM a Natalie Portman fan account, asking for leads.Life of M by Rachel Cusk review – is this story of a film star based on Natalie Portman?Read moreAs has been widely reported, M’s character is based on Portman. One journalist wascreditedwith the scoop, but she simply finished her advance copy sooner than the rest of us; it’s clear from page three, when Cusk describes M’s breakout film as having “immediately brought her childhood to an end” (obviously Léon: The Professional; Portman was 11 when she was cast) and a later film about obsessive, wild ballerinas (Black Swan). But the rumor that Portman is unhappy with her portrayal – an impression that cannot immediately be gleaned from the book itself, especially depending on interpretation of its final lines – has trickled down to the raggiest of tabloids.Cusk’s “literary scandal”, so dubbed byPage Six, adds Life of M to the canon of biogossip, AKA novels that stoke intense speculation over the person they’rereally about– and if the source material is all but confirmed by the author, then how much is exactly as it happened? How close have we, the readers, been allowed to get?View image in fullscreenCusk photographed in Barcelona in 2025.Photograph: Enric Fontcuberta/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockNearly a century ago, Virginia Woolf had high society ablaze withOrlando, her time- and gender-bending romantic experiment. The Daily Mail treated it as nothing but straight gossip from the heart of the Bloomsbury Group, confirmation of Woolf’s affair with Vita Sackville-West. As if anyone actually in the scene didn’t already know that was going on (and had ended by the time of publication).Women’s Wear Daily reported in 2002 that The Devil Wears Prada by Lauren Weisberger, who was a former assistant to Vogue’s Anna Wintour, sold to Doubleday for around $250,000. When Wintour heard, she allegedly replied, “I cannot remember who that girl is.” Though Weisberger maintained in the press that her ice-cold magazine editor Miranda Priestly was not based on Anna, the court of public opinion, not to mention Hollywood, decided otherwise. After years of side-stepping questions about the book and 2006 film adaptation, Wintour finally decided toget in on the jokein time for the film’s sequel earlier this year.In 2018, Lisa Halliday’s debut novelAsymmetrywas a literary event for it offered what the New Yorker called the “voyeuristic thrill” of imagining what it would be like to date Philip Roth – which Halliday did, for a time – or at least a man who greatly resembles him. There were just enough tasteful details (baseball, back pain, anxiety) to point a reader’s imagination to the esteemed American author; the magazine likened the prose to “one of Rachel Cusk’s cool-voiced narrators”.View image in fullscreenScarlett Johansson, Azhy Robertson and Adam Driver in 2019 film Marriage Story.Photograph: Netflix/AllstarThe biogossip micro-genre functions like all gossip does: it’s the most fun when you’re on the outside. Not so far away to not know the players, but not close enough to feel real hurt or deep sympathy or dubiousness because they’re more than caricatures to you. Though if you’re a Jennifer Jason Leigh superfan, Noah Baumbach’s Marriage Story would have been a hard watch (the film is thought to be about the director’s eight-year marriage to the actor, though Baumbach has said it’s “not autobiographical; it’s personal”).Biogossip tends to set the scene and to establish familiarity. The voyeuristic thrill of The Devil Wears Pradais, well, to read about people who wear Prada. And Armani, and Oscar de la Renta and Bottega Veneta – spelled wrong in the first edition, by the way! The Vogue-like magazine may present as Runway, with a Condé Nast-ish parent company renamed Elias-Clark, but all the delicious free-market proper nouns that complete the fantasy of working in high fashion remain. Even the Diet Coke mentions serve a purpose (beyond an opportunity for coherent product placement in the sequel film): to communicate that the narrative exists in our recognizable world.View image in fullscreenStreep as Miranda Priestly in the 2006 film adaptation of The Devil Wears Prada.Photograph: AllstarCusk sits on the other side of the looking glass. She strips away all those signifiers of class and taste, to instead present a sketch of something you thought you knew, but actually, the harder you inspect, it’s really quite hard to say. This is typical of her style and preoccupations; she’ll eventually exhaust the alphabet with her first-initial-only muses of novels like Second Place, long-listed for the Booker, and Parade, winner of the 2024 Goldsmiths Prize. But M is different because M is mega-famous.View image in fullscreenCusk’s Life of M.Photograph: Farrar, Straus and Giroux/APCusk onceproposedthat character doesn’t exist anymore, and it’s because we have begun to live out a collective homogenous experience. Yet M can’t do things like go to a restaurant normally, and that’s because of how we treat her. The subject pronoun “we” is employed throughout the novel, and this is where biogossip shifts into a meta register. We fancy ourselves individuals, but we are slavish to the same principles of parasociality: “Like the ugly tower we see everything from where we are, except ourselves,” Cusk writes. “Fame is perhaps this tower, an ultimate entrapment in the self that is also a deliverance from it.” Who wouldn’t feel some way about being in proximity to Natalie Portman? Cusk gets us to admit that we crave juicy details. But because Cusk refuses to provide them, we don’t feel like we’re allowed to get close to M at all.Even without the pulpiness and dead-giveaway cover art of, say, The Wig, The Bitch & The Meltdown, a satirical novel by former America’s Next Top Model right-hand man Jay Manuel, the allure of the mere suggestion of biogossip can do the near impossible and propel a work of literary fiction beyond a newspaper’s book review section and squarely onto the homepages of gossip blogs. I have to wonder if that was part of Cusk’s calculus from the jump. She’s been a tabloid fascination before, ripped to shreds by the British press for her books about motherhood and marriage. After publishing A Life’s Work, her 2001 memoir about, among other things, the struggle to maintain a sense of self when caring for a newborn, she wasaccused of child-hating, doom-mongering and epitomizing the crisis of contemporary feminism. “I’ve coped artistically by believing the criticisms weren’t right,” Cusksaid. “They upset me, but they didn’t challenge my understanding of how to write, nor of how morality functions in literature.”Gossip tests the morals, teeters on a line. It’s not the concept of fame that Cusk critiques on moral grounds but our behavior in the face of it. My rabid sleuthing for the inspiration behind the “rather turgid and awkward” bookstore event in Life of M is, I’ll freely admit, a disgusting waste of the precious hours that comprise my own life. Perhaps that realization means I passed a test of Cusk’s own.Explore more on these topicsRachel CuskNatalie PortmanFictionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Dog Stars review – Ridley Scott’s lethargic postapocalyptic drama is a misfire | Ridley Scott | The Guardian
description: An adaptation of Peter Heller’s 2012 novel never finds its footing with overly familiar survival beats and a glum lack of energy
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: An adaptation of Peter Heller’s 2012 novel never finds its footing with overly familiar survival beats and a glum lack of energy
Content: Jacob Elordi in The Dog Stars.Photograph: Fabio Lovino/20th Century Studios/APView image in fullscreenJacob Elordi in The Dog Stars.Photograph: Fabio Lovino/20th Century Studios/APRidley ScottReviewThe Dog Stars review – Ridley Scott’s lethargic postapocalyptic drama is a misfireAn adaptation of Peter Heller’s 2012 novel never finds its footing with overly familiar survival beats and a glum lack of energyBenjamin LeeTue 25 Aug 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 13.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLooking towards the end of an August moviedumping ground littered with more unwanted trash than usual, there seemed to be a faint glimmer of hope, a shiny treasure poking out through the dusty mass ofunnecessary sequelsandsex purge romcoms. Somehow, there was a $110m-budget adaptation of an acclaimed novel directed by Ridley Scott, led by a recently Oscar-nominated rising star with support from two Oscar-nominated actors and an Oscar winner. But why then would such a film be unveiled in between the summer blockbuster season and the upcoming deluge of prestige fall festival big hitters? A cursed weekend that’s recently been home to Jay Roach’s heinous War of the Roses remake, Dennis Quaid’s Ronald Reagan biopic and George Miller’s hard-to-define and even harder-to-love flop Three Thousand Years of Longing.It Ends review – gripping micro-budget horror ranks among the year’s bestRead moreEver since The Dog Stars, based on Peter Heller’s 2012 novel, had been yanked from its far more encouraging date at the end of March, there were multiple red flags flying and the rotten end of August has ultimately become an appropriate punishment for a limp and lethargic film that only briefly fascinates in pushing us to wonder what anyone was really hoping this would end up being. It’s yet another grubby postapocalyptic survival tale, an overcrowded subgenre that hasn’t just reached maximum capacity on the big screen but on the small one too. In a world of seven Walking Dead shows, the beats are now far too familiar – artfully dishevelled actors grieve for the past and fear for the future as they scramble to find and protect resources – and there’s nothing new or notable here to conjure anything but deja vu.In The Dog Stars, a flu pandemic has wiped out most of humanity and turned those who remain against each other. Mechanic Hig (Jacob Elordi) lives a simple, if stressful, life with dog Jasper and grizzled former marine Bangley (Josh Brolin) as they protect their remote Colorado compound and scavenge for supplies. But the pair share differing views on how to survive and what might come next, Hig the optimist and Bangley the opposite. The script, from Twisters writer Mark L Smith, tends to detail these differences a little too loudly, as if these characters were having such conversations for the very first time just for our benefit. It’s the kind of writing that, for all the film’s attempts to whip up a folksy charm, never feels convincingly lived-in, our investment then at a minimum when chaos inevitably lands.Hig’s belief that something more is out there causes him to leave for a nearby hub and, on the way, encounter a father-daughter pairing (Guy Pearce and Margaret Qualley) who end up joining him just as so-called “reapers” – essentially bloodthirsty goth invaders – come a’knocking.It’s not that the action entering the fray so late into the movie is the problem here (I’m all for a more subdued character-based end-of-days drama a laZ for Zachariah) or that the set pieces are all a little too cut-and-paste to truly excite (where the $110m budget went is a mystery). It’s that the plot and its characters are too maddeningly insubstantial to justify such human-over-spectacle storytelling.Elordi, who was easily the best part of Guillermo del Toro’s otherwise mostly wretched Frankenstein, is on less sure footing here, a vast acting challenge followed by something considerably less interesting, and he seems as fatigued by playing Hig as we are at watching him. It’s a boringly absent lead performance of empty, stoic stares, although with a puddle-deep script that asks very little and gives even less as reward, there’s not much more anyone could have done (young man is impulsive, older man is cynical and, at its most thankless, young woman is nurturing). Smith’s dialogue is initially clumsy in its attempts to fill in the gaps (if you’re choosing to avoid a more straightforward introduction to the world and its rules then your exposition should be less awkwardly crammed in) before it graduates to stiff and obvious instead. A third act sequence, involvingAllison Janneydoing the very most, might have seemed more sudden and shocking in Heller’s book but it’s too derivative and unscary to wake us up on screen.It’s an oddly directed yet not odd enough section that questions Scott’s once unimpeachable ability to put us on edge arriving in a film that makes us broadly wonder what he’s doing here in the first place. The scenery – rural Italy doubling for rural America – is genuinely stunning (and surely afforded all those involved a lovely vacation) but, as in Gladiator II, there are some weirdly janky visual effects (one explosion looks laptop-made) and a general uninvolved shrug to the proceedings, as if he replaced a more impassioned director late in the day. Scott’s disinterest in retiring is admirable (he’sopenly loathsomeof the idea), I just wish he seemed more interested in the day job.The Dog Stars is out in Australian cinemas on 27 August and in the US and UK on 28 AugustExplore more on these topicsRidley ScottAction and adventure filmsScience fiction and fantasy filmsDrama filmsJacob ElordiJosh BrolinGuy PearcereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sami Abu Wardeh Hates You review – a clown strides into the mainstream with style | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The comedian delivers a tour of his peripatetic childhood, with stops for risque gags and to ponder his resemblance to a ‘porn Super Mario’
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: The comedian delivers a tour of his peripatetic childhood, with stops for risque gags and to ponder his resemblance to a ‘porn Super Mario’
Content: Teasing at the boundaries of the permissible … Sami Abu Wardeh pictured outside Pleasance Courtyard.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTeasing at the boundaries of the permissible … Sami Abu Wardeh pictured outside Pleasance Courtyard.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewSami Abu Wardeh Hates You review – a clown strides into the mainstream with stylePleasance Courtyard, EdinburghThe comedian delivers a tour of his peripatetic childhood, with stops for risque gags and to ponder his resemblance to a ‘porn Super Mario’Brian LoganWed 26 Aug 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 10.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleComedy fans have seen Sami Abu Wardeh in several guises, from acapering clowncatching cherry tomatoes in his mouth, to teller (on last year’s fringe) of the historical stories behind the Gaza crisis. But we’ve never seen him deliver straight autobiographical standup – until now. The new direction, the 40-year-old tells us, is thanks to his agent, who’s told him that audiences need to get to know him better. And who may be concerned, Wardeh implies, by recent dust-ups between this “anti-fascist”/pro-Palestine performer and one or two audience members to whom that worldview was unwelcome.View image in fullscreenFar more than just chat … Sami Abu Wardeh.Photograph: Dylan WoodleySami Abu Wardeh Hates You (its title notwithstanding) presents us with a more palatable act, one effortlessly capable of delivering mainstream comedy. From the opening gag about walk-on music, to the tour of his peripatetic childhood (from Kuwait via southwest London to Dubai), to the risque gags about wanking and his resemblance to a “porn Super Mario”, the show might have been designed to demonstrate the Irish-Palestinian’s mastery of standup topics and techniques. But he gives them his own spin; whether that’s workshopping racist slurs with his bully, or orchestrating his Middle Eastern schoolmates in a rap-along to Will Smith’s Men in Black.All of this is greatly embellished by our host’s clowning skills, which ensure that most of those routines are far more than just chat. Body, vocals and gurning, leering face are all bent towards caricature here, as Wardeh brings to larger-than-life the demonic-seeming rituals of the Catholic church, say, or the sex appeal of his Arabic teacher. An anecdote about voicing an audiobook platforms his accent abilities, forever teasing at the boundaries of the permissible.Courtney Büchner: One of the Girls review – all aboard for a rollercoaster relationshipRead moreYou wait in vain for the show’s premise – “a chaotic exploration of the value of hate today” – to be fulfilled, but the subject is addressed just briefly. Only the later stages bring us into the present day, with a story about a comically ineffective protest he launched against racist policing. We get a veiled picture of who Sami Abu Wardeh is now, but a vivid and funny one of who he was while getting here.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalEdinburgh festival 2022FestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Kirsty Mann: Corpse review – a comedy so creepy you’ll fear the next revelation | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The comedian brings a calm authority to her tale of a haunted house and digs out maximum horror from a minimal staging
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: The comedian brings a calm authority to her tale of a haunted house and digs out maximum horror from a minimal staging
Content: Powerful presence … Kirsty Mann in Corpse at Summerhall, Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPowerful presence … Kirsty Mann in Corpse at Summerhall, Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewKirsty Mann: Corpse review – a comedy so creepy you’ll fear the next revelationSummerhall, EdinburghThe comedian brings a calm authority to her tale of a haunted house and digs out maximum horror from a minimal stagingChris WiegandWed 26 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome shows work their magic on you slowly but Kirsty Mann will have you hooked in under a minute. A thunderous sound effect, a flash of blood-red lighting and a DIY ghost costume is all it takes to get the audience strapped in for her comic tale of a haunting. “Are you a believer?” she asks us. Mann may not convince you of supernatural powers but she overwhelmingly proves the power of storytelling.It succeeds partly because our host is such a natural on stage and so rational, too. Mann quickly comes across as an ordinary neighbour, even while detailing the most uncommon events of moving into her new home. When she and her husband snapped up a semi in east London they knew it was a fixer-upper but it turns out the knotweed is the least of their problems. The previous resident died in the same bed in which they consummate their moving in and it gets creepier by the day. Why does the toilet seemingly flush itself? Are those scratch marks on the bedroom door? What the hell is going on under the apple tree?View image in fullscreenA natural … Kirsty Mann in Corpse.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianMann is a doctor as well as a comedian (“So when I’m not killing it on stage …”) and her spooked state begins to cause problems at work and test her marriage. She plays assorted characters including her often absent husband, who nicknames her Piglet – accentuating their tenderness yet also her increasingly jangled nerves. The story unfolds amid removal boxes to add an extra air of uncertainty. Once you’ve seen the previous owner’s paintings you will never unsee them.Soft Spot review – this wine-glass circus has a lot of bottleRead moreThere are sparing references to horror cinema and Mann operates with the knowledge, as proven by The Woman in Black, that less is more when scaring on stage. Her clinical examination to verify a patient’s death is breathtakingly done and there is a moment of darkness when you fear what you’ll discover when the lights go up. The scenes of comical hysteria, with her clambering amid the audience, are more run-of-the-mill. If the final flourish is not quite unsettling enough it is still a relief, leaving the venue after this afternoon show, to not walk home in the dark.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 30 August and atShedinburgh, Edinburgh, on 29 August. Then atSoho theatre, London, 2-13 February.All our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalHorror filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Adam Riches: The Captain review – the extraordinary glory of a ‘half man, half fish’ Victorian hero | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: An endurance test for a standup already starring in a fringe hit, this show resurrects the man who drilled the first ever cross-Channel swimmer
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: An endurance test for a standup already starring in a fringe hit, this show resurrects the man who drilled the first ever cross-Channel swimmer
Content: Deep dive … Adam Riches: The Captain.Photograph: Matt StrongeView image in fullscreenDeep dive … Adam Riches: The Captain.Photograph: Matt StrongeEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewAdam Riches: The Captain review – the extraordinary glory of a ‘half man, half fish’ Victorian heroSummerhall, EdinburghAn endurance test for a standup already starring in a fringe hit, this show resurrects the man who drilled the first ever cross-Channel swimmerBrian LoganWed 26 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Who are these people that do what [the rest of us] cannot?”Adam Riches’ solo play The Captain teases at the daredevil spirit, incarnate here in Capt Matthew Webb, the first man to swim the Channel unaided. Riches plays Fred Beckwith, a swimming coach who trains the young Webb for his tilt at greatness. The show takes the form of a lecture-cum-eulogy to the “half man, half fish” Webb, whose body lies under a shroud on a table in the apt surroundings of Summerhall’s Anatomy theatre.A comedian by trade, Riches offers up a version of the true story here that’s as funny as his comedy elsewhere on the fringe,The Critic’s Way. The gentle sendup of Victorian values is droll. The swimming workshops and cheerleading of Webb’s channel crossing, to which the audience is co-opted with gusto (this is an Adam Riches show, after all), are stirring good fun. And there’s a real relish forthe story’s bizarre details– such as Beckwith’s “mystical fifth swimming technique”, the sidestroke. Or the American rival to Webb who completes the crossing before him, albeit in a rubber suit that strongly resembles a boat.‘Audiences ask to feel my calves!’ The endurance extremists pounding treadmills and pumping pedals at the fringeRead moreYou could argue that that comic instinct undermines the seriousness of Riches’ exploration of what drives some people to strive for the impossible – and what mark they leave on the rest of us. Riches can seldom resist a joke, and even at his most earnest – as Beckwith hymns the manly strength and firmness of his hero’s endeavours – you sense the next gag pregnant on his lips.But the sincerity of his interest shines through. Perhaps unsurprisingly for a man whose whole oeuvre has explored extreme masculinity, and whose every Edinburgh fringe (two shows this year, three next) is itself a heroic feat of stamina, Riches considers Webb’s grasp-exceeding reach, and the role glory plays in a life well lived, with real depth of feeling. Why swim 21 miles when you can swim 39? It might as well be Riches’ motto, and he makes an engaging case for it in this tribute to Victorian pluck and watery derring-do.AtSummerhall, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Adam RichesTheatreComedy (Stage)Swimming (Sport)Swimming (Life and style)Comedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Whimsical shortlist announced for Edinburgh comedy award 2026 | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: A shortlist rich in kookiness sees Lara Ricote tipped for the main prize, alongside returning nominees and a new generation of eccentric fringe acts
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: A shortlist rich in kookiness sees Lara Ricote tipped for the main prize, alongside returning nominees and a new generation of eccentric fringe acts
Content: Woozy … UK-based Li Jin Hao from Singapore is nominated for Falling from a Moon.Photograph: Rebecca Need MenearView image in fullscreenWoozy … UK-based Li Jin Hao from Singapore is nominated for Falling from a Moon.Photograph: Rebecca Need MenearEdinburgh festival 2026Whimsical shortlist announced for Edinburgh comedy award 2026A shortlist rich in kookiness sees Lara Ricote tipped for the main prize, alongside returning nominees and a new generation of eccentric fringe actsBrian LoganWed 26 Aug 2026 13.23 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 13.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe shortlist has been announced for the annual Edinburgh comedy award, and it’s a list that majors in whimsy. With an act hymning his belief in healing crystals, another dreamily counting sheep and a third whose show is about “mystery and messages” – and that’s before we even get to the loopy DIY comedy of TV veteran Spencer Jones – this year’s “Oscars of comedy” nominees (for both the best show and best newcomer prize) suggest an art form exploding with creativity but also increasingly oriented towards woo-woo: in full flight, perhaps, from our troubled times.The award favourite is Mexican-American comic Lara Ricote, co-star of Sam Campbell’s Channel 4 mockumentaryMake That Movieand former fringe best newcomer. Ricote’sInklingis a remarkable hour about picking up on the messages that come one’s way, and how that’s complicated by, in the 29-year-old’s case, being hard of hearing.View image in fullscreenAward favourite … Lara Ricote.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanReturning to the annual shortlist, for an award once known as the Perrier, are Chris Cantrill (a three-time nominee whose double act sidekickAmy Gledhillwon in 2024), shouty MancunianDan Tiernan(nominated twice before) with Quartz and All and goofball prop comic Jones (also nominated twice before). Jones is the veteran of this year’s list with his own BBC show, The Mind of Herbert Clunkerdunk, already under his belt.On a shorter list than we’ve seen in recent years, they are joined by Cornwall’sHarriet Dyer, recently announced as a participant in the Halloween edition of Amazon Prime’s smash hit Last One Laughing UK, and whose show Easily Distra … celebrates her inability to stay on topic; andLi Jin Hao, the UK-based Singaporean whose show Falling from a Moon develops the brand of woozy philosophical comedy pioneered in his2024 show Swimming in a Submarine.The most egregious omissions from the lineup, which is selected by industry and public panellists, are Elf Lyons with The Woman on the Edge,an extraordinary breakup showthat’s got everyone talking; Aussie stunt-comedy offeringMan Sings the Same Song Over and Over Again for an Hour; and the Radio 4 sketch trioCrybabieswith their brilliantly executed horror pastiche The Scaring.View image in fullscreenInventive … Limerick comic Marty Gleeson.Photograph: Rachel SherlockOn the best newcomer shortlist – for an award previously won by Sarah Millican, Tim Minchin and Harry Hill – there’s more whimsy still. Too many kooks, you might say, at a festival where socially engaged or political comedy is vanishingly thin on the ground. Or you could celebrate the surfeit of invention among acts that include Limerick’s Marty Gleeson, a quartet of US clowns performing theirUnderground Monk Show, and Birmingham teacher turned oddball Tom Towelling, with a show that binds its audience together in wool.Completing the newcomer nominees, at a time when the proficiency of first-time Edinburgh acts seems to be rocketing, there are Dom McGovern with Prize Hog, TV regular but fringe rookie Fatiha El-Ghorri withCockney Stacking Doll, Freddie Meredith with the terrific Need a Light? and Omar Badawy with Guided Detour.Chair of the judging panel Liz Lewin, director of comedy series at Netflix UK, said of the lists: “These are the people shaping the comedy landscape and we can’t wait for audiences beyond Edinburgh to enjoy them as much as we did”. The awards will be handed out at a ceremony this Saturday by2016 winner Richard Gaddand last year’s best newcomer and now SNL:UK starAyoade Bamgboye. The winners will receive £10,000 for best show (sponsored by Audible), and £5,000 for best newcomer. Recent winners of the main award include Rose Matafeo, Hannah Gadsby and last year’s champ Sam Nicoresti.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalAwards and prizesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Two women accuse former Fat White Family member Saul Adamczewski of physical and emotional abuse | Music | The Guardian
description: Insecure Men singer has now been dropped by his record label and had tour dates cancelled after two women shared allegations about his behaviour
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: Insecure Men singer has now been dropped by his record label and had tour dates cancelled after two women shared allegations about his behaviour
Content: Saul Adamczewski performing with the Fat White Family in 2014.Photograph: Hugo Marie/EPA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSaul Adamczewski performing with the Fat White Family in 2014.Photograph: Hugo Marie/EPA/ShutterstockMusicTwo women accuse former Fat White Family member Saul Adamczewski of physical and emotional abuseInsecure Men singer has now been dropped by his record label and had tour dates cancelled after two women shared allegations about his behaviourLaura SnapesWed 26 Aug 2026 11.42 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 15.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSaul Adamczewski of Insecure Men and formerly ofFat White Familyhas been dropped by his record label and had tour dates cancelled after two women shared allegations of physical and emotional abuse against the musician.One woman said that the pair had a short relationship that resulted in a pregnancy, after which, she alleged, Adamczewski “made it his duty to make me suffer. He has been violent, pushed me, thrown glass bottles at me, showered me with beer […] insulted me, taken my passport from me, stolen my money and more, all while I had our baby.”She claimed that Adamczewski – who has been candid about his use of crack cocaine and heroin, and was kicked out of Fat White Family and sent to rehab – used her “as an excuse to get more money for doing smack, while I would have no money to feed myself and had to steal after he promised he would take care of me.”She said that in her third month of pregnancy, she moved to “be with my family and away from him” and shared screenshots appearing to show abusive messages from Adamczewski.The musician Jessica Winter commented on the post saying she had “witnessed this man’s physical and emotional abuse on two women and other men”, and claimed that Adamczewski had “threatened and abused me to try and silence me”.Another alleged victim described multiple incidences of physical violence. She also alleged that he folded her inside a sofa bed and “held me inside”.The Guardian has contacted representatives for Adamczewski for comment. The band’s management and UK publicist have severed ties and the Instagram profile for Insecure Men has been removed.Insecure Men were signed to the US indie label Fat Possum and have now been dropped. In a statement, the label said: “We take the accusations against Saul Adamczewski very seriously. Fat Possum will no longer be working with Insecure Men.” The band have been removed from the label’s online roster.The band’s set at the Green Man festival did not go ahead this weekend, nor a planned date in Manchester. A subsequent date at Rough Trade Liverpool has also been cancelled, a staff member confirmed to the Guardian, along with the band’s November tour of the UK. No official reason for the cancellation has been shared.Adamczewski co-founded the Metros in 2006 and found minor indie sleaze-era success including having a song on the soundtrack to US teen TV series Gossip Girl.In 2011, he co-founded Fat White Family, a band that gained notoriety and acclaim for their debauched behaviour. He left the band before the completion of their 2024 album Forgiveness Is Yours. He was also a member of Warmduscher from 2014 to around 2018.Explore more on these topicsMusicFat White FamilynewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: the search for the murderer of Northern Irish journalist Lyra McKee | Television | The Guardian
description: A documentary gains impressive access to the detectives who have been hunting for the killer since 2019. Plus: Mark Gatiss returns as a bookish postwar sleuth. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: A documentary gains impressive access to the detectives who have been hunting for the killer since 2019. Plus: Mark Gatiss returns as a bookish postwar sleuth. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Det Supt Jason Murphy, the lead investigator in the Lyra McKee murder trial in Northern Ireland.Photograph: Polly Garnett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDet Supt Jason Murphy, the lead investigator in the Lyra McKee murder trial in Northern Ireland.Photograph: Polly Garnett/The GuardianTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: the search for the murderer of Northern Irish journalist Lyra McKeeA documentary series gains impressive access to the detectives who have been hunting for the killer since 2019. Plus: Mark Gatiss returns as a bookish postwar sleuth. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Graeme VirtueandSimon WardellWed 26 Aug 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Murder Detective9pm, Channel 4The 2019 murder of the journalist Lyra McKee in Derry was a grim reminder that, while the Troubles are in abeyance, it’s still a stretch to describe them as being over. Filmed across seven years, this three-part documentary gains impressive access to the detectives hunting for Lyra’s killer. It’s intense and gripping: the team struggle to persuade any witnesses (there were more than 150) to come forward and gradually realise that they are, in fact, investigating the leadership of the New IRA.Phil HarrisonSurviving Earth8pm, Sky OneThis Walking With Dinosaurs-style series is parked in the Triassic era, a period when evolution was forcibly redirected by extinction events. But the programme makers know you can make a looming ice age relatable by telling the story of a plucky little critter: in this case, a squat young ischigualastia dealing with food scarcity.Graeme VirtueBookish8pm, U&AlibiBack to 1946 London for more genteel, meticulous detective work with Mark Gatiss’s bibliophile sleuth, Gabriel Book. Series two begins in the world of mediums as Book examines a seance resulting in the apparent killing of Harold Sneed (an enjoyably louche Jason Watkins). For all the supernatural woo-woo, could the answer be surprisingly earthbound?PHProfessor T9pm, ITV1There’s a whiff of The Thursday Murder Club to the latest outing for Ben Miller’s compulsive criminologist as he finds himself at the scene of a violent murder in a posh retirement village. The fact that DS Winters (Barney White) hates his guts could derail the case. Might a joint therapy session help?GVThe Never Ending Murder10pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenOne of the most serious unsolved crimes in British history … the disappearance of Nicola Payne.Photograph: Channel4This series promises new revelations concerning one of the most serious unsolved crimes in British legal history. In 1991, somewhere between her home and that of her parents, 18-year-old Nicola Payne vanished. She hasn’t been seen since, but the police have been unable to make any progress towards uncovering her fate.PHRainbow Warrior10pm, Sky DocumentariesBack in 1985, the ideas propagated by Greenpeace hadn’t quite reached the mainstream. However, its campaign to stop French nuclear testing in the South Pacific – which culminated in the bombing of the titular boat – was a turning point. This lively, fascinating documentary hears from many of those directly involved.PHFilm choiceView image in fullscreenEndearing … Moses Al Shabazz (Marchánt Davis) in The Day Shall ComeThe Day Shall Come (Christopher Morris, 2019), 1.25am, Film4Chris Morris’s scathing 2019 satire about the US government’s “war on terror” and the innocents caught up in it may be the most neglected of his brilliant career, but in its plausibility (“Based on a hundred true stories,” a title card notes) and bleak comedy it deserves more love. Moses Al Shabazz (an endearing Marchánt Davis) is a delusional Miami preacher who leads a radical black power movement (members: three) that is infiltrated by an FBI branch desperate for a win, despite posing no actual threat. Not as surreal as Four Lions, but it still possesses a sharp bite.Simon WardellExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Passage by Colin Thubron review – mortality and memory in a gem of a novel | Books | The Guardian
description: A terminally ill woman makes a final trip to Egypt in an exquisitely wrought portrait of end-of-life reckoning
Author: John Banville
Headline: A terminally ill woman makes a final trip to Egypt in an exquisitely wrought portrait of end-of-life reckoning
Content: Karnak temple, Egypt.Photograph: Jose A Bernat Bacete/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKarnak temple, Egypt.Photograph: Jose A Bernat Bacete/Getty ImagesBook of the dayBooksReviewPassage by Colin Thubron review – mortality and memory in a gem of a novelA terminally ill woman makes a final trip to Egypt in an exquisitely wrought portrait of end-of-life reckoningJohn BanvilleWed 26 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 02.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVirginia Woolf said of Middlemarch that it is one of the few English novels written for grown-up people. In the shallow and infantilising age through which we are living, Colin Thubron dares to assume that his readers are adults. Passage is a very beautiful, very moving, authentic work of art. Hardly more than a novella, it sits lightly in the hand, but its emotional and aesthetic weight overtips the balance.Thubron began his career as a travel writer and a large part of the action of Passage is set in a vividly but economically evoked Egypt. This is not the teeming Egypt of Cairo or Alexandria, but of the countryside, the villages, and the great immemorial tombs and ancient monuments. The best travel writers know that “abroad” is most convincingly evoked not by awed exclamations at the world’s wonders, but by an attitude of relaxed familiarity. Thubron is obviously an old Egypt hand, or at least has the skill to convince us that he is.The story he tells is both simple and subtle. The main character is Kathleen, an Anglicised Australian actor whose father had emigrated from Slovenia. She is in her 40s, beautiful and gravely ill, and the brief first chapter is a toe-curlingly stark description of an operation on her brain to investigate a tumour which, as we will learn, is incurable.As it happens, Kathleen’s husband, Robert, is himself a brain specialist, and has elected, unwisely, to be present at the operation, “standing as far away as space allows … He finds himself staring speechless into his wife’s brain. It is a turmoil of ink and crimson coils, faintly pulsing under the surgeon’s instrument.” Kathleen is awake, and answering questions that will help the doctor to identify cancerous tissue.double quotation markThe book sits lightly in the hand, but its emotional and aesthetic weight overtips the balanceRobert and Kathleen’s marriage has gone stale; also, it has a historical blemish, since it was Robert’s younger brother, Alan, who first met Kathleen and fell in love with her when they were both in their teens. The one who loved the most was Alan; Kathleen, having returned home to Melbourne, wrote to him more and more infrequently, then not at all. “It was not until six years later that she reappeared, on Robert’s arm.”Kathleen is a wonderful creation: strong-willed, outspoken, and above all clear-eyed, about herself and others. She knows how ill she is, but is determined not to give in to self-pity and to live her life as fully as she can to the end, even if the end should prove bitter. Although the surgeon advises against it, she insists, only weeks after the operation, on setting off, with Robert and Alan – yes, Alan does seem a glutton for heartache – on the Egyptian holiday that had been planned before she became ill.One of the most admirable aspects of the book is Thubron’s restraint in exploiting the symbolic possibilities that this journey holds out to him. Egypt, after all, or the parts of it that the travellers visit, is itself a kind of afterworld. “The temple city that was gathering around them, with its unreadable carvings and maimed statues, was a ruined monument to death and memory.”Death and memory: these are the poles between which Kathleen’s dwindling existence is strung. What for the other tourists are more or less interesting sites, and sights, are for her the points of exit that she must soon step through: “When her eyes adjusted to the dark, she saw in front of her a gold-lit corridor that appeared to reach into infinity. In its walls, painted gods marched or floated through an ocean of hieroglyphs. Above her spread a constellation of stars.”When she encounters a local guide, the soft-spoken and quietly considerate Ashraf, it seems she is being offered another and surely final chance at love. However, she knows it is an impossibility: “She imagined his hands encountering with horror the sutures under her hair.” What she does not know is that Ashraf, a political activist, is already a marked man, as she is a marked woman, in a different way, and for different reasons.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPassage is an exquisitely wrought novel which, for all its understated, filigree texture, reverberates in the mind with poetic force. The record of Kathleen’s passage from life into the not-life is at once tragic and affirmative. “No matter, she was moving through a sacred theatre where gods and humans transformed into each other, as if they shared one essence, the immortal and the transient interfused.”Passage by Colin Thubron is published by Chatto & Windus (£14.99).
