title: De Gaulle: Résistance review – a galloping bromance for Churchill and France’s wartime hero | Movies | The Guardian
description: This biopic of the great Gallic general – which culminates at Bir Hakeim, in advance of a second film – is a fine, quietly amusing romp with a touch of classic 60s war films
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: This biopic of the great Gallic general – which culminates at Bir Hakeim, in advance of a second film – is a fine, quietly amusing romp with a touch of classic 60s war films
Content: French fancy … Simon Abkarian as Charles de Gaulle.Photograph: Malgosia Abramowska/Pathé Films/TF1 Films ProductionView image in fullscreenFrench fancy … Simon Abkarian as Charles de Gaulle.Photograph: Malgosia Abramowska/Pathé Films/TF1 Films ProductionMoviesReviewDe Gaulle: Résistance review – a galloping bromance for Churchill and France’s wartime heroThis biopic of the great Gallic general – which culminates at Bir Hakeim, in advance of a second film – is a fine, quietly amusing romp with a touch of classic 60s war filmsPeter BradshawWed 26 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 09.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePerhaps because it is based on a biography by an Englishman – Julian Jackson’s A Certain Idea of France: The Life ofCharles de Gaulle– this very enjoyable and gallopingly eventful biopic, directed by Antonin Baudry, has an element of amused detachment. The first of two parts, it offers a good-humoured, though naturally sympathetic, perspective on France’s great wartime hero, played with martyred and faintly preposterous hauteur by Franco-Armenian actor Simon Abkarian.De Gaulle is the lofty exile in London, refusing to accept the dishonour of the Vichy government and its capitulation to the Nazis, symbolised by Marshal Philippe Pétain (Alain Libolt) and Adm François Darlan (Mathieu Kassovitz). For reasons that will later become clear, De Gaulle’s own story is mysteriously intertwined with that of a hothead young patriot, Fernand Bonnier de la Chapelle (Florian Lesieur), who is De Gaulle’s biggest fan. A tiny touch of comedy is part of what makes this resemble an old-fashioned 60s war film, although it has evidently taken until 2026 for French cinema to come to terms with its contentious national icon. No one here is cheeky enough to comment on the nominative determinism of a Gallic hero being called “De Gaulle”.His great supporter (and even, in some ways, creator) after the fall of France in 1940 is Winston Churchill, played with great gusto and charm bySimon Russell Beale– incidentally, it is a relief to see a commercial movie role worthy of the man. I can’t think of any other film portrayal of Churchill in which most of his dialogue is in French; this is how he mostly talks with De Gaulle. Was Churchill’s French really as good as that? Churchill’s attitude is exasperated, affectionate and occasionally furious, but he recognises in De Gaulle a kindred spirit: a romantic maverick and patriot. Beale gives his extended dialogue scenes with Abkarian, genially quaffing champagne, a touch of Shakespeare. I wonder if the second film will include the legendary moment when De Gaulle is asked who the three most important Europeans are, and promptly replies: “Dante, Goethe, Chateaubriand.” When asked about Shakespeare, he shrugs: “European?”The film also breathlessly gives us De Gaulle’s arrival in Britain after the French collapse, where he is cunningly promoted by Churchill as the true keeper of the French flame to undermine Vichy. He is given staff, a house and permitted to make BBC broadcasts rallying the cause of French resistance, for all of which De Gaulle is hilariously ungrateful. He then assembles a ragtag group of expatriates as his cabinet, like the prisoners in John Sturges’s The Great Escape joining the great plan. De Gaulle impassively accepts the horror ofChurchill’s ruthless bombing of the French fleetat the Algerian port of Mers-el-Kébir in 1940, killing nearly 1,300 French servicemen, to prevent this force falling into Nazi hands. The film suggests that De Gaulle, with a ruthless realpolitik of his own, saw the importance of propitiating Churchill, while seeing Mers-el-Kébir as a judgment on Vichy cowardice.View image in fullscreenNiels Schneider as Gen Philippe Leclerc de Hauteclocque in De Gaulle: Résistance.Photograph: Malgosia Abramowska/Pathé Films/TF1 Films ProductionThen, we get the high comedy of De Gaulle’s chaotic personal adventures in Africa, finding support for his Free French in Chad and Cameroon, which Churchill admires as audacious if absurd. But Africa is important. An Anglo-Hollywood movie might have seen Britain’s turning point in the war as a matter of dramatising Montgomery’s brilliance atEl-Alamein. This French movie instead emphasisesthe heroism of an outnumbered Free French brigadein the desert at Bir Hakeim under Gen Marie-Pierre Kœnig (Benoît Magimel); inspired by De Gaulle, they hold out against Rommel’s superior forces, giving British forces a chance to retreat and regroup.And so, De Gaulle falls in and out of favour with the British, who are nervous that the comic opera of his political career in London will undermine Britain in the eyes of US President Franklin D Roosevelt (Campbell Scott). And the film shows us De Gaulle and Churchill’s differing views of the American saviour. The film rattles along with De Gaulle’s return to the inner circles of allied power after sensational events in Africa – and stops. The second film will presumably take the story on from there. But this one, entertainingly, is a kind of bromance or double-act with Churchill, a wartime duo heading for glory and then the long fadeout of post imperial peacetime.De Gaulle: Résistance is in UK and Irish cinemas from 28 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmBiopicsCharles de GaulleSecond world warSimon Russell BealeFranceEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Last Sunrise review – Amazon’s soapy YA romance is thankless and bland | Romance films | The Guardian
description: Another familiar concoction fails to make use of its sunny location and chooses cheap melodrama over romantic charm
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Another familiar concoction fails to make use of its sunny location and chooses cheap melodrama over romantic charm
Content: Maia Reficco and Fernando Lindez in The Last Sunrise.Photograph: Lucia Faraig/PrimeView image in fullscreenMaia Reficco and Fernando Lindez in The Last Sunrise.Photograph: Lucia Faraig/PrimeRomance filmsReviewThe Last Sunrise review – Amazon’s soapy YA romance is thankless and blandAnother familiar concoction fails to make use of its sunny location and chooses cheap melodrama over romantic charmRafaela BassiliWed 26 Aug 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 03.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAtitular sunrise, a summer fling fantasy, exorbitant wealth, impossibly sculpted bodies: such are the profitable story ingredients that make up The Last Sunrise, the latest offering in Amazon’s endless catalogue of “romance content”. I wouldn’t ordinarily use that term to describe a film, but it fits The Last Sunrise (indifferently directed by Carlson Young) like a glove. The movie is an adaptation of the 2025 novel of the same title by Anna Todd, whoseAfter series– itself adapted from Todd’sphenomenally popularOne Direction fan fiction – was wrung dry between 2019 and 2024.Spa Weekend review – female answer to The Hangover spreads the slush with the massage oilRead moreIn recent years, a particular romance category has yielded high returns for Amazon: from this summer’sEvery Year AftertoThe Summer I Turned Pretty’s memorable run, these stories are easily palatable, set in idyllic locations, and orbit attractive, heterosexual, wealthy couples. Nothing new there – one need look no further than any run-of-the-mill 2000s romcom to find the same tropes. But the narrative simplicity that once made room for electric chemistry between leads, perfectly tailored wardrobes and irresistibly depicted locales has given way to cheap melodrama. With its improbable plot twists, family secrets and at least one across-the-face slap, The Last Sunrise is more soap opera than Under the Tuscan Sun.The soapy mood is accentuated by the presence of Eva Longoria, who gave life to Gabrielle Solis in ABC’s long-running prime-time soap Desperate Housewives. Here, Longoria plays Isolde Pera, the mother of protagonist Oriah (Maia Reficco), a young dancer who suffers from tuberous sclerosis, a rare genetic condition that causes tumors to grow in different organs. Oriah joins her mom on a summer-long trip to the Spanish island of Mallorca, where Isolde grew up and where her company, Redwyn, is preparing to build a swanky new hotel. The trip comes at a good time for Oriah, who finds herself at a medical crossroads after suffering a seizure on stage: she can either increase her medication dosage or have surgery.The pills numb Oriah’s feelings, but surgery would put her at risk of losing her memory. She opts for the former, though upon arriving in Mallorca, she quickly dispenses with treatment altogether – she wants to feel every passionate second of her summer fling with Julián Garcia (Fernando Lindez), a curly haired local fisher. Oriah insists that the pills make her numb, but we never see any evidence to back up the statement. There is scarcely any dramatic modulation in Oriah’s character at all, whether imposed by the story or Reficco’s performance. In fact, despite being the main character, Oriah makes little impact on the plot – mostly, things happentoher. Even then, these events are not dramatized; instead, they are described by characters in dialogue.Take, as an example, the fact that Redwyn is angling to buy the fishing docks owned by the Garcias, thereby destroying a century-old business and breaking Julián’s heart. This conflict is supposed to raise the stakes of Oriah and Julián’s involvement; it is their major obstacle, the cross-purpose that leads Oriah to describe their romance as “Romeo-and-Juliet-serious” to a friend. But apart from some papers that are dutifully waved around, any work that would have gone into this deal goes unseen. The disputed land – of which Julián is so fond that he goes into debt with a gangster-ish loan shark in a vague, off-screen attempt to save it – is never shown, either. The Garcias’ fishing boat could have just as easily been at port in Gloucester, Massachusetts, so perfunctorily is its mooring depicted.For a story ostensibly concerned with the fierce attachments a person might feel to the place they call home, The Last Sunrise is bizarrely devoid of texture. Mallorca is photographed like a stock image, its specificities digitally scrubbed clean. Films like Under the Tuscan Sun and Eat, Pray, Love endure in part because their fantasy versions of Italy are rendered in minute, loving detail; it’s impossible not to wonder how much The Last Sunrise might have benefited from a cinematographer and production designer committed to transporting the viewer to Mallorca. Paired with the lack of interest in the dramatic mechanics of the plot, this disregard for visual storytelling raises the question: why make a movie at all?Oh, right: money. In recent years, romance – which has long been maligned as an “unserious” genre – has regained prominence in the cultural spotlight. The romcom died and was reborn as steamy television; commercial romance fiction filled with graphic detail. But as the genre returns to its position as a pillar of the entertainment industry, the human-scale simplicity that gave us Bridget Jones’s Diary has been neglected and replaced by half-baked efforts like The Last Sunrise – the main value of which is to expose, all too clearly, how indifferently streaming platforms regard their audience.The Last Sunrise is now available on Amazon Prime VideoExplore more on these topicsRomance filmsAmazon Prime VideoreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hanging By a Wire review – cable car rescue documentary dangles viewers on the edge of disaster | Movies | The Guardian
description: The extraordinary fate of eight people trapped above a chasm in Pakistan makes for a tense, skilfully assembled survival story with unexpected flashes of comedy
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: The extraordinary fate of eight people trapped above a chasm in Pakistan makes for a tense, skilfully assembled survival story with unexpected flashes of comedy
Content: High drama … Hanging By a Wire.View image in fullscreenHigh drama … Hanging By a Wire.MoviesReviewHanging By a Wire review – cable car rescue documentary dangles viewers on the edge of disasterThe extraordinary fate of eight people trapped above a chasm in Pakistan makes for a tense, skilfully assembled survival story with unexpected flashes of comedyLeslie FelperinWed 26 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 12.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSurvival documentaries are a weird little genre of nonfiction film-making that recount the stories of accidents and natural catastrophes – and more often than not, the daring rescues of people caught up in them. Eyewitnesses and the loved ones of those endangered are top of the interview list, to keep the sense of danger and emotional stakes at the top of everyone’s mind. Survivors can also have their say, and more adventurous film-makers might care to recreate the action with actors or the actual survivors themselves.This account of how eight people – six teenage boys and two adult men – were left suspended over a chasm in northernPakistanin 2023, when a wire on the cable car they were travelling on broke, is a pretty conventional example of the form. For obvious reasons, no one tries to recreate the situation, but since it was quite recent there is no shortage of news footage and amateur clips to fill out the particulars. The downside of doing a story that’s so recent is that some of the audience may remember what happened anyway, but still there’s plenty of nail-nibbling suspense here, and sequences that will give anyone with acrophobia the heebie jeebies – especially the drone shots that zoom close on the terrified faces of those trapped inside the dangling car.Credit is due to director Mohammed Ali Naqvi for pulling it all together adeptly, as well as to the seamless editing by William Grayburn that nourishes the suspense and draws out some of the surprising moments of comedy. It’s good to have a bit of a giggle amid all the tension; we meet one heroic zip line enthusiast who brags about his amazing body as he struts around the gym he runs, looking buff but not outrageously so. The fact that he’s introduced halfway through the story lets us know he’ll survive, as will his best buddy, who has a lot less braggadocio.At one point, the two of them are surprised to find a third would-be rescuer on top of the precarious cable car and they all get into an argument while the people inside hurl insults at them (correctly) for putting more strain on the already frayed cables. Indeed, the one thing the film doesn’t do – which an American or British movie would probably go big on – is investigate the safety failures that allowed all this to happen. Instead, the Pakistani interviewees just take it as bad luck that, for example, the army didn’t have any working walkie-talkies when they first showed up, just some of the kit that might have sped up the rescue effort.Hanging By a Wire is in UK cinemas from 28 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsPakistanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: How to turn the dregs of a ketchup bottle into a classic Marie Rose dressing – recipe | Sauces and gravies | The Guardian
description: Shake up the remnants of a bottle of ketchup with a splash of sprits, a heap of mayonnaise and a few other simple additions, and turn it into one of the culinary world’s most famous sauces
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Shake up the remnants of a bottle of ketchup with a splash of sprits, a heap of mayonnaise and a few other simple additions, and turn it into one of the culinary world’s most famous sauces
Content: Tom Hunt’s ketchup bottle Marie Rose sauce goes as well on lettuce wedges as in a prawn cocktail.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s ketchup bottle Marie Rose sauce goes as well on lettuce wedges as in a prawn cocktail.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notSauces and graviesHow to turn the dregs of a ketchup bottle into a classic Marie Rose dressing – recipeShake up the remnants of a bottle of ketchup with a splash of sprits, a heap of mayonnaise and a few other simple additions, and turn it into one of the culinary world’s most famous saucesTom HuntWed 26 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy new favourite preparation for sauces, marinades and dressings is in a near-empty jar, tub or bottle, so I can upcycle all the remains. Rather than washing it and putting it in the recycling, I instead add a few store-cupboard ingredients to create a dressing or sauce, often re-exploring classics such as a retro Marie Rose sauce or myyoghurt-pot chicken. It’s a convenient way to use up the last dregs of a ketchup bottle, for instance, which often seems to harbour exactly the right amount of sauce.My Marie Rose recipe is inspired by the one inSimon HopkinsonandLindsey Bareham’s 1997The Prawn Cocktail Years. It’s wonderfully simple, with the sophisticated addition of a dash of cognac, though other recipes use brandy. I had neither, however, but I did have some sweet vermouth left over, which worked exceptionally well, so feel free to experiment with whatever spirits you have to hand – vodka, for instance, works brilliantly, and gives the sauce a nice kick.Serve tossed with prawns, avocado, lettuce and cucumber in a classic prawn cocktail, or splat on to burger buns, or do as I did and serve drizzled over wedges of iceberg lettuce garnished with celery leaves and capers, and dusted with paprika. Glass or plastic bottles both work, though squeezy ones help to deliver a chef-like drizzle.Ketchup bottle Marie RoseWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appWhen I was a kid, I used to love ketchup on just about everything, so these days it seems a rather odd concept to mix it with mayonnaise and prawns. Even so, it is surprisingly good – well, of course it is – and a great way to use up the annoying last dregs in the bottom of the bottle. Besides the other dishes mentioned above, Marie Rose also goes really well withavocado fries, if you happen to also have an under-ripe avocado to hand.4-5 tbsp mayonnaise1 tsp sweet vermouth, or other spirit (vodka, cognac, brandy)1-3 tbsp sriracha, Tabasco or other chilli sauce, to taste1 small squeeze lemon juiceFlaky sea salt and black pepper1 part-empty ketchup bottle, with roughly 1-2 tbsp remainingPaprika, to finish, optionalUsing a funnel, if you have one, add the mayonnaise, vermouth, Tabasco (or other chilli sauce), lemon juice, a small pinch of sea salt and generous grind of black pepper to the near-empty ketchup bottle. Screw the lid back on and shake well. Taste, adjusting for seasoning, heat and acidity as required, then squeeze directly over your chosen dish. Finish with a pinch of paprika, if you like.Explore more on these topicsSauces and graviesWaste notFoodFood wasteShellfishfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A Tamil summer vegetarian feast: Cynthia Shanmugalingam’s cucumber yoghurt curry and gooseberry pickle  | Curry | The Guardian
description: Serve this cold curry with a hot, fenugreek-flavoured preserve for a seasonal refresher
Author: Cynthia Shanmugalingam
Headline: Serve this cold curry with a hot, fenugreek-flavoured preserve for a seasonal refresher
Content: Cynthia Shanmugalingam’s cucumber yoghurt curry with gooseberry pickle.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Liam Baker.View image in fullscreenCynthia Shanmugalingam’s cucumber yoghurt curry with gooseberry pickle.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Hanna Miller. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Liam Baker.CurryA Tamil summer vegetarian feast: Cynthia Shanmugalingam’s cucumber yoghurt curry and gooseberry pickleServe this cold curry with a hot, fenugreek-flavoured preserve for a seasonal refresherCynthia ShanmugalingamWed 26 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis lovely summery “curry” is a cold, refreshing dish from Karnataka in India, and is eaten widely in Tamil Nadu, just 20 miles across the Palk Strait from my ancestral Tamil homeland in north and eastern Sri Lanka. Along with chefs Louis and Seb in our development kitchen, we decided that smacking the cucumbers helps give them a silky texture, and means the fragrant yoghurt base can get into all the nooks and crannies. It’s wonderful with plain rice and a side of fenugreek-heavy hot Tamil pickle, made with English gooseberries rather than superfood nelli, both of which are said to make your skin shine and hair bouncy.Hot gooseberry pickleWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenCynthia Shanmugalingam’s hot gooseberry pickle.Prep10 minCook10 minPickle10 minChill2 hr+Serves4250g gooseberries250ml apple cider vinegar1 tbsp caster sugar1 tsp salt1 tsp fenugreek seeds1 tbsp mustard seeds4 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed3 tbsp vegetable oil4 tbsp Kashmiri chilli powderSome saltWash the gooseberries well, then spread them out on a cloth and leave to dry.Put the vinegar, 250ml water, the sugar and salt in a saucepan and cook on a high heat until the sugar and salt have dissolved and the liquid is simmering. Add the gooseberries, turn off the heat and leave to pickle for 10 minutes.In a small frying pan, dry roast the fenugreek for about 60 seconds, until fragrant, then leave to cool. Tip the cooled fenugreek into a small spice grinder or mortar, add the mustard seeds and crushed garlic, then blitz or grind to a paste. Scrape the mix into a small bowl, add the drained gooseberries, the oil, chilli powder and salt, then cover and put in the fridge for at least two hours.Cucumber yoghurt curryWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenCynthia Shanmugalingam’s cucumber yoghurt curry.Prep15 minCook10 minServes42 cucumbers80g desiccated coconut (frozen or freshly grated), soaked in water for 15 minutes, then drained2 green chillies, roughly chopped4 garlic cloves, peeled and roughly chopped30g fresh coriander, stalks and leaves½ tsp black peppercorns2 tsp sesame seeds100g natural yoghurtSalt, to tasteBoiled white rice, to serveFor the temper4 tsp vegetable oil, or coconut oil10 fresh curry leaves1 tsp fenugreek seeds(optional)2 tsp mustard seeds2 tsp cumin seeds3 dried red chillies, ideally cascabelFirst, make a coconut-cucumber paste. Peel the cucumbers, reserving the skins. Wrap each cucumber in clingfilm, then bash them lightly with a rolling pin. Remove the clingfilm, keeping the seeds, and cut the flesh on a slight diagonal into 1cm slices. Put a few of the chopped cucumbers, the cucumber seeds and skins into a blender, add the drained coconut, green chillies, garlic, coriander, black peppercorns and sesame seeds, then blitz smooth.Put the yoghurt in a medium bowl, and whisk until smooth, then beat in enough water, if need be, to get it to a pouring consistency. Add salt to taste, stir in the cucumber paste and remaining chopped cucumber, then pour into a serving bowl and put in the fridge to chill.When you’re ready to eat, make the temper. Put the oil in a small frying pan on a highheat, add the curry leaves and, after about 30 seconds, when they’re sizzling, stir in the fenugreek (if using), mustard seeds, cumin seeds and red chillies – stand well back, because the spices will probably splutter. Pour the hot temper, oil and all, over the cucumber yoghurt curry and serve with plain boiled white rice.Cynthia Shanmugalingam is chef/proprietor ofRambutan, London SE1Explore more on these topicsCurryFoodMain courseSide dishesHerbs and spicesPickling, fermenting and preservingFruitrecipesShareReuse this content
